source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XI (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio primi capituli: Liber generationis Jesu Christi
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ”

paras.t: Liber generationis Jesu Christi, filii David, filii Abraham. Sicut in Prologo protestatur Hieronymus, Matthæus ante ceteros Evangelistas suum conscripsit evangelium in Judæa. Scripsit autem Judæis conversis stilo Hebræo. Chrysostomus vero refert, quod facta magna persecutione fidelium in Palæstina, fratres dispersi precabantur Matthæum, ut eis verborum et operum Christi veritatem describeret, quatenus librum evangelicæ legis ad manum haberent, secumque deferrent quocumque venirent. Hæc autem simul stare possunt. Quamvis enim in Judæa scripserit, potuit tamen plebs christiana in Palæstina exsistens, esse occasio hujus scripturæ: præsertim quum plurimi Judæorum in Palæstina morati conversique fuerint.
paras.en: [[1:1|The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.|Liber generationis Jesu Christi, filii David, filii Abraham.]] As Jerome declares in his Prologue, Matthew wrote his Gospel in Judaea before the other Evangelists. He wrote it for the converted Jews, in the Hebrew tongue. Chrysostom, for his part, relates that when a great persecution of the faithful had arisen in Palestine, the scattered brethren begged Matthew to write down for them the truth of Christ's words and works, so that they might have the book of the Gospel law at hand and carry it with them wherever they went. These two accounts can stand together. For although he wrote in Judaea, the Christian people living in Palestine could still have been the occasion of this writing, especially since a great many of the Jews who had settled in Palestine had been converted.

paras.t: Porro intentio Matthæi fuit ostendere Christum veraciter incarnatum, atque ex semine David progenitum: quoniam infideles Judæi ex hoc arguebant Jesum Nazarenum non esse Messiam seu Christum, eo quod a Nazareth urbe Galilææ fuerat oriundus; Scriptura vero prædixit Christum de Bethlehem Juda et semine David venturum. Hinc enim principes Judæorum locuti sunt Nicodemo: Numquid a Galilæa venit Christus? nonne Scriptura dicit, quia ex semine David, et de Bethlehem castello, ubi erat David, venit Christus?
paras.en: Now Matthew's purpose was to show that Christ was truly made flesh and was begotten of the seed of David. For the unbelieving Jews argued from this that Jesus of Nazareth was not the Messiah, that is, the Christ: that He came from Nazareth, a city of Galilee, whereas the Scripture had foretold that the Christ would come from Bethlehem of Juda and from the seed of David[[Matt 2:5||]][[Mich 5:2||]]. Hence the rulers of the Jews spoke thus to Nicodemus: [[John 7:41|Doth the Christ come out of Galilee?|Numquid a Galilæa venit Christus?]] [[John 7:42|Doth not the scripture say: That Christ cometh of the seed of David and from Bethlehem the town where David was?|nonne Scriptura dicit, quia ex semine David, et de Bethlehem castello, ubi erat David, venit Christus?]]

paras.t: Declarans ergo Matthæus Jesum esse filium David, sic orsus est: Liber generationis Jesu Christi, id est, liber præsens a generatione Christi intitulatur. Solent enim Hebræi libros denominare ab eo de quo in exordio pertractatur: quemadmodum primus liber Moysis dicitur Genesis, quia de mundi creatione sumit initium; liber quoque in cujus principio Dominus fertur jussisse numerari filios Israel, vocatus est liber Numerorum. Itaque iste est liber generationis Jesu Christi, id est describens humanam seu temporalem generationem Christi, de cujus divinitate ac divina generatione Joannes plenius sermocinatur.
paras.en: Setting out, then, to declare that Jesus is the son of David, Matthew began thus: [[1:1|The book of the generation of Jesus Christ|Liber generationis Jesu Christi]], that is, the present book takes its title from the generation of Christ. For the Hebrews are accustomed to name books from what is treated at their beginning: so the first book of Moses is called Genesis, because it begins with the creation of the world; and the book at whose beginning the Lord is said to have commanded the children of Israel to be numbered is called the book of Numbers. This, then, is [[1:1|the book of the generation of Jesus Christ|liber generationis Jesu Christi]], that is, the book describing the human or temporal generation of Christ; of His Godhead and divine generation John discourses more fully.

paras.t: Quamvis autem in veteri Testamento plures dicti sunt Jesus, ut Josue, alias Jesus filius Nave, et Jesus filius Josedec sacerdos magnus; plures quoque vocati sunt Christi, per quamdam participationem et nuncupationem, imperfectamque rationem, videlicet, quoniam populum Israel temporaliter seu corporaliter, vel dispositive et solum instrumentaliter liberaverunt, et oleo sancto uncti fuerunt corporaliter, vel spiritualiter, vel modo utroque: nullus tamen secundum perfectam rationem ac plenam proprietatem dici potest Jesus aut Christus, nisi Unigenitus Dei, homo factus, qui solus perfectam animæ et corporis liberationem nobis promeruit, fecit, ac tribuit, omniumque divinorum charismatum unctione plenissime est perfusus: quia non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum homini Christo. Unde in Psalmo canitur: Unxit te Deus oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis. Proprie itaque, Christus est nomen personæ in duplici natura subsistentis, divinæ videlicet et humanæ. Imo tam Jesus quam Christus, supponunt æternam et increatam hypostasim Verbi, ita ut hæ vere sint: Jesus est æternus, immensus, omnipotens; Christus ubique est, omnia implet, omnia continet.
paras.en: Now in the Old Testament several men were called Jesus, such as Josue, otherwise Jesus the son of Nave[[Ecclus 46:1||]], and Jesus the son of Josedec, the high priest[[Agg 1:1||]][[Zach 3:1||]]; and several were also called christs [that is, anointed ones], by a certain sharing in the name, as a title, and in an imperfect sense: namely, because they delivered the people of Israel in a temporal or bodily way, or by way of preparation and only as instruments, and were anointed with holy oil bodily, or spiritually, or in both ways. Yet no one in the perfect sense and with full propriety can be called Jesus or Christ except the Only-begotten of God made man, who alone merited, wrought and bestowed on us the perfect deliverance of soul and body, and who was most fully steeped in the anointing of all the divine gifts; for [[John 3:34|God doth not give the Spirit by measure|non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum]] to the man Christ. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: God [[Ps 44:8|hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows|Unxit te Deus oleo lætitiæ præ participibus tuis]]. Properly, then, Christ is the name of a Person subsisting in two natures, the divine and the human. Indeed, both "Jesus" and "Christ" stand for the eternal and uncreated hypostasis of the Word [supponunt: in the logic of the schools, a name "supposits" for the person it actually designates; since the Person named is the Word, divine attributes may truly be said of the man Jesus], so that these statements are true: Jesus is eternal, immense, almighty; Christ is everywhere, fills all things, contains all things.

paras.t: Hic ergo est liber generationis Jesu Christi, filii David, filii Abraham, id est, qui secundum assumptam humanitatem est filius David regis, et Abrahæ patriarchæ: juxta quod Gabriel apud Lucam disseruit Virgini benedictæ, Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus; et Apostolus ad Romanos, Qui factus est ei ex semine David secundum carnem. Secundum Hieronymum, horum duorum dumtaxat filius nominatur jam Christus, quia ad hos tantum de Christo facta est divina promissio. Ad David etenim dictum est: De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam; ad Abraham autem, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Sed huic obviare videtur, quod in Genesi hæc eadem promissio legitur Isaac facta: ad quem inter cetera contestatus est Dominus, Multiplicabo semen tuum; et, Benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terræ. Imo et Jacob patriarchæ in Genesi legitur Dominus hoc ipsum promisisse. Præterea Jacob quoque patriarcha manifeste prædixit Judæ, quod de semine ejus nasceretur Christus, exspectatio gentium. Arbitror ergo idcirco Christum potissimum dici filium David et Abrahæ, quoniam ceteris principaliores et forte sanctiores fuerunt. David namque regum, Abraham vero Patriarcharum maximus fuit.
paras.en: This, then, is [[1:1|the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham|liber generationis Jesu Christi, filii David, filii Abraham]]: that is, of Him who according to the humanity He assumed is the son of King David and of the patriarch Abraham. So Gabriel declared to the blessed Virgin in Luke: [[Luke 1:32|And the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father|Dabit illi Dominus Deus sedem David patris ejus]]; and the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 1:3|who was made to him of the seed of David, according to the flesh|Qui factus est ei ex semine David secundum carnem]]. According to Jerome, Christ is here named the son of these two only, because to them alone was the divine promise concerning Christ made. For to David it was said: [[Ps 131:11|of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne|De fructu ventris tui ponam super sedem tuam]]; and to Abraham: [[Gen 22:18|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes]]. But against this it seems that in Genesis this same promise is read as made to Isaac, to whom among other things the Lord solemnly declared: [[Gen 26:4|I will multiply thy seed|Multiplicabo semen tuum]]; and, [[Gen 26:4|in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed|Benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes terræ]]. Indeed, in Genesis the Lord is read to have promised this very thing to the patriarch Jacob also[[Gen 28:14||]]. Moreover the patriarch Jacob plainly foretold to Juda that of his seed would be born the Christ, [[Gen 49:10|the expectation of nations|exspectatio gentium]]. I think, therefore, that Christ is called above all the son of David and of Abraham because they were more eminent, and perhaps holier, than the rest: for David was the greatest of the kings, and Abraham of the Patriarchs.

paras.t: Sed quum per Isaiam de Christo prædictum sit, Generationem ejus quis enarrabit? quid est, quod Matthæus et Lucas Christi generationem describunt? Ad hoc Hieronymus Chrysostomusque respondent, quod Isaias de divina Christi generatione loquatur, Evangelistæ autem de generatione humana. Quamvis autem hoc verum sit, quantum ad hoc quod divina Christi generatio præcipue inenarrabilis est, quæ secundum Dionysium, posuit tenebras latibulum suum; nihilo minus verbum Isaiæ jam introductum de humana quoque Christi generatione intelligi potest, quemadmodum Leo Papa ubertim fatetur: Quis enim viator concipere, comprehendere, aut eloqui valeat, quomodo virgo æternam personam, verum et incommutabilem Deum concipiat? quomodo de clauso utero ejus Christus procedat, quod sine penetratione dimensionum omnem rationem excedente, non potuit fieri? Imo ut aliqui probabiliter adstruunt, verbum Isaiæ jam allegatum, ad litteram intelligendum est, nec de divina, nec de humana, sed de spirituali Christi generatione, qua homines ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto renascuntur in Christo, et per Apostolorum prædicationem cœlestisque gratiæ infusionem, ad ipsum conversi sunt. Prædictis enim verbis Isaias adjecit: Quia abscissus est de terra viventium, id est, Christus per mortem ablatus est a consortio hominum in mundo viventium. Hæc vero abscissio non est causa inenarrabilitatis divinæ vel humanæ generationis Christi, sed generationis ejus spiritualis: quum hoc sit valde mirabile, quod in hominem crucifixum totus pene crediderit mundus.
paras.en: But since it was foretold of Christ through Isaias, [[Is 53:8|who shall declare his generation?|Generationem ejus quis enarrabit?]], how is it that Matthew and Luke describe the generation of Christ? To this Jerome and Chrysostom answer that Isaias speaks of the divine generation of Christ, and the Evangelists of His human generation. This is true, inasmuch as the divine generation of Christ is above all beyond telling, for, as Dionysius says, it [[Ps 17:12|made darkness his cover|posuit tenebras latibulum suum]][[2 Kings 22:12||]]. Nevertheless the word of Isaias just cited can be understood of the human generation of Christ also, as Pope Leo abundantly acknowledges: "For what wayfarer [viator: a man still on the journey of this life, as distinct from the blessed in heaven] could conceive, comprehend or utter how a virgin conceives an eternal Person, true and unchangeable God? how Christ comes forth from her closed womb, which could not come about without a passing of body through body [penetratio dimensionum: two bodies occupying the same place at once, which surpasses every natural reason]?" Indeed, as some argue with probability, the word of Isaias just alleged is to be understood literally neither of the divine nor of the human, but of the spiritual generation of Christ, by which men are born again in Christ of water and the Holy Ghost[[John 3:5||]], and have been converted to Him through the preaching of the Apostles and the pouring in of heavenly grace. For to the words already given Isaias added: [[Is 53:8|because he is cut off out of the land of the living|Quia abscissus est de terra viventium]], that is, Christ was taken away by death from the fellowship of men living in the world. Now this cutting off is not the reason why the divine or the human generation of Christ is beyond telling, but why His spiritual generation is: for this is a great marvel, that almost the whole world should have believed in a crucified man.

paras.t: Quamvis itaque quælibet harum trium Christi generationum inenarrabilis sit, ita quod perfecte comprehendi recitarique nequit, singulæ tamen aliqualiter describuntur. De divina siquidem generatione ait Christus sapientia Dei: Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram; ante colles ego parturiebar. In Ecclesiastico quoque: Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam. Unde in Sapientiæ libro legitur: Vapor est virtutis Dei, et emanatio quædam claritatis omnipotentis Dei sincera; candor est enim lucis æternæ. Spiritualis autem generatio Christi jam dicta, in Actibus Apostolorum, ceterisque legendis Sanctorum describitur.
paras.en: So although each of these three generations of Christ is beyond telling, in that it cannot be perfectly comprehended or recounted, yet each is described in some measure. Of the divine generation Christ, the wisdom of God, says: [[Prov 8:24|The depths were not as yet, and I was already conceived|Nondum erant abyssi, et ego jam concepta eram]]; [[Prov 8:25|before the hills, I was brought forth|ante colles ego parturiebar]]. And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 24:5|I came out of the mouth of the most High, the firstborn before all creatures|Ego ex ore Altissimi prodivi, primogenita ante omnem creaturam]]. Hence we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 7:25|she is a vapour of the power of God, and a certain pure emmanation of the glory of the Almighty God|Vapor est virtutis Dei, et emanatio quædam claritatis omnipotentis Dei sincera]]; [[Wis 7:26|For she is the brightness of eternal light|candor est enim lucis æternæ]]. The spiritual generation of Christ just mentioned is described in the Acts of the Apostles and in the other lives of the Saints.

paras.t: Abraham genuit Isaac supernaturaliter, de Sara nonagenaria naturaliter sterili, quando et ipse fere centenarius erat. De Ismaele autem primogenito Abrahæ non fit mentio, sicut nec de ceteris filiis Abrahæ, quia ex eorum semine non prodiit Christus. Nec mystica ratio compulit eos commemorari, sicut inferius commemorantur fratres Judæ et Jechoniæ, de quibus tamen non est natus Salvator. Iste est Abraham quem Deus per Isaiam appellat amicum, qui fuit perfectæ obedientiæ forma, fideique ac spei exemplum. Unde in Genesi Dominus ait ad eum: Ego protector tuus et merces tua magna nimis. Cujus præconia in Genesi describuntur. Quoniam ergo ex Isaac natus est Christus, dictum est Abrahæ in eodem Genesis libro: In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen. Apostolus quoque ad Galatas dicit Ismaelem natum secundum carnem, Isaac autem secundum spiritum, id est secundum Spiritus Sancti promissionem et operationem, ac typicam Christi præfigurationem. In multis siquidem erat figura Christi, videlicet, quia divinitus promissus, supernaturaliter conceptus ac genitus, et quia ad sui ipsius immolationem ligna portavit, sicut et Christus bajulans sibi crucem exivit ad passionem. Isaac quoque interpretatur risus seu gaudium. Nam eo nato, Sara mater ejus: Risum, inquit, fecit mihi Dominus; omnis qui audierit, corridebit mihi. Quis autem est spiritualis risus et gaudium electorum, desideratusque gentium, nisi is de quo angelus pastoribus, Ecce, ait, annuntio vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo, quia natus est vobis Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus? — Spiritualiter per Abraham, qui interpretatur pater multarum gentium, intelligitur quilibet virtuosus, qui est principium multarum operationum bonarum. Talis generat Isaac, id est, spiritualem habet lætitiam, quoniam actibus virtuosis sincera delectatio est annexa.
paras.en: [[1:2|Abraham begot Isaac|Abraham genuit Isaac]] in a way above nature, of Sara, a woman of ninety and barren by nature, when he himself was almost a hundred. No mention is made of Ismael, Abraham's firstborn, nor of Abraham's other sons, because Christ did not come forth from their seed; nor did any mystical reason require them to be named, as further on the brethren of Juda and of Jechonias are named, though the Saviour was not born of them. This is the Abraham whom God through Isaias calls His friend, who was the pattern of perfect obedience and the example of faith and hope. Hence in Genesis the Lord says to him: [[Gen 15:1|I am thy protector, and thy reward exceeding great|Ego protector tuus et merces tua magna nimis]]. His praises are set out in Genesis. Since, then, Christ was born of Isaac, it was said to Abraham in the same book of Genesis: [[Gen 21:12|in Isaac shall thy seed be called|In Isaac vocabitur tibi semen]]. The Apostle too, writing to the Galatians, says that Ismael was born according to the flesh, but Isaac according to the spirit, that is, according to the promise and working of the Holy Ghost, and as a figure foreshadowing Christ. For he was a figure of Christ in many things: namely, because he was promised by God, conceived and born above nature, and because he carried the wood for his own sacrifice, as Christ also, [[John 19:17|bearing his own cross, he went forth|bajulans sibi crucem exivit]] to His passion. Isaac, moreover, is interpreted "laughter" or "joy". For when he was born, Sara his mother said: [[Gen 21:6|God hath made a laughter for me: whosoever shall hear of it will laugh with me|Risum, inquit, fecit mihi Dominus; omnis qui audierit, corridebit mihi]]. And who is the spiritual laughter and joy of the elect, and the desired of the nations, if not He of whom the angel said to the shepherds: [[Luke 2:10|behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy that shall be to all the people|Ecce, ait, annuntio vobis gaudium magnum, quod erit omni populo]]: [[Luke 2:11|this day is born to you a Saviour, who is Christ the Lord|quia natus est vobis Salvator, qui est Christus Dominus]]? — In the spiritual sense, by Abraham, which is interpreted "father of many nations"[[Gen 17:5||]], is understood any virtuous man, who is the source of many good works. Such a man begets Isaac, that is, he has spiritual gladness, because a pure delight is joined to virtuous acts.

paras.t: Isaac autem genuit Jacob, qui erat vir simplex, in tabernaculis habitans. De quo Augustinus sentire videtur, quod fuerit in utero sanctificatus. Unde et apud Malachiam prophetam loquitur Dominus: Nonne frater erat Jacob Esau? Et Jacob dilexi, Esau autem odio habui. Hic Jacob angelorum visionibus frequenter potitus est, qui ab angelo dictus est Israel. Porro quam præclarissimus propheta exstiterit, quamque sanctissimum vitæ finem habuerit, ex Genesi elucescit. — Spiritualiter Isaac, id est gaudium in Domino, generat Jacob, id est vitiorum supplantatorem. Qui enim delectatur in Domino et actibus sanctis, vitiis fortiter reluctatur, ac alios ad vitiorum eradicationem inducit: secundum quod dicitur, Gustato spiritu, desipit omnis caro.
paras.en: [[1:2|And Isaac begot Jacob|Isaac autem genuit Jacob]], who was [[Gen 25:27|a plain man|vir simplex]], dwelling in tents. Augustine seems to hold that he was sanctified in the womb. Hence the Lord says through the prophet Malachias: [[Mal 1:2|Was not Esau brother to Jacob|Nonne frater erat Jacob Esau]]? [[Mal 1:2|and I have loved Jacob|Et Jacob dilexi]], [[Mal 1:3|But have hated Esau|Esau autem odio habui]]. This Jacob was often granted visions of angels[[Gen 28:12||]][[Gen 32:1||]] [the margin note here is only partly readable; these are the visions of angels in Genesis], and was named Israel by an angel[[Gen 32:28||]]. How very illustrious a prophet he was, and how holy an end of life he had, is clear from Genesis[[Gen 48:1||]][[Gen 49:1||]]. — In the spiritual sense Isaac, that is, joy in the Lord, begets Jacob, that is, the supplanter of vices. For he who delights in the Lord and in holy deeds strives mightily against vices, and leads others to root them out; according to the saying: "Once the spirit has been tasted, all flesh grows insipid" [a saying of St Bernard].

paras.t: Jacob autem genuit Judam et fratres ejus, undecim Patriarchas, videlicet Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zabulon. Hi sex de Lia exorti sunt. Joseph quoque et Benjamin ex Rachele; Dan vero et Nephthali ex Bala; Gad autem et Aser ex Zelpha. — Jacob pater duodecim Patriarcharum, figura est Christi, patris duodecim Apostolorum. Judas autem interpretatur confessio. Qui ergo spiritualiter Jacob est, vitia supplantando, generat Judam, id est confessionem laudis divinæ, dicens cum Psalmista: Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo; itemque, Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo. Talis quippe dignus est Deum laudare, quum non sit speciosa laus in ore peccatoris. De hoc Juda scriptum est in libro Paralipomenon: Judas fortissimus erat inter fratres suos.
paras.en: [[1:2|And Jacob begot Judas and his brethren|Jacob autem genuit Judam et fratres ejus]], the eleven Patriarchs, namely Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, Zabulon: these six [counting Juda] were born of Lia[[Gen 35:23||]]; Joseph and Benjamin of Rachel[[Gen 35:24||]]; Dan and Nephthali of Bala[[Gen 35:25||]]; Gad and Aser of Zelpha[[Gen 35:26||]]. — Jacob, the father of the twelve Patriarchs, is a figure of Christ, the father of the twelve Apostles. Judas is interpreted "confession"[[Gen 29:35||]]. He, then, who is spiritually Jacob, by supplanting vices, begets Judas, that is, the confession of God's praise, saying with the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:2|I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth|Benedicam Dominum in omni tempore, semper laus ejus in ore meo]]; and again: [[Ps 9:2|I will give praise to thee, O Lord, with my whole heart|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo]][[Ps 110:1||]][[Ps 137:1||]]. Such a man is indeed worthy to praise God, since [[Ecclus 15:9|praise is not seemly in the mouth of a sinner|non sit speciosa laus in ore peccatoris]]. Of this Juda it is written in the book of Paralipomenon that Juda [[1 Par 5:2|was the strongest among his brethren|fortissimus erat inter fratres suos]].

paras.t: Judas autem genuit Phares et Zaram de Thamar nuru sua. Cui quum Judas dare nollet filium suum in maritum, ut suscitaret semen fratrum suorum maritorum Thamar sine liberis defunctorum, illa prolem habere desiderans, mutato habitu, sedit in via qua noverat Judam iturum: qui putans eam esse scortum, concubuit cum ea, concepitque et peperit filios duos jam nominatos.
paras.en: [[1:3|And Judas begot Phares and Zara of Thamar|Judas autem genuit Phares et Zaram de Thamar]], his daughter-in-law. When Judas would not give her his son as husband, to raise up seed for his brothers, Thamar's husbands, who had died without children, she, desiring to have offspring, changed her garments and sat by the road on which she knew Judas would pass; and he, taking her for a harlot, lay with her, and she conceived and bore the two sons just named[[Gen 38:14||]][[Gen 38:30||]].

paras.t: Hoc loco dicit Hieronymus, in genealogia Salvatoris nullam sanctarum assumi feminarum, sed eas quas Scriptura reprehendit: ut qui propter peccatores venerat, de peccatricibus nascens, omnium peccata deleret. Contra quod dictum Lyra argumentatur, quia inferius virgo Maria, quæ erat sanctissima, ponitur. Hieronymus etiam asserit, tres reges propter iniquitatem patris eorum omissos, ne in sanctæ nativitatis ordine ponerentur. Non ergo hæ mulieres ponuntur hoc loco quoniam peccatrices. — Certum est autem, quod harum objectionum prima non sit contra mentem Hieronymi: sicut nec illa quæ aliquis dicere posset contra verba Hieronymi, quibus ait quod Matthæus nominat Christum filium David et Abrahæ tantum. Posset enim quis objicere, quod etiam nominat eum filium Mariæ. — De secunda objectione dubium esse potest quid Hieronymus senserit. Non autem opinor eum sensisse, quod hæ quatuor mulieres, quas appellat non sanctas, sed peccatrices, videlicet Thamar, Rahab, Ruth et Bethsabee, sint in vitiis consummatæ seu condemnatæ. Unde Ambrosius eas multum excusat, etiam ipsam Thamar, quæ inexcusabilior esse videtur, quoniam rea incesti. Sed quoniam teste Dionysio, sanctum dicitur quasi immaculatum, Hieronymus vocat eas non sanctas et peccatrices, eo quod aliqua reprehensibilia commiserint, de quibus pœnituisse creduntur. Fuerant ergo peccatrices, eo modo quo de Maria Magdalene jam pœnitente in Evangelio legitur: Mulier quæ erat in civitate peccatrix, ut cognovit quod Jesus accubuit in domo Simonis, etc. De virtutibus autem earum statim dicetur.
paras.en: Here Jerome says that in the genealogy of the Saviour none of the holy women is taken up, but those whom Scripture blames: so that He who had come for the sake of sinners, being born of sinful women, might blot out the sins of all. Against this saying Lyra argues that further on the Virgin Mary, who was most holy, is set down[[1:16||]]. Jerome also asserts that three kings were left out because of their father's wickedness, so as not to be set in the line of the holy nativity. Therefore, Lyra concludes, these women are not set down here because they were sinners. — It is certain, however, that the first of these objections is not against Jerome's mind; any more than the objection someone might raise against Jerome's words where he says that Matthew names Christ the son of David and Abraham only[[1:1||]]: for one could object that he also names Him the son of Mary. — About the second objection there may be doubt as to what Jerome meant. But I do not think he meant that these four women whom he calls not holy but sinners, namely Thamar, Rahab, Ruth and Bethsabee, were hardened in their vices or condemned. Hence Ambrose excuses them a great deal, even Thamar herself, who seems the least excusable, being guilty of incest. But since, on the testimony of Dionysius, "holy" means as it were "spotless", Jerome calls them not holy, and sinners, because they had committed some blameworthy things, of which they are believed to have repented. They were sinners, then, in the way it is said in the Gospel of Mary Magdalen, already repentant: [[Luke 7:37|a woman that was in the city, a sinner, when she knew that he sat at meat|Mulier quæ erat in civitate peccatrix, ut cognovit quod Jesus accubuit]] in the house of Simon, etc. Of their virtues we shall speak presently.

paras.t: Bona est igitur ratio S. Hieronymi, quod hæ feminæ peccatrices in genealogia Christi ponuntur propter exemplum sperandæ salutis, et propter spem excitandam: non solum in quantum peccatrices, sed in quantum peccatrices pœnitentes, ut dum audimus Sanctum Sanctorum de peccatricibus mediate natum, nullatenus desperemus, sed peccatricum illarum pœnitentiam imitemur. Interea, quod de regibus illis omissis objicitur, non est contra intellectum Hieronymi. Non enim dicit eos dumtaxat omissos, quia injusti fuerunt, nam simili ratione Roboam, Achaz, Amon, et alii quidam omissi fuissent; sed propter commixtionem patris eorum, videlicet Joram regis Juda, cum filia impiissimæ Jezabel, muliere gentili atque idololatra: unde propter labem gentilitatis omissi sunt. Sicque opposita ratio est de omissione regum istorum et prædictarum mulierum, eo quod Rahab et Ruth gentilitate relicta, ad Judaismum conversæ sunt; Joram vero legitimo toro contempto, acceperit uxorem gentilem in gentilitate manentem.
paras.en: St Jerome's reason is therefore a good one: these sinful women are set in the genealogy of Christ as an example of the salvation we may hope for, and to stir up hope; not only as sinners, but as repentant sinners, so that when we hear that the Holy of Holies was born, through others, of sinful women [mediate: not directly, but through the intervening generations], we may in no way despair, but may imitate the repentance of those women. As for the objection about the kings left out, it is not against Jerome's meaning. For he does not say that they were left out simply because they were unjust; for by the same reasoning Roboam, Achaz, Amon and certain others would have been left out. Rather it was because of their father's union, that is, of Joram king of Juda, with the daughter of the most impious Jezabel, a Gentile woman and an idolater[[2 Par 21:6||]][[2 Par 24:7||]]: so they were left out because of the stain of heathenism. And so the reason for omitting these kings is the opposite of the reason for including the women named, because Rahab and Ruth left heathenism and were converted to Judaism, whereas Joram, scorning a lawful marriage, took a Gentile wife who remained in her heathenism.

paras.t: Phares autem genuit Esron; Esron autem genuit Aram; Aram autem genuit Aminadab; Aminadab autem genuit Naasson. Hic Phares cum patre suo Juda Ægyptum ingressus est, in qua genuit Esron; Esron quoque in Ægypto genuit Aram, et ille Aminadab. Sed et Aminadab in Ægypto genuit Naasson, quorum uterque egressus est Ægyptum cum Moyse. Dicunt quoque Hebræi, quod mari Rubro diviso et Moyse illud ingresso, quum ceteræ tribus formidarent eum sequi, Aminadab cum tribu Juda, in qua principalior fuit, primo secutus est Moysen: quo viso, aliæ tribus secutæ sunt. Unde per hoc dicunt tribum Juda meruisse principatum et regnum. Potius tamen tenendum est, quod tribus hæc sine suo merito ad regnum electa atque promota est propter reverentiam Christi, qui de ea incarnari elegit.
paras.en: [[1:3|And Phares begot Esron. And Esron begot Aram|Phares autem genuit Esron; Esron autem genuit Aram]]. [[1:4|And Aram begot Aminadab. And Aminadab begot Naasson|Aram autem genuit Aminadab; Aminadab autem genuit Naasson]]. This Phares went into Egypt with his father Juda[[Gen 46:12||]], and there begot Esron; Esron too begot Aram in Egypt, and Aram begot Aminadab. And Aminadab also begot Naasson in Egypt, and both of these went out of Egypt with Moses[[Num 1:7||]]. The Hebrews also say that when the Red Sea was divided and Moses had entered it, while the other tribes were afraid to follow him, Aminadab with the tribe of Juda, in which he was the chief man, followed Moses first; and seeing this the other tribes followed. Hence, they say, the tribe of Juda earned the leadership and the kingdom. It is rather to be held, however, that this tribe was chosen and raised to the kingdom without any merit of its own, out of reverence for Christ, who chose to take flesh from it. [[Num 2:3||]]

paras.t: Naasson autem genuit Salmon. Iste Naasson fuit princeps Judæ: cujus sororem nomine Elisabeth accepit Aaron in uxorem; qui etiam Naasson fuit unus duodecim principum quos Dominus jussit in patibulis poni propter peccata filiorum Israel cum filiabus et idolis Madianitarum fornicantium.
paras.en: [[1:4|And Naasson begot Salmon|Naasson autem genuit Salmon]]. This Naasson was prince of Juda; Aaron took his sister, named Elisabeth, to wife[[Ex 6:23||]]. This Naasson was also one of the twelve princes whom the Lord commanded to be hung on gibbets because of the sins of the children of Israel[[Num 25:4||]], who committed fornication with the daughters and the idols of the Madianites.

paras.t: Salmon autem genuit Booz de Rahab. Salmon iste cum Josue terram Chanaan introivit. Non enim fuit numeratus in prima numeratione inter filios Israel. Accepit autem Rahab meretricem in conjugem, gignens ex ea Booz. Quamvis enim filiis Israel esset prohibitum inire conjugium cum mulieribus alienigenis, maxime Chananæis, hoc tamen intelligendum fuit de mulieribus in infidelitate durantibus; sed quando conversæ erant ad Judaismum, et notabiliter virtuose vivebant, poterant in matrimonium recipi. Talem autem fuisse hanc Rahab constat ex libro Josue. Recepit enim, abscondit atque dimisit exploratores missos a Josue; et omnipotentiam Dei Israel confitebatur; deinde gentilitate contempta, cum omni sua progenie apposita est ad filios Israel. Unde propter hanc fidem, veritatem atque justitiam, meruit a viro nobili in conjugem recipi, scilicet a filio Naasson.
paras.en: [[1:5|And Salmon begot Booz of Rahab|Salmon autem genuit Booz de Rahab]]. This Salmon entered the land of Chanaan with Josue; for he had not been counted among the children of Israel in the first numbering [and so was not among those who died in the desert]. He took Rahab the harlot to wife, and begot Booz of her. For although the children of Israel were forbidden to marry foreign women, above all Chanaanites[[Ex 34:16||]][[Deut 7:3||]], this was to be understood of women who persisted in unbelief; but when they had been converted to Judaism and were living with notable virtue, they could be received in marriage. That this Rahab was such a woman is plain from the book of Josue[[Jos 2:1||]]. For she received, hid and sent away the spies sent by Josue, and confessed the almighty power of the God of Israel[[Jos 2:11||]]; then, having renounced heathenism, she was added with all her family to the children of Israel[[Jos 6:25||]]. Hence, for this faith, truthfulness and justice, she was found worthy to be taken in marriage by a man of noble rank, namely by the son of Naasson.

paras.t: Quidam tamen asserit hanc Rahab non fuisse meretricem, quamvis sic nominetur, sicut frequenter aliquis pauper dicitur dux, qui non est dux. Dicit enim in Hebræo haberi, Mulierem hospitatricem, ubi nostra translatio continet, Mulierem meretricem. Non videtur etiam verisimile, quod Salmon potentissimus pene et maximus in tribu Juda, recepisset meretricem in conjugem. Sed hoc dictum non consonat communibus dictis Sanctorum, qui asserunt Rahab meretricem fuisse. Tale quoque agnomen non fit communiter in eodem casu; nec tam turpe agnomen convenisset mulieri honestæ. Idcirco meretrix non videtur fuisse dumtaxat agnomen feminæ hujus. Sed nec probabile arbitror, quod B. Hieronymus in lingua Hebræa tam eruditus, loco hospitatricis transtulisset, Meretricem: imo potius æstimo, quod nomen Hebraicum sit æquivocum ad hospitatricem et meretricem. Sic enim frequenter invenio, quod Lyra dicit aliter haberi in Hebræo, quam nostra habeat translatio. Tamen in libris Hieronymi invenio, quod sermo Hebraicus sit æquivocus, possitque diversimode interpretari. Unde Hieronymus significationem convenientiorem accepit, et ita non proprie habetur in Hebræo aliter quam Hieronymus transtulit. Denique, quod arguitur, non esse probabile Salmon accepisse meretricem in conjugem: respondendum est secundum Chrysostomum, quod propter virtutes ejus accepit eam post suam emendationem, quando etiam magna et sublimata fuerat in populo Israel. Est quoque consuetudo Scripturæ, ut mulieres incontinentes et lubricæ, meretrices vocentur, quamvis non sint publicum scortum. Unde ad salvandum quod Rahab fuerit meretrix, non oportet opinari quod omnibus se exposuit.
paras.en: One writer, however, asserts that this Rahab was not a harlot, although she is so called, just as a poor man is often nicknamed "Duke" who is no duke. For he says that the Hebrew has "a woman who kept an inn" where our translation has "a harlot woman"[[Jos 2:1||]][[Jos 6:22||]]. Nor does it seem likely, he says, that Salmon, almost the most powerful and greatest man in the tribe of Juda, would have taken a harlot to wife. But this saying does not agree with the common teaching of the Saints, who assert that Rahab was a harlot. Moreover, such a byname is not commonly given in a case like this; nor would so shameful a byname have suited an honourable woman. Therefore "harlot" does not seem to have been merely a byname of this woman. Nor do I think it probable that blessed Jerome, so learned in the Hebrew tongue, would have translated "harlot" in place of "innkeeper"; rather I judge that the Hebrew word is ambiguous, meaning both innkeeper and harlot. For I often find Lyra saying that the Hebrew reads otherwise than our translation has it; yet in Jerome's books I find that the Hebrew expression is ambiguous and can be interpreted in different ways. Hence Jerome took the more fitting meaning, and so the Hebrew does not, properly speaking, read otherwise than as Jerome translated. Lastly, to the argument that it is not probable that Salmon took a harlot to wife, the answer, following Chrysostom, is that he took her for her virtues, after her amendment, when she had become great and highly honoured among the people of Israel. It is also the custom of Scripture to call incontinent and wanton women harlots, even though they are not public prostitutes. Hence, to maintain that Rahab was a harlot, we need not suppose that she gave herself to all.

paras.t: Booz autem genuit Obed ex Ruth. Ista est Ruth Moabitis, quæ ut legitur in libro Ruth, venit cum Noemi a terra Moab in terram Juda: quam Booz accepit in conjugem, eo quod esset propinquus priori marito Ruth filio Noemi sine prole defuncto. Quamvis enim illicitum fuerat Israelitis contrahere cum Moabitis (imo tale matrimonium non erat verum matrimonium, propter disparem cultum personarum: propter quod Esdras abjecit a filiis Israel uxores eorum Moabitidas): nihilominus, quando conversæ fuerunt feminæ tales ad Judaismum, et virtuosæ effectæ, recipi poterant, saltem ex dispensatione. Quam autem virtuosa et fidelissima, humilis atque obediens fuerit Ruth, patet in ejus historia. Unde et Booz dixit ad eam: Scit omnis populus urbis meæ mulierem te esse virtutis. Quoniam vero inter matrimonium Salmon et Rahab, quod fuit tempore Josue, et matrimonium Booz et Ruth, quod fuit tempore Heli, vel circiter, tempus trecentorum annorum transierit, ut potest probari, computando tempora judicum intermediorum; mirum apparet quomodo Salmon genuit Booz maritum Ruth. Ad quod aliqui dicunt, tres fuisse Booz, quorum primus erat filius Salmon et avus hujus Booz: comprehenduntur tamen sub nomine uno. Sed ista responsio ex nulla canonica Scriptura auctoritatem sortitur: imo ubicumque in novo et veteri Testamento describitur ordo generationis istorum, de uno dumtaxat Booz fit mentio. Non tamen pro præsenti occurrit responsio melior, nisi hic Booz dicatur tempore tam longo vixisse. Erat autem hic Booz homo magnarum opum, vir bonus et justus.
paras.en: [[1:5|And Booz begot Obed of Ruth|Booz autem genuit Obed ex Ruth]]. This is Ruth the Moabitess, who, as we read in the book of Ruth, came with Noemi from the land of Moab into the land of Juda[[Ruth 1:19||]]; and Booz took her to wife because he was a kinsman of Ruth's first husband, Noemi's son, who had died without issue[[Ruth 4:10||]][[Ruth 4:13||]]. For although it was unlawful for Israelites to marry Moabites (indeed such a marriage was no true marriage, because of the difference of worship between the persons [disparitas cultus: the impediment that makes void a marriage between a believer and an unbeliever], for which reason Esdras put away from the children of Israel their Moabite wives[[1 Esd 10:3||]]), nevertheless, when such women had been converted to Judaism and had become virtuous, they could be received, at least by dispensation. How virtuous and most faithful, how humble and obedient Ruth was, is plain from her story. Hence Booz said to her: All the people of my city [[Ruth 3:11|know that thou art a virtuous woman|Scit omnis populus urbis meæ mulierem te esse virtutis]]. But since between the marriage of Salmon and Rahab, which was in the time of Josue, and the marriage of Booz and Ruth, which was in the time of Heli or thereabouts, a period of three hundred years passed, as can be proved by reckoning the times of the judges in between, it seems strange how Salmon begot Booz, the husband of Ruth. To this some say that there were three called Booz, the first of whom was the son of Salmon and the grandfather of this Booz, though they are included under one name. But this answer draws no authority from any canonical Scripture; on the contrary, wherever in the New and Old Testaments the line of descent of these men is set out, only one Booz is mentioned. Yet for the present no better answer offers itself, unless it be said that this Booz lived for so long a time. This Booz was a man of great wealth, a good and just man[[Ruth 2:1||]].

paras.t: Obed autem genuit Jesse. Jesse trinomius fuit. Dictus est enim Isai et Naas: unde secundo Regum habetur, quod Amasa fuit filius Jethra Jezraelitis, qui ingressus est ad Abigail filiam Naas sororem Sarviæ, quæ fuit soror David, et mater Joab. Naas ergo erat pater David atque Sarviæ. Et quia Matthæus loquitur jam de Isai, secundum quod Christus ex eo natus est, ideo nominat eum Jesse, quia sic appellatur apud Isaiam, ubi Christus de eo nasciturus asseritur. Sic enim habemus: Egredietur virga de radice Jesse. Sic ergo ostenditur prophetia illa in ipso completa. De hoc Jesse primo Regum inducitur, quod in diebus Saul erat vir grandævus et magnus inter viros Israel. Jesse autem genuit David regem. Nominatur solus David rex propter excellentiam gratiæ sibi concessæ, et quoniam nullus præcedentium rex fuit, eorum videlicet qui nunc ante David expressi sunt, et quoniam primus electus est ad regnum tanquam stabiliendus in eo. Hic David, homo secundum cor Dei, pene in omnibus Christi erat figura.
paras.en: [[1:5|And Obed begot Jesse|Obed autem genuit Jesse]][[Ruth 4:17||]][[Ruth 4:22||]]. Jesse had three names: he was also called Isai and Naas. Hence it is found in the second book of Kings that Amasa was the son of Jethra of Jezrael, [[2 Kings 17:25|who went in to Abigail the daughter of Naas, the sister of Sarvia|qui ingressus est ad Abigail filiam Naas sororem Sarviæ]], who was David's sister and the mother of Joab. Naas, then, was the father of David and of Sarvia. And because Matthew is now speaking of Isai as the one from whom Christ was born, he names him Jesse, since that is what he is called in Isaias, where it is declared that Christ will be born of him. For there we have: [[Is 11:1|And there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse|Egredietur virga de radice Jesse]]. So it is shown that that prophecy was fulfilled in Christ. Of this Jesse it is related in the first book of Kings that in the days of Saul he was a man of great age, and great among the men of Israel[[1 Kings 17:12||]]. [[1:6|And Jesse begot David the king|Jesse autem genuit David regem]]. David alone is named king because of the excellence of the grace granted to him; and because none of those before him was a king, that is, of those named so far before David; and because he was the first chosen to the kingdom as one in whom it was to be established. This David, a man after God's heart[[Acts 13:22||]], was a figure of Christ in almost everything.

paras.t: David autem rex genuit Salomonem ex ea quæ fuit Uriæ, id est ex Bethsabee, quæ fuerat uxor Uriæ Hethæi, viri justi, qui merito suæ virtutis hoc loco exprimitur. Genuit autem David ex Bethsabee filium unum in adulterio, qui et mortuus est infans; accepitque eam in conjugem antequam ex ea genuit Salomonem. Porro, quod Bethsabee justa fuerit, constat ex libro Proverbiorum, ubi Salomon recitat quomodo a matre sua instructus sit. Iste est Salomon, qui inclinavit femora sua mulieribus, et dedit maculam in gloria sua. Reliquit quoque post se stultitiam, id est filium stultum, de quo subditur:
paras.en: [[1:6|And David the king begot Solomon, of her that had been the wife of Urias|David autem rex genuit Salomonem ex ea quæ fuit Uriæ]], that is, of Bethsabee, who had been the wife of Urias the Hethite[[2 Kings 11:3||]], a just man, who is named here on account of his virtue. David begot one son of Bethsabee in adultery[[2 Kings 11:4||]], who died as an infant[[2 Kings 12:18||]]; and he took her to wife before he begot Solomon of her[[2 Kings 12:24||]]. That Bethsabee was a just woman is plain from the book of Proverbs, where Solomon tells how he was taught by his mother[[Prov 4:3||]]. This is the Solomon who bowed himself to women and stained his glory[[Ecclus 47:21||]][[Ecclus 47:22||]]. He also left folly behind him[[Ecclus 47:27||]], that is, a foolish son, of whom it follows:

paras.t: Salomon autem genuit Roboam, propter cujus stultam responsionem, decem tribus omnino recesserunt a domo David, constituentes sibi Jeroboam Ephrateum in regem. Roboam autem genuit Abiam, ex filia Absalonis fratris sui, quam secundum legem habere non potuit propter cognationis propinquitatem.
paras.en: [[1:7|And Solomon begot Roboam|Salomon autem genuit Roboam]], because of whose foolish answer ten tribes wholly fell away from the house of David[[3 Kings 12:13||]][[3 Kings 12:16||]] and set up Jeroboam the Ephrathite as king over them[[3 Kings 12:20||]]. [[1:7|And Roboam begot Abia|Roboam autem genuit Abiam]], of the daughter of Absalom[[2 Par 11:20||]] his brother [so the printed text; Absalom was Solomon's brother, and so Roboam's uncle], whom he could not lawfully have according to the Law because of the nearness of kinship.

paras.t: Abias autem genuit Asa; Asa autem genuit Josaphat. Magnificentia atque præconia Asa et Josaphat, in libro Paralipomenon plenissime describuntur. Erant namque plurimum virtuosi et boni: quibus et maximas victorias atque divitias Deus concessit. Josaphat autem genuit Joram virum pravissimum, qui Athaliam filiam Achab et Jezabel sumpsit in conjugem, cujus consilio plurima mala operatus est.
paras.en: [[1:7|And Abia begot Asa|Abias autem genuit Asa]]. [[1:8|And Asa begot Josaphat|Asa autem genuit Josaphat]]. The great deeds and praises of Asa and Josaphat are set out most fully in the book of Paralipomenon[[2 Par 14:2||]]; for they were very virtuous and good men, and God granted them very great victories and riches. [[1:8|And Josaphat begot Joram|Josaphat autem genuit Joram]], a most wicked man, who took to wife Athalia, the daughter of Achab and Jezabel[[4 Kings 8:18||]], by whose counsel he did a great many evil things.

paras.t: Joram autem genuit Oziam. In libro Regum fertur quod Joram genuit Ochoziam, Ochozias autem genuit Joas, de quo natus est Amasias, qui genuit Oziam, qui alio nomine vocatus est Azarias, sub quo Isaias orsus est prophetare. Tres ergo hoc loco reges omissi sunt, videlicet Ochozias, Joas et Amasias. Cujus ratio una est, secundum Hieronymum, Hilarium et Chrysostomum, quoniam Joram accepit filiam Jezabel feminæ gentilis ac pessimæ in uxorem: idcirco filii ejus de iniquo et maledicto semine nati, usque ad quartam generationem tolluntur, ne in sanctæ nativitatis ordine commemorentur aut collocentur. Aliam rationem ponit Hieronymus. Nam Evangelistæ propositum erat, tres quaterdenas generationum, id est ter quatuordecim, in Christi genealogia disponere, et hoc, in diverso temporum statu, ut plenius ostendetur, ita ut a David usque ad transmigrationem Babylonis esset una quaterdena. Quoniam ergo decem et septem generationes inter David et transmigrationem fuerunt, hi tres reges convenientius quam alii fuerant omittendi, propter causam inductam. Joram ergo genuit immediate Ochoziam, mediate vero Oziam: qui quum thurificare vellet in templo, lepra percussus est, mansitque leprosus usque ad mortem; quem constat justum fuisse, et de sua præsumptione pœnituisse, plagam quoque paternæ correctionis Dei patienter tulisse.
paras.en: [[1:8|And Joram begot Ozias|Joram autem genuit Oziam]]. In the book of Kings it is related that Joram begot Ochozias[[4 Kings 8:24||]], and Ochozias begot Joas[[4 Kings 11:2||]], of whom was born Amasias[[4 Kings 12:21||]], who begot Ozias, who by another name was called Azarias[[4 Kings 14:21||]], under whom Isaias began to prophesy[[Is 1:1||]]. Three kings, then, are left out here, namely Ochozias, Joas and Amasias. One reason for this, according to Jerome, Hilary and Chrysostom, is that Joram took to wife the daughter of Jezabel, a Gentile and most wicked woman; therefore his sons, born of a wicked and accursed seed, are removed down to the fourth generation, so as not to be named or placed in the line of the holy nativity. Jerome gives another reason. For it was the Evangelist's purpose to arrange the genealogy of Christ in three fourteens of generations, that is, three times fourteen, and this according to the different states of the times, as will be shown more fully, so that there should be one fourteen [[1:17|from David to the transmigration of Babylon|a David usque ad transmigrationem Babylonis]]. Since, then, there were seventeen generations between David and the transmigration, these three kings were more fittingly left out than others, for the reason already given. So Joram begot Ochozias immediately, but Ozias mediately [that is, through the intervening generations]. When Ozias wished to burn incense in the temple he was struck with leprosy, and remained a leper until his death[[2 Par 26:16||]]; yet it is certain that he was a just man, that he repented of his presumption, and that he bore patiently the stroke of God's fatherly correction.

paras.t: Ozias autem genuit Joatham, qui rexit palatium, patre ejus propter lepram habitante seorsum. Hunc Joatham dicit Hieronymus super Isaiam, fuisse justissimum. Joatham autem genuit Achaz, hominem prorsus malignum, cujus idololatria, perversitas et infortunia, in libris Regum et Paralipomenon recitantur. Achaz autem genuit Ezechiam, qui tantæ perfectionis et gloriæ exstitit, ut de ipso in libro Regum legatur, quod nec ante eum, nec post eum aliquis ei similis fuerit. Denique ipse bona conscientia ausus est dicere coram Deo: Memento, Domine, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate, et in corde perfecto, et quod bonum est in oculis tuis fecerim. Ad cujus instantiam reversus est sol decem lineis, per quas descenderat in horologio Achaz, ita quod dies illa prolongata fuit horis viginti (unde Dionysius in epistola ad Polycarpum affirmat diem illam pene triplicatam fuisse); angelus quoque percussit centum octoginta quinque millia virorum Assyriorum. Quumque Ezechias ab Isaia audisset se moriturum, flevit uberrime: non ex formidine mortis, nec desiderio vitæ præsentis, sed quoniam promissionem patribus suis factam de Christi nativitate ex eis, vidit frustrari in se: nondum enim habuit filium. Misertus Dominus Ezechiæ, prolongavit vitam ejus per quindecim annos.
paras.en: [[1:9|And Ozias begot Joatham|Ozias autem genuit Joatham]], who governed the palace while his father, because of his leprosy, lived apart[[4 Kings 15:5||]]. Jerome, on Isaias, says that this Joatham was most just. [[1:9|And Joatham begot Achaz|Joatham autem genuit Achaz]], an utterly wicked man, whose idolatry, perversity and misfortunes are recounted in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon[[4 Kings 16:2||]][[2 Par 28:1||]]. [[1:9|And Achaz begot Ezechias|Achaz autem genuit Ezechiam]], who was of such perfection and glory that we read of him in the book of Kings that none like him was before him or after him[[4 Kings 18:5||]]. Indeed, with a good conscience he dared to say before God: [[Is 38:3|O Lord, remember how I have walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight|Memento, Domine, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate, et in corde perfecto, et quod bonum est in oculis tuis fecerim]]. At his petition the sun went back the ten lines by which it had gone down on the dial of Achaz[[4 Kings 20:10||]][[Is 38:8||]], so that that day was lengthened by twenty hours (hence Dionysius, in his letter to Polycarp, affirms that that day was almost tripled); and an angel struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand men of the Assyrians[[4 Kings 19:35||]]. And when Ezechias heard from Isaias that he was to die, he wept most bitterly[[4 Kings 20:1||]]: not from fear of death, nor from desire of the present life, but because he saw that the promise made to his fathers, that Christ would be born of them, was coming to nothing in himself, for he did not yet have a son. The Lord had pity on Ezechias, and lengthened his life by fifteen years[[4 Kings 20:6||]].

paras.t: Ezechias autem genuit Manassen, cujus gravissima scelera in libris Regum et Paralipomenon recoluntur. Observavit somnia atque auguria, servivit omni militiæ cœli, replevitque Jerusalem sanguine innocentium, usque ad os; Isaiam quoque patruum suum jussit lignea serra secari. Refert Chrysostomus, quod Ezechias ægrotans, præsente Isaia docere cœpit Manassen, quomodo Deo servire, legem servare, et populum gubernare deberet. Dixit autem Isaias: Vere verba tua non descendunt in cor ejus, et ego ab eo occidendus sum. Quod audiens Ezechias, voluit Manassen occidere: Melius (inquiens) mihi est sine filio mori, quam talem relinquere. Isaias vero tenuit eum, ne illum occideret. Postremo Manasses propter peccata sua a rege Assyriorum captus, incarceratus et dire ligatus, egit pœnitentiam valde, toto corde conversus ad Deum; et liberatus, ad regnum suum reductus est.
paras.en: [[1:10|And Ezechias begot Manasses|Ezechias autem genuit Manassen]], whose most grievous crimes are recorded in the books of Kings and Paralipomenon. He observed dreams and auguries[[4 Kings 21:6||]], served all the host of heaven[[4 Kings 21:3||]], and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood up to the brim[[4 Kings 21:16||]]; and he commanded Isaias, his uncle, to be sawn asunder with a wooden saw. Chrysostom relates that Ezechias, when he was sick, began in the presence of Isaias to teach Manasses how he ought to serve God, keep the law and govern the people. But Isaias said: "Truly, thy words do not go down into his heart, and I am to be slain by him." Hearing this, Ezechias wished to kill Manasses, saying: "It is better for me to die without a son than to leave such a one behind." But Isaias held him back, so that he should not kill him. At last Manasses, for his sins, was taken by the king of the Assyrians, imprisoned and cruelly bound[[2 Par 33:11||]]; he did great penance, turned to God with his whole heart, and was set free and brought back to his kingdom[[2 Par 33:12||]][[2 Par 33:13||]].

paras.t: Manasses autem genuit Amon, qui secutus est peccata patris sui, non tamen pœnitentiam ejus. Amon autem genuit Josiam, virum sanctissimum, qui in pueritia sua quæsivit Dominum: sub quo Jeremias orsus est vaticinari. De cujus laude scriptum est: Memoria Josiæ in compositione odoris facta, opus pigmentarii; in omni ore quasi mel indulcabitur, et ut musica in convivio vini. Occisus est autem a sagittariis Pharaonis Nechao regis Ægypti: quem Jeremias maxime deploravit. Hujus Josiæ nomen per annos pene quadringentos divinitus prænuntiatum fuerat a Propheta qui dixit coram Jeroboam rege Israel: Ecce nascetur domui David filius, Josias nomine, etc.
paras.en: [[1:10|And Manasses begot Amon|Manasses autem genuit Amon]], who followed his father's sins but not his penance[[2 Par 33:22||]]. [[1:10|And Amon begot Josias|Amon autem genuit Josiam]], a most holy man, who sought the Lord in his boyhood[[2 Par 34:3||]], and under whom Jeremias began to prophesy[[Jer 1:2||]]. Of his praise it is written: [[Ecclus 49:1|The memory of Josias is like the composition of a sweet smell made by the art of a perfumer|Memoria Josiæ in compositione odoris facta, opus pigmentarii]]; it [[Ecclus 49:2|shall be sweet as honey in every mouth, and as music at a banquet of wine|in omni ore quasi mel indulcabitur, et ut musica in convivio vini]]. He was slain by the archers of Pharao Nechao, king of Egypt[[2 Par 35:23||]], and Jeremias mourned him greatly[[2 Par 35:25||]]. The name of this Josias had been foretold by God almost four hundred years before, by the Prophet who said in the presence of Jeroboam king of Israel: [[3 Kings 13:2|Behold a child shall be born to the house of David, Josias by name|Ecce nascetur domui David filius, Josias nomine]], etc.

paras.t: Josias autem genuit Jechoniam et fratres ejus in transmigrationem Babylonis. In libro Regum legitur Joachaz filius Josiæ immediate regnasse post patrem suum: qui quum mensibus tribus regnasset, captus et in Ægyptum perductus est a Pharaone Nechao jam expresso, qui loco Joachaz constituit Eliacim fratrem Joachaz filium Josiæ in regem, vocavitque eum Joakim, qui etiam dictus est Jechonias: et iste jam dicitur genitus a Josia. Qui quum undecim annis regnasset, obsessus et captus est a Nabuchodonosor rege Babylonis: quem aliqui dicunt translatum in Babylonem. Certum est autem quod Nabuchodonosor eum remisit in Jerusalem ut regnaret, accepta ab eo promissione quod non rebellaret. Unde secundum quosdam, in via remisit eum rex Babylonis. Quum autem tribus annis servisset regi Babylonis subditus, repugnavit. Propter quod ab exercitu ejus interfectus est; projeceruntque eum extra portas Jerusalem insepultum, quemadmodum dixerat Jeremias: Sepultura asini sepelietur. Quo mortuo, regnavit filius ejus pro eo: qui etiam appellatus est Joachin et Jechonias, sicut pater ipsius, quamvis diversis litteris scribantur. Quum vero et iste regnasset mensibus tribus, a rege Babylonis vallatus est; cernensque se non posse resistere, exivit ad regem, qui misit eum cum matre, uxoribus atque principibus suis in Babylonem, et fecit Mathaniam avunculum ejus filium Josiæ regem pro eo, appellans eum Sedeciam: qui tandem rebellans, captus, excæcatus, et in Babylonem perductus est, sicut Jeremias ei prædixit: Babylonem intrabis, et eam non videbis. Sic ergo Josias genuit Jechoniam et fratres ejus jam nominatos in transmigrationem Babylonis, id est, transmigratione seu translatione Judæorum in Babylonem jam imminente, quæ post generationem istorum secuta est, evolutis annis circiter viginti septem.
paras.en: [[1:11|And Josias begot Jechonias and his brethren in the transmigration of Babylon|Josias autem genuit Jechoniam et fratres ejus in transmigrationem Babylonis]]. In the book of Kings we read that Joachaz, the son of Josias, reigned immediately after his father[[4 Kings 23:30||]]; and when he had reigned three months he was taken and carried into Egypt by the Pharao Nechao already mentioned, who in place of Joachaz made Eliacim, Joachaz's brother and a son of Josias, king, and called him Joakim[[4 Kings 23:34||]]; he was also called Jechonias, and it is he who is here said to have been begotten by Josias. When he had reigned eleven years he was besieged and taken by Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon[[2 Par 36:6||]]; some say he was carried off to Babylon. But it is certain that Nabuchodonosor sent him back to Jerusalem to reign, having received from him a promise that he would not rebel; so according to some the king of Babylon sent him back while on the way. But when he had served the king of Babylon as his subject for three years, he rebelled[[4 Kings 24:1||]]. For this he was slain by the king's army, and they cast him out unburied outside the gates of Jerusalem, as Jeremias had said: [[Jer 22:19|He shall be buried with the burial of an ass|Sepultura asini sepelietur]]. After his death his son reigned in his stead[[4 Kings 24:6||]], who was also called Joachin and Jechonias like his father, though the names are written with different letters. When he too had reigned three months he was besieged by the king of Babylon[[4 Kings 24:8||]]; and seeing that he could not resist, he went out to the king, who sent him with his mother, his wives and his princes to Babylon[[4 Kings 24:12||]], and made Mathanias, his uncle, a son of Josias, king in his place, calling him Sedecias[[4 Kings 24:17||]]. Sedecias at length rebelled, and was taken, blinded and carried to Babylon[[4 Kings 25:7||]], as Jeremias had foretold to him: [[Jer 34:3|thou shalt go to Babylon|Babylonem intrabis]], and thou shalt not see it [the second half is from Ezechiel 12:13, "he shall not see it"]. So, then, [[1:11|Josias begot Jechonias and his brethren|Josias genuit Jechoniam et fratres ejus]], already named, [[1:11|in the transmigration of Babylon|in transmigrationem Babylonis]], that is, when the transmigration or carrying away of the Jews to Babylon was already at hand; it followed after the begetting of these men, some twenty-seven years later.

paras.t: Et post transmigrationem Babylonis, id est, postquam Judæi in Babylonem translati fuerunt, Jechonias (iste secundus, filius prioris Jechoniæ et nepos Josiæ) genuit Salathiel: de quo dicit Chrysostomus, Putamus eum sanctum fuisse et in captivitate Dominum assidue exorasse pro liberatione populi sui. Verum Hilarius et Chrysostomus sentiunt eumdem esse Jechoniam, qui ante et post transmigrationem fuit. Sed verum est quod ait Hieronymus, quod unus fuerit pater alterius. Si enim idem esset, non invenirentur quatuordecim generationes post transmigrationem usque ad Christum: cujus contrarium infra habetur. Unde Hieronymus: Si voluerimus, inquit, Jechoniam in fine primæ tessaradecadis ponere, hoc est ultimo loco secundæ seu mediæ quaterdenæ, in sequenti, id est in ultima quaterdena, non erunt quatuordecim, sed tredecim. Sciamus ergo Jechoniam priorem, ipsum esse quem et Joakim; secundum autem, filium non patrem: quorum prior per k et m, sequens per ch et n scribitur.
paras.en: [[1:12|And after the transmigration of Babylon|Et post transmigrationem Babylonis]], that is, after the Jews had been carried away to Babylon, [[1:12|Jechonias|Jechonias]] (this is the second, the son of the first Jechonias and grandson of Josias) [[1:12|begot Salathiel|genuit Salathiel]]. Of him Chrysostom says: "We think that he was a holy man, and that in the captivity he prayed to the Lord unceasingly for the deliverance of his people." Hilary and Chrysostom, however, hold that it was the same Jechonias who lived before and after the transmigration. But what Jerome says is true, that the one was the father of the other. For if they were the same, there would not be found fourteen generations after the transmigration down to Christ, the contrary of which is stated below[[1:17||]]. Hence Jerome says: "If we wish to put Jechonias at the end of the first fourteen" (that is, in the last place of the second or middle fourteen), "in the following one" (that is, in the last fourteen) "there will not be fourteen but thirteen. Let us know, then, that the first Jechonias is the same as Joakim, and the second is the son, not the father; the former is written with k and m, the latter with ch and n" [that is, Joakim and Joachin].

paras.t: Salathiel autem genuit Zorobabel, cujus præconia in apocryphis Esdræ narrantur: ad ejus quippe petitionem Darius rex Persarum dedit Judæis licentiam redeundi a Babylone in sua. De quo in Ecclesiastico inducitur: Quomodo amplificemus Zorobabel? Ipse enim quasi signum in manu dextera Israel. Et apud Aggæum: In die illo, dicit Dominus, assumam te, Zorobabel fili Salathiel serve meus, et ponam te quasi signaculum, quoniam te elegi. Zorobabel autem genuit Abiud. In libro Paralipomenon legitur Zorobabel genuisse Mosollam et alios quosdam, inter quos non ponitur Abiud. Ad quod respondendum, quod unus illorum alio nomine appellatus est Abiud, vel non omnes filii ejus ibi ponuntur.
paras.en: [[1:12|And Salathiel begot Zorobabel|Salathiel autem genuit Zorobabel]], whose praises are told in the apocryphal books of Esdras [the margin cites III Esdras iv–v, a book not in this Bible]: for it was at his request that Darius, king of the Persians, gave the Jews leave to return from Babylon to their own land. Of him it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 49:13|How shall we magnify Zorobabel? for he was as a signet on the right hand|Quomodo amplificemus Zorobabel? Ipse enim quasi signum in manu dextera]] of Israel. And in Aggeus: [[Agg 2:24|In that day|In die illo]], saith the Lord, [[Agg 2:24|I will take thee, O Zorobabel the son of Salathiel, my servant|assumam te, Zorobabel fili Salathiel serve meus]], [[Agg 2:24|and will make thee as a signet, for I have chosen thee|et ponam te quasi signaculum, quoniam te elegi]]. [[1:13|And Zorobabel begot Abiud|Zorobabel autem genuit Abiud]]. In the book of Paralipomenon we read that Zorobabel begot Mosollam and certain others, among whom Abiud is not set down[[1 Par 3:19||]]. To this the answer is that one of them was called Abiud by another name, or else not all his sons are set down there.

paras.t: De reliquis generationibus quæ sequuntur, usque ad Joseph, nihil habetur in scriptura canonica veteris Testamenti. Aliqui tamen Judæi diligenter scripserunt genealogias patrum suorum: præsertim ex catena et semine David, de quo noverant Christum nasciturum, propter quod ejus, scilicet David, posteritatem diligentius descripserunt.
paras.en: Of the remaining generations that follow, down to Joseph, nothing is found in the canonical scripture of the Old Testament. Some Jews, however, carefully wrote down the genealogies of their fathers, especially of the line and seed of David, from whom they knew Christ would be born; for this reason they recorded the posterity of David with special care.

paras.t: Jacob autem genuit Joseph virum Mariæ, de qua natus est Jesus, qui vocatur Christus. Erat autem Joseph veraciter vir Mariæ. Nam inter eos verum exstitit matrimonium, quamvis non fuerit consummatum. De qua Maria, id est ex cujus purissimis sanguinibus loco seminis a Spiritu Sancto formatus, natus est Jesus secundum humanam naturam, qui vocatur et est Christus, id est Deus et homo in una persona, duplicique natura.
paras.en: [[1:16|And Jacob begot Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ.|Jacob autem genuit Joseph virum Mariæ, de qua natus est Jesus, qui vocatur Christus.]] Joseph was truly the husband of Mary, for there was a true marriage between them, although it was not consummated. [[1:16|Of whom|De qua]] Mary, that is, from whose most pure blood, formed by the Holy Ghost in place of seed, [[1:16|was born Jesus|natus est Jesus]] according to His human nature, [[1:16|who is called|qui vocatur]] and is [[1:16|Christ|Christus]], that is, God and man in one Person and two natures.

paras.t: Omnes ergo generationes ab Abraham inclusive usque ad David inclusive, fuerunt generationes quatuordecim; et a David exclusive usque ad transmigrationem Babylonis, videlicet usque ad primum Jechoniam inclusive, fuerunt generationes quatuordecim, loquendo de generationibus hic enumeratis, videlicet omissis tribus generationibus prædictis propter causam inductam; et a transmigratione Babylonis, id est a secundo Jechonia inclusive, usque ad Christum inclusive, fuerunt generationes quatuordecim: ita ut quartadecima generatio in Christo compleatur. Hoc planum est numeranti personas præscriptas.
paras.en: [[1:17|So all the generations from Abraham|Omnes ergo generationes ab Abraham]] inclusive [[1:17|to David|usque ad David]] inclusive [[1:17|are fourteen generations|fuerunt generationes quatuordecim]]. [[1:17|And from David|et a David]] exclusive [[1:17|to the transmigration of Babylon|usque ad transmigrationem Babylonis]], that is, down to the first Jechonias inclusive, [[1:17|are fourteen generations|fuerunt generationes quatuordecim]], speaking of the generations listed here, that is, leaving out the three generations mentioned above for the reason given. [[1:17|And from the transmigration of Babylon|et a transmigratione Babylonis]], that is, from the second Jechonias inclusive, [[1:17|to Christ|usque ad Christum]] inclusive, [[1:17|are fourteen generations|fuerunt generationes quatuordecim]], so that the fourteenth generation is completed in Christ. This is plain to anyone who counts the persons listed above.

1.title: Determinatio dubiorum concernentium locum istum
1.title_en: Resolution of the difficulties concerning this passage

paras.t: Difficultatem interea facit lectori in primis, quod beatissimi evangelistæ Matthæus et Lucas, describendo genealogiam Christi, in aliquibus dissonare videntur et opposito modo procedere. Primo itaque dubitatur, quomodo Lucas asserat Joseph esse filium Heli, Matthæus vero affirmet quod Joseph sit filius Jacob. Et respondendum, quod Joseph fuit filius naturalis ipsius Jacob, filius vero legalis Heli. Mathat enim et Mathan fratres fuerunt, qui successive eamdem habuere uxorem, de qua Mathan genuit Jacob, Mathat vero genuit ex ea Heli, ita quod Jacob et Heli fuerunt fratres uterini. Heli vero accepta conjuge, mortuus est non relicto semine: propter quod Jacob frater ejus, de præcepto legis accepit conjugem fratris sui defuncti, ut suscitaret semen fratri suo; genuitque ex ea Joseph, qui fuit filius Jacob secundum naturam, et filius Heli secundum legem Mosaicam, quæ præcepit, ut fratre aliquo uxorato sine liberis mortuo, frater ejus seu propinquus uxorem ejus acciperet, et filium ex ea natum, defuncto adscriberet, ne nomen ejus deleretur ex Israel. Sed tunc dubium occurrit, quomodo duo fratres poterant eamdem habere uxorem, ita quod unusquisque eorum ex ea proprium semen habebat. Ad hoc aliqui dicunt, quod quando aliquis non habuit nisi unam prolem ex conjuge sua, non reputabatur semen relinquere, et sic propinquus seu frater ipsius cum uxore sua contrahere potuit, ac si nullum semen reliquisset. Unde in Deuteronomio pluraliter dicitur, Si frater sine liberis mortuus fuerit, propinquus accipiat uxorem ejus, etc.
paras.en: First of all, the reader finds a difficulty in this: that the most blessed evangelists Matthew and Luke, in describing the genealogy of Christ, seem in some points to disagree and to proceed in opposite ways. The first doubt, then, is how Luke can assert that Joseph is the son of Heli[[Luke 3:23||]], while Matthew affirms that Joseph is the son of Jacob. The answer is that Joseph was the natural son of Jacob, but the legal son of Heli. For Mathat and Mathan were brothers who had the same wife one after the other: of her Mathan begot Jacob, and Mathat begot Heli, so that Jacob and Heli were brothers on the mother's side. Heli took a wife and died without leaving issue; therefore Jacob his brother, by the precept of the law, took the wife of his dead brother to raise up seed for his brother, and of her he begot Joseph, who was the son of Jacob according to nature and the son of Heli according to the law of Moses[[Deut 25:5||]][[Deut 25:6||]]. That law commanded that when a married man died without children, his brother or kinsman should take his wife, and should ascribe to the dead man the son born of her, so that his name should not be blotted out of Israel. But then a doubt arises: how could two brothers have the same wife, in such a way that each of them had his own seed of her? To this some answer that when a man had only one child by his wife he was not reckoned to leave seed, and so his kinsman or brother could marry his wife as though he had left no seed. Hence in Deuteronomy it is said in the plural: "If a brother die without children [liberi, 'children', is a plural noun], let his kinsman take his wife, etc."[[Deut 25:5||]]

paras.t: Secundo dubitatur, quomodo Matthæus asserat Salathiel filium Jechoniæ, quum Lucas dicat eum esse filium Neri. Dicendum, quod Salathiel fuerat filius Jechoniæ naturalis, Neri vero legalis vel adoptivus. — Tertio quæritur, quomodo Zorobabel hic dictus sit filius Salathiel, quum primo Paralipomenon appelletur filius Phadaiæ. Respondent aliqui, quod Salathiel alio nomine nuncupabatur Phadaia. Sed hoc non videtur, quum loco præallegato, in quo filii Jechoniæ describuntur, inter Salathiel et Phadaiam alius medius nominetur. Ideo alii dicunt, quod Zorobabel filius Salathiel fuit alius ab isto Zorobabel filio Phadaiæ.
paras.en: The second doubt is how Matthew can assert that Salathiel was the son of Jechonias, when Luke says he was the son of Neri[[Luke 3:27||]]. The answer is that Salathiel was the natural son of Jechonias, but the legal or adopted son of Neri. — The third question is how Zorobabel is here called the son of Salathiel, when in the first book of Paralipomenon he is called the son of Phadaia[[1 Par 3:19||]]. Some answer that Salathiel was called by another name Phadaia. But this does not seem right, since in the place cited, where the sons of Jechonias are listed, another is named between Salathiel and Phadaia[[1 Par 3:17||]][[1 Par 3:18||]]. Others therefore say that Zorobabel the son of Salathiel was a different man from the Zorobabel who was the son of Phadaia.

paras.t: Quarto principaliter dubitatur, quomodo Lucas dicat Christum descendisse a David per Nathan, Matthæus per Salomonem. Ad hoc diversi diversimode responderunt. Quidam, quod Nathan iste fuit filius David adoptivus, non naturalis: et horum aliqui dixerunt, quod fuit Nathan propheta, quem propter suam sanctitatem David adoptavit in filium. Alii, quod fuit filius Sammaa fratris David: quem Nathan Jesse avus ejus adoptavit in filium; defunctoque Jesse, ipse David eumdem sibi filium adoptavit. Et hoc dicit Magister in historiis. Lyra autem potius sentit, quod fuit Nathan propheta. Quod enim non fuerit filius naturalis David, probat per hoc, quod Salomon in Proverbiis de se ipso testatur: Fui tenellus et unigenitus coram matre mea, videlicet ex parte matris. Nam quamvis Bethsabee habuerit filium de David ante Salomonem, ille tamen non computatur, quoniam ante circumcisionem defunctus est, secundum Hebræos.
paras.en: The fourth and chief doubt is how Luke can say that Christ descended from David through Nathan[[Luke 3:31||]], and Matthew through Solomon. To this different men have answered in different ways. Some say that this Nathan was David's adopted son, not his natural son; and of these, some have said that he was Nathan the prophet, whom David adopted as his son because of his holiness. Others say that he was the son of Sammaa, David's brother, and that Jesse, his grandfather, adopted this Nathan as his son, and when Jesse died David himself adopted him as his own son. This is what the Master says in the Histories [Peter Comestor, the "Master of the Histories", in the Historia Scholastica]. Lyra, however, rather holds that he was Nathan the prophet. For he proves that Nathan was not David's natural son from this, that Solomon testifies of himself in Proverbs: I was [[Prov 4:3|tender, and as an only son in the sight of my mother|tenellus et unigenitus coram matre mea]] [unigenitus: literally "only-begotten"], that is, on his mother's side. For although Bethsabee had a son by David before Solomon, that son is not counted, since, according to the Hebrews, he died before his circumcision.

paras.t: Sed his obviat quod in libro Paralipomenon manifeste habetur, quod in Jerusalem nati sunt David quatuor filii de Bethsabee, quorum unus ibidem Nathan vocatur. Nec videtur sufficere, quod dicatur filius naturalis Bethsabee ex Uria et filius David adoptivus, ut aliqui dicunt, asserentes quod tres illic nominati fuerint filii Uriæ, quos David adoptavit in filios, dum matrem eorum accepit in conjugem. Si enim sic esset, non proprie dicerentur nati ipsi David ex Bethsabee. Ideo probabilius reor, quod Nathan fuit verus et naturalis filius David ex Bethsabee. Ad quod valet dictum Damasceni, libro quarto, ubi declarat beatam Virginem descendisse de David per Nathan. Si ergo Nathan non erat naturalis filius David, sed fratris sui, vel alterius, diceretur Christus potius descendisse de Jesse per Sammaa, quam per David, vel de alio aliquo etiam secundum carnem: quum tamen Apostolus dicat, eum factum ex semine David secundum carnem. Imo secundum hoc Christus non diceretur præcipue filius David. Præterea, secundum Ambrosium super Lucam, Christus secundum carnem veraciter natus est ex semine Nathan. Quod autem allegatur in oppositum ex Proverbiis, solvitur, si dicatur Salomonem notanter dixisse, Fui unigenitus et unicus, et non, Sum: hoc enim refert de se ipso pro tempore pueritiæ suæ, quando et mater ejus docuit eum sicut subjungit. Potuit autem accidere quod usque ad illud tempus fuerit unicus, unigenitus, aliis postmodum natis: quod tamen dici non potest, si cum Hieronymo asseratur Salomon non fuisse nisi undecim annorum quum cœpit regnare: cujus oppositum alii satis probabiliter tenent.
paras.en: But against these opinions stands what is plainly found in the book of Paralipomenon: that four sons were born to David of Bethsabee in Jerusalem, one of whom is there called Nathan[[1 Par 3:5||]]. Nor does it seem enough to say, as some do, that he was Bethsabee's natural son by Urias and David's adopted son, asserting that the three named there besides Solomon were sons of Urias whom David adopted as sons when he took their mother to wife. For if that were so, they would not properly be said to have been born to David himself of Bethsabee. I therefore think it more probable that Nathan was the true and natural son of David by Bethsabee. In support of this is the saying of Damascene, in his fourth book, where he declares that the blessed Virgin descended from David through Nathan. If, then, Nathan was not the natural son of David but of his brother or of someone else, Christ would rather be said to have descended from Jesse through Sammaa than through David, or even from someone else according to the flesh; whereas the Apostle says that He was made [[Rom 1:3|of the seed of David, according to the flesh|ex semine David secundum carnem]]. Indeed, on that view Christ would not be called the son of David in a special way. Moreover, according to Ambrose on Luke, Christ according to the flesh was truly born of the seed of Nathan. As for what is alleged to the contrary from Proverbs, it is answered if we say that Solomon pointedly said "I was" an only-begotten and only son, and not "I am"; for he says this of himself with regard to the time of his boyhood, when his mother also taught him, as he goes on to say[[Prov 4:4||]]. And it may have happened that up to that time he was the only one, the only-begotten, and that others were born afterwards. This, however, cannot be said if, with Jerome, it is asserted that Solomon was only eleven years old when he began to reign; though others hold the opposite with fair probability.

paras.t: Quinto quæritur, cur Lucas genealogiam Christi describat ascendendo, Matthæus descendendo. Respondendum, quod Matthæus principaliter loquitur de carnali et naturali Christi generatione, secundum quod venit ad nos, et carnem assumpsit: ideo a superiori incipit, descendendo usque ad Joseph et S. Mariam. Lucas vero loquitur de Christi generatione, prout per eam ad Deum reducimur, et ejus filii adoptivi efficimur: ideo incipit ascendendo a Joseph usque ad Adam. Sed quare non sistit in Abraham, a quo Matthæus exorsus est?
