Dicendum quod ideo, ut ostendat omnes electos in quacumque mundi ætate exstiterint, per Christum ad Deum reductos atque salvatos. — Sexto quæritur, cur inter Joseph et Abraham multo plures patres ponantur a Luca, quam a Matthæo: Lucas quippe enumerat quinquaginta, Matthæus quadraginta duos. Dicendum, quod Lucas ponit triplices patres, videlicet naturales, legales et adoptivos; Matthæus, naturales dumtaxat: qui etiam ex certa causa quosdam naturales patres omisit, sicut ostensum est.
paras.en: The fifth question is why Luke describes the genealogy of Christ ascending and Matthew descending. The answer is that Matthew speaks chiefly of the carnal and natural generation of Christ, according as He came to us and took flesh; therefore he begins from above and comes down to Joseph and holy Mary. Luke, on the other hand, speaks of the generation of Christ as it is the means by which we are brought back to God and made His adopted sons; therefore he begins from Joseph and goes up to Adam. But why does he not stop at Abraham, where Matthew began? He does so in order to show that all the elect, in whatever age of the world they lived, have been brought back to God and saved through Christ. — The sixth question is why many more fathers between Joseph and Abraham are set down by Luke than by Matthew: Luke counts fifty, Matthew forty-two. The answer is that Luke sets down three kinds of fathers, namely natural, legal and adoptive; Matthew natural fathers only, and even of these he left some out for a definite reason, as has been shown.

paras.t: Septimo quæritur, quomodo secundum Ambrosium atque Hilarium, Lucas genealogiam Christi describere dicitur secundum gradum sacerdotalis originis, Matthæus vero secundum successionem regalis propaginis. Ad hoc aliqui responderunt quod ideo, quia Matthæus ponit Salomonem, qui fuerat rex, Lucas autem Nathan, quem dicunt fuisse sacerdotem, juxta illud: Filii autem David sacerdotes erant. Sed hoc non videtur sufficere. Non enim sic intelligendum est, quod legales hostias in templo more sacerdotum Leviticorum offerebant, et in altari ministrabant (quia non erant de genere Aaron); sed quia religiosi, vel, ut alii dicunt, principales et primi ad honores fuerunt. Unde in Paralipomenon scriptum est: Filii autem David erant primi ad manum regis. Convenientius ergo dicendum, quod tribus Juda et Levi seu regia et sacerdotalis principales fuerunt, idcirco frequenter conjunctæ fuerunt vinculo matrimoniali, etiam ante David. Nam Aaron uxorem habuit Elisabeth, filiam Aminadab de tribu Juda. David quoque, ut tangit Hilarius, conjugium iniit cum tribu sacerdotali: quod secundum eum, a Salathiel atque Zorobabel confirmatum fuit ex genere. Sicque Nathan et alii quidam a Luca positi, ex una parte de tribu sacerdotali fuerunt: quemadmodum et Maria, quod innotescit per hoc, quod Elisabeth uxor Zachariæ ejus cognata, ex filiabus Aaron duxit originem, ut in Luca habetur.
paras.en: The seventh question is how, according to Ambrose and Hilary, Luke is said to describe the genealogy of Christ by the degrees of a priestly descent, and Matthew by the succession of a royal line. To this some have answered that it is because Matthew sets down Solomon, who was a king, and Luke Nathan, who they say was a priest, according to the text: [[2 Kings 8:18|the sons of David were the princes|Filii autem David sacerdotes erant]] [the Vulgate has sacerdotes, literally "priests"; the Douay-Rheims renders the sense, "princes"]. But this does not seem enough. For it is not to be understood that they offered the sacrifices of the Law in the temple after the manner of the Levitical priests and ministered at the altar (for they were not of the race of Aaron), but that they were devout men, or, as others say, chief men and first in honours. Hence it is written in Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 18:17|the sons of David were chief about the king|Filii autem David erant primi ad manum regis]]. It is more fitting, then, to say that because the tribes of Juda and Levi, that is, the royal and the priestly tribes, were the chief ones, they were often joined by the bond of marriage, even before David. For Aaron had as his wife Elisabeth, the daughter of Aminadab[[Ex 6:23||]] of the tribe of Juda[[Num 7:12||]]. David too, as Hilary mentions, contracted marriage with the priestly tribe; and this, according to him, was confirmed in the line by Salathiel and Zorobabel. And so Nathan and certain others set down by Luke were on one side of the priestly tribe; as was Mary also, which is known from this, that Elisabeth the wife of Zachary, her kinswoman, took her origin from the daughters of Aaron, as is found in Luke[[Luke 1:5||]].

paras.t: Octavo inquiritur, cur Matthæus generationes has tripartitur, seu in tres quaterdenas partitur. Quum enim summatim dicere potuisset, Omnes generationes ab Abraham usque ad Christum quadraginta duæ fuerunt; distincte locutus est, dicens: Omnes generationes ab Abraham usque ad David, generationes quatuordecim, etc., sicut in fine præcedentis dicebatur articuli. Respondet Chrysostomus: quoniam status hominum in Judæis ter mutatus est, generationibus quatuordecim ter completis. Ab Abraham enim usque ad David fuerunt sub judicibus; a David usque ad transmigrationem, sub regibus; a transmigratione usque ad Christum, sub pontificibus. Hoc ergo vult demonstrare, quod sicut bis mutatus est hominum status binis quaterdenis completis, ita completa quaterdena a transmigratione usque ad Christum, oportuit hominum statum mutari a Christo: quemadmodum factum est. Post ejus namque adventum, cœpit humanum genus esse non sub multis judicibus, regibus, et pontificibus, sed sub uno judice, rege, atque pontifice Christo, qui trium illorum statuum ac personarum sortitus est dignitatem. Pater quippe judicium omne dedit Filio. Et ipse est sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech; habetque in vestimento et in femore suo scriptum: Rex regum, et Dominus dominantium. His verbis Chrysostomi objici posset, quod Judæi ante David habuerunt regem Saulem; et ante Christi adventum Joannem Hyrcanum, itemque Herodem. Ad quod dici potest, quod Saul non fuit assumptus ad permanendum in regno; Joannes quoque Hyrcanus non diu regnavit, sicque tempus illud non reputabatur; Herodes vero alienigena fuit.
paras.en: The eighth question is why Matthew divides these generations into three parts, that is, into three fourteens. For though he could have said in sum, "All the generations from Abraham to Christ were forty-two", he spoke distinctly, saying: [[1:17|all the generations from Abraham to David, are fourteen generations|ad David, generationes quatuordecim]], etc., as was said at the end of the preceding article. Chrysostom answers: because the state of men among the Jews was changed three times, as three sets of fourteen generations were completed. For from Abraham to David they were under judges; from David to the transmigration, under kings; from the transmigration to Christ, under high priests. He means to show, then, that as the state of men was changed twice, when two fourteens had been completed, so when the fourteen from the transmigration to Christ was completed, the state of men had to be changed by Christ; as indeed it was. For after His coming the human race began to be not under many judges, kings and high priests, but under one judge, king and high priest, Christ, who received the dignity of those three states and persons. For the Father [[John 5:22|hath given all judgment to the Son|judicium omne dedit Filio]]. And He is [[Ps 109:4|a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech|sacerdos in æternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech]]; [[Apoc 19:16|And he hath on his garment and on his thigh written: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS.|habetque in vestimento et in femore suo scriptum: Rex regum, et Dominus dominantium.]] Against these words of Chrysostom it could be objected that the Jews had a king, Saul, before David, and before the coming of Christ had John Hyrcanus, and also Herod. To this it can be said that Saul was not taken up to remain in the kingdom; John Hyrcanus did not reign long, and so that period was not taken into account; and Herod was a foreigner.

paras.t: Nono inquiritur, cur potius Joseph quam Mariæ origo describitur, quum tamen propositum Evangelistæ fuerit demonstrare Christum ex semine David natum, qui non de Joseph, sed de Maria natus agnoscitur. Ad hoc omnium una responsio est, consuetudinem non esse divinæ Scripturæ mulierum genealogiam describere: et quoniam Evangelista docuit Joseph justum fuisse, satis declaravit eum atque Mariam ad eamdem tribum spectare, quum secundum legem quælibet tribus contrahere debuit cum personis propriæ tribus. Sed objici potest, quod consequentia ista non teneat, eo quod tribus Levitica cum qualibet tribu contrahere potuit. Ad hoc pro præsenti aliam responsionem non video, nisi ut dicatur Evangelista id supposuisse quod omnibus suo innotuit tempore, utpote patrem Mariæ fuisse de tribu Juda et David, vel secutum esse communem cursum, secundum quod uterque conjugum ad eamdem tribum spectabat. Sed tunc rursus occurrit, cur non potius origo Joachim patris Mariæ, quam Joseph enarretur. Dici potest quod ideo, quoniam major est unitas mariti et conjugis, quam patris et prolis, juxta quod scriptum est: Erunt duo in carne una, et relinquet homo patrem et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ.
paras.en: The ninth question is why the descent of Joseph rather than of Mary is described, since the Evangelist's purpose was to show that Christ was born of the seed of David, and He is known to have been born not of Joseph but of Mary. To this all give one answer: that it is not the custom of divine Scripture to describe the genealogy of women; and since the Evangelist taught that Joseph was a just man, he made it sufficiently plain that he and Mary belonged to the same tribe, since according to the law each tribe was to marry with persons of its own tribe[[Num 36:6||]][[Num 36:8||]]. But it may be objected that this inference does not hold, because the tribe of Levi could marry with any tribe. To this, for the present, I see no other answer than to say that the Evangelist took for granted what was known to everyone in his time, namely that Mary's father was of the tribe of Juda and of David; or else that he followed the common course, according to which both spouses belonged to the same tribe. But then the question arises again: why is the descent of Joachim, Mary's father, not related rather than that of Joseph? It can be said that this is because the union of husband and wife is greater than that of father and child, according to what is written: [[Gen 2:24|they shall be two in one flesh|Erunt duo in carne una]], and [[Gen 2:24|a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife|relinquet homo patrem et matrem, et adhærebit uxori suæ]].

paras.t: Denique de ortu et genealogia superlaudabilis benedictæque Virginis, Damascenus libro quarto, sic ait: David inter ceteros duos habuit filios, Salomonem et Nathan. Ex catena itaque Nathan Levi genuit Melchi et Panthera; Panthera genuit Barpanthera, qui genuit Joachim patrem Mariæ. Ex catena vero Salomonis Mathan descendens, habuit conjugem de qua genuit Jacob; Mathan autem defuncto, Melchi duxit ejus uxorem, videlicet matrem Jacob, de qua genuit Heli fratrem uterinum ipsius Jacob. Heli vero sine liberis mortuo, frater ejus Jacob duxit ejus uxorem, de qua genuit Joseph. Joachim insuper nupsit Annæ matri Mariæ; soror vero Annæ nomine Hismeria genuit Elisabeth, quæ genuit Joannem Baptistam.
paras.en: Lastly, of the birth and genealogy of the most praiseworthy and blessed Virgin, Damascene in his fourth book speaks thus: "David, among others, had two sons, Solomon and Nathan. Of the line of Nathan, Levi begot Melchi and Panthera; Panthera begot Barpanthera, who begot Joachim, the father of Mary. Of the line of Solomon, Mathan had a wife of whom he begot Jacob; and when Mathan died, Melchi married his wife, that is, Jacob's mother, and of her begot Heli, Jacob's brother on the mother's side. And when Heli died without children, his brother Jacob married his wife, and of her begot Joseph." Joachim, moreover, married Anne, the mother of Mary; and Anne's sister, named Hismeria, bore Elisabeth, who bore John the Baptist[[Luke 1:57||]][[Luke 1:63||]].

1.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus capituli primi, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Christi autem generatio sic erat
1.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this first chapter, from the place where it says: “Now the generation of Christ was in this wise”

paras.t: Descripta consueta ac naturali generatione patrum, nunc nova et supernaturalis generatio Christi describitur. Christi autem generatio sic erat. Tanquam dicat: Prædicti solito modo generati sunt, sicut prædixi, per seminis descensionem; Christi autem generatio singulari modo et ordine facta est, quemadmodum subditur. Quum esset desponsata, id est promissa vel in matrimonium tradita, mater Jesu Maria Joseph, id est viro sic dicto de ejusdem Mariæ cognatione exorto, qui secundum Hieronymum, cogebatur eam accipere ut propinquam; antequam convenirent ad cohabitandum, ut aliqui dicunt, vel ad carnalem conjunctionem, secundum alios, ad quam nec postea convenerunt, inventa est, Maria a Joseph ejus diligenti custode ac sponso, in utero habens, id est filio impregnata, de Spiritu Sancto, id est virtute et operatione Spiritus Sancti, qui ex purissimis Virginis sanctæ sanguinibus corpus Christi formavit, organizavit, et anima rationali decoravit: quæ omnia facta sunt in instanti a tota superbeatissima Trinitate, quamvis adscribantur et approprientur Spiritui Sancto, eo quod ad misericordiam bonitatemque Dei pertineant, tanquam effectus ineffabilis clementiæ Dei. Clementia autem et bonitas appropriantur Spiritui Sancto.
paras.en: Having described the usual and natural generation of the fathers, the Evangelist now describes the new and supernatural generation of Christ. [[1:18|Now the generation of Christ was in this wise|Christi autem generatio sic erat]]. As if to say: those named above were begotten in the usual way, as I have said, by the descent of seed; but the generation of Christ came about in a singular manner and order, as follows. [[1:18|When as his mother Mary was espoused|Quum esset desponsata]], that is, promised or given in marriage, [[1:18|to Joseph|Joseph]], that is, to a man so called, sprung from the kindred of this same Mary, who according to Jerome was obliged to take her as his near kinswoman; [[1:18|before they came together|antequam convenirent]], to dwell together, as some say, or in carnal union, according to others, in which they never came together afterwards either, [[1:18|she was found|inventa est]], that is, Mary was found by Joseph, her careful guardian and spouse, [[1:18|with child|in utero habens]], that is, pregnant with a son, [[1:18|of the Holy Ghost|de Spiritu Sancto]], that is, by the power and working of the Holy Ghost, who from the most pure blood of the holy Virgin formed the body of Christ, organized it, and adorned it with a rational soul. All these things were done in an instant by the whole most blessed Trinity, although they are ascribed and appropriated to the Holy Ghost [appropriation: attributing to one divine Person a work common to all three, because of its likeness to what is proper to that Person], since they belong to the mercy and goodness of God, as the effect of God's ineffable clemency; and clemency and goodness are appropriated to the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: De desponsatione autem et conventione Mariæ et Joseph multa leguntur, quæ pro magna parte apocrypha sunt: idcirco talia prætermitto. — Cur autem Unigenitus Dei de virgine desponsata nasci voluit potius quam de non desponsata, multæ rationes traduntur. Prima, secundum beatum Ignatium martyrem, ut partus Virginis lateret diabolum. Dicit tamen Thomas, et alii multi, quod si Deus permisisset, diabolus aliunde bene perpendisset Mariam esse virginem, non obstante ejus desponsatione. Poterat enim sua naturali industria faciliter percipere quod corpore integra fuit. Secunda ratio, ne Virgo sanctissima a Judæis reputaretur adultera; maluitque Christus Judæos de suo ortu ambigere, quam de Matris pudore perverse sentire. Tertia, ne Judæi occasionem haberent abjiciendi Christum, quasi de fornicaria natum. Quarta, ut Virgo beata haberet casti viri solatium atque obsequium, et Christus nutricium. Alias plurimas causas assignant doctores, quæ satis notæ videntur. — Denique conventionem prædictam Hieronymus accipit de conventione concubitus. Dicit enim quod nec postea convenerunt.
paras.en: Many things are read about the espousal and coming together of Mary and Joseph which are for the most part apocryphal; therefore I pass over such things. — As to why the Only-begotten of God willed to be born of an espoused virgin rather than of one not espoused, many reasons are given. The first, according to blessed Ignatius the martyr, is that the Virgin's childbearing might be hidden from the devil. Thomas, however, and many others say that, had God permitted it, the devil could well have perceived by other means that Mary was a virgin, her espousal notwithstanding; for by his natural cunning he could easily have perceived that she was untouched in body. The second reason is that the most holy Virgin might not be reputed an adulteress by the Jews; and Christ preferred that the Jews should be in doubt about His birth rather than think perversely of His Mother's modesty. The third, that the Jews might have no occasion to reject Christ as one born of a fornicatress. The fourth, that the blessed Virgin might have the comfort and service of a chaste husband, and Christ a foster-father. The doctors assign very many other reasons, which seem well enough known. — Lastly, Jerome takes the coming together mentioned above as the coming together of intercourse; for he says that they did not come together afterwards either.

paras.t: Joseph autem, vir ejus, quum esset justus, et nollet eam traducere, id est Judæis quasi adulteram tradere, seu puniendam exponere, vel publice accusare, voluit occulte dimittere eam. Secundum Hieronymum et Bernardum, S. Joseph certus fuit de castitate Mariæ. Si enim cognovisset eam fuisse adulteram et non traduxisset eam, fuisset injustus, quia secundum legem, non solum actor sceleris, sed et conscius ejus obnoxius est peccato si taceat. Dum ergo Evangelista affirmat Joseph justum fuisse, atque ob id Mariam non traduxisse, innuit quod de castimonia sponsæ suæ non dubitavit. Et si Christus noluit Judæos de suæ Matris pudore sinistrum quid suspicari, probabile est quod non permisit justum Joseph de tanta Virgine adulterium opinari. Sed cur tunc voluit eam occulte dimittere? Ideo, quoniam reputavit se cohabitatione præsentiaque Mariæ indignum. Quam ob rem et Petrus repulit Christum, dicendo: Exi a me, Domine, quia homo peccator sum; et centurio: Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum.
paras.en: [[1:19|Whereupon Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing publicly to expose her|Joseph autem, vir ejus, quum esset justus, et nollet eam traducere]], that is, to hand her over to the Jews as an adulteress, or expose her to punishment, or accuse her publicly, [[1:19|was minded to put her away privately|voluit occulte dimittere eam]]. According to Jerome and Bernard, St Joseph was certain of Mary's chastity. For if he had known her to be an adulteress and had not exposed her, he would have been unjust, since according to the law not only the doer of a crime but also one who knows of it is liable to sin if he keeps silent[[Lev 5:1||]]. When, therefore, the Evangelist affirms that Joseph was just, and for that reason did not expose Mary, he implies that Joseph had no doubt of his spouse's purity. And if Christ did not wish the Jews to suspect anything sinister of His Mother's modesty, it is probable that He did not permit just Joseph to think such a Virgin guilty of adultery. But why then did he wish to put her away privately? Because he reckoned himself unworthy to live with Mary and be in her presence. For this reason too Peter put Christ from him, saying: [[Luke 5:8|Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord|Exi a me, Domine, quia homo peccator sum]]; and the centurion: [[Matt 8:8|Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof|Domine, non sum dignus ut intres sub tectum meum]].

paras.t: Chrysostomus vero testatur, quod Joseph desponsata sibi Virgine, accepit eam in domum suam: ubi quum angelus Gabriel ignorante Joseph Virgini conceptionem Filii Dei nuntiasset, et ipsa jam concepisset, suamque cognatam Elisabeth concepisse audisset, mox surgens accepta a sponso suo licentia, abiit et visitavit Elisabeth, ut ei congratularetur, obsequeretur, et ex Christi præsentia magnus profectus accresceret, tam ipsi Elisabeth quam ejus infanti. Reversa autem Maria post trium mensium spatia, videns Joseph eam jam impregnatam, prima facie suspicatus est malum de ea; excusatione vero ab ea recepta, attenta etiam sanctitate suæ conversationis, ambiguus fuit quid finaliter de ea sentiret. Idcirco voluit eam occulte dimittere, ne vel innocentem traduceret, vel adulteræ consentiret. — Verba divi Chrysostomi quæ in diversis locis de hac materia introducit, intelligenda sunt sapienter, quoniam sibi invicem contrariari videntur. Alicubi enim ait, quod Joseph putavit eam adulteram, alibi vero dicit, quod (inæstimabilis laus Mariæ) magis credebat Joseph castitati ejus quam ventri ejus, et magis gratiæ quam naturæ. Conceptionem manifeste videbat, et fornicationem suspicari non poterat: possibilius credidit mulierem sine viro posse concipere, quam Mariam posse peccare. Quod ergo dicit Joseph, putasse Mariam fuisse adulteram, referendum est ad tempus quo primo vidit eam prole fecundam. Quod vero dicit, eum non potuisse fornicationem suspicari de ea, referendum est ad tempus excusationis receptæ et sanctitatis pensatæ. Dubium enim non est, quin interior gratia, sanctitas, castitasque Mariæ, mirabiliter ac potenter refulsit, non solum in ejus vultu, sed in toto corporis gestu et apparatu, in tantum quod qui ejus conversationem diligenter advertit, fornicationem aut crimen aliquod de ipsa suspicari non potuit.
paras.en: Chrysostom, however, testifies that Joseph, when the Virgin had been espoused to him, took her into his house. There, when the angel Gabriel, without Joseph's knowledge, had announced to the Virgin the conception of the Son of God[[Luke 1:31||]], and she had already conceived and had heard that her kinswoman Elisabeth had conceived[[Luke 1:36||]], she rose at once and, having obtained leave from her spouse, went and visited Elisabeth[[Luke 1:39||]], to rejoice with her, to serve her, and so that from the presence of Christ great profit might grow both to Elisabeth herself and to her infant[[Luke 1:41||]]. When Mary returned after the space of three months[[Luke 1:56||]], Joseph, seeing her now with child, at first sight suspected evil of her; but when he had received her explanation, and considered also the holiness of her life, he was in doubt what finally to think of her. Therefore he wished to put her away privately, so as neither to expose an innocent woman nor to consent to an adulteress. — The words which the divine Chrysostom brings in at various places on this matter must be understood wisely, since they seem to contradict one another [much of what Denis cites as Chrysostom on Matthew comes from the Opus imperfectum in Matthæum, then thought to be his]. For in one place he says that Joseph thought her an adulteress; but elsewhere he says that (O inestimable praise of Mary!) Joseph believed her chastity more than her womb, and grace more than nature: “He saw the conception plainly, and could not suspect fornication: he believed it more possible for a woman to conceive without a man than for Mary to sin.” What he says, then, that Joseph thought Mary an adulteress, is to be referred to the time when he first saw her great with child; but what he says, that Joseph could not suspect her of fornication, is to be referred to the time after he had received her explanation and weighed her holiness. For there is no doubt that the inward grace, holiness and chastity of Mary shone out wonderfully and powerfully, not only in her face but in the whole bearing and carriage of her body, so much so that whoever carefully observed her manner of life could not suspect fornication or any crime of her.

paras.t: Præterea aliqui asserunt, quod Joseph profectus est cum Maria ad visitandum Elisabeth, tanquam obsequiosus ac diligens commissæ sibi Virginis custos. Aliqui etiam dicunt, quod Joseph nondum recepit Mariam in domum suam, sed quod desponsatione peracta, ipse descendit in propriam domum, quasi nuptiis necessaria præparaturus; Maria vero interim fuit in domo parentum suorum. Quumque reversa fuisset ab Elisabeth, cernens eam Joseph gravidam, noluit eam in domum suam recipere. Quid horum sit verius, ignoratur.
paras.en: Some, moreover, assert that Joseph set out with Mary to visit Elisabeth, as the dutiful and careful guardian of the Virgin entrusted to him. Others again say that Joseph had not yet received Mary into his house, but that, once the espousal was made, he went down to his own house, as if to prepare what was needed for the wedding, while Mary meanwhile stayed in her parents' house; and when she had returned from Elisabeth, Joseph, seeing her with child, would not receive her into his house. Which of these is the truer is not known.

paras.t: Hæc autem eo, videlicet Joseph, cogitante, utpote quod Mariam occulte dimitteret, ecce angelus Domini apparuit in somnis ei, id est ipsi Joseph dormienti. Apparuit autem ei apparitione visionis imaginariæ: et hoc, tempore somni, in quo revelationes divinæ atque propheticæ solent fieri, quia tunc anima aptior est ad talium receptionem propter exteriorum sensuum clausuram, et a sensibilium perceptione vacantiam, et præsertim propter imaginationis ampliorem quietem. Propter quod dicitur: Per somnium in visione nocturna, aperit aures virorum, et instruit eos. Apparuit ergo Joseph, dicens: Joseph fili David, non solum carnis propagine, sed fidei atque justitiæ imitatione. Unde ad commendandam justitiam Joseph nominat eum filium David. Noli timere accipere Mariam conjugem tuam, id est audacter eam recipias ad cohabitandum, nec aliquid mali suspiceris de illa; quod enim in ea natum est, id est proles quam habet in utero, de Spiritu Sancto est, hoc est, virtute et operatione Spiritus Sancti concepta est, non humano semine, sed deifico lumine, sine virginitatis injuria.
paras.en: [[1:20|But while he|Hæc autem eo]], namely Joseph, [[1:20|thought on these things|cogitante]], that is, of putting Mary away privately, [[1:20|behold the Angel of the Lord appeared to him in his sleep|ecce angelus Domini apparuit in somnis ei]], that is, to Joseph himself as he slept. He appeared to him in an imaginary vision [that is, one formed in the imagination, as distinct from a bodily or a purely intellectual vision], and this in the time of sleep, in which divine and prophetic revelations are wont to be made; for the soul is then more apt to receive such things, because the outward senses are closed and it is free from perceiving the things of sense, and above all because the imagination is more fully at rest. Hence it is said: [[Job 33:15|By a dream in a vision by night|Per somnium in visione nocturna]] [[Job 33:16|he openeth the ears of men|aperit aures virorum]], and [[Job 33:16|instructeth them|instruit eos]]. He appeared, then, to Joseph, [[1:20|saying: Joseph, son of David|dicens: Joseph fili David]], not only by descent of the flesh but by imitation of faith and justice; hence, to commend Joseph's justice, he names him son of David. [[1:20|Fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife|Noli timere accipere Mariam conjugem tuam]], that is, receive her boldly to dwell with thee, and suspect nothing evil of her; [[1:20|for that which is conceived in her|quod enim in ea natum est]] [the Latin natum means literally “born”; Denis explains the word in the next paragraph], that is, the child she has in her womb, [[1:20|is of the Holy Ghost|de Spiritu Sancto est]], that is, was conceived by the power and working of the Holy Ghost, not of human seed but by divine light, without injury to her virginity.

paras.t: Cur non potius ait Evangelista, Quod in ea conceptum est, quam, Quod in ea natum est? Respondendum, quod nativitas seu generatio, est productio seu acquisitio esse substantialis. Res ergo tunc nascitur quum formam substantialem sortitur. Hanc autem proles recipit primum in utero matris: ideo prima est nativitas in utero, deinde ex utero, quum fetus separatur a matre incipitque apparere, et in se perfecte subsistere. Quamdiu nempe manet in utero, est quasi aliquid matris, quemadmodum pomum est aliquid arboris. Alia ratio est, ad insinuandum quod conceptio Christi non fuit successiva ac naturalis, procedens ab imperfecto ad perfectum, sed instantanea et supernaturalis, ita quod in eodem instanti completa est corporis Christi organizatio ac animatio. Ideo dicit, Quod in ea natum est: quoniam puer quem concepit, a primo conceptionis suæ instanti fuit homo perfectus, imo et vir, non corporis quantitate, sed animæ perfectione. Unde Jeremias dicit: Novum creavit Dominus super terram, mulier circumdabit virum.
paras.en: Why does the Evangelist not rather say “that which is conceived in her” than “that which is born in her”? The answer is that nativity or generation is the production or acquiring of substantial being. A thing, then, is born when it receives its substantial form. Now offspring receives this first in the mother's womb: therefore the first birth is in the womb, and the second from the womb, when the fetus is separated from the mother and begins to appear and to subsist perfectly in itself. For as long as it remains in the womb it is, as it were, something of the mother, just as an apple is something of the tree. Another reason is to suggest that the conception of Christ was not gradual and natural, proceeding from the imperfect to the perfect, but instantaneous and supernatural, so that the organizing and ensouling of Christ's body were complete in the same instant. Therefore he says “that which is born in her”: because the child she conceived was a perfect man from the first instant of His conception, and indeed a grown man [vir, a man in his full strength, as opposed to homo, a human being], not in size of body but in perfection of soul. Hence Jeremias says: [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall compass a man|Novum creavit Dominus super terram, mulier circumdabit virum]].

paras.t: Pariet autem filium: de quo Isaias: Puer, inquit, natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis; et vocabis, in die circumcisionis, quando Judæi nomina pueris imponebant, nomen ejus, nominatum, id est ipsummet puerum, Jesu, id est nomine tali. Vel: Vocabis, id est, vocando dices, nomen ejus nominans esse Jesum, id est, quod nomen pueri sit Jesus. Cur autem ita vocandus sit, subditur: Ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum, id est omnes electos peccato obnoxios, a peccatis eorum originali et actuali. Christus enim merito suæ incarnationis, sanctissimæ conversationis, atque dirissimæ passionis, liberavit genus humanum ab omni peccato sufficienter, quantum in se est: solos autem electos salvavit efficienter. Oportet tamen ut meritum Christi, seu virtus suæ passionis, nobis applicetur per sacramenta Ecclesiæ, seu fidem et caritatem, ad hoc quod liberemur a Christo. Jesus autem interpretatur salvator, aut salutaris. Consuetudo vero Judæorum fuit, rebus imponere nomina ab aliqua proprietate, quemadmodum in Isaia, puer iste qui spoliavit infernum, vocatur Velociter spolia detrahe, cito prædare. Convenienter ergo filius Virginis, salus mundi, dictus est Jesus. In cujus figura Josue et filius Josedec sacerdos magnus dicti sunt Jesus.
paras.en: [[1:21|And she shall bring forth a son|Pariet autem filium]]: of whom Isaias says: [[Is 9:6|A child|Puer]], he says, [[Is 9:6|is born to us, and a son is given to us|natus est nobis, et filius datus est nobis]]. [[1:21|And thou shalt call|et vocabis]], on the day of circumcision, when the Jews gave names to children, [[1:21|his name|nomen ejus]], the one named, that is, the child himself, [[1:21|Jesus|Jesu]], that is, by that name [Denis takes nomen, “name”, for the person named, and reads Jesu as “by the name Jesus”]. Or: [[1:21|thou shalt call|Vocabis]], that is, in calling thou shalt say, [[1:21|his name|nomen ejus]], naming it to be [[1:21|Jesus|Jesum]], that is, that the child's name is Jesus. Why He is to be so called is added: [[1:21|For he shall save his people|Ipse enim salvum faciet populum suum]], that is, all the elect who are liable to sin, [[1:21|from their sins|a peccatis eorum]], original and actual. For Christ, by the merit of His incarnation, His most holy life and His most bitter passion, freed the human race from all sin sufficiently, as far as lies in Him; but He saved the elect alone effectively [sufficiently: the price paid was enough for all; effectively: it actually takes effect in them]. Yet the merit of Christ, or the power of His passion, must be applied to us through the sacraments of the Church, or through faith and charity, in order that we may be set free by Christ. Now Jesus is interpreted Saviour, or saving. It was the custom of the Jews to give things names from some property of theirs, as in Isaias this child, who despoiled hell, is called [[Is 8:3|Hasten to take away the spoils: Make hast to take away the prey|Velociter spolia detrahe, cito prædare]]. Fittingly, then, the Virgin's son, the salvation of the world, was called Jesus; in figure of whom Josue[[Ecclus 46:1||]], and the son of Josedec the high priest[[Agg 1:1||]][[Zach 3:1||]], were called Jesus [Josue is “Jesus the son of Nave” in Ecclesiasticus 46:1, and the high priest is “Jesus the son of Josedec” in Aggeus 1:1].

paras.t: Quæritur quomodo secundum Matthæum angelus vocet nomen filii hujus Jesum, post ejus conceptionem, quum Lucas dicat: Vocatum est nomen ejus Jesus, quod vocatum est ab angelo, priusquam in utero conciperetur. Dicendum, quod Lucas loquitur de vocatione angeli ad Mariam, quum dixit: Ecce concipies in utero, et paries filium, et vocabis nomen ejus Jesum.
paras.en: It is asked how, according to Matthew, the angel calls the name of this son Jesus after His conception, when Luke says: [[Luke 2:21|his name was called Jesus, which was called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb|Vocatum est nomen ejus Jesus, quod vocatum est ab angelo, priusquam in utero conciperetur]]. The answer is that Luke is speaking of the angel's naming addressed to Mary, when he said: [[Luke 1:31|Behold thou shalt conceive in thy womb and shalt bring forth a son: and thou shalt call his name Jesus|Ecce concipies in utero, et paries filium, et vocabis nomen ejus Jesum]].

paras.t: Hoc autem totum factum est, scilicet, quod Virgo de Spiritu Sancto concepit, quod Salvatorem peperit, quod nomen pueri vocatum est Jesus, ut impleretur quod dictum est a Domino per Prophetam Isaiam dicentem: Ecce virgo in utero habebit, et pariet filium, et vocabitur nomen ejus Emmanuel, quod est interpretatum (id est expositum), nobiscum Deus: hoc est, per hoc nomen, Emmanuel, designatur quod puer iste sit Deus nobis per nostræ naturæ assumptionem unitus, et per humanæ vitæ conversationem conjunctus: juxta illud Baruch, Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est. Unde apud Isaiam testatur: Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum. Allegat autem Evangelista potius sensum quam verba Isaiæ. Sic enim ait Propheta: Ecce virgo concipiet.
paras.en: [[1:22|Now all this was done|Hoc autem totum factum est]], namely, that the Virgin conceived of the Holy Ghost, that she bore the Saviour, that the child's name was called Jesus, [[1:22|that it might be fulfilled which the Lord spoke by the prophet|ut impleretur quod dictum est a Domino per Prophetam]] Isaias, [[1:22|saying|dicentem]]: [[1:23|Behold a virgin shall be with child, and bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is|Ecce virgo in utero habebit, et pariet filium, et vocabitur nomen ejus Emmanuel, quod est interpretatum]] (that is, expounded), [[1:23|God with us|nobiscum Deus]]: that is, by this name Emmanuel it is signified that this child is God united to us by taking on our nature, and joined to us by living a human life among us; according to that of Baruch: [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est]]. Hence He testifies in Isaias: [[Is 52:6|Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself that spoke, behold I am here|Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum]]. The Evangelist cites the sense rather than the words of Isaias; for the Prophet says: [[Is 7:14|Behold a virgin shall conceive|Ecce virgo concipiet]].

paras.t: Porro, per hoc quod filius Virginis appellatur Jesus, quia salvat a peccatis, et Emmanuel, quia nobiscum Deus, declaratur duplex natura, puta divina et humana, in una Christi persona: nullus enim nisi Deus a peccatis valet salvare; et nobiscum Deus, est Deus et homo.
paras.en: Moreover, in that the Virgin's son is called Jesus, because He saves from sins, and Emmanuel, because He is [[1:23|God with us|nobiscum Deus]], a twofold nature, divine and human, is declared in the one Person of Christ: for none but God can save from sins; and [[1:23|God with us|nobiscum Deus]] is God and man.

paras.t: Arguunt autem Judæi hoc loco adversum nos, asserentes Evangelistam nostrum mendaciter allegasse scripturam propheticam. Isaias namque secundum Hebraicam veritatem sic ait: Ecce adolescentula concipiet et pariet. Adolescentula autem est nomen commune virgini et corruptæ. Respondendum secundum B. Hieronymum, quod in Hebræo pro eo quod Evangelista dixit, Ecce virgo, ita habetur: Ecce alma. Alma autem duo significat, scilicet adolescentulam, et absconditam; nuncque accipitur pro abscondita, id est pro puella abscondita, seu diligenter custodita, adspectibusque virorum subtracta, in tantum ut de ejus integritate dubitari non possit. Talis autem exstitit S. Maria, quæ usque ad tempus suæ desponsationis mansit Dominoque servivit in templo. Unde Matthæus Spiritu Sancto repletus, mentem Isaiæ certissime sciens, allegavit sensum magis quam verba. De hoc plenius dixi in expositione Isaiæ proprio loco.
paras.en: Here the Jews argue against us, asserting that our Evangelist cited the prophetic scripture falsely. For Isaias, according to the Hebrew verity [Jerome's phrase for the Hebrew original], says: “Behold, a young woman shall conceive and bear.” And “young woman” is a name common to a virgin and to one who is not. The answer, according to blessed Jerome, is that in the Hebrew, in place of what the Evangelist said, [[1:23|Behold a virgin|Ecce virgo]], we have: Ecce alma [“Behold, an almah”]. Now alma signifies two things, namely a young woman, and one hidden away; and here it is taken for one hidden away, that is, for a girl kept hidden, or carefully guarded and withdrawn from the sight of men, so much so that there can be no doubt of her integrity. Such was holy Mary, who until the time of her espousal remained in the temple and served the Lord there. Hence Matthew, filled with the Holy Ghost and knowing most certainly the mind of Isaias, cited the sense rather than the words. Of this I have spoken more fully in the exposition of Isaias, in its proper place.

paras.t: De nativitate autem Christi ex Virgine Psalmista fatetur: Descendet sicut pluvia in vellus, et sicut stillicidia stillantia super terram. Et in Zacharia disseruit Dominus: Ecce ego adducam servum meum Orientem (videlicet Christum), et cælabo sculpturam ejus, id est, corpus ejus in utero Virginis supernaturaliter præparabo. Hoc idem in Isaia pulchre legitur prophetatum quum de Christo illic inducitur: Et ascendet sicut virgultum coram eo, et sicut radix de terra sitienti. Quemadmodum enim virgultum oritur de terra non ab hominibus culta, sed cælesti influentia fecundata, sic Christus de matre non ab homine tacta, sed divinitus imprægnata. Quemadmodum etiam radix de terra sitienti, id est sicca, non compluta, pullulat; sic Christus de matre non virili semine impregnata processit.
paras.en: Of Christ's birth from the Virgin the Psalmist declares: [[Ps 71:6|He shall come down like rain upon the fleece; and as showers falling gently upon the earth|Descendet sicut pluvia in vellus, et sicut stillicidia stillantia super terram]]. And in Zacharias the Lord said: [[Zach 3:8|behold, I will bring my servant the Orient|Ecce ego adducam servum meum Orientem]] (that is, Christ), and [[Zach 3:9|I will grave the graving thereof|cælabo sculpturam ejus]], that is, I will supernaturally prepare His body in the Virgin's womb. The same is beautifully read as prophesied in Isaias, where it is said of Christ: [[Is 53:2|And he shall grow up as a tender plant before him, and as a root out of a thirsty ground|Et ascendet sicut virgultum coram eo, et sicut radix de terra sitienti]]. For as a tender plant [virgultum, a young shoot] springs up from ground not tilled by men but made fruitful by heavenly influence, so Christ came from a mother not touched by man but made fruitful by God. And as [[Is 53:2|a root out of a thirsty ground|radix de terra sitienti]], that is, dry ground not rained upon, puts forth shoots, so Christ came forth from a mother not made fruitful by the seed of man.

paras.t: Circa hæc quæritur, cur dicat Evangelista, Hoc totum factum est, ut impleretur, etc., et non potius, Hoc totum prædictum fuit, quia sic fuit agendum. Non enim ideo factum est, quia prædictum, sed ideo prædictum, quia sic erat futurum. Et respondendum, quod in talibus sermonibus hoc quod dicitur, ut, tenetur non causaliter, sed concomitanter, ut sit sensus: Hoc factum est, ut impleretur quod dictum est per Prophetam, id est, ideo est prædictum, quia sic fuit futurum. Et hoc etiam dicit Albertus in libro de Laudibus Virginis gloriosæ.
paras.en: On these words it is asked why the Evangelist says, [[1:22|all this was done that it might be fulfilled|Hoc totum factum est, ut impleretur]], etc., and not rather, “All this was foretold, because it was so to be done.” For it was not done because it was foretold, but foretold because it was so to come about. The answer is that in such sayings the word “that” [ut, “so that”, “in order that”] is taken not causally but concomitantly [that is, as marking what goes along with the event, not what causes it], so that the sense is: [[1:22|this was done that it might be fulfilled|Hoc factum est, ut impleretur]] what was spoken [[1:22|by the prophet|per Prophetam]], that is, it was foretold because it was so to come about. Albert too says this in his book On the Praises of the Glorious Virgin [the De laudibus beatæ Mariæ, long ascribed to Albert the Great, is now generally attributed to Richard of Saint-Laurent].

paras.t: Exsurgens autem Joseph a somno, fecit sicut præcepit ei angelus Domini, et accepit conjugem suam, quam decrevit dimittere. Accepit autem eam vel ad cohabitandum et obsequendum, secundum eos qui asserunt quod nondum suscepit eam in propriam domum, vel ad permanendum cum ea ex animo, secundum eos qui dicunt quod jam ante in domum suam eam accepit. Unde Chrysostomus: Non in domum accepit eam, nondum enim de domo dimiserat eam; sed de animo suo deposuerat eam, et iterum in animum suum recepit eam. Itaque eam accepit, tanquam de cetero jugiter permansurus cum ea sine suspicione, cum ingenti humilitate, puritate ac reverentia ministrando ei in omnibus, velut dignissimæ genitrici creatoris salvatorisque sui.
paras.en: [[1:24|And Joseph rising up from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took unto him his wife|Exsurgens autem Joseph a somno, fecit sicut præcepit ei angelus Domini, et accepit conjugem suam]], whom he had decided to put away. He took her either to dwell with her and serve her, according to those who assert that he had not yet received her into his own house, or to remain with her in heart, according to those who say that he had already taken her into his house before. Hence Chrysostom: “He did not take her into his house, for he had not yet put her out of his house; but he had put her out of his mind, and he took her back into his mind.” And so he took her, as one who would henceforth abide with her continually without suspicion, serving her in all things with immense humility, purity and reverence, as the most worthy mother of his Creator and Saviour.

paras.t: Et non cognoscebat eam, donec peperit filium suum primogenitum. Hæc Chrysostomus de intellectuali cognitione satis subtiliter veraciterque exponit. Nam ante Virginis partum, ipse Joseph perfecte non scivit quantæ dignitatis et gloriæ esset hæc virgo. Post partum vero ipsius, plenius ejus excellentiam novit, quia ex tunc in animo Joseph facta est speciosior atque præstantior quam totus mundus. Quidam exponunt de cognitione sensitiva, dicentes, quod Christo in utero Virginis consistente, tantus in vultu ejus splendor claritatis ex præsentia Christi refulsit, quod Joseph eam intueri non valuit, sicut nec filii Israel poterant vultum inspicere Moysis propter ejus fulgorem ex consortio angeli. — Litteraliter vero exponitur de cognitione copulæ carnalis, ita quod Joseph non accessit ad eam maritali affectu, donec peperit Christum.
paras.en: [[1:25|And he knew her not, till she brought forth her first born son|Et non cognoscebat eam, donec peperit filium suum primogenitum]]. Chrysostom expounds these words, subtly enough and truly, of the knowledge of the mind. For before the Virgin's childbearing Joseph himself did not perfectly know of how great dignity and glory this virgin was; but after she had given birth he knew her excellence more fully, because from then on she became in Joseph's mind more beautiful and more excellent than the whole world. Some expound it of knowledge by the senses, saying that while Christ was in the Virgin's womb so great a splendour of brightness shone in her face from the presence of Christ that Joseph could not look upon her, just as the children of Israel could not look upon the face of Moses[[2 Cor 3:7||]] because of the brightness it had from his converse with the angel[[Ex 34:30||]]. — Literally, however, it is expounded of the knowledge of carnal union: that Joseph did not come to her with a husband's desire until she had brought forth Christ.

paras.t: Sed numquid postmodum eam cognovit? Non utique. Tunc enim impiissimus et præsumptuosissimus exstitisset, si templum Filii Dei, si sacrarium Spiritus Sancti, si uterum puritatis violare tentasset. Maria quoque ingrata fuisset, si tanto filio non fuisset contenta. Sciendum ergo, quod dictio donec interdum importat tempus determinatum, quo evoluto fit aliquid. Sic Job ait: Quis mihi tribuat, ut in inferno protegas me, donec pertranseat furor tuus? Sicque communiter dicimus: Non faciam hoc, donec veneris. Interdum vero accipitur pro tempore indeterminato: sicque includit omnem differentiam temporis. Excludendo enim illud tempus quo magis videbatur aliquid esse, vel non esse, consequenter excludit alia tempora, quibus minus tale quid videtur. Et ita habetur in Psalmo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum; et iterum, Oculi nostri ad Dominum Deum nostrum, donec misereatur nostri; et rursus, Deus, ne derelinquas me, donec annuntiem brachium tuum, etc. Non est sensus, quod postquam hostes Christi fuerint ei subjecti, tunc ipse cessabit sedere ad dexteram Patris: imo tunc major est ratio ut sedeat. Unde quum Scriptura dicit eum sedere ad dexteram Patris, donec ponantur adversarii scabellum pedum ejus, innuitur quod postea æternaliter sedeat. Hoc itaque modo sumitur donec, in proposito. Possibilius quippe videbatur, quod Joseph cognoverit sponsam et conjugem suam ante conceptionem Filii Dei, quam postea. Ideo, quum Evangelista edocuit, quod non cognovit eam ante Christi generationem, pro certo reliquit, quod nec postmodum eam accesserit. Juxta hunc sensum dicit de Christo Apostolus: Oportet autem illum regnare, donec ponantur inimici scabellum pedum ejus. Numquid postea non regnabit? Hinc ait Chrysostomus: Hoc quod fieri potuit, dixit Evangelista factum non esse; id autem quod fieri non potuit, quid necessarium habuit dicere quia factum non est?
paras.en: But did he know her afterwards? By no means. For then he would have been most impious and most presumptuous, had he tried to violate the temple of the Son of God, the sanctuary of the Holy Ghost, the womb of purity. Mary too would have been ungrateful had she not been content with such a son. It must be understood, then, that the word “till” [donec] sometimes implies a fixed time, after which something happens. So Job says: [[Job 14:13|Who will grant me|Quis mihi tribuat]], [[Job 14:13|that thou mayst protect me in hell|ut in inferno protegas me]], [[Job 14:13|till thy wrath pass|donec pertranseat furor tuus]]? And so we commonly say: “I will not do this till you come.” But sometimes it is taken for an indefinite time, and so it includes every difference of time. For by excluding the time in which something seemed more likely to be, or not to be, it consequently excludes the other times in which such a thing seems less likely. And so we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 109:1|Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool|Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum]]; and again, [[Ps 122:2|our eyes unto the Lord our God, until he have mercy on us|Oculi nostri ad Dominum Deum nostrum, donec misereatur nostri]]; and again, [[Ps 70:18|O God, forsake me not, Until I shew forth thy arm|Deus, ne derelinquas me, donec annuntiem brachium tuum]], etc. The sense is not that after Christ's enemies have been made subject to Him, He will then cease to sit at the right hand of the Father; rather, there is then greater reason that He should sit there. Hence when Scripture says that He sits at the right hand of the Father until His adversaries are made the footstool of His feet, it is implied that afterwards He sits there eternally. In this way, then, “till” is taken in the present passage. For it seemed more possible that Joseph should have known his spouse and wife before the conception of the Son of God than afterwards. Therefore, when the Evangelist taught that he did not know her before Christ's birth, he left it certain that he did not come to her afterwards either. In this sense the Apostle says of Christ: [[1 Cor 15:25|For he must reign, until|Oportet autem illum regnare, donec]] His enemies are made the footstool of His feet[[Heb 10:13||]] [Denis's wording here blends 1 Cor 15:25 with Heb 10:13, and the margin gives both; in 1 Corinthians the Apostle has “until he hath put all his enemies under his feet”]. Will He not reign afterwards? Hence Chrysostom says: “What could have happened, the Evangelist said did not happen; but what could not have happened, what need had he to say that it did not happen?”

paras.t: Ex his patet error Helvidii hæretici, qui erat sacerdos et idiota, dicens, quod Joseph non cognovit Mariam ante partum Christi, sed postea, eo quod scriptum sit: Non cognovit eam donec peperit. Item, quoniam Christus nunc dicitur primogenitus Mariæ, ergo et postea alium genuit: præsertim quum in Evangeliis legatur Christus fratres habuisse, sicut patebit. Dicendum, quod in Scriptura primogenitus nominatur, non solum respectu sequentis, sed etiam quia priorem non habuit. Sic enim in Exodo legitur, Dominum percussisse omne primogenitum in terra Ægypti, nec erat domus in Ægypto, in qua non jaceret defunctus. Numquid in qualibet domo erant plures filii? Sic etiam in lege Moysis fuit præceptum, omne primogenitum Deo offerri; et si parentes non habuerunt nisi unigenitum, tamen vi hujus præcepti tenebantur illum offerre. Postremo, fratres Christi dicuntur, quia cognati, quomodo Abraham dixit ad Lot, Fratres sumus; et Joab ad Amasam, Salve, mi frater. Et in libro Judicum habetur: Dixit Judas Simeoni fratri suo. Contra istum Helvidium prorsus turpissimum et insanum, composuit S. Hieronymus librum.
paras.en: From this the error of the heretic Helvidius is plain, who was a priest and an unlettered man [idiota], and who said that Joseph did not know Mary before the birth of Christ but did afterwards, because it is written: [[1:25|He knew her not, till she brought forth|cognovit eam donec peperit]]. Again, since Christ is here called Mary's firstborn, he argued that she afterwards bore another as well; especially since we read in the Gospels that Christ had brethren[[Matt 12:46||]][[Matt 13:55||]], as will appear. The answer is that in Scripture one is called firstborn not only with respect to one who follows, but also because he had none before him. For so we read in Exodus that the Lord slew [[Ex 12:29|every firstborn in the land of Egypt|omne primogenitum in terra Ægypti]], and [[Ex 12:30|there was not a house|nec erat domus]] in Egypt [[Ex 12:30|wherein there lay not one dead|in qua non jaceret defunctus]]. Were there several sons in every house? So too in the law of Moses it was commanded that every firstborn be offered to God[[Ex 13:2||]] [the margin's reference here is partly unreadable (Exod. xiii?); Ex 13:2 gives the precept]; and if the parents had only one son, they were still bound by force of this precept to offer him. Lastly, they are called Christ's brethren because they were His kinsmen, as Abraham said to Lot, [[Gen 13:8|we are brethren|Fratres sumus]]; and Joab to Amasa, [[2 Kings 20:9|God save thee, my brother|Salve, mi frater]]; and in the book of Judges we have: [[Judg 1:3|Juda said to Simeon, his brother|Dixit Judas Simeoni fratri suo]]. Against this Helvidius, altogether most base and senseless, St Jerome composed a book [On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary, against Helvidius].

paras.t: Quod vero subjungitur, Et vocavit nomen ejus Jesum, hoc tam de Maria quam de Joseph intelligi potest. Utrique enim seorsum præceperat angelus, ut puerum Jesum vocarent: quod utique nomen secundum suam plenariam proprietatem, id est salvativam virtutem, a Deo impositum, et appropriatum est Filio Virginis, qui solus perfecte salvat, et universaliter liberat. Propter quod Isaias dicit: Dominus ab utero vocavit me, de ventre matris meæ recordatus est nominis mei.
paras.en: As for what is added, [[1:25|and he called his name Jesus|Et vocavit nomen ejus Jesum]], this can be understood of Mary as well as of Joseph [the Latin vocavit can mean either “he called” or “she called”]. For the angel had commanded each of them separately to call the child Jesus. And this name, in its full property, that is, its saving power, was imposed by God and appropriated to the Virgin's Son, who alone saves perfectly and delivers universally. For this reason Isaias says: [[Is 49:1|The Lord hath called me from the womb, from the bowels of my mother he hath been mindful of my name|Dominus ab utero vocavit me, de ventre matris meæ recordatus est nominis mei]].

2.title: Elucidatio capituli secundi: Quum ergo natus esset Jesus, etc.
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: “When Jesus therefore was born,” etc.

paras.t: Descripta Christi generatione præcedenti capitulo, nunc ejus apparitio seu manifestatio describitur. Quum ergo natus esset Jesus in Bethlehem Juda. Secundum quod Lucas plenius enarrat: Quum (egresso edicto Augusti ut describeretur orbis) Joseph cum Maria ascendisset a Galilæa in Bethlehem Judæ, impleti sunt dies ut pareret Virgo, peperitque Deum infantem in stabulo, reclinans eum in præsepio, quia non vacavit ei locus in diversorio. Dicitur autem in Bethlehem Juda, ad differentiam alterius Bethlehem in Galilæa, pertinentis ad tribum Zabulon, ut habetur in libro Josue.
paras.en: Having described the generation of Christ in the preceding chapter, the Evangelist now describes His appearing, or manifestation. [[2:1|When Jesus therefore was born in Bethlehem of Juda|Quum ergo natus esset Jesus in Bethlehem Juda]]. As Luke tells it more fully: when (an edict having gone out from Augustus that the world should be enrolled) Joseph had gone up with Mary from Galilee to Bethlehem of Juda, the days were accomplished that the Virgin should bring forth, and she brought forth the infant God in a stable, laying Him in a manger, because there was no room for Him in the inn[[Luke 2:1||]][[Luke 2:4||]][[Luke 2:7||]]. It says “Bethlehem of Juda” to distinguish it from the other Bethlehem, in Galilee, belonging to the tribe of Zabulon, as is found in the book of Josue[[Jos 19:15||]].

paras.t: In diebus Herodis regis Ascalonitæ, natione Idumæi, cujus filius dictus Herodes Antipas, occidit Joannem, et Christum in passione illusit. Fuit et alter Herodes Agrippa, qui Jacobum decollavit, et Petrum incarceravit: qui ab angelo percussus, consumptus est a vermibus, sicut in Actibus Apostolorum recolitur. Nominatur autem hoc loco Herodes, secundum Chrysostomum, ad ostendendum quod prophetia Danielis de nativitate Christi post septuaginta hebdomadas annorum a tempore Danielis, sit in Christo impleta: quia ab illo tempore usque ad regnum Herodis tot hebdomadæ transierunt. Una autem hebdomada continet septem annos, omnesque simul continent circa quadringentos* annos. Alia ratio est, ut prophetia patriarchæ Jacob declaretur impleta in Christo. Prædixit enim: Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, et dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est; et ipse erit exspectatio gentium. Quoniam ergo tempore Herodis alienigenæ ablatum fuit sceptrum, hoc est dominium, de Juda, et dux de ejus prosapia, certum est Christum tunc advenisse, qui est exspectatio gentium, prout in Aggæo habetur: Veniet Desideratus cunctis gentibus. Nam usque ad tempus Herodis, aliqui de tribu Juda præfuerunt Judæis. Quamvis enim tempore captivitatis Babylonicæ regia dignitas sit ablata a Juda, tamen post captivitatem illam rursus præfuerunt aliqui de tribu Juda, videlicet Zorobabel, cum quo redierunt de Babylone, et Machabæi, qui erant de Juda et Levi, et aliqui alii.
paras.en: [[2:1|in the days of king Herod|In diebus Herodis regis]], the Ascalonite, an Idumean by nation, whose son, called Herod Antipas, killed John[[Matt 14:10||]] and mocked Christ in His passion[[Luke 23:11||]]. There was also another, Herod Agrippa, who beheaded James[[Acts 12:2||]] and imprisoned Peter[[Acts 12:4||]]; struck by an angel, he was eaten up by worms, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles[[Acts 12:23||]]. Herod is named in this place, according to Chrysostom, to show that the prophecy of Daniel concerning the birth of Christ after seventy weeks of years from the time of Daniel[[Dan 9:24||]] was fulfilled in Christ; for from that time to the reign of Herod that many weeks had passed. One week contains seven years, and all of them together contain about four hundred years [so the printed text, which marks the figure with an asterisk; seventy weeks of years make 490]. Another reason is that the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob might be shown to be fulfilled in Christ. For he foretold: [[Gen 49:10|The sceptre shall not be taken away from Juda, nor a ruler from his thigh, till he come that is to be sent, and he shall be the expectation of nations|Non auferetur sceptrum de Juda, et dux de femore ejus, donec veniat qui mittendus est; et ipse erit exspectatio gentium]]. Since, then, in the time of Herod the foreigner the sceptre, that is, the dominion, was taken away from Juda, and the ruler from his stock, it is certain that Christ had then come, who is the expectation of nations, as is found in Aggeus: [[Agg 2:8|The desired of all nations shall come|Veniet Desideratus cunctis gentibus]]. For up to the time of Herod some of the tribe of Juda ruled over the Jews. Although in the time of the Babylonian captivity the royal dignity was taken away from Juda, yet after that captivity some of the tribe of Juda ruled again: namely Zorobabel, with whom they returned from Babylon[[1 Esd 2:1||]], and the Machabees, who were of Juda and Levi, and some others.

paras.t: Ecce Magi, id est sapientes viri, ab oriente, id est a Perside, quæ est in plaga orientali respectu Judææ, venerunt cum grandi comitatu, utpote reges (illis namque temporibus sapientes regnare solebant, quales etiam erant amici Job, qui in libro Tobiæ, et a S. Ambrosio, reges vocantur), Jerosolymam, dicentes. Viri isti magi vocantur non ab arte magica, seu quia malefici, ut magi Pharaonis, nec quia illusores, sed quoniam sapientes. Nam qui apud Hebræos dicuntur scribæ, hi a Græcis appellantur philosophi, a Latinis doctores, a Persis magi. Quidam vero affirmant, quod secundum Chrysostomum dicti sunt magi, quia fuerunt malefici, quamvis conversi sint postea. Verumtamen Chrysostomus hoc loco dicit, quod fuerunt viri orientales a Perside, et quod apud Persas magi, non malefici, sed sapientes vocantur. Unde nescio si hoc dicat Chrysostomus. Magi isti secundum Hieronymum, fuerunt successores Balaam prophetæ, et de eo nati feruntur.
paras.en: [[2:1|behold|Ecce]] [[2:1|wise men|Magi]] [Latin magi, which the Douay-Rheims renders “wise men”], that is, men of wisdom, [[2:1|from the East|ab oriente]], that is, from Persia, which lies in the eastern quarter with respect to Judea, [[2:1|there came|venerunt]] with a great retinue, being kings (for in those times wise men were wont to reign, such as were also the friends of Job, who are called kings in the book of Tobias[[Tob 2:15||]] and by St Ambrose), [[2:1|to Jerusalem|Jerosolymam]], [[2:2|Saying|dicentes]]. These men are called magi not from the magic art, or because they were sorcerers, like the magicians of Pharao[[Ex 7:11||]][[Ex 7:22||]], nor because they were deceivers[[Wis 17:7||]], but because they were wise. For those who among the Hebrews are called scribes are called philosophers by the Greeks, doctors by the Latins, and magi by the Persians. Some, however, affirm that according to Chrysostom they were called magi because they were sorcerers, although they were afterwards converted. Yet Chrysostom says in this place that they were men of the East, from Persia, and that among the Persians those called magi are not sorcerers but wise men. So I do not know whether Chrysostom says this. These Magi, according to Jerome, were successors of the prophet Balaam, and are said to be descended from him.

paras.t: Ubi est qui natus est rex Judæorum? Quam certa atque secura interrogatio! Jam Romani legem dederunt, ut sub periculo mortis, nemo aliquem regem vocaret sine eorum consensu. Fuit quoque præceptum et Magis non ignotum, quod qui rege vivente, alium regem pronuntiat, aut adorat, punitur in sanguine. Quomodo ergo Magi audebant vivente et regnante Herode, in ejus præsentia sine Romanorum licentia, regem alium profiteri? Procul dubio, istam eis audaciam puer natus influxit. Dicit enim Chrysostomus, quod non curabant de sanguine. Quod si curassent de morte, ita locuti non essent. Nondum viderant Christum, et jam parati erant mori pro Christo. Denique verbo, opere, atque muneribus Magi professi sunt Christum esse verum hominem, verum regem, verumque Deum: verbo quidem, quia dum dicunt, Ubi est qui natus est? humanitatem ejus fatentur; quumque adjiciunt, Rex Judæorum, regiam ejus potestatem declarant; dum vero annectunt, Et venimus adorare eum, divinitatem ejus testantur. Quomodo autem idem egerunt opere, et muneribus, infra dicetur.
paras.en: [[2:2|Where is he that is born king of the Jews?|Ubi est qui natus est rex Judæorum?]] How sure and fearless a question! The Romans had already made a law that, under peril of death, no one should call anyone king without their consent. It was also a precept, not unknown to the Magi, that whoever proclaims or adores another king while the king is living is punished with his blood. How then did the Magi dare, while Herod was living and reigning, in his presence and without leave of the Romans, to profess another king? Without doubt the new-born Child inspired this boldness in them. For Chrysostom says that they cared nothing for their blood: had they cared about death, they would not have spoken so. They had not yet seen Christ, and already they were ready to die for Christ. Further, by word, by deed and by gifts the Magi professed Christ to be true man, true king and true God: by word, since in saying [[2:2|Where is he that is born?|Ubi est qui natus est?]] they confess His humanity; when they add [[2:2|king of the Jews|Rex Judæorum]], they declare His royal power; and when they go on, [[2:2|and are come to adore him|Et venimus adorare eum]], they bear witness to His divinity. How they did the same by deed and by gifts will be told below.

paras.t: Insuper causam cur tam secure interrogent de ortu regis Judæorum aperiunt. Vidimus enim stellam ejus, id est stellam suæ nativitatis declarativam, in oriente, quia in terra eorum apparuit eis, ita quod stetit prope in conspectu ipsorum. Non enim sic intelligendum est, quod ipsi existentes in oriente, viderunt stellam hanc in Judæa. Et venimus adorare eum adoratione latriæ, qua soli Deo debetur: quod Isaias testatus est: Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum; gloriam meam alteri non dabo. Secundum doctores, Magi notitiam stellæ apparituræ, ex vaticinio Balaam patris sui sumpserunt. Sic enim in Numeris legitur prophetasse: Orietur stella ex Jacob, id est causa Christi nati de semine Jacob, videlicet ad manifestandum ipsius nativitatem; et consurget virga de Israel. Crediderunt ergo hanc stellam apparituram, ejusque ortum seu apparitionem præstolabantur, et observabant. Quumque in hora nativitatis Christi vidissent coram se quamdam novam ac radiosissimam stellam, mox Deo inspirante intellexerunt hanc esse stellam diutissime exspectatam: propter quod statim surgentes, paratis parandis, secuti sunt stellæ ducatum.
paras.en: Moreover, they disclose the reason why they ask so confidently about the birth of the king of the Jews: [[2:2|For we have seen his star|Vidimus enim stellam ejus]], that is, the star that declared His birth, [[2:2|in the East|in oriente]], because it appeared to them in their own land, so that it stood close by, in their sight. For it is not to be understood that they, being in the East, saw this star in Judea. [[2:2|and are come to adore him|Et venimus adorare eum]] with the adoration of latria, which is due to God alone, as Isaias witnessed: [[Is 42:8|I the Lord, this is my name: I will not give my glory to another|Ego Dominus, hoc est nomen meum; gloriam meam alteri non dabo]][[Is 48:11||]]. According to the doctors, the Magi took their knowledge of the star that was to appear from the prophecy of Balaam their father. For thus he is read in Numbers to have prophesied: [[Num 24:17|A star shall rise out of Jacob|Orietur stella ex Jacob]], that is, because of Christ, born of the seed of Jacob, namely to make His birth known; [[Num 24:17|and a sceptre shall spring up from Israel|et consurget virga de Israel]] [Latin virga, “rod”, where the Douay-Rheims has “sceptre”]. They believed, then, that this star would appear, and they awaited and watched for its rising or appearing. And when, at the hour of Christ's birth, they saw before them a certain new and most radiant star, at once, by God's inspiration, they understood that this was the star so long awaited; wherefore, rising up straightway and making ready what was needful, they followed the star's leading.

paras.t: Refert Chrysostomus (quod tamen ipse non asserit, sicut nec reprobat) fuisse gentem quamdam in principio orientis juxta Oceanum, quæ ex doctrina Seth didicit futuram hanc stellam. Propter quod elegerunt ex se duodecim viros sapientes, atque cœlestium mysteriorum amatores, qui nominabantur Magusæi, quoniam in silentio Deum glorificabant: qui et observabant ortum stellæ istius. Quum vero aliquis istorum duodecim moriebatur, alius substituebatur. Quum igitur quodam tempore essent in monte altissimo, quem vocabant montem victorialem, apparuit eis stella descendens super hunc montem, habens in se formam pueri parvuli, crucem bajulantis in humeris, et locuta est eis ut tenderent in Judæam. Quibus per biennium itinerantibus, nec cibus nec potus defecit in peris eorum stellam istam sequentium.
paras.en: Chrysostom relates (though he neither asserts it nor rejects it) [the story comes from the Opus imperfectum in Matthæum, then ascribed to Chrysostom] that there was a certain people at the beginning of the East, by the Ocean, who had learned from the teaching of Seth that this star would come. Therefore they chose from among themselves twelve wise men, lovers of heavenly mysteries, who were called Magusæi because they glorified God in silence; and these watched for the rising of this star. Whenever one of these twelve died, another was put in his place. Once, then, when they were on a very high mountain which they called the Mount of Victory, there appeared to them a star coming down upon this mountain, having in it the form of a little child carrying a cross on his shoulders; and it spoke to them, bidding them make for Judea. As they journeyed for two years following this star, neither food nor drink failed in their wallets.

paras.t: Præterea, Magis Judæam ingressis, stella ad tempus disparuit. Dicuntque aliqui, quod idcirco disparuit, quoniam Magi recurrentes ad humanum præsidium, scilicet ad Jerosolymitas, perdere meruerunt divinum ducatum. Et ita ingressi fuissent, vel ingredi Jerosolymam proposuissent, antequam stella disparuit, nec ejus ducatum secuti fuissent assidue. Quod non est verisimile, quoniam avidissima ac devotissima mente sectabantur hanc stellam. Unde et ea denuo visa, gavisi sunt gaudio magno valde. Probabilius itaque dicitur, quod stella ex divina dispensatione disparuit: qua non apparente, Magi opinati sunt regium puerum in urbe regali Jerusalem esse quærendum. Voluit ergo Deus ut Jerosolymam introirent, ad majorem sui confirmationem, et Judæorum confusionem ac condemnationem, videlicet, ut testimonio prophetali certificarentur de puero nato, et ut Judæi inexcusabiles fierent, eorumque cæcitas atque desidia confunderetur, dum gentibus Christum confitentibus, ac desideranter quærentibus, ipsi nec crediderunt, nec quæsierunt, imo regem suum, quem ex libris Prophetarum aliis monstraverunt, ipsi videre neglexerunt.
paras.en: Furthermore, when the Magi had entered Judea, the star disappeared for a time. Some say that it disappeared because the Magi, by having recourse to human help, namely to the people of Jerusalem, deserved to lose the divine leading. In that case they would have entered Jerusalem, or meant to enter it, before the star disappeared, and would not have followed its leading steadily. This is not likely, since they followed this star with a most eager and devout mind; and so, when it was seen again, [[2:10|they rejoiced with exceeding great joy|gavisi sunt gaudio magno valde]]. It is more probably said, therefore, that the star disappeared by divine dispensation; and while it did not appear, the Magi supposed that the royal Child was to be sought in the royal city of Jerusalem. God willed, then, that they should enter Jerusalem, for their own greater confirmation and for the confusion and condemnation of the Jews: namely, that they might be made certain of the Child's birth by the testimony of the prophets, and that the Jews might be left without excuse and their blindness and sloth put to shame; since, while the Gentiles confessed Christ and sought Him with longing, they themselves neither believed nor sought; nay, their own king, whom they pointed out to others from the books of the Prophets, they themselves neglected to see.

paras.t: Audiens autem Herodes rex verba Magorum, turbatus est, non solum turbatione admirationis, propter rei novitatem, sed etiam turbatione inordinatæ affectionis: quia quum esset ambitiosus et alienigena, formidavit regno privari, et velut alienigena a populo Judæorum, cui proprius rex natus esset, repelli. In quo impletum est illud Job: Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii, et quum pax sit, ille semper insidias suspicatur. Et omnis Jerosolyma cum illo, id est, omnes et maxime principales habitatores Jerusalem, cum Herode turbati, commoti, et admirati sunt; non quia Herodem et ejus principatum amabant, sed quoniam ejus crudelitatem scientes, timebant maxima bella concitari ab eo adversus regem natum et ejus fautores. Et ita Judæi propriæ vitæ ac rebus timebant. Multi quoque turbabantur, quoniam Herodi applaudere atque favere volebant, conformantes se domino suo, quia, ut dicitur in Ecclesiastico: Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus; et qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea. Ex quo innotescit, quam periculosus nocivusque sit indignus impiusque prælatus. In hac turbatione impletum est quod Psalmista prædixit: Quoniam ecce reges congregati sunt, convenerunt in unum; ipsi videntes sic admirati sunt, conturbati sunt, commoti sunt, etc.
paras.en: [[2:3|And king Herod hearing|Audiens autem Herodes rex]] the words of the Magi [[2:3|was troubled|turbatus est]]: not only with the trouble of wonder, at the newness of the thing, but also with the trouble of disordered affection; for, being ambitious and a foreigner, he dreaded to be deprived of the kingdom and to be driven out, as a foreigner, by the Jewish people, to whom their own king had been born. In this was fulfilled that word of Job: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always|Sonitus terroris semper]] in the ears of the wicked man, [[Job 15:21|and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|et quum pax sit, ille semper insidias suspicatur]]. [[2:3|and all Jerusalem with him|Et omnis Jerosolyma cum illo]], that is, all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and especially the chief men, were troubled, moved and astonished with Herod; not because they loved Herod and his rule, but because, knowing his cruelty, they feared that very great wars would be stirred up by him against the new-born king and his supporters. And so the Jews feared for their own lives and goods. Many, too, were troubled because they wished to applaud and side with Herod, conforming themselves to their master; for, as is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:2|As the judge of the people is himself, so also are his ministers: and what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein|Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus; et qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea]]. From this it is plain how dangerous and harmful an unworthy and wicked prelate is. In this troubling was fulfilled what the Psalmist foretold: [[Ps 47:5|For behold the kings|Quoniam ecce reges]] [[Ps 47:5|assembled themselves: they gathered together|congregati sunt, convenerunt in unum]]. [[Ps 47:6|So they saw, and they wondered, they were troubled, they were moved|ipsi videntes sic admirati sunt, conturbati sunt, commoti sunt]], etc.

paras.t: Et congregans Herodes omnes principes sacerdotum, quorum unus succedere alteri solebat in pontificatu, quamvis pro eodem tempore non esset nisi unus princeps sacerdotum, et Scribas populi, id est doctores et legisperitos Judæorum, sciscitabatur, id est inquirebat, ab eis ubi Christus nasceretur. Ex hoc constat, quod Herodes per regem Judæorum, non quemlibet regem, sed regem Messiam, summum et verum regem Judæis promissum, intellexit. Erat quippe proselytus, id est ad Judaismum conversus. Sed imperfecte instructus fuit in lege, putans Christum in primo suo adventu temporaliter regnaturum. Quod et multi excæcati putant Judæi, quum tamen Prophetæ primum ejus adventum in paupertate et humilitate futurum descripserint: juxta quod ait Isaias, Inglorius erit inter viros adspectus ejus; et Zacharias, Ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam.
paras.en: [[2:4|And assembling together all the chief priests|Et congregans Herodes omnes principes sacerdotum]], of whom one used to succeed another in the high priesthood, although at any one time there was only one chief priest, [[2:4|and the scribes of the people|et Scribas populi]], that is, the doctors and lawyers of the Jews, [[2:4|he inquired|sciscitabatur]], that is, asked, [[2:4|of them where Christ should be born|ab eis ubi Christus nasceretur]]. From this it is clear that by “king of the Jews” Herod understood not just any king, but the King Messias, the supreme and true King promised to the Jews. For he was a proselyte, that is, a convert to Judaism. But he was imperfectly instructed in the law, thinking that Christ at His first coming would reign in temporal fashion. Many blinded Jews think so too, though the Prophets described His first coming as to be in poverty and humility; as Isaias says: [[Is 52:14|so shall his visage be inglorious among men|Inglorius erit inter viros adspectus ejus]]; and Zacharias: [[Zach 9:9|he is poor, and riding upon an ass|Ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam]].

paras.t: At illi dixerunt ei: In Bethlehem Judæ. Sic enim scriptum est per Prophetam Michæam: Et tu, Bethlehem terra Juda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Juda; ex te enim exiet dux qui regat populum meum Israel. Nostra translatio aliter sonat: quæ talis est: Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata, parvulus es in millibus Juda; ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel. Christus enim et Apostoli ac Evangelistæ allegando Scripturas veteris Testamenti, frequenter potius sensum quam verba commemorant. Interdum quoque allegant secundum aliam translationem. Allegatio autem Evangelistæ, quantum ad sensum, redit in idem cum nostra translatione.
paras.en: [[2:5|But they said to him: In Bethlehem of Juda. For so it is written by the prophet|At illi dixerunt ei: In Bethlehem Judæ. Sic enim scriptum est per Prophetam]] Micheas: [[2:6|And thou Bethlehem the land of Juda art not the least among the princes of Juda: for out of thee shall come forth the captain that shall rule my people Israel|Et tu, Bethlehem terra Juda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Juda; ex te enim exiet dux qui regat populum meum Israel]]. Our translation [the Vulgate, Jerome's version from the Hebrew] reads otherwise, as follows: [[Mich 5:2|And thou Bethlehem Ephrata, art a little one among the thousands of Juda, out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be the ruler in Israel|Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata, parvulus es in millibus Juda; ex te mihi egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel]]. For Christ and the Apostles and Evangelists, in citing the Scriptures of the Old Testament, frequently recall the sense rather than the words; and sometimes, too, they cite according to another translation. But the Evangelist's citation comes to the same, as to the sense, as our translation.

paras.t: Est itaque sensus: Et tu, Bethlehem terra Juda, id est pertinens ad Judæam, vel ad sortem tribus Juda, nequaquam minima es in principibus Juda, hoc est inter principales urbes, seu præcipuos cives Juda. Quamvis enim fuerit parva quantitate ædificiorum, vel paucitate habitatorum, tamen præclara fuit dignitate civium, scilicet David et aliorum dignissimorum, qui erant nati ex Bethlehem, et maxime ex nativitate Christi in ea, sicut subjungitur. Ex te enim exiet, id est, procedet et orietur, dux, id est Christus, de quo in Daniele legitur: Ab exitu sermonis usque ad Christum ducem, etc. Christus namque ex loco et civibus Bethlehem natus est. Qui regat spirituali regimine populum meum Israel, id est electos ac fideles Israelitas, in quorum cordibus Christus per fidem gratiamque regnavit, juxta quod Archangelus loquitur: Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum.
