Christus etiam per se ipsum, deinde per Apostolos aliosque discipulos, rexit plurimos Judæorum, docendo eos, quando conversabatur et videbatur in terris.
paras.en: The sense, then, is this: [[2:6|And thou Bethlehem the land of Juda|Et tu, Bethlehem terra Juda]], that is, belonging to Judea, or to the lot of the tribe of Juda, [[2:6|art not the least among the princes of Juda|nequaquam minima es in principibus Juda]], that is, among the chief cities, or the foremost citizens, of Juda. For although it was small in the number of its buildings and the fewness of its inhabitants, yet it was renowned for the dignity of its citizens, namely David and other most worthy men who were born of Bethlehem, and above all for the birth of Christ in it, as follows: [[2:6|for out of thee shall come forth|Ex te enim exiet]], that is, shall proceed and arise, [[2:6|the captain|dux]], that is, Christ, of whom we read in Daniel: [[Dan 9:25|from the going forth of the word|Ab exitu sermonis]] [[Dan 9:25|unto Christ, the prince|usque ad Christum ducem]] [Latin ducem, the same word as dux, “captain”, in the verse above], etc. For Christ was born of the place and the citizens of Bethlehem. [[2:6|that shall rule|Qui regat]] with spiritual rule [[2:6|my people Israel|populum meum Israel]], that is, the elect and faithful Israelites, in whose hearts Christ reigned by faith and grace, as the Archangel says: [[Luke 1:32|he shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever|Regnabit in domo Jacob in æternum]]. Christ also, by Himself and then through the Apostles and other disciples, ruled very many of the Jews, teaching them while He lived and was seen on earth[[Bar 3:38||]].

paras.t: Porro sensus nostræ translationis concurrit in idem, videlicet: Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata, id est, quæ alio nomine appellata es Ephrata (ut patet in Genesi), parvulus es locus in millibus Juda, id est inter cetera loca et oppida Juda, quæ propter suam multitudinem millia nuncupantur: parvulus, inquam, spatio, non dignitate. Ex te mihi, id est ad honorem et gloriam meam, egredietur qui sit dominator in Israel, id est in populo Judæorum, non corporaliter præsidendo, sed spiritualiter principando.
paras.en: The sense of our translation, moreover, comes to the same, namely: [[Mich 5:2|And thou Bethlehem Ephrata|Et tu, Bethlehem Ephrata]], that is, thou who by another name art called Ephrata (as appears in Genesis[[Gen 35:19||]]), [[Mich 5:2|art a little one|parvulus es]] (a little place) [[Mich 5:2|among the thousands of Juda|in millibus Juda]], that is, among the other places and towns of Juda, which on account of their multitude are called thousands: a little one, I say, in extent, not in dignity. [[Mich 5:2|out of thee|Ex te]] [[Mich 5:2|unto me|mihi]], that is, to My honour and glory, [[Mich 5:2|shall he come forth|egredietur]] [[Mich 5:2|that is to be the ruler in Israel|qui sit dominator in Israel]], that is, among the Jewish people, not by presiding in bodily fashion, but by ruling spiritually.

paras.t: Secundum Chrysostomum, princeps sacerdotum et Scribæ peccabant, dicendo Herodi locum nativitatis Christi: nam noverant Herodem velle Christo insidiari.
paras.en: According to Chrysostom, the chief priest and the scribes sinned in telling Herod the place of Christ's birth; for they knew that Herod meant to lay snares for Christ.

paras.t: Tunc Herodes clam vocatis Magis: noluit enim propositum suum indicare Judæis, quia nec in eis confidentiam habuit, et verebatur ne ipsi sibi resisterent, adhærendo proprio regi ex eorum semine nato; diligenter didicit ab eis tempus stellæ, hoc est certum et determinatum diem apparitionis stellæ, quæ apparuit eis, quando videlicet eis primo apparuit. Hoc inquisivit, ut cognita nati regis ætate, melius puerum cognosceret istum, ad interficiendum. Et mittens, id est, ire suadens, illos in Bethlehem, dixit: Ite in equis seu aliis jumentis: non enim pedestres venerant, sed in dromedariis, secundum Hieronymum; et interrogate diligenter a civibus Bethlehem, de puero, scilicet, in quo loco sit, et cujus potentiæ; et quum inveneritis eum, renuntiate mihi, revertendo ad me, vel per alium mihi insinuando, determinatam domum in qua puer sit, ut et ego veniens adorem eum. Hoc simulatorie dixit, ut per falsam obsequii promissionem, induceret Magos ad renuntiandum sibi de puero. Talis nempe est consuetudo pessimorum, ut dum aliquem in occulto gravius lædere quærunt, humilitatem ei et amicitias fingant. Unde tunc amplius metuendum et præcavendum est a nocumento, dum adversarius magis arridet. Non puto quod Herodes voluerit puerum natum in præsentia Magorum accedere vel occidere; sed eis ad sua reversis, decrevit cum suis satellitibus Christum exstinguere. Non ergo sic voluit sibi de puero renuntiari, ut Magis adhuc in Bethlehem constitutis veniret.
paras.en: [[2:7|Then Herod, privately calling the wise men|Tunc Herodes clam vocatis Magis]] (for he did not wish to reveal his purpose to the Jews, since he had no confidence in them, and feared that they would resist him by cleaving to their own king, born of their seed), [[2:7|learned diligently of them the time of the star|diligenter didicit ab eis tempus stellæ]], that is, the certain and fixed day of the star's appearing, [[2:7|which appeared to them|quæ apparuit eis]], namely when it first appeared to them. He inquired into this so that, knowing the age of the new-born king, he might the better identify this child, to kill him. [[2:8|And sending|Et mittens]], that is, urging to go, [[2:8|them into Bethlehem, said: Go|illos in Bethlehem, dixit: Ite]] on horses or other beasts (for they had not come on foot, but on dromedaries, according to Jerome), [[2:8|and diligently inquire|et interrogate diligenter]] of the citizens of Bethlehem [[2:8|after the child|de puero]], namely in what place he is, and of what power; [[2:8|and when you have found him, bring me word again|et quum inveneritis eum, renuntiate mihi]], by coming back to me, or by letting me know through another, the particular house in which the child is, [[2:8|that I also may come and adore him|ut et ego veniens adorem eum]]. This he said deceitfully, so that by a false promise of homage he might induce the Magi to report to him about the child. Such indeed is the custom of the worst men: when they seek to do someone grave harm in secret, they feign humility and friendship towards him. Hence harm is all the more to be feared and guarded against when an adversary smiles the more. I do not think Herod meant to approach or kill the new-born child in the presence of the Magi; but he resolved, once they had gone home, to destroy Christ with his henchmen. So he did not wish to be told about the child in such a way as to come while the Magi were still in Bethlehem.

paras.t: Qui quum audissent regem, id est verba Herodis, de quo nil mali contra puerum suspicabantur, abierunt a Jerusalem versus Bethlehem cum festinatione non modica, quoniam ardens affectus nati regis impulsit eos. Et ecce stella quam viderant in oriente, antecedebat eos. Quemadmodum enim Deo disponente, circa Jerusalem disparuit, sic rursus Deo volente, mox ut Jerosolymam egressi sunt eis apparuit, atque præcessit in aere, mota ab angelo. Usque dum veniens staret supra domum ubi, id est in qua domo; vel, supra caput, ut alii asserunt, puta in domo ubi erat puer regalis: quasi diceret, Ecce quem quæritis. Videntes autem stellam, quum egrederentur Jerusalem, gavisi sunt gaudio magno valde, sicut et ante de ejus disparitione vehementissime tristabantur. His verbis Evangelista ostendit Magos inæstimabili et ultra humanum modum gaudio esse lætatos, stella rursus conspecta, tanquam dupliciter certificati de pueri inventione jam proxima. Dum enim aliquid cum desiderio quæritur, tanto majus est gaudium, quanto desiderati inventio certior fuerit atque vicinior.
paras.en: [[2:9|Who having heard the king|Qui quum audissent regem]], that is, the words of Herod, of whom they suspected no evil against the child, [[2:9|went their way|abierunt]] from Jerusalem towards Bethlehem with no small haste, since their burning love for the new-born king drove them on. [[2:9|and behold the star which they had seen in the East, went before them|Et ecce stella quam viderant in oriente, antecedebat eos]]. For just as by God's disposing it disappeared near Jerusalem, so again by God's will it appeared to them as soon as they had gone out of Jerusalem, and went before them in the air, moved by an angel, [[2:9|until it came and stood over|Usque dum veniens staret supra]] the house [[2:9|where|ubi]], that is, over which house; or over His head, as others assert, that is, in the house [[2:9|where the child was|ubi erat puer]], the royal child: as if to say, “Behold Him whom you seek.” [[2:10|And seeing the star|Videntes autem stellam]], as they went out of Jerusalem, [[2:10|they rejoiced with exceeding great joy|gavisi sunt gaudio magno valde]], just as before they had been most grievously saddened at its disappearing. By these words the Evangelist shows that the Magi were gladdened with an inestimable joy, beyond human measure, when they saw the star again, being doubly assured that the finding of the child was now near. For when something is sought with longing, the joy is the greater the more certain and the nearer the finding of what is desired.

paras.t: Et intrantes domum, videlicet stabulum seu diversorium, brutis potius quam hominibus aptum, ad quod nemo declinare solebat, nisi itineris necessitate inductus, secundum Chrysostomum, invenerunt puerum cum Maria matre ejus, et forte in gremio ejus. Joseph vero, secundum aliquos, Deo ordinante, tunc abfuit, ne pater pueri putaretur; vel forte adfuit, quatenus visa tanta pueri veneratione, eum de cetero amplius revereretur. Potuit enim puer hic a corde Magorum talem suspicionem excludere, quos in aliis mirabilioribus supernaturaliter docuit. Et procidentes humiliter cum maxima reverentia coram puero super genua sua, vel proni in terram, adoraverunt eum adoratione latriæ, tanquam Dominum majestatis, Regem cœlestem, et omnium Salvatorem de quo locuti erant Prophetæ. Viderunt enim procul dubio non solum intellectualibus, sed et corporalibus oculis, aliquid supernaturale in puero, videlicet quemdam deiformem fulgorem in vultu ipsius. Intus quoque instruxit eos Spiritus Sanctus, omnem exteriorem paupertatem et abjectionem in puero ejusque matre apparentem, non esse humanæ necessitatis, sed divinæ dispositionis, in signum quod puer iste non temporalem opulentiam atque mundanam prosperitatem, sed veram, et item cœlestem ac sempiternam beatitudinem in se credentibus impertiret: ideo moti non sunt ex stabuli vilitate, ex matris inopia, ex pueri solitudine, imo quo exteriora videbantur abjectiora, eo interiora intellexerunt esse diviniora.
paras.en: [[2:11|And entering into the house|Et intrantes domum]], namely the stable or lodging, fit for beasts rather than for men, at which no one was wont to stop unless driven by the necessity of the journey, according to Chrysostom, [[2:11|they found the child with Mary his mother|invenerunt puerum cum Maria matre ejus]], perhaps in her lap. Joseph, according to some, was absent at that time by God's ordering, lest he should be thought the child's father; or perhaps he was present, so that, having seen such veneration paid to the child, he might revere Him the more thereafter. For this Child could shut out such a suspicion from the hearts of the Magi, whom He taught supernaturally in other, more wonderful things. [[2:11|and falling down|Et procidentes]] humbly, with the greatest reverence, before the child, upon their knees, or prostrate on the ground, [[2:11|they adored him|adoraverunt eum]] with the adoration of latria, as the Lord of majesty, the heavenly King, and the Saviour of all, of whom the Prophets had spoken. For without doubt they saw, not only with the eyes of the mind but also with bodily eyes, something supernatural in the child, namely a certain godlike radiance in His face. Inwardly, too, the Holy Ghost taught them that all the outward poverty and abjection appearing in the child and His mother was not of human necessity but of divine disposition, as a sign that this child would bestow on those who believe in Him not temporal wealth and worldly prosperity, but true, heavenly and everlasting beatitude. Therefore they were not put off by the meanness of the stable, the want of the mother, or the loneliness of the child; nay, the more abject the outward things appeared, the more divine they understood the inward things to be.

paras.t: Et apertis thesauris suis, id est repositoriis divitiarum suarum, quas secum detulerant, obtulerunt ei munera, utpote aurum, thus, et myrrham. Hæc tria singuli obtulerunt: Primo, quoniam Persæ et Arabes his rebus abundant, easque magnis personis offerre solebant. Hi vero Magi Persæ fuerunt, qui et in Arabia minori regnasse creduntur: quæ Arabia non multum distat a Judæa et Perside. Unde in oblatione ista Magorum ex parte impletum conspicimus, quod Isaias prædixit: Omnes de Saba venient, aurum et thus deferentes, et laudem Domino annuntiantes; et quod ait Psalmista, Reges Tharsis et insulæ munera offerent, reges Arabum et Saba dona adducent. Secunda ratio oblationis munerum horum, est spiritualis et mystica. Magi namque, ut dictum est, cognoverunt puerum istum esse verum hominem, regem, ac Deum. Aurum ergo obtulerunt ei ut regi, myrrham ut mortali, thus ut Deo. Tertia ratio, quia videbant matris paupertatem, pueri teneritudinem, et stabuli fœditatem. Aurum itaque obtulerunt ad sublevamen inopiæ matris, thus ad expulsionem fœtoris, myrrham ad membrorum pueri consolidationem.
paras.en: [[2:11|and opening their treasures|Et apertis thesauris suis]], that is, the stores of the riches which they had brought with them, [[2:11|they offered him gifts|obtulerunt ei munera]], namely [[2:11|gold, frankincense, and myrrh|aurum, thus, et myrrham]]. Each of them offered these three. First, because the Persians and Arabians abound in these things, and were wont to offer them to great persons; and these Magi were Persians, who are believed also to have reigned in Lesser Arabia, which is not far from Judea and Persia. Hence in this offering of the Magi we see fulfilled in part what Isaias foretold: [[Is 60:6|all they from Saba shall come, bringing gold and frankincense: and shewing forth praise to the Lord|Omnes de Saba venient, aurum et thus deferentes, et laudem Domino annuntiantes]]; and what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 71:10|The kings of Tharsis and the islands shall offer presents: the kings of the Arabians and of Saba shall bring gifts|Reges Tharsis et insulæ munera offerent, reges Arabum et Saba dona adducent]]. The second reason for the offering of these gifts is spiritual and mystical. For the Magi, as has been said, knew this child to be true man, king and God. They offered Him gold, then, as to a king, myrrh as to a mortal, frankincense as to God. The third reason is that they saw the poverty of the mother, the tenderness of the child, and the squalor of the stable. So they offered gold to relieve the mother's want, frankincense to drive out the stench, and myrrh to strengthen the child's limbs.

paras.t: Hæc quoque munera, et nos spiritualiter Christo quotidie offerre debemus. Per aurum enim significatur fides illuminata, vel donum sapientiæ, vel caritas fervida. Unde in Apocalypsi legitur: Suadeo tibi emere aurum ignitum probatum; et secundum Apostolum, Alius superædificat aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos. Per thus vero figuratur bonæ famæ suavitas, vita exemplaris, vel affectuosa et dulcis oratio. Dicit enim Apostolus: Christi bonus odor sumus in omni loco; et Psalmista, Dirigatur (inquit) oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo. In Apocalypsi quoque habetur: Ascendit fumus incensorum de orationibus Sanctorum coram Deo. Per myrrham autem signatur mortificatio carnis, seu opera bona. Nam sicut myrrha corpora defunctorum præservat a putredine vermium, et a corruptionis dissolutione; sic mortificatio carnis custodit hominem a putredine vitiorum, et dissolutione divisionis a Deo. Debemus ergo Deo offerre fidem illuminatam, ardentem affectum, seu animam sapientia decoratam: hoc est aurum. Item bonam famam, atque devotam orationem (juxta quod scriptum est, Curam habe de bono nomine; et rursus, Oportet semper orare, et non deficere): hoc est thus. Tertio, immolare debemus corporis mortificationem, seu corpus mortificatum per opera pœnitentiæ. Qui enim sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis.
paras.en: These gifts we too ought to offer to Christ spiritually every day. For by gold is signified enlightened faith, or the gift of wisdom, or fervent charity. Hence we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:18|I counsel thee to buy|Suadeo tibi emere]] [[Apoc 3:18|gold, fire tried|aurum ignitum probatum]]; and, according to the Apostle, [[1 Cor 3:10|another buildeth thereon|Alius superædificat]] [[1 Cor 3:12|gold, silver, precious stones|aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos]]. By frankincense is figured the sweetness of a good name, an exemplary life, or loving and sweet prayer. For the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 2:15|we are the good odour of Christ|Christi bonus odor sumus]] [[2 Cor 2:14|in every place|in omni loco]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 140:2|Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight|Dirigatur (inquit) oratio mea sicut incensum in conspectu tuo]]. In the Apocalypse too we find: [[Apoc 8:4|the smoke of the incense of the prayers of the saints ascended up before God|Ascendit fumus incensorum de orationibus Sanctorum coram Deo]]. By myrrh is signified the mortification of the flesh, or good works. For as myrrh preserves the bodies of the dead from the rotting of worms and from the dissolution of corruption, so the mortification of the flesh guards a man from the rot of vices and from the dissolution of separation from God. We ought, then, to offer God enlightened faith, burning affection, or a soul adorned with wisdom: this is the gold. Again, a good name and devout prayer (according to what is written: [[Ecclus 41:15|Take care of a good name|Curam habe de bono nomine]]; and again: [[Luke 18:1|we ought always to pray and not to faint|Oportet semper orare, et non deficere]]): this is the frankincense. Thirdly, we ought to sacrifice the mortification of the body, or the body mortified by works of penance; for [[Gal 5:24|they that are Christ's have crucified their flesh, with the vices and concupiscences|Qui enim sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis]].

paras.t: Et responso accepto in somnis, id est tempore dormitionis eorum in aliquo hospitio in Bethlehem, ne redirent ad Herodem, videlicet, ne Herodes cognito loco pueri, eum occideret. Hoc responsum habuerunt ab angelo, vel a puero nato eis in somnis visione imaginaria apparente. Responsum autem proprie datur interroganti, et sic Magi interrogasse videntur forsitan a Maria, an ad Herodem redire deberent; vel responsum istud datum est non sermoni, sed operationi eorum, quoniam suo obsequio meruerunt sic admoneri a Deo. Per aliam viam reversi sunt in regionem suam. Sic et nos quum ab Herode, id est mundi ac dæmonis cultu, per pœnitentiam ad Christum accessimus, per aliam viam, quam est via iniquorum, in qua ambulavimus olim, reverti debemus in regionem nostram, videlicet in societatem Ecclesiæ militantis ac triumphantis, seu paradisum cœlestem.
paras.en: [[2:12|And having received an answer in sleep|Et responso accepto in somnis]], that is, while they slept in some lodging in Bethlehem, [[2:12|that they should not return to Herod|ne redirent ad Herodem]], namely, lest Herod, learning where the child was, should kill Him. This answer they had from an angel, or from the new-born child Himself appearing to them in sleep in an imaginary vision [that is, a vision formed in the imagination, as in dreams, as distinct from a bodily or a purely intellectual vision]. Now an answer is properly given to one who asks; and so the Magi seem to have asked, perhaps of Mary, whether they ought to return to Herod. Or else this answer was given not to their words but to their deeds, since by their homage they deserved to be so warned by God. [[2:12|they went back another way into their country|Per aliam viam reversi sunt in regionem suam]]. So we too, when we have come from Herod, that is, from the service of the world and the devil, to Christ through penance, ought to return by another way than the way of the wicked in which we once walked, into our own country, namely into the fellowship of the Church militant and triumphant, or the heavenly paradise.

paras.t: Præterea hi tres Magi omnium gentium conversionem figuraverunt: ternarius namque est numerus perfectionis. In quibus impleri cœpit illud Isaiæ: Ecce gentem quam nesciebas vocabis, et gentes quæ non cognoverunt te, ad te current. Per fulgorem insuper stellæ, præsignata est claritas gratiæ per quam corda gentilium contemplata sunt Christum. Bethlehem quoque interpretatur, domus panis: per quam intelligitur anima religiosa, quæ pane obedientiæ, pane lacrimarum, et pane sacramentali, fovetur. In tali anima nascitur Christus: quo cognito, Magi, id est pœnitentes, veniunt, et Christum in anima tali honorant.
paras.en: Moreover, these three Magi figured the conversion of all the nations; for three is the number of perfection. In them began to be fulfilled that word of Isaias: [[Is 55:5|Behold thou shalt call a nation, which thou knewest not: and the nations that knew not thee shall run to thee|Ecce gentem quam nesciebas vocabis, et gentes quæ non cognoverunt te, ad te current]]. By the brightness of the star, again, was foreshown the brightness of grace, through which the hearts of the Gentiles have contemplated Christ. Bethlehem, too, is interpreted “house of bread”: by which is understood the religious soul, which is nourished with the bread of obedience, the bread of tears, and the sacramental bread. In such a soul Christ is born; and when this is known, the Magi, that is, penitents, come and honour Christ in such a soul.

2.title: Prosecutio expositionis hujus secundi capituli: Qui quum recessissent
2.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this second chapter: “And after they were departed”

paras.t: Descripta pueri Jesu veneratione, in qua ejus divinitas patuit, consequenter describitur ejus persecutio, in qua sua humanitas clare innotuit. Qui quum recessissent, id est, quum Magi a Bethlehem ad sua redire cœpissent per aliam viam, ecce angelus Domini apparuit in somnis Joseph, dicens ei: Surge, et accipe puerum et matrem ejus, et fuge in Ægyptum, et esto ibi usque dum dicam tibi, id est tamdiu donec annuntiem tibi de reditu. Causa autem hujus commissionis subjungitur: futurum est enim ut Herodes quærat puerum ad perdendum eum, id est interficiendum, non ad adorandum sicut vulpino corde spopondit. Ista apparitio et allocutio angeli facta est S. Joseph post præsentationem pueri Jesu in templo, ubi Simeon accepit eum in ulnas suas, et Anna prophetissa confessa est Domino, omnibusque habitatoribus Jerusalem de Christo locuta est. Herodes quippe cernens Magos non reverti ad se, æstimavit eos per phantasticam stellam illusos, sicque ex verecundia non redisse ad eum, sed clam abscessisse: ideo non curavit requirere puerum. Verum, post purificationem Mariæ percipiens verba Simeonis, Annæ, atque pastorum perhibentium testimonium Christo, tunc credens Magos non esse deceptos, vehementer turbatus est, suspicatus successorem regni. Hæc est enim implacabilis regum iracundia, dum sentiunt regnum suum ab alio impeti.
paras.en: Having described the veneration of the child Jesus, in which His divinity was made plain, the Evangelist next describes His persecution, in which His humanity was clearly made known. [[2:13|And after they were departed|Qui quum recessissent]], that is, when the Magi had begun to return from Bethlehem to their own country by another way, [[2:13|behold an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph, saying|ecce angelus Domini apparuit in somnis Joseph, dicens]] to him: [[2:13|Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt: and be there until I shall tell thee|Surge, et accipe puerum et matrem ejus, et fuge in Ægyptum, et esto ibi usque dum dicam tibi]], that is, until I bring thee word of the return. The reason for this charge is then added: [[2:13|For it will come to pass that Herod will seek the child to destroy him|futurum est enim ut Herodes quærat puerum ad perdendum eum]], that is, to kill Him, not to adore Him, as with a fox’s heart he had promised. This appearing and speaking of the angel to St Joseph took place after the presentation of the child Jesus in the temple, where Simeon [[Luke 2:28|took him into his arms|accepit eum in ulnas suas]], and Anna the prophetess gave praise to the Lord and spoke of Christ to all the dwellers in Jerusalem[[Luke 2:38||]]. For Herod, seeing that the Magi did not come back to him, supposed that they had been deluded by an illusory star, and so out of shame had not returned to him but had gone away secretly; therefore he did not trouble to seek out the child. But after the purification of Mary, hearing of the words of Simeon and of Anna, and of the shepherds bearing witness to Christ, he then believed that the Magi had not been deceived, and was greatly troubled, suspecting a successor to his kingdom. For such is the implacable wrath of kings when they perceive their kingdom to be threatened by another.

paras.t: Qui Joseph consurgens a somno, sine dilatione, quia de pueri præservatione atque custodia diligentissimus exstitit, accepit puerum et matrem ejus nocte, id est, suo itineri eos associavit: et forte in propriis ulnis vel scapulis puerum bajulavit, nisi dicatur Mariam et Jesum jumento vexisse, propter itineris prolixitatem, sicut et Virginem sacram in asino creditur deduxisse ad Bethlehem, hora nativitatis Christi jam proxima. Accepitque eos nocte, forte eadem qua angelum vidit, quoniam tempus nocturnum magis aptum est fugæ, ne de fuga accusaretur ab aliquo.
paras.en: [[2:14|Who arose|Qui Joseph consurgens]], that is, Joseph, rising from sleep without delay, because he was most diligent in preserving and guarding the child, [[2:14|and took the child and his mother by night|accepit puerum et matrem ejus nocte]], that is, he took them with him on his journey; and perhaps he carried the child in his own arms or on his shoulders, unless it be said that he carried Mary and Jesus on a beast of burden because of the length of the journey, just as he is believed to have brought the holy Virgin to Bethlehem on an ass when the hour of Christ’s birth was already near. And he took them by night, perhaps the same night in which he saw the angel, since the night-time is better suited to flight, so that no one might inform against him for fleeing.

paras.t: Secundum principem theologorum divinum Dionysium, ecclesiastica hierarchia ab angelica gubernatur, et omnia opera Dei ordinatissima sunt. Quamvis ergo puer natus poterat S. Joseph intus docere, imo et foris affari de fuga arripienda, tamen hoc fecit per angelum, ut ordo hierarchicus servaretur. Poterat quoque Jesus alio modo evadere manum Herodis, quemadmodum evasit manus Judæorum, eum præcipitare et lapidare volentium. Sed quia nostram assumpsit naturam, et ad patiendum atque ad exhibendum totius perfectionis exemplum advenit, voluit humano modo procedere, fugiendo, adversa patiendo, et exemplum præbendo, sicut in Evangelio loquitur: Quum vos persecuti fuerint in una civitate, fugite in aliam.
paras.en: According to the prince of theologians, the divine Dionysius, the ecclesiastical hierarchy is governed by the angelic, and all the works of God are most perfectly ordered. Although, then, the new-born child could have taught St Joseph inwardly, and indeed have spoken to him outwardly, about taking flight, yet He did this through an angel, so that the order of the hierarchy might be kept. Jesus could also have escaped the hand of Herod in another way, just as He escaped the hands of the Jews when they wished to cast Him down headlong[[Luke 4:29||]][[Luke 4:30||]] and to stone Him[[John 8:59||]]. But since He had taken our nature, and had come to suffer and to show an example of all perfection, He willed to proceed in a human way: by fleeing, by suffering adversity, and by giving an example, as He says in the Gospel: [[Matt 10:23|when they shall persecute you in this city, flee into another|Quum vos persecuti fuerint in una civitate, fugite in aliam]].

paras.t: Et secessit Joseph cum Maria et infantulo in Ægyptum: prout per Isaiam fuerat prophetatum: Ecce Dominus ascendet super nubem levem, et ingredietur Ægyptum, et commovebuntur simulacra Ægypti a facie ejus. Fertur equidem in Scholastica historia, quod Christo Ægyptum ingrediente, omnia idola in fanis Ægyptiorum in terram collapsa sunt, Christi præsentiam ferre nequaquam valentia, sicut nec Dagon præsentiam arcæ, sed corruit. Per quod figurabatur idololatriam penitus destruendam in toto mundo Christi virtute, juxta illud: In die illa, dicit Dominus, disperdam nomina idolorum de terra. — Quæritur, cur potius Ægyptum ingressus sit Christus. Respondendum primo, quoniam Ægyptii olim tempore Joseph, circa populum Israel multum benevoli erant. Nam et Jacob patriarcham primo septuaginta diebus, deinde septem planxerunt, ut in Genesi dicitur. Secundo, quoniam Deus, qui non in perpetuum irascitur, postquam percussit, rursus medetur: ideo, sicut quondam gravissime cecidit Ægyptum propter populum Israel, sic nunc eam curandam misericorditer visitat. Tertio, quia Ægyptus fuit evidens mundi hujus figura, ideo eam intravit, ad præsignandum quod per Apostolorum prædicationem toti mundo inveheretur.
paras.en: [[2:14|And retired|Et secessit]] Joseph, with Mary and the little child, [[2:14|into Egypt|in Ægyptum]], as had been prophesied through Isaias: [[Is 19:1|Behold the Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud, and will enter into Egypt, and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence|Ecce Dominus ascendet super nubem levem, et ingredietur Ægyptum, et commovebuntur simulacra Ægypti a facie ejus]]. It is related indeed in the Scholastic History [the Historia scholastica of Peter Comestor] that when Christ entered Egypt all the idols in the temples of the Egyptians fell to the ground, being quite unable to bear the presence of Christ, just as Dagon could not bear the presence of the ark, but fell down[[1 Kings 5:3||]][[1 Kings 5:4||]]. By this it was foreshown that idolatry would be utterly destroyed in the whole world by the power of Christ, according to the words: [[Zach 13:2|in that day, saith the Lord|In die illa, dicit Dominus]], [[Zach 13:2|I will destroy the names of idols out of the earth|disperdam nomina idolorum de terra]]. — It is asked why Christ went into Egypt rather than elsewhere. The answer is, first, that the Egyptians were formerly, in the time of Joseph, very well disposed towards the people of Israel; for they mourned the patriarch Jacob first for seventy days and then for seven, as is said in Genesis[[Gen 50:3||]][[Gen 50:10||]]. Secondly, because God, who is not angry for ever[[Ps 102:9||]], heals again after He has struck; and therefore, as He once struck Egypt most grievously for the sake of the people of Israel, so now He mercifully visits it to heal it. Thirdly, because Egypt was a plain figure of this world, He entered it to foreshow that He would be carried to the whole world by the preaching of the Apostles.

paras.t: Et erat Joseph ibi, videlicet in Ægypto cum matre et puero, manibus suis victum conquirens, usque ad obitum Herodis, utpote septem annis, ut fertur. Herodes enim triginta septem annis dicitur regnasse, ejusque imperii tricesimo anno Christus legitur natus fuisse. Ut impleretur in Christi reversione ab Ægypto post mortem Herodis, quod dictum est a Domino per Prophetam Osee dicentem: Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum.
paras.en: [[2:14|and he was there|Et erat Joseph ibi]], Joseph, that is, in Egypt with the mother and the child, earning their living with his own hands, [[2:14|until the death of Herod|usque ad obitum Herodis]], namely for seven years, as is said. For Herod is said to have reigned thirty-seven years, and Christ is read to have been born in the thirtieth year of his rule. [[2:15|That it might be fulfilled|Ut impleretur]] (in Christ’s return from Egypt after the death of Herod) [[2:15|which the Lord spoke by the prophet|quod dictum est a Domino per Prophetam]] Osee, [[2:15|saying: Out of Egypt have I called my son|dicentem: Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum]].

paras.t: Hoc Judæi ad litteram exponunt de populo Israel, qui dicitur filius, imo et primogenitus Dei, juxta illud: Israel primogenitus meus; dixi tibi, Dimitte filium meum ut serviat mihi: quod certum est dici de populo Judæorum ad Pharaonem. Sic in proposito asserunt per filium designari populum Israel, non Christum. Unde in Osee ita habetur: Puer Israel, et dilexi eum; et ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum. Verumtamen, Evangelista docente, compellimur profiteri, hoc ad litteram de Christo prædictum. Probatio namque per allegationem Scripturæ non valet, nisi ex sensu litterali, secundum Augustinum. Oportet itaque scire, quod quum aliquid dicitur de populo, vel certa persona veteris Testamenti, prout erat figura Christi sive Ecclesiæ, quamvis ad litteram de illis exponatur, principalius tamen ac litteralius exponitur de Christo, vel Ecclesia: quemadmodum illud de Salomone, Ego ero illi in patrem, et ipse erit mihi in filium, Apostolus introducit de Christo prædictum. Dictum est enim de Salomone, in quantum Christi figuram gerebat: idcirco de Christo principalius intelligitur. Sic quod apud Osee habetur, Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum, quamvis ad litteram dictum sit de populo Judæorum, litteralius principaliusque de Christo accipitur: quia de populo illo prædictum est, secundum quod erat figura Christi, qui non solum per determinatas personas, sed per totum populum Synagogæ multoties præfiguratur.
paras.en: This the Jews expound literally of the people of Israel, which is called the son, and indeed the firstborn, of God, according to the words: [[Ex 4:22|Israel is my son, my firstborn|Israel primogenitus meus]]; [[Ex 4:23|I have said to thee: Let my son go, that he may serve me|dixi tibi, Dimitte filium meum ut serviat mihi]], which, it is certain, was said to Pharao of the Jewish people. So in the present case they assert that by “son” is meant the people of Israel, not Christ; whence in Osee it reads thus: [[Osee 11:1|Israel was a child, and I loved him: and I called my son out of Egypt|Puer Israel, et dilexi eum; et ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum]]. Nevertheless, taught by the Evangelist, we are compelled to profess that this was foretold literally of Christ. For, according to Augustine, a proof by the citing of Scripture is not valid except from the literal sense [the principle St Thomas states, citing Augustine’s letter against Vincentius the Donatist: an argument can be drawn only from the literal sense, not from what is said by way of allegory]. We must know, then, that when something is said of the people, or of a particular person, of the Old Testament, insofar as that people or person was a figure of Christ or of the Church, although it is expounded literally of them, yet it is expounded more principally and more literally of Christ or of the Church; just as the Apostle brings forward the words spoken of Solomon, [[2 Kings 7:14|I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son|Ego ero illi in patrem, et ipse erit mihi in filium]], as foretold of Christ[[Heb 1:5||]]. For it was said of Solomon insofar as he bore the figure of Christ, and therefore it is understood more principally of Christ. So what is found in Osee, [[Osee 11:1|I called my son out of Egypt|Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum]], although literally it was said of the Jewish people, is taken more literally and more principally of Christ; because it was foretold of that people according as it was a figure of Christ, who is many times prefigured not only by particular persons but by the whole people of the Synagogue.

paras.t: Tunc, utpote crescente rumore de Christo, propter Simeonis et Annæ, pastorumque verba (puto etiam quod Zacharias et Elisabeth parentes Joannis, non tacuerunt de Christo), Herodes videns, id est considerans, quoniam illusus, id est deceptus atque contemptus, esset a Magis non redeuntibus ad ipsum juxta condictum, iratus est valde, indigne ferens se esse derisum, et de puero nato vindicare se cupiens, quem ad suam injuriam natum putavit.
paras.en: [[2:16|Then|Tunc]], that is, as the rumour about Christ was growing because of the words of Simeon and Anna and of the shepherds (I think too that Zachary and Elizabeth, the parents of John, were not silent about Christ), [[2:16|Herod perceiving|Herodes videns]], that is, considering, [[2:16|that he was deluded|quoniam illusus]], that is, deceived and scorned, [[2:16|by the wise men|a Magis]], who did not come back to him as had been agreed, [[2:16|was exceeding angry|iratus est valde]], taking it ill that he had been mocked, and longing to avenge himself on the new-born child, who he thought had been born to do him wrong.

paras.t: Et mittens crudeles satellites, occidit per manum servorum suorum, omnes pueros mares qui erant in Bethlehem et in omnibus finibus ejus, id est in locis et in villis vicinis ad eam pertinentibus. Secundum historias, istud non contigit statim postquam se illusum pensavit. Quamvis enim tunc statim decrevit occidere pueros, tamen propter accusationem filiorum suorum coactus est Romam venire, et ibi cum filiis suis coram imperatore comparere. Obtenta autem sententia pro se, videns se confirmatum in regno, quum redisset, implevit quod de nece infantium concepit, interfici faciens omnes pueros, a bimatu, id est ab ætate seu tempore duorum annorum, videlicet omnes infantes biennes seu duorum annorum tempus habentes, et infra, id est etiam illos qui erant minoris ætatis, usque ad pueros unius diei inclusive, ut videtur insinuari per hoc quod dicitur, Infra, secundum tempus quod exquisierat a Magis, id est juxta mensuram temporis evoluti ab hora apparitionis stellæ, nativitatisque pueri: quod tempus, videlicet diem apparitionis stellæ, exquisivit et didicit a Magis: per quod agnovit quantæ ætatis consisteret Christus. Herodes quippe certificari volens de Christi occisione, et sciens eum jam esse unius anni et modicum amplius (tantum enim temporis fluxit a nativitate ejus usque ad regressum Herodis a Roma), præcepit occidi pueros majoris ætatis usque ad bimos, itemque minoris ætatis usque ad pueros diei unius, ne puer requisitus evaderet. Ista est expositio præsentis loci communior, procedens secundum eos qui dicunt quod stella in die nativitatis Christi Magis apparuit, eosque infra tredecim dies usque ad Christum perduxit: et ita hæc dictio, Infra, denotat ordinem temporis.
paras.en: [[2:16|and sending|Et mittens]] cruel henchmen, he [[2:16|killed|occidit]], by the hand of his servants, [[2:16|all the menchildren that were in Bethlehem, and in all the borders thereof|omnes pueros mares qui erant in Bethlehem et in omnibus finibus ejus]], that is, in the places and villages near by that belonged to it. According to the histories, this did not happen immediately after he reckoned himself deluded. For although he resolved at once to kill the children, yet because of an accusation brought by his sons he was forced to go to Rome and appear there with his sons before the emperor. Having obtained judgement in his favour, and seeing himself confirmed in the kingdom, on his return he carried out what he had conceived concerning the slaughter of the infants, having all the boys put to death [[2:16|from two years old|a bimatu]], that is, from the age or time of two years, namely all infants of two years, or having two years’ time, [[2:16|and under|et infra]], that is, also those who were of lesser age, down to boys of one day inclusive, as seems to be suggested by the words “and under”; [[2:16|according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men|secundum tempus quod exquisierat a Magis]], that is, according to the measure of time that had passed since the hour of the star’s appearing and of the child’s birth: which time, namely the day of the star’s appearing, he had inquired into and learned from the Magi, and by it he knew of what age Christ was. For Herod, wishing to be made certain of the killing of Christ, and knowing that He was now a year old and a little more (for so much time had passed from His birth to Herod’s return from Rome), ordered the boys of greater age, up to those of two years, to be killed, and likewise those of lesser age, down to boys of one day, lest the child he sought should escape. This is the more common exposition of this place, following those who say that the star appeared to the Magi on the day of Christ’s birth and brought them to Christ within thirteen days; and so the word “under” [Latin infra, “below”, “within”] denotes the order of time.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur, prout denotat ordinem numeri, ut sit sensus: A bimatu, id est a pueris duorum annorum, et infra, id est etiam illos qui erant infra ætatem duorum bimatuum, scilicet pueros quatuor annorum usque ad pueros quinquennes, secundum tempus quod exquisierat a Magis, a quibus secundum exponentes hoc modo, didicit stellam apparuisse eis per duos annos antequam Jerosolymam intraverunt. Herodes ergo putans Christum tunc natum quum stella apparuit, æstimavit eum jam plus esse quam trium annorum: quia jam annus fluxit a recessu Magorum, antequam ipse a Roma reversus est. Ideo interfecit omnes pueros bimos usque ad quinquennes, ne Christus evaderet, si forte solito majoris aut minoris exsisteret quantitatis. Ista expositio fertur esse Chrysostomi, eo quod dicat stellam diu apparuisse Magis ante Christi nativitatem. Verum (ut tetigi) hoc Chrysostomus non dicit asserendo, sed quamdam scripturam apocrypham recitando. Nihilo minus huic opinioni apparentiam confert, quod quorumdam Innocentium ossa adeo magna sunt, quod biennium vix esse credantur. — Alio modo exponitur quod dictum est, Infra, ut sit sensus, quod pueros duorum annorum, usque ad pueros unius diei, fecit occidi: quod verius æstimatur.
paras.en: Secondly, it is expounded according as it denotes the order of number [that is, “under” is taken to count the years upward from two, not downward to the newborn], so that the sense is: [[2:16|from two years old|A bimatu]], that is, from boys of two years, [[2:16|and under|et infra]], that is, also those who were within the age of two two-year spans, namely boys of four years, up to boys of five, [[2:16|according to the time which he had diligently inquired of the wise men|secundum tempus quod exquisierat a Magis]]; from whom, according to those who expound it in this way, he learned that the star had appeared to them for two years before they entered Jerusalem. Herod, then, thinking that Christ was born when the star appeared, reckoned that He was now more than three years old, since a year had already passed from the departure of the Magi before he himself returned from Rome. Therefore he killed all the boys from two years old up to five, lest Christ should escape if He happened to be larger or smaller than is usual. This exposition is said to be Chrysostom’s, because he says that the star appeared to the Magi long before the birth of Christ. But (as I have touched on already) Chrysostom does not say this by way of assertion, but in reciting a certain apocryphal writing. Nevertheless this opinion is made likely by the fact that the bones of some of the Innocents are so large that they can scarcely be believed to be of two years. — The words “and under” are expounded in yet another way, so that the sense is that he had the boys of two years, down to boys of one day, put to death; and this is reckoned the truer.

paras.t: Ecce quanta crudelitas impiissimi regis! Sed quoniam dictum est, Herodem fuisse proselytum, et credidisse Scripturis de Christi adventu, mirum videtur quod tentavit eum exstinguere, quasi posset Dei consilium et Prophetarum Scripturas mutare. Respondendum, quod credidit fide informi, vel opinione humana, sicut credit hæreticus, qui nec fidem formatam habet. Nihilo minus malitia et passionum vehementia ita obtenebraverunt intellectum Herodis, quod non attendit neminem posse resistere Deo, vel ejus immobile consilium variare, vel divinas Scripturas falsificare. Sed tentavit suis passionibus satisfacere, malo superatus affectu, qui non advertit judicium. Et quid hoc mirum de Herode, quum et Salomon, qui tempore suæ sapientiæ dixit, scripsitque, Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum, a mulieribus infatuatus tentaverit simile aliquid perpetrare? Quum enim audisset a Deo regnum suum esse scindendum, percepissetque a propheta Ahia, prænuntiatum esse Jeroboam Ephrathæo, quod super decem tribus regnaret, tentavit occidere ipsum Jeroboam, qui in Ægyptum aufugit.
paras.en: Behold how great the cruelty of this most impious king! But since it has been said that Herod was a proselyte and had believed the Scriptures concerning the coming of Christ, it seems strange that he tried to destroy Him, as though he could change the counsel of God and the Scriptures of the Prophets. The answer is that he believed with unformed faith [fides informis: faith without charity, a true assent of the mind that does not of itself make a man pleasing to God; “formed” faith is faith given life by charity], or by human opinion, as a heretic believes, who has not even formed faith. Nevertheless, malice and the violence of his passions so darkened Herod’s understanding that he did not consider that no one can resist God, or alter His unchangeable counsel, or falsify the divine Scriptures. But he tried to satisfy his passions, overcome by an evil affection, which pays no heed to judgement. And what wonder is this in Herod, when even Solomon, who in the time of his wisdom said and wrote, [[Prov 21:30|There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord|Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum]], when he had been infatuated by women, tried to do something similar? For when he had heard from God that his kingdom was to be divided[[3 Kings 11:11||]], and had learned that the prophet Ahias had foretold to Jeroboam the Ephrathite that he would reign over ten tribes[[3 Kings 11:31||]][[3 Kings 11:35||]], he tried to kill Jeroboam himself, who fled into Egypt[[3 Kings 11:40||]].

paras.t: Tunc adimpletum est quod dictum est per Jeremiam prophetam dicentem: Vox in Rama, id est in sublimi, audita est, utpote longe et late diffusa, propter vehementiam soni: vox, inquam, ploratus, id est plorationis puerorum, qui a matribus avellebantur et occidebantur, matribusque lamentantibus miserabilius flebant; vox quoque et ululatus matrum, quæ de filiorum separatione et interfectione dupliciter et incredibiliter cruciabantur, quas sola tantæ crudelitatis memoria supra modum afflixit. Rachel, id est congregatio feminarum Bethlehemitarum: quæ nomine Rachelis signantur: Primo, quoniam Rachel juxta Bethlehem est sepulta, et ex corpusculi hospitio nomen matris accepit, secundum Hieronymum. Secundo, quoniam tribus Juda et Benjamin junctæ erant loco et sorte. Herodes autem jussit non tantum in Bethlehem, sed in locis quoque adjacentibus pueros trucidari: sicque ex propinquitate locorum non solum filii Liæ habitantis in Bethlehem, quæ pertinebat ad tribum Judæ nati ex Lia; sed et multi ex filiis Rachel matris Benjamin, hoc est de tribu Benjamin, interfecti fuerunt. Propter quod Rachel, id est posteritas ejus, dicitur plorare filios suos ab Herode necatos. Et noluit consolari, id est, matres filiorum occisorum consolationem recipere noluerunt de morte filiorum: sicut nec Jacob, quum putavit Joseph a fera pessima devoratum; quia non sunt, id est, quoniam filii earum ab hac vita subtracti sunt eis per mortem crudelem: quod fuit eis inconsolabilis causa doloris.
paras.en: [[2:17|Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremias the prophet, saying|Tunc adimpletum est quod dictum est per Jeremiam prophetam dicentem]]: [[2:18|A voice in Rama|Vox in Rama]], that is, on high, [[2:18|was heard|audita est]], as being spread far and wide by the violence of the sound: a voice, I say, of [[2:18|lamentation|ploratus]], that is, of the weeping of the children, who were torn from their mothers and slain, and who wept the more piteously as their mothers lamented; a voice also, and [[2:18|mourning|ululatus]], of the mothers, who were tormented doubly and beyond belief at the separation and slaying of their sons, and whom the mere memory of so great a cruelty afflicted beyond measure. [[2:18|Rachel|Rachel]], that is, the gathering of the women of Bethlehem, who are signified by the name of Rachel: first, because Rachel was buried near Bethlehem[[Gen 35:19||]], and from the lodging of her poor body there received the name of mother, according to Jerome; secondly, because the tribes of Juda and Benjamin were joined in place and in lot. Now Herod ordered the boys to be slaughtered not only in Bethlehem but also in the places round about; and so, because the places were near together, there were killed not only the sons of Lia living in Bethlehem (which belonged to the tribe of Juda, who was born of Lia), but also many of the sons of Rachel, the mother of Benjamin, that is, of the tribe of Benjamin. For this reason Rachel, that is, her posterity, is said to be [[2:18|bewailing her children|plorare filios suos]] slain by Herod. [[2:18|and would not be comforted|Et noluit consolari]], that is, the mothers of the slain sons would not receive comfort for the death of their sons, just as Jacob would not either when he thought that Joseph had been devoured by an evil wild beast[[Gen 37:33||]]; [[2:18|because they are not|quia non sunt]], that is, because their sons had been taken from them out of this life by a cruel death, which was for them a cause of grief past all comfort.

paras.t: Rama interdum est proprium nomen loci; interdum vero est nomen commune, et interpretatur excelsum: sicque accipitur nunc. Unde in Jeremia habetur: Vox in excelsis audita est lamentationis et planctus, etc. Quod autem asseritur, vox ista in excelsis audita, sic quoque intelligi potest, quia in cœlum coram Deo ascendit: secundum quod a Jacobo de pauperibus dicitur, Clamor eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit; et alibi, Oratio humiliantis se, penetrat nubes.
paras.en: Rama is sometimes the proper name of a place, but sometimes it is a common noun and is interpreted “high”; and so it is taken here. Whence in Jeremias it reads: [[Jer 31:15|A voice was heard on high of lamentation, of mourning|Vox in excelsis audita est lamentationis et planctus]], etc. That this voice is said to have been heard on high can also be understood in this way: that it went up to heaven before God; as James says of the poor, [[Jas 5:4|the cry of them hath entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth|Clamor eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit]]; and elsewhere, [[Ecclus 35:21|The prayer of him that humbleth himself, shall pierce the clouds|Oratio humiliantis se, penetrat nubes]].

paras.t: Defuncto autem Herode, ecce angelus Domini apparuit in somnis Joseph in Ægypto, dicens: Surge, et accipe puerum et matrem ejus, et vade ex Ægypto in terram Israel. Determinatam autem urbem ad quam revertatur non ei exprimit angelus, quia de hoc postea instructurus erat S. Joseph, quando specialis ratio hoc exegit. Defuncti sunt enim, qui quærebant animam pueri, id est Herodes et ejus fautores, qui animam, id est vitam animalem, pueri quærebant exstinguere. Per quod, secundum Hieronymum et Chrysostomum, datur intelligi sacerdotes et Scribas de morte Christi cogitasse, et Herodis studio consensisse. Quod intelligi potest de Christo materialiter et formaliter: materialiter, quia consenserunt in mortem ejus qui fuit verus Christus, quem ipsi non crediderant esse Christum; formaliter, quia et Christum etiam cognitum optaverunt occidi. An hoc secundo modo intelligi possit, difficile est, et satis ambiguum, quum Apostolus dicat: Si enim cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent. Et Petrus Judæis loquens, dicit: Scio quod per ignorantiam fecistis, sicut et principes vestri. Et Dominus in cruce pendens, dixit: Pater, dimitte illis, non enim sciunt quid faciunt.
paras.en: [[2:19|But when Herod was dead, behold an angel of the Lord appeared in sleep to Joseph in Egypt|Defuncto autem Herode, ecce angelus Domini apparuit in somnis Joseph in Ægypto]], [[2:20|Saying: Arise, and take the child and his mother, and go|dicens: Surge, et accipe puerum et matrem ejus, et vade]] out of Egypt [[2:20|into the land of Israel|in terram Israel]]. The angel does not tell him the particular city to which he is to return, because he was to instruct St Joseph about this afterwards, when a special reason required it. [[2:20|For they are dead that sought the life of the child|Defuncti sunt enim, qui quærebant animam pueri]], that is, Herod and his abettors, who sought to put out the soul [Latin anima, which the Douay-Rheims renders “life”], that is, the animal life, of the child. By this, according to Jerome and Chrysostom, we are given to understand that the priests and Scribes had been thinking of the death of Christ and had consented to Herod’s design. This can be understood of Christ materially and formally: materially, because they consented to the death of Him who was the true Christ, though they did not believe Him to be the Christ; formally, because they wished even the Christ, known as such, to be killed. Whether it can be understood in this second way is difficult and quite doubtful, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:8|For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory|Si enim cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriæ crucifixissent]]. And Peter, speaking to the Jews, says: [[Acts 3:17|I know that you did it through ignorance: as did also your rulers|Scio quod per ignorantiam fecistis, sicut et principes vestri]]. And the Lord, hanging on the cross, said: [[Luke 23:34|Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do|Pater, dimitte illis, non enim sciunt quid faciunt]].

paras.t: Qui consurgens, accepit puerum et matrem ejus, et venit in terram Israel. Audiens autem Joseph quod Archelaus filius Herodis regnaret in Judæa pro Herode patre suo. Refert Josephus, quod Herodes totum regnum suum dimisit Archelao, quem diligebat præ ceteris filiis. Herodes ergo et Philippus, filii hujus Herodis et fratres Archelai, petierunt ab imperatore partem regni paterni: qui consilio habito, divisit regnum majoris Herodis in duas partes, dans unam medietatem Archelao; aliam vero medietatem in duas partitus est, dans unam Herodi minori, videlicet Galilæam, aliamque Philippo, puta Ituræam et Trachonitidem regionem. Medietas vero Archelao concessa, tenuit nomen Judææ: ideo Archelaus dicitur in Judæa regnasse. Et quoniam a patre suo constitutus erat hæres totius regni, et carior patri, idcirco favit machinationibus patris sui de Christi occisione et aliis malis. Unde Joseph proditionem formidans, non audebat ad terram Archelai reverti, sicut subjungitur: timuit illo ire, id est ad Judæam transire. Et admonitus in somnis, haud dubium quin ab angelo, secessit in partes Galilææ, id est, per loca et terminos Galilææ transivit, quia Herodes dominus Galilææ patrem suum non dilexit, a quo regno erat privatus: ideo Joseph in terra ejus securius morabatur.
paras.en: [[2:21|Who arose, and took the child and his mother, and came into the land of Israel|Qui consurgens, accepit puerum et matrem ejus, et venit in terram Israel]]. [[2:22|But hearing|Audiens autem]], Joseph, that is, that Archelaus, the son of Herod, [[2:22|reigned in Judea in the room of Herod his father|regnaret in Judæa pro Herode patre suo]]. Josephus relates that Herod left his whole kingdom to Archelaus, whom he loved more than his other sons. Herod and Philip, then, sons of this Herod and brothers of Archelaus, asked the emperor for a share of their father’s kingdom; and he, having taken counsel, divided the kingdom of the elder Herod into two parts, giving one half to Archelaus, and dividing the other half in two, giving one part, namely Galilee, to the younger Herod, and the other to Philip, that is, Iturea and the country of Trachonitis. The half granted to Archelaus kept the name of Judea; that is why Archelaus is said to have reigned in Judea. And since he had been appointed by his father heir of the whole kingdom, and was dearer to his father, he favoured his father’s schemes for the killing of Christ, and other evils. Hence Joseph, fearing betrayal, did not dare to return to the land of Archelaus, as is added: [[2:22|he was afraid to go thither|timuit illo ire]], that is, to cross into Judea. [[2:22|and being warned in sleep|Et admonitus in somnis]], doubtless by an angel, he [[2:22|retired into the quarters of Galilee|secessit in partes Galilææ]], that is, he passed through the places and borders of Galilee, because Herod, the lord of Galilee, had no love for his father, by whom he had been deprived of the kingdom; and so Joseph lived more safely in his land.

paras.t: Et veniens Joseph habitavit cum Maria et puero in civitate quæ vocatur Nazareth, in qua angelus Virgini Christi conceptionem annuntiavit; ut adimpleretur in Christi habitatione in Nazareth, quod dictum est per Prophetas: Quoniam Nazaræus vocabitur Christus, quia in Nazareth fuit moratus, conceptus atque nutritus. Hoc in Isaia secundum Hebraicam veritatem sic legitur: Egredietur virga de radice Jesse, et Nazaræus de radice ejus consurget. Loco cujus nos habemus: Et flos de radice ejus ascendet. Et forsitan alii Prophetæ, quorum scripta non habentur, idem dixerunt. Non enim omnium Prophetarum libros habemus, et tamen omnes Prophetæ de Christo locuti sunt. Unde Philippus sciens hoc a Prophetis prædictum, ait ad Nathanael: Quem scripsit Moyses et Prophetæ, invenimus Jesum filium Joseph a Nazareth. Cui concordans Nathanael: A Nazareth, inquit, potest aliquid boni esse?
paras.en: [[2:23|And coming|Et veniens]], Joseph [[2:23|dwelt|habitavit]] with Mary and the child [[2:23|in a city called Nazareth|in civitate quæ vocatur Nazareth]], in which the angel announced to the Virgin the conception of Christ[[Luke 1:26||]][[Luke 1:31||]]; [[2:23|that it might be fulfilled|ut adimpleretur]], in Christ’s dwelling in Nazareth, [[2:23|which was said by the prophets: That he shall be called a Nazarene|quod dictum est per Prophetas: Quoniam Nazaræus vocabitur]], Christ, that is, because in Nazareth He lived, was conceived and was brought up. This is read in Isaias, according to the Hebrew original, thus: [[Is 11:1|there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse|Egredietur virga de radice Jesse]], and a Nazarene shall rise up from his root [the Hebrew has neṣer, “shoot” or “branch”, the word St Jerome takes to lie behind “Nazarene”]. In its place we have: [[Is 11:1|and a flower shall rise up out of his root|Et flos de radice ejus ascendet]]. And perhaps other Prophets, whose writings we do not have, said the same; for we do not have the books of all the Prophets, and yet all the Prophets spoke of Christ. Hence Philip, knowing that this had been foretold by the Prophets, said to Nathanael: [[John 1:45|We have found him of whom Moses, in the law and the prophets did write, Jesus the son of Joseph of Nazareth|Quem scripsit Moyses et Prophetæ, invenimus Jesum filium Joseph a Nazareth]]. And Nathanael, agreeing with him, says: [[John 1:46|Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?|A Nazareth, inquit, potest aliquid boni esse?]] [Denis takes these words as assent, as St Augustine does, reading them “From Nazareth something good can come”]

paras.t: Postremo in fine capituli recolo, quod pene excidit mente, videlicet stellam quæ Magis apparuit, non dici stellam univoce cum veris stellis. Differebat nempe ab illis, sicut corruptibile ab incorruptibili. Formata est enim angelico ministerio de materia elementari et corruptibili, peractoque suo obsequio, in præjacentem est resoluta materiam. Sed et motu, loco ac tempore, differebat a veris sideribus, sicut in diversis libris satis ostenditur: idcirco pertranseo.
paras.en: Lastly, at the end of the chapter, I recall something that almost slipped my mind: namely, that the star which appeared to the Magi is not called a star univocally with the true stars [univocally: in one and the same sense of the word]. For it differed from them as the corruptible from the incorruptible: it was formed by the ministry of angels out of elemental and corruptible matter, and when its service was done it was dissolved into the matter from which it had been made. It differed from the true stars also in motion, place and time, as is shown well enough in various books; and so I pass over it.

paras.t: Item circa illud quod dictum est, Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum, dicit Hieronymus: Possumus hunc locum aliter conciliare propter contentiosos, et testimonium proferimus ex Numeris, dicente Balaam: Deus ex Ægypto vocavit eum; gloria ejus ut unicornis. Loco cujus habemus, Fortitudo ejus sicut rhinocerotis: hoc enim in Numeris scriptum est. Sed agnoscendum, quod hoc non minus litteraliter dictum est de populo Israel, quam præinductum verbum Osee. Quum enim Balaam retulisset, Non est idolum in Jacob nec simulacrum in Israel, subdidit: Dominus Deus eduxit eum de Ægypto, etc.
paras.en: Again, concerning the words [[2:15|Out of Egypt have I called my son|Ex Ægypto vocavi filium meum]], Jerome says: “We can reconcile this passage in another way, for the sake of the contentious, and we bring forward a testimony from Numbers, where Balaam says: God called him out of Egypt; his glory is as of the unicorn” [Jerome quotes Balaam’s words as the Greek Septuagint has them; the Vulgate reads “God hath brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like to the rhinoceros”]. In its place we have: [[Num 23:22|whose strength is like to the rhinoceros|Fortitudo ejus sicut rhinocerotis]]; for this is what is written in Numbers. But it must be recognized that this was said no less literally of the people of Israel than the word of Osee brought forward above. For when Balaam had said, [[Num 23:21|There is no idol in Jacob, neither is there an image god to be seen in Israel|Non est idolum in Jacob nec simulacrum in Israel]], he added: the Lord [[Num 23:22|God hath brought him out of Egypt|Deus eduxit eum de Ægypto]], etc.

3.title: Expositio capituli tertii: In diebus autem illis venit Joannes
3.title_en: Exposition of the third chapter: “And in those days cometh John”

paras.t: Tractaturus beatissimus Evangelista in sequentibus de conversatione, doctrina atque miraculis Christi, primo de præcursore ipsius mentionem inducit, sanctitatem, idoneitatem, doctrinam et vitam Joannis describens, ut innotescat quam dignum et credibile sit testimonium ejus de Christo. Christus ergo, qui est lux vera, summa et infinita, sciens mundum sui immediate non esse capacem, præmisit magnum quemdam sui adventus præparatorem, qui corda Judæorum ad Christi receptionem disponeret.
paras.en: The most blessed Evangelist, being about to treat in what follows of the life, teaching and miracles of Christ, first makes mention of His forerunner, describing the holiness, fitness, teaching and life of John, so that it may be known how worthy and credible is his testimony concerning Christ. Christ, then, who is the true light[[John 1:9||]], supreme and infinite, knowing that the world was not capable of receiving Him immediately, sent before Him a great preparer of His coming, to dispose the hearts of the Jews to receive Christ.

paras.t: In diebus autem illis, quando videlicet Jesus adhuc habitabat in Nazareth, puta circa tricesimum annum Christi, non quando rediit de Ægypto, venit Joannes Baptista. Unde? nisi a latibulis eremi, in quibus hucusque solitariam vitam duxit. Venit ergo ab occulto loco deserti ad loca ejusdem deserti publica, ubi hominibus se videndum exhibuit. Prædicans in deserto Judææ: in quo utique deserto fuerat enutritus; et dicens: Pœnitentiam agite, id est, peccata vestra deflete, et per opera pœnitentiæ pro eis satisfacite, nec deplorata reiterate. Pœnitentia tripliciter sumitur: primo, pro sacramento; secundo, pro virtute morali quæ est pars justitiæ; tertio, pro actu pœnitentis: sic modo accipitur. Appropinquabit enim regnum cœlorum, id est, jam in proximo est ut janua patriæ aperiatur per Christum, ut gratia et veritas fiat per Salvatorem, ut beatitudo cœlestis condonetur electis. Christus namque per suam passionem regnum cœlorum aperuit. Regnum ergo cœlorum vocatur patria, vel præmium electorum, seu triumphans Ecclesia. Hoc regnum primum publice prædicatum est a Joanne. In veteri etenim Testamento promittebantur bona terrena aperte, cœlestia vero quasi implicite.
paras.en: [[3:1|And in those days|In diebus autem illis]], that is, when Jesus was still living in Nazareth, about the thirtieth year of Christ, not when He returned from Egypt, [[3:1|cometh John the Baptist|venit Joannes Baptista]]. From where? From the hiding-places of the wilderness, surely, in which until then he had led a solitary life. He came, then, from a hidden spot in the desert to the public places of the same desert, where he showed himself to be seen by men; [[3:1|preaching in the desert of Judea|Prædicans in deserto Judææ]], in which desert indeed he had been brought up; [[3:2|and saying: Do penance|et dicens: Pœnitentiam agite]], that is, weep for your sins, and make satisfaction for them by works of penance, and do not commit again what you have wept for. Penance is taken in three ways: first, for the sacrament; secondly, for the moral virtue which is a part of justice; thirdly, for the act of the penitent; and it is taken so here. [[3:2|for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Appropinquabit enim regnum cœlorum]] [Denis reads the future, “will draw near”], that is, it is now close at hand that the gate of the fatherland be opened through Christ, that grace and truth come by the Saviour[[John 1:17||]], that heavenly beatitude be granted to the elect. For Christ opened the kingdom of heaven by His passion. The kingdom of heaven, then, is the name given to the fatherland, or the reward of the elect, or the Church triumphant. This kingdom was first preached publicly by John; for in the Old Testament earthly goods were promised openly, but heavenly ones only as it were implicitly.

paras.t: Consequenter dignitas Joannis prophetico testimonio declaratur. Hic, id est iste Joannes Baptista, est enim qui dictus, id est prænuntiatus, est per Isaiam prophetam, dicentem: Vox clamantis in deserto, id est sermo Joannis in solitudine prædicantis, est iste qui subditur: Parate viam Domini, id est, corda vestra disponite ad receptionem inhabitationemque Christi, vitiorum obliquitates, seu gratiæ obicem repellendo, et quod in vobis est faciendo; rectas facite semitas ejus, id est, divina præcepta atque consilia, quibus itur ad Deum, pure et irreprehensibiliter observate. Itaque Domino viam parare, est pœnitentiam agere. Quemadmodum autem terrenus rex urbem aliquam ingressurus, habet præcursores, qui viarum sordes amoveant, vias complanent, hospitium ornent; sic Christus rex cœlestis ad hominum corda venturus præmisit Joannem, qui viam sibi pararet inducendo homines ad virtutes. Ipse quoque Joannes, vox clamantis vocatur. Sic enim respondit Judæis: Ego vox clamantis, etc. Dicitur enim vox per similitudinem, seu ratione officii: primo, quoniam sicut vox prior est verbo ordine naturæ, sic Joannes præcessit Christum; secundo, quia ut vox rem significatam notificat, sic Joannes Christum monstravit. Dicitur autem vox clamantis, id est Christi seu Dei per ipsum loquentis, in deserto: quia non ipse erat qui loquebatur, sed Spiritus Sanctus, et Christus per eum, secundum quod Paulus ait: An experimentum quæritis ejus qui in me loquitur Christus?
paras.en: Next, the dignity of John is declared by the testimony of prophecy. [[3:3|For this|Hic]], that is, this John the Baptist, [[3:3|is he that was spoken of|est enim qui dictus]], that is, foretold, [[3:3|by Isaias the prophet, saying: A voice of one crying in the desert|est per Isaiam prophetam, dicentem: Vox clamantis in deserto]], that is, the word of John preaching in the wilderness, is this which follows: [[3:3|Prepare ye the way of the Lord|Parate viam Domini]], that is, dispose your hearts to receive Christ and to have Him dwell in them, by putting away the crookedness of vices, or the obstacle to grace, and by doing what lies in you; [[3:3|make straight his paths|rectas facite semitas ejus]], that is, keep purely and blamelessly the divine precepts and counsels by which men go to God. And so to prepare the way for the Lord is to do penance. Just as an earthly king about to enter some city has forerunners to clear away the filth of the roads, level the ways and adorn his lodging, so Christ, the heavenly King, being about to come into the hearts of men, sent John before Him to prepare His way by leading men to the virtues. John himself, too, is called the voice of one crying; for so he answered the Jews: [[John 1:23|I am the voice of one crying|Ego vox clamantis]], etc. He is called a voice by a likeness, or by reason of his office: first, because just as the voice comes before the word in the order of nature, so John went before Christ [the Latin verbum, “word”, is also the name of the Son, the Word]; secondly, because as the voice makes known the thing it signifies, so John pointed out Christ. And he is called [[3:3|a voice of one crying|vox clamantis]], that is, of Christ or of God speaking through him, [[3:3|in the desert|in deserto]]; for it was not he who spoke, but the Holy Ghost, and Christ through him, according to what Paul says: [[2 Cor 13:3|Do you seek a proof of Christ that speaketh in me|An experimentum quæritis ejus qui in me loquitur Christus]]?

paras.t: Deinde describitur austeritas vitæ Joannis in victu et vestibus. Ipse autem Joannes habebat vestimentum de pilis camelorum, videlicet vestem cilicinam, seu pellem cameli, unaque veste erat contentus, et zonam pelliceam, id est grossam corrigiam, circa lumbos suos, quemadmodum et Elias, eratque de duris et crudis pellicearum minutiis facta. Esca autem ejus erat locusta. Locusta significat tria, videlicet herbam, radicem, et avem minutam. Chrysostomus autem et alii multi hoc loco per locustas intelligunt animalia parva non alte volantia, quæ in deserto Judææ abundabant, et frixa cum oleo esca sunt pauperum. Alii per locustas intelligunt herbas deserti, quum non videatur probabile, quod Joannes, qui nec pane vescebatur, carnes animalium aut aliquid coctum comederit. Et mel silvestre, id est, quod in silvis reperitur, et arborum truncis. Rabanus autem per mel silvestre intelligit quoddam genus foliorum, quæ alba et tenera, manibusque attrita, melleum habent saporem.
paras.en: Then the austerity of John’s life in food and clothing is described. [[3:4|And the same John had his garment of camel's hair|Ipse autem Joannes habebat vestimentum de pilis camelorum]], that is, a garment of haircloth, or a camel’s skin, and he was content with a single garment; [[3:4|and a leathern girdle|et zonam pelliceam]], that is, a coarse strap, [[3:4|about his loins|circa lumbos suos]], as Elias also had[[4 Kings 1:8||]], and it was made of hard, raw scraps of hide. [[3:4|And his meat was locusts|Esca autem ejus erat locusta]]. The word locusta means three things: a herb, a root, and a small winged creature. Chrysostom and many others understand by locusts in this place small creatures that do not fly high, which abounded in the desert of Judea and which, fried in oil, are the food of the poor. Others understand by locusts the herbs of the desert, since it does not seem probable that John, who did not even eat bread, ate the flesh of animals or anything cooked. [[3:4|and wild honey|Et mel silvestre]], that is, honey that is found in the woods and in the trunks of trees. Rabanus, however, understands by wild honey a kind of leaves which, being white and tender, when rubbed in the hands have the taste of honey.

paras.t: Tunc exibat ad eum, videlicet ad Joannem in desertum (et postea, quando Joannes descendit ad Jordanem, ut Lucas dicit, venit ad eum illuc), Jerosolyma, id est habitatores Jerusalem etiam in maxima multitudine. Unde Marcus enarrat, quod egrediebantur ad eum Jerosolymitæ universi. Et omnis Judæa, id est aliqui de omni genere populi Judæorum, et omnis regio circa Jordanem, id est etiam illi qui circa Jordanem morabantur, videlicet Galilæi. Ponitur hoc loco continens pro contento, et locus pro locato. Et baptizabantur, id est, corporaliter lavabantur, non intus purgabantur a culpa, ab eo in Jordane, confitentes peccata sua, in communi, non confessione sacramentali distincta atque plenaria, prout Confessio est sacramentum novæ legis et gratiæ. Sic enim instituta est a Salvatore, nec erat in veteri lege, in qua data non erat potestas hominibus ligandi atque solvendi, seu vitia relaxandi: imo nec Joanni data est ista potestas.
paras.en: [[3:5|Then went out to him|Tunc exibat ad eum]], that is, to John in the desert (and afterwards, when John went down to the Jordan, as Luke says[[Luke 3:3||]], it came to him there), [[3:5|Jerusalem|Jerosolyma]], that is, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and in very great numbers; whence Mark relates that [[Mark 1:5|there went out to him|egrediebantur ad eum]] [[Mark 1:5|all they of Jerusalem|Jerosolymitæ universi]]. [[3:5|and all Judea|Et omnis Judæa]], that is, some of every kind of the Jewish people, [[3:5|and all the country about Jordan|et omnis regio circa Jordanem]], that is, those too who lived about the Jordan, namely the Galileans. Here the container is put for what it contains, and the place for those in the place. [[3:6|And were baptized|Et baptizabantur]], that is, they were washed in body, not cleansed inwardly from guilt, [[3:6|by him in the Jordan, confessing their sins|ab eo in Jordane, confitentes peccata sua]], in general, not by a sacramental confession, distinct and complete, such as Confession is as a sacrament of the new law and of grace. For it was so instituted by the Saviour, and did not exist in the old law, in which men had not been given the power of binding and loosing, or of remitting sins; nay, not even to John was this power given.

paras.t: Denique Damascenus (libri quarti capitulo nono) ponit octo genera baptismatum. Primum vocat diluvium, secundum transitum maris Rubri, tertium ablutionem legalem, quartum baptisma Joannis, quintum baptisma Christi, quo ipse a Joanne baptizari dignatus est, sextum baptisma pœnitentiæ seu lacrimarum, septimum sanguinis seu martyrii, octavum Flaminis seu Spiritus. Gregorius vero Nazianzenus non ponit nisi quinque genera baptismatum. Nam tria prima genera comprehendit sub uno, quod nominat baptisma figurativum. Baptisma quoque quod Joannes dedit, et Christus accepit, sub uno videtur genere comprehendisse. Primum itaque genus baptismi secundum eum, vocatur figurativum, ut erat transitus maris Rubri, et lotio corporalis in aqua, secundum Mosaicam legem. Secundum genus vocatur præparatorium, puta baptisma Joannis, quod disponebat ad Christi Baptismum a Christo institutum. Tertium dicitur purgativum, quo regeneramur ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto, et purgamur ab omni piaculo. Quartum vocatur supererogativum, videlicet baptismus sanguinis. Quintum est quotidianum, videlicet lacrimarum baptismus.
paras.en: Damascene, moreover (book IV, chapter 9), sets down eight kinds of baptism. The first he calls the flood; the second, the crossing of the Red Sea; the third, the washing of the law; the fourth, the baptism of John; the fifth, the baptism of Christ, with which He deigned to be baptized by John; the sixth, the baptism of penance or of tears; the seventh, that of blood or of martyrdom; the eighth, that of the Breath, or of the Spirit [Latin flamen, “breath”: what is now called baptism of desire]. Gregory Nazianzen, however, sets down only five kinds of baptism. For he includes the first three kinds under one, which he names figurative baptism; and he seems to have included the baptism that John gave and Christ received under one kind as well. The first kind of baptism, then, according to him, is called figurative, such as was the crossing of the Red Sea, and the bodily washing in water according to the law of Moses[[Lev 12:1||]]. The second kind is called preparatory, namely the baptism of John, which disposed men for the Baptism of Christ instituted by Christ. The third is called purifying, by which we are born again of water and the Holy Ghost and are cleansed from every sin. The fourth is called supererogatory, namely the baptism of blood. The fifth is the daily one, namely the baptism of tears.

paras.t: Sciendum ergo, secundum Thomam super quartum Sententiarum, unum dumtaxat esse Baptisma proprie dictum, quod celebratur in aqua sub determinata et certa verborum forma a Christo præfixa: de quo Matthæus ait, Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti. Alia vero nomen baptismi sortiuntur secundum ordinem quemdam ad istud Baptisma: et hoc tripliciter. Primo, in quantum aliquid fuerat signum hujus Baptismatis. Sicque diluvium appellatur baptisma, prout nostrum Baptisma præfiguravit, quantum ad spiritualis vitæ salvationem, ex salvatione naturalis vitæ humani generis facta in arca Noe. Unde scriptum est apud Petrum apostolum: In arca pauci, id est octo animæ salvæ factæ sunt per aquam: quod et vos nunc similis formæ salvos facit Baptisma. Transitus quoque maris Rubri baptisma asseritur, quoniam nostrum Baptismum præfiguravit quoad liberationem a potestate diaboli, sicut per transitum maris liberabantur Hebræi a potestate regis Ægypti. Hinc dicit Apostolus: Omnes in Moyse baptizati sunt, in nube et in mari. Nubes autem significavit Spiritum Sanctum et gratiam ejus; mare vero, aquam Baptismi. Ablutiones etiam legis figurabant Baptismum, secundum quod mundat a macula culpæ, quemadmodum ablutiones illæ mundabant ab immunditiis corporalibus. Alio modo dicitur aliquid baptismus, quia aliquo modo causa fuit nostri Baptismi: sicque baptismus Joannis vocatur baptismus, tanquam disponens ad eum, et baptismus Christi passivus, tanquam dans efficaciam ei. Tertio aliquid nuncupatur baptismus, secundum proportionem ad eumdem effectum Baptismi proprie sumpti: et ita martyrium, pœnitentia, et Spiritus Sancti infusio, baptismata appellantur. De baptismate autem Spiritus ait Salvator Apostolis: Vos baptizabimini Spiritu Sancto, non post multos hos dies. De baptismo insuper sanguinis: Ego, inquit, baptismo habeo baptizari.
paras.en: It is to be known, then, according to Thomas on the fourth book of the Sentences, that there is only one Baptism properly so called, which is celebrated in water under a determined and fixed form of words laid down by Christ; of which Matthew says: [[Matt 28:19|Going therefore, teach ye all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost|Euntes docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti]]. The others receive the name of baptism by a certain relation to this Baptism, and that in three ways. First, inasmuch as something had been a sign of this Baptism. And so the flood is called a baptism, inasmuch as it prefigured our Baptism with respect to the saving of the spiritual life, by the saving of the natural life of the human race that was wrought in Noe’s ark.
