Est quoque alia ratio cur non debeamus jurare sine necessitate, vel magna utilitate, quamvis sint vera qua dicimus : quia hoc cedit ad irreverentiam Dei, quod homo tam leviter, inadvertenter et intimorate assumit tantæ sanctitatis majestatem in testem. Quod autem jurare non sit prorsus illicitum, innotescit per hoc quod Paulus in suis epistolis toties invenitur jurasse, dicendo : Testis est mihi Deus ; et, Testificor coram Deo, etc.
paras.en: [[5:34|But I say to you not to swear at all|Ego autem dico vobis, non jurare omnino]]. According to Jerome, Christ does not forbid swearing by God, but by the things that follow, namely, [[5:34|neither by heaven|neque per cælum]], etc. But since it is added at once, [[5:37|But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no|Sit autem sermo vester, est, est: non, non]], it is understood, according to some, that Christ dissuaded or forbade even an oath by God; not because it is always evil and unlawful, but, as Augustine says, lest by the habit of swearing a man fall into perjury. There is also another reason why we ought not to swear without necessity or great usefulness, even though what we say is true: because it tends to irreverence towards God that a man should so lightly, heedlessly and fearlessly take the majesty of so great a holiness as his witness. But that swearing is not altogether unlawful is made known by the fact that Paul is found to have sworn so often in his epistles, saying: [[Rom 1:9|For God is my witness|Testis enim mihi est Deus]]; and, [[1 Tim 5:21|I charge thee, before God|Testor coram Deo]], etc.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Hieronymum super illud Jeremiæ, Jurabis, Vivit Dominus, in veritate, et judicio, et justitia, tres sunt comites juramenti, videlicet veritas, judicium, et justitia; et quodcumque horum defuerit, juramentum erit illicitum. Imo sic jurans, eo ipso quo jurat, perjurus efficitur, secundum Thomam, quia hæc observare tenetur in quolibet casu. Si enim desit veritas, juramentum est mendax ; si judicium desit, juramentum est temerarium et incautum ; si justitia, iniquum est, leve atque inutile. Veritas itaque ad juramentum ordinata, requiritur ex parte rei de qua juratur; judicium vero seu discretio, ex parte jurantis; Justitia autem, ex parte causæ, ut sit necessitas ad jurandum. Juratio ergo debite circumstantionata, videlicet, ut fiat ex causa necessaria, tune ubi taliter fit et propter congruum finem, non solum est licita, sed et actus virtutis quæ dicitur latria. Qui enim sic jurat, exhibet reverentiam Deo, presupponens eum habere infallibilem veritatem, omniumque certam notitiam, ac universalem providentiam. Unde ait Scriptura : In omni corde suo juraverunt Domino, et invenerunt ; et Psalmista, Laudabuntur omnes qui jurant in eo. Hieronymus quoque affirmat, quod jurans veneratur vel diligit eum per quem jurat.
paras.en: Further, according to Jerome on the words of Jeremias, [[Jer 4:2|And thou shalt swear: As the Lord liveth, in truth, and in judgment, and in justice|Et jurabis: Vivit Dominus in veritate, et in judicio, et in justitia]], there are three companions of an oath, namely truth, judgment and justice; and if any of these is lacking, the oath will be unlawful. Indeed one who swears so becomes a perjurer by the very fact that he swears, according to Thomas, because he is bound to observe these in every case. For if truth is lacking, the oath is lying; if judgment is lacking, the oath is rash and incautious; if justice, it is wicked, light and useless. Truth, then, as ordered to an oath, is required on the side of the thing sworn to; judgment or discretion on the side of the one swearing; and justice on the side of the cause, that there be a necessity for swearing. An oath, therefore, clothed with its due circumstances, namely that it be made from a necessary cause, at a time when it is fitting, and for a fitting end, is not only lawful but also an act of the virtue called latria [the worship due to God alone]. For he who swears in this way shows reverence to God, presupposing that He has infallible truth, certain knowledge of all things, and universal providence. Hence Scripture says: [[2 Par 15:15|for with all their heart they swore|in omni enim corde suo juraverunt]], [[2 Par 15:15|and they found him|et invenerunt]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 62:12|all they shall be praised that swear by him|laudabuntur omnes qui jurant in eo]]. Jerome also affirms that he who swears venerates or loves him by whom he swears.

paras.t: Sic ergo intelligenda est littera : Dico vobis non jurare omnino, hoc est non jurare omnibus modis indifferenter, seu ex qualibet causa, sed solum modo jam dicto, videlicet neque per cœlum, quia thronus, id est sedes et habitatio, Dei est. Quamvis enim incircumscriptus immensusque Deus loco nullo claudatur, ibi tamen esse asseritur, ubi operatur et se ipsum ostendit. Quum ergo in cœlo empyreo maxime operetur, illicque facie ad faciem conspiciatur, merito coelum empyreum appellatur thronus ejus. Unde Unigenitus Dei : Ego (inquit) vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus. Neque per terram juraveris, quia scabellum pedum ejus est, id est divinæ potestati subjecta, et a Deo in ultimo ac infimo rerum ordine collocata. Per pedes itaque Dei, designatur operatio seu provisio ejus, pertingens usque ad infima. Hoc idem in Isaia scriptum est : Hæc dicit Dominus : Cœlum mihi sedes est, et terra scabellum pedum meorum. Non est itaque sic intelligendum, quasi Deus in divinitatis natura eorporalia habeat lineamenta, et situaliter sedeat, præsertim quum de ipso scriptum sit : Excelsior cœlo est, et profundior inferno ; longior terra mensura ejus, et latior mari. Neque per Jerosolymam juraveris, quia civitas est magni regis : de quo legitur in libro Esther : Domine rex omnipotens, in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita ; et in Psalmo, Quoniam Deus magnus Dominus, et rex magnus super omnes deos. Fuit enim Jerusalem deputata ad hujus regis obsequium. Neque per caput tuum juraveris, quia non potes unum capillum album facere aut nigrum, propria potestate et solo imperio, quamvis per artem et naturalium rerum applicationem possit homo diversos colores crinibus capitis sui inducere.
paras.en: So, then, the letter is to be understood: [[5:34|But I say to you not to swear at all|Ego autem dico vobis, non jurare omnino]], that is, not to swear in every manner indifferently, or from any cause whatever, but only in the way just stated; namely [[5:34|neither by heaven for it is the throne of God|neque per cælum, quia thronus Dei est]], that is, His seat and dwelling. For though God, being uncircumscribed and immense, is shut in by no place, He is said to be there where He works and shows Himself. Since, then, He works most of all in the empyrean heaven, and is there seen face to face[[1 Cor 13:12||]], the empyrean heaven is rightly called His throne. Hence the Only-begotten of God says: [[Apoc 3:21|I also have overcome and am set down with my Father in his throne|ego vici, et sedi cum Patre meo in throno ejus]]. [[5:35|Nor by the earth, for it is his footstool|neque per terram, quia scabellum est pedum ejus]], that is, subject to the divine power, and set by God in the last and lowest order of things. By the feet of God, then, is signified His working or providence, reaching even to the lowest things. The same is written in Isaias: [[Is 66:1|Thus saith the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth my footstool|Hæc dicit Dominus: Cælum sedes mea, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum]]. It is not, then, to be understood as though God in the nature of His Godhead had bodily features and sat in a place, especially since it is written of Him: [[Job 11:8|He is higher than heaven|Excelsior cælo est]], and [[Job 11:8|deeper than hell|profundior inferno]]; [[Job 11:9|The measure of him is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea|Longior terra mensura ejus, et latior mari]]. [[5:35|Nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great king|neque per Jerosolymam, quia civitas est magni regis]], of whom we read in the book of Esther: O Lord, almighty king, [[Esth 13:9|for all things are in thy power|in ditione enim tua cuncta sunt posita]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 94:3|For the Lord is a great God, and a great King above all gods|quoniam Deus magnus Dominus, et rex magnus super omnes deos]]. For Jerusalem was set apart for the service of this King. [[5:36|Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black|neque per caput tuum juraveris, quia non potes unum capillum album facere, aut nigrum]], by thine own power and by command alone; although by art and by the application of natural things a man can put various colours on the hair of his head.

paras.t: Ecce non solum per Deum, sed etiam per creaturas jurare prohibuit vel dissuasit. Sed quomodo intelligendum est hoc? Nonne per Evangelium et per Sanctos fit lieitum juramentum ? Nonne Joseph per salutem Pharaonis juravit? Nonne Apostolus dicit, Ego testem invoco Deum in animam meam? Quæritur ergo, quando et quomodo liceat per creaturas jurare. Respondet B. Thomas, quod juramentum fit dupliciter : primo, per simplicem contestationem ; secundo, per exsecrationem. Juramentum primo modo factum, principaliter divine veritati innititur. Secundario autem assumuntur aliqua creaturæ ad jurandum, non secundum se, sed in quantum divina in eis veritas manifestatur : sicque juratur per Evangelium, id est per Deum, cujus veritas in Evangelio continetur ; et item per Sanctos, qui hanc veritatem crediderunt. In juramento autem quod fit per exsecrationem, assumitur creatura tanquam id in quo divinum exerceatur judicium, si non verum asseritur, ut quum homo jurat per caput, vel filium suum, seu aliam rem dilectam. Denique, sicut licitum est jurare per Deum pro loco, causa et tempore, sic et per creaturas, tam per simplicem contestationem, quam per exsecrationem. Per exsecrationem namque juravit Apostolus : Ego, inquiens, testem invoco Deum in animam meam. Quod vero Joseph per salutem Pharaonis juraverit, utroque modo intelligi potest, videlicet : per modum exsecrationis, ita quod Pharaonis salutem obligavit Deo ; et per modum contestationis, contestando veritatem divina justitiæ, ad cujus exsecutionem principes terræ constituuntur, quorum unus fuit Pharao : sicque per ejus salutem juravit Joseph, in quantum divina justitia in Pharaonis imperio monstrabatur. Quum ergo per creaturas juratur, jurans obligatur implere jurata, ac si per Deum juraret : quia non jurat per creaturas, nisi in quantum divina virtus in eis relucet. Ideo quoque non licet per eas jurare, nisi circumstantiis debitis observatis, quemadmodum nec per Deum.
paras.en: Behold, He forbade or dissuaded swearing not only by God but also by creatures. But how is this to be understood? Is not a lawful oath made by the Gospel and by the Saints? Did not Joseph swear by the health of Pharao[[Gen 42:15||]][[Gen 42:16||]]? Does not the Apostle say, [[2 Cor 1:23|I call God to witness upon my soul|Ego autem testem Deum invoco in animam meam]]? It is asked, then, when and how it is lawful to swear by creatures. Blessed Thomas answers that an oath is made in two ways: first, by simple attestation; secondly, by execration [that is, by calling down a curse on oneself or on what one holds dear, if what is sworn be false]. An oath made in the first way rests principally on the divine truth; but secondarily certain creatures are taken up for swearing, not for their own sake, but inasmuch as the divine truth is shown forth in them. So one swears by the Gospel, that is, by God, whose truth is contained in the Gospel; and likewise by the Saints, who believed this truth. But in an oath made by execration, a creature is taken up as that upon which the divine judgment is to be exercised if what is asserted is not true, as when a man swears by his head, or by his son, or by some other beloved thing. Further, as it is lawful to swear by God with due regard to place, cause and time, so too by creatures, both by simple attestation and by execration. For the Apostle swore by execration, saying: [[2 Cor 1:23|I call God to witness upon my soul|Ego autem testem Deum invoco in animam meam]]. That Joseph swore by the health of Pharao can be understood in both ways: by way of execration, in that he pledged Pharao’s health to God; and by way of attestation, by calling to witness the truth of the divine justice, for the carrying out of which the princes of the earth are appointed, one of whom was Pharao: and so Joseph swore by his health inasmuch as the divine justice was shown in Pharao’s rule. When, then, one swears by creatures, the one swearing is bound to fulfil what he has sworn, as if he swore by God, because he swears by creatures only inasmuch as the divine power shines in them. And for this reason too it is not lawful to swear by them unless the due circumstances are observed, just as it is not lawful by God.

paras.t: Est etiam alia ratio cur Christus per creaturas jurare prohibuit : quia speciem idololatriæ habet hujusmodi juramentum. Idololatre enim sic jurant; et ei per quod juratur divinus honor impendi videtur, ut tangit hoc loco Hieronymus. Quid enim est jurare, nisi infallibilem testem ad confirmationem verborum inducere ? Christus vero insinuat, ideo per creaturas non esse jurandum sine causa necessaria, quia in eis aliquid divine virtutis relucet. Dicit enim : Neque per cœlum, quia thronus Dei est, id est, gloria Dei manifestatur in cœlo; neque per terram, quia scabellum pedum ejus est, id est, in terra relucet dispositio potestatis divinæ : sicque jurando per cœlum aut terram, juratur per eum cujus majestas presentatur in cœlo, vel cujus dispositio relucet in terra. Per hoc quoque quod non possumus unum capillum capitis nostri facere album vel nigrum, evidenter patescit quod non a nobis, sed a Deo ipsum caput accepimus.
paras.en: There is also another reason why Christ forbade swearing by creatures: because an oath of this kind has the appearance of idolatry. For idolaters swear in this way; and divine honour seems to be paid to that by which one swears, as Jerome touches on in this place. For what is swearing, but bringing in an infallible witness to confirm one’s words? But Christ suggests that one must not swear by creatures without necessary cause precisely because something of the divine power shines in them. For He says: [[5:34|neither by heaven for it is the throne of God|neque per cælum, quia thronus Dei est]], that is, the glory of God is manifested in heaven; [[5:35|Nor by the earth, for it is his footstool|neque per terram, quia scabellum est pedum ejus]], that is, the ordering of the divine power shines in the earth: and so in swearing by heaven or earth one swears by Him whose majesty is present in heaven, or whose ordering shines in the earth. And by the fact that we cannot make one hair of our head white or black, it is plainly shown that we have received the head itself not from ourselves but from God.

paras.t: Sit autem sermo vester, Est, est ; Non, non : id est, simpliciter affirmate quod verum est, et negate quod falsum est, nee adhibeatur juratio sine necessitate. Quod autem his abundantius est, id est, juramentum quod affirmationi seu negationi superadditur, a malo est, id est, ex malo culpæ, vel malo pœna procedit, videlicet ex infirmitate, incredulitate, vel suspicione ejus qui exigit juramentum, vel ex malo jurantis, qui jurat omissis tribus prædictis juramenti comitibus. Non dixit, Quod his abundantius est, malum est; sed, malo : quia juramentum non est semper peccatum, sed origo juramenti est malum quoddam, videlicet quoniam homines sibi invicem discredunt.
paras.en: [[5:37|But let your speech be yea, yea: no, no|Sit autem sermo vester, est, est: non, non]]; that is, simply affirm what is true and deny what is false, and let no oath be added without necessity. [[5:37|And that which is over and above these|quod autem his abundantius est]], that is, an oath added over and above the affirmation or denial, [[5:37|is of evil|a malo est]], that is, proceeds from the evil of fault or the evil of punishment: namely from the weakness, unbelief or suspicion of him who demands the oath, or from the evil of him who swears, when he swears leaving out the three companions of an oath mentioned above. He did not say, “That which is over and above these is evil”, but, “is of evil”: because an oath is not always a sin, but the origin of an oath is a certain evil, namely that men do not believe one another.

5.title: Elucidatio sequentis partis hujus capituli, usque ad finem ipsius, videlicet: Audistis quia dictum est
5.title_en: Explanation of the following part of this chapter, to its end, namely: “You have heard that it hath been said”
5.note: This article goes on into chapter 6 (vv. 1–4); that part is shown there. A line in each column of p. 73 is unreadable in the scan; the gaps are marked […].

paras.t: Consequenter Salvator informat discipulos circa judiciale legis præceptum de pœna talionis. Audistis quia dictum est, id est, per Moysen denuntiatum est filiis Isræl : Oculum pro oculo requires, dentem pro dente exiges : id est, si quis tibi excutiat dentem vel oculum, fiat ei similiter. Dixit enim Moyses : Qualem læsionem quis intulerit, talem sustinere cogetur, ut livorem pro livore, vulnus pro vulnere, animam pro anima. Hæc ultio licita erat in lege rudibus data, quatenus timore eadem patiendi retraherentur ab injuriatione, et ne læsi ex impatientia et crudelitate excederent modum in ulciscendo. Est enim commune hominibus, ut velint plus læsionis rependere, quam passi sunt, eo quod alius prior in eos peccavit, sicque non solum læsionem, sed et contemptum injustitiamque perpessi sunt. Lex ergo aliqualiter reduxit ad pacem, et præparavit ad patientiam, dum jubet non plus inferre quam illatum est. Judæorum vero nonnulli circa verba prædicta dupliciter erraverunt : primo, quoniam æstimabant vindictam propter se appetendam ; secundo, quia putabant hæc verba sic dici per modum præcepti, ut non liceret aliter agere, seu penitus indulgere : non pensantes illud in Psalmo, Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis. Jeremias quoque virum perfectum describens, ait : Dabit percutienti se maxillam, saturabitur opprobriis. Christus ergo istos errores excludens, subjecit :
paras.en: Next the Saviour instructs the disciples concerning the judicial precept of the law on the penalty of retaliation [poena talionis, the penalty of like for like]. [[5:38|You have heard that it hath been said|Audistis quia dictum est]], that is, it was declared through Moses to the children of Israel: [[5:38|An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth|Oculum pro oculo requires, dentem pro dente exiges]] [Denis reads: “Thou shalt require an eye for an eye, thou shalt exact a tooth for a tooth”]; that is, if anyone strike out thy tooth or thine eye, let the like be done to him. For Moses said: [[Lev 24:20|What blemish he gave, the like shall he be compelled to suffer|Qualem læsionem quis intulerit, talem sustinere cogetur]]: [[Ex 21:25|stripe for stripe|livorem pro livore]], [[Ex 21:25|wound for wound|vulnus pro vulnere]], [[Ex 21:23|life for life|animam pro anima]][[Deut 19:21||]]. This vengeance was lawful in the law given to an untaught people, so that by the fear of suffering the same they might be held back from doing injury, and that the injured might not, out of impatience and cruelty, exceed the measure in taking revenge. For it is common among men to want to repay more harm than they have suffered, because the other sinned against them first, and so they have suffered not only harm but also contempt and injustice. The law, then, in some measure led back to peace and prepared for patience, by commanding that no more be inflicted than was inflicted. But some of the Jews erred in two ways about these words: first, because they thought that vengeance was to be sought for its own sake; secondly, because they thought these words were said by way of precept, so that it was not lawful to act otherwise, or to forgive altogether; not weighing the words of the Psalm: [[Ps 7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils, let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies|Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis]]. Jeremias too, describing the perfect man, says: [[Lam 3:30|He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him, he shall be filled with reproaches|Dabit percutienti se maxillam, saturabitur opprobriis]]. Christ, then, shutting out these errors, added:

paras.t: Ego autem dico vobis, non resistere malo, id est non repugnare, non reddere malum pro malo, non litigare, nec repercutere. Per hoc non datur intelligi, vitia non esse coercenda, nec excessus esse corrigendos ab his quibus ratione officii competit servare justitiam ; sed ne privata persona vindicet semetipsam, et ne aliquis affectu vindicet potius quam zelo justitiæ, corrigendique animo, resistat malo, id est peccatori seu peccato. Si autem per hoc quod non resistitur malo, periret ordo justitiæ, ac rigor disciplinæ, et impii in suis malignitatibus indurarentur ac foverentur, resistendum esset secundum ordinem juris ex caritate, præsertim ne iniqui in æternum perirent. Si vero ex resistentia mali, oritur grave scandalum infirmorum, vel majus malum, tenetur homo non resistere malo, ne ponat offendiculum proximo, aut pejor fiat scissura; vel scandalum tale alio modo sedandum est. Si autem desistat homo resistere malo vindictam non quærendo, quamvis resistendo non oriretur scandalum prædictum majusve malum, tunc erit opus supererogationis atque consilii non resistere. Hinc ergo dicit Apostolus : Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum. Denique imperfectis et passionatis hominibus tutius atque salubrius est, ut assuescant non resistere malo, quamvis possint. Nam etsi æstiment se resistere secundum ordinem juris, timendum est tamen quod potius impellantur passione quam ratione, impatientia quam justitia, privato amore quam sincera dilectione. Itaque vindicta non est optanda neque quærenda sub ratione vindictæ, sed medicinæ atque justitia, utpote ut transgressor in hoc sæculo corrigatur, ordo justitiæ observetur, alii terreantur, vel propter aliquid simile.
paras.en: [[5:39|But I say to you not to resist evil|Ego autem dico vobis, non resistere malo]], that is, not to fight back, not to render evil for evil, not to quarrel, nor to strike back. By this we are not given to understand that vices are not to be restrained, nor excesses corrected, by those whose office it is to uphold justice; but that a private person should not avenge himself, and that no one should resist evil, that is, the sinner or the sin, from a desire for revenge rather than from zeal for justice and with a mind to correct. But if by not resisting evil the order of justice and the rigour of discipline would perish, and the wicked would be hardened and encouraged in their malice, evil would have to be resisted according to the order of law, out of charity, above all lest the wicked perish for ever. But if from resisting evil there arises grave scandal of the weak, or a greater evil, a man is bound not to resist evil, lest he put a stumbling-block before his neighbour, or a worse rent be made; or else such scandal must be quieted in some other way. And if a man refrains from resisting evil by not seeking revenge, even though no such scandal or greater evil would arise from resisting, then not to resist will be a work of supererogation and of counsel. Hence the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good|Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]]. Moreover, for imperfect men, and men ruled by their passions, it is safer and more wholesome to accustom themselves not to resist evil, even though they could. For although they think they are resisting according to the order of law, it is to be feared that they are driven rather by passion than by reason, by impatience than by justice, by private love than by sincere charity. Vengeance, therefore, is not to be desired nor sought under the aspect of vengeance, but of medicine and justice: namely, that the transgressor may be corrected in this world, the order of justice kept, and others deterred, or for some similar reason.

paras.t: Præterea, secundum Christi perfectissima documenta, parum est non resistere. Subditur enim : Sed si quis te percusserit in dexteram maxillam tuam, præbe ei et alteram vel secundum realem exhibitionem, si ratio id deposcat ad ostendendam patientiam, et aliorum ædificationem, vel ad demonstrandum caritatis fervorem, quo homo paratus est ad omnia sustinenda pro fide et Christo. Si autem nil tale occurrat, præbenda est altera maxilla, seu alia pars corporis (sicut B. Martinus præbuit dorsum cædentibus) secundum animi præparationem, ita ut homo paratus sit plura perferre : quia non semper corporaliter præbenda est altera maxilla, præsertim quum Christus alapa recepta dixerit sacrilego : Si male locutus sum, testimonium perhibe de malo ; si autem bene, quid me cædis? Paulus quoque apostolus, quum a militibus cæderetur, dixit : Si civem Romanum et indemnatum licet vobis flagellare? Et tamen utique non solum flagellari, sed et mori pro Christo paratus fuit ; sed desideravit primo Romam videre et informare.
paras.en: Moreover, according to the most perfect teachings of Christ, it is little not to resist. For it is added: [[5:39|but if one strike thee on thy right cheek|Sed si quis te percusserit in dexteram maxillam tuam]], [[5:39|turn to him also the other|præbe ei et alteram]], either by actually offering it, if reason calls for this, to show patience and for the edification of others, or to display the fervour of charity by which a man is ready to bear all things for the faith and for Christ. But if nothing of the kind is at stake, the other cheek, or another part of the body (as blessed Martin offered his back to those who were beating him), is to be offered by the readiness of the mind, so that a man is prepared to bear more; for the other cheek is not always to be offered bodily, especially since Christ, having received a blow, said to the sacrilegious servant: [[John 18:23|If I have spoken evil, give testimony of the evil; but if well, why strikest thou me?|Si male locutus sum, testimonium perhibe de malo ; si autem bene, quid me cædis?]] Paul the apostle too, when he was about to be scourged by the soldiers, said: [[Acts 22:25|Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman and uncondemned?|Si civem Romanum et indemnatum licet vobis flagellare?]] And yet he was certainly ready not only to be scourged but also to die for Christ[[Acts 21:13||]]; but he desired first to see Rome and to instruct it.

paras.t: Videtur tamen prædictis contrarium, quod illico jussus cædi, dixit pontifici id jubenti : Percutiet te Deus, paries dealbate. Thomas quoque apostolus in vultu percussus, satis horrendam legitur ultionem impetrasse, ita ut percussorem leo occideret. Ad primum respondet Augustinus, quod verba Apostoli erant prophetia, non imprecatio mali. Ad aliud dicit, quod non cogimur illi historiæ credere. Possumus autem dicere, quod ex misericordia potius quam ex crudelitate Thomas hoc fecerit, ut Deus parceret anima percussoris, et ceteri divinam potestatem agnoscerent.
paras.en: Yet against what has been said there seems to be the fact that the Apostle, when ordered to be struck on the spot, said to the high priest who gave the order: [[Acts 23:3|God shall strike thee, thou whited wall|Percutiet te Deus, paries dealbate]]. Thomas the apostle too, when struck in the face, is read to have obtained a quite dreadful vengeance, so that a lion killed the man who struck him. To the first Augustine answers that the Apostle’s words were a prophecy, not an imprecation of evil. To the other he says that we are not obliged to believe that story. We can also say that Thomas did this out of mercy rather than cruelty, that God might spare the soul of the one who struck him, and that the rest might acknowledge the divine power.

paras.t: Et ei qui vult tecum judicio contendere, et tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei et pallium. Istud, secundum Augustinum, intelligitur non quoad operis ostensionem, sed animi præparationem. Sed quia Apostolus dicit : Jam omnino delictum est in vobis, quod judicia habetis inter vos; quare non magis injuriam accipitis ? quare non magis fraudem patimini? Hinc ergo oportet diligentius intellectum horum verborum inquirere. Chrysostomus itaque hoc loco multis persuasionibus videtur velle probare, nequaquam servum Dei debere coram judice pro temporalibus causam habere vel apparere, propter peccati periculum, quod vix evitari potest, et scandalum aliorum, et quoniam Christus majora rependere potest, si ejus amore vitetur judicium. Idem videtur Augustinus sentire, exponendo prememorata verba Apostoli dicens : Hoc ipsum vestro peccato agitur, quod inter vos negotia judicio determinanda habetis, quia peccatum est habere judicium contra fratrem.
paras.en: [[5:40|And if a man will contend with thee in judgment, and take away thy coat, let go thy cloak also unto him|Et ei qui vult tecum judicio contendere, et tunicam tuam tollere, dimitte ei et pallium]]. This, according to Augustine, is to be understood not as to the showing of the deed but as to the readiness of the mind. But since the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 6:7|Already indeed there is plainly a fault among you, that you have law suits one with another|omnino delictum est in vobis, quod judicia habetis inter vos]]: [[1 Cor 6:7|Why do you not rather take wrong? Why do you not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?|quare non magis fraudem patimini?]], we must therefore inquire more carefully into the meaning of these words. Chrysostom in this place seems to wish to prove by many persuasions that a servant of God ought by no means to have a suit or appear before a judge for temporal things, because of the danger of sin, which can scarcely be avoided, and the scandal of others, and because Christ can repay greater things if a lawsuit is avoided for love of Him. Augustine seems to think the same, expounding the aforesaid words of the Apostle, saying: “This very thing is done by your sin, that you have business among you to be settled by judgment; for it is a sin to have a lawsuit against a brother.”

paras.t: Verum si hoc absolute intelligatur, daretur impiis magna libertas atque occasio spoliandi et rapiendi, præsertim bona simplicium, fierentque innumerabilia mala. Glossa igitur, quasi exponens verba Augustini, adjecit : Perfectis licet repetere sua simpliciter, utpote sine lite, sine causa, sine judicio; sed non convenit eis inde movere causam ante judicem. Infirmis vero licet repetere sua coram judice, judiciumque habendo contra fratrem, sed non contentiose, vel fraudulenter, vel apud judices infideles.
paras.en: But if this were understood absolutely, great licence and occasion would be given to the wicked to plunder and rob, especially the goods of simple people, and countless evils would follow. The Gloss, therefore, as if expounding Augustine’s words, added: “It is lawful for the perfect to ask back what is theirs simply, that is, without strife, without a suit, without a judgment; but it is not fitting for them to bring a suit about it before a judge. The weak, however, may ask back what is theirs before a judge, and have a lawsuit against a brother, but not contentiously, or fraudulently, or before unbelieving judges.”

paras.t: Verum nec istud videtur aliis satis resolutum. Ecclesia namque non peccat habendo judicia, et religiosi possunt coram judice sua repetere. Fideles quoque in terris infidelium habitantes, nec fideles judices habere potentes, possunt ad judices infideles recurrere. Alii ergo respondent, quod liceat, non autem expediat, sæcularia habere judicia, et quod religiosi ac perfecti possunt sua repetere coram judice, quasi bona communia, non ut propria. Aliqui etiam breviter dicunt, quod non licet repetere sua in judicio, si ex repetitione oriatur scandalum et malum deterius. Sed tunc scire oportet, quando et quomodo bona temporalia dimittenda sunt propter vitanda scandala aliorum. Ad quod Thomas respondet, quod temporalium bonorum quædam sunt nobis commissa, quemadmodum bona Ecclesiæ committuntur prælatis, et bona reipublicæ committuntur rectoribus. Horum itaque conservatio imminet his quibus commissa sunt, de necessitate, sicut et depositorum. Ideo propter scandalum vitandum dimittenda non sunt, sicut nec alia quæ sunt de necessitate salutis. Unde B. Thomas Cantuariensis episcopus, repetiit bona Ecclesiæ cum grandi scandalo regis. Alia bona temporalia, sunt nostra seu propria ; et hæc propter scandalum dimittenda sunt, vel largiendo ea aliis, si apud nos sint, vel dimittendo ea aliis, si apud nos non sunt, quando scandalum ex infirmitate vel ignorantia oritur, quod est scandalum infirmorum : dimittenda sunt, inquam, vel scandalum alio modo sedandum est, ut errans instruatur, et scandalizari desistat. Quod si noluerit, jam scandalum ejus erit scandalum Pharisæorum. Dum igitur scandalum ex malitia scandalizati procedit, non sunt bona temporalia, quamvis propria, propter id vitandum dimittenda, quia hoc vergeret in detrimentum boni communis, et rapientibus hoc noceret in anima.
paras.en: But to others this does not seem sufficiently resolved either. For the Church does not sin in having lawsuits, and religious may ask back what is theirs before a judge. The faithful too, living in the lands of unbelievers and unable to have believing judges, may have recourse to unbelieving judges. Others therefore answer that it is lawful, but not expedient, to have secular lawsuits; and that religious and the perfect may ask back what is theirs before a judge as common goods, not as their own. Some also say briefly that it is not lawful to ask back one’s own in court if from asking it back there arises scandal and a worse evil. But then we must know when and how temporal goods are to be given up to avoid the scandal of others. To this Thomas answers that some temporal goods are committed to us, as the goods of the Church are committed to prelates and the goods of the commonwealth to rulers. The keeping of these, then, falls by necessity on those to whom they are committed, as with things deposited. Therefore they are not to be given up to avoid scandal, any more than other things that are of necessity for salvation. Hence blessed Thomas, bishop of Canterbury, sought back the goods of the Church to the great scandal of the king. Other temporal goods are ours, or our own; and these are to be given up because of scandal, either by bestowing them on others if they are in our possession, or by leaving them to others if they are not, when the scandal arises from weakness or ignorance, which is the scandal of the weak. They are to be given up, I say, or else the scandal must be quieted in another way, so that the one in error is instructed and ceases to be scandalized. But if he will not, his scandal will then be the scandal of the Pharisees. So when the scandal proceeds from the malice of the one scandalized, temporal goods, even our own, are not to be given up to avoid it, because this would tend to the detriment of the common good, and would harm the souls of those who seize them.

paras.t: Quod ergo ait Salvator, et ejus Apostolus, intelligendum est secundum promptitudinem animi, ita quod homo paratior sit pati fraudem atque injuriam, quam judicio agere, desiderio pacis interne et quietis, et ne alii offendantur, dummodo aliunde expediat. Ex his aliqualiter elucescit, quomodo intelligendum sit, quod alibi præcipit Christus : Qui aufert quæ tua sunt, ne repetas, scilicet cum lite et contentione, vel cum scandalo pusillorum.
paras.en: What the Saviour says, then, and His Apostle, is to be understood of the readiness of the mind, so that a man be more ready to suffer fraud and injury than to go to law, from a desire for inward peace and quiet, and lest others be offended, provided that it is otherwise expedient. From this it becomes in some measure clear how we are to understand what Christ commands elsewhere: [[Luke 6:30|of him that taketh away thy goods, ask them not again|Qui aufert quæ tua sunt, ne repetas]], namely with strife and contention, or with scandal to the little ones.

paras.t: Et quicumque te angariaverit, id est, coegerit seu violenter compulerit, mille passus, hoc est ambulare secum per mille passuum spatium (quinque autem pedes faciunt passum), vade cum illo et alia duo millia passuum, secundum animi præparationem, vel secundum operis exsecutionem, si sine majoris mali et scandali ortu vitare non poteris : id est, si aliquis a te exegerit indebitam servitutem, sed licitam, debes animo esse paratus plus facere, quam ille angariando requirit. Si autem in omnibus præinductis percutiens, rapiens, sive angarians, ex nostra patientia in sua malitia confirmetur ac foveatur, expedit ei resistere secundum juris processum. Si tamen habeatur spes de ejus emollitione, videlicet, quod ejus pravitas per nostram pietatem, caritatem et patientiam corrigatur, sustinendum est, sicut Apostolus loquitur : Vince in bono malum. Unde Chrysostomus : Patientia, inquit, tua illius vincat crudelitatem, et ostende quod major sit benignitas Dei in sanctis, quam malitia diaboli in iniquis hominibus. Interea, si servus Christi libenter eat cum impio, vel serviat violento, non angariatur, sed ille æstimat se istum angariare.
paras.en: [[5:41|And whosoever will force thee|et quicumque te angariaverit]], that is, shall constrain or violently compel thee, [[5:41|one mile|mille passus]], that is, to walk with him for the space of a thousand paces (five feet make a pace), [[5:41|go with him other two|vade cum illo et alia duo]] thousand paces, by the readiness of the mind, or by actually doing it if thou canst not avoid it without giving rise to a greater evil and scandal: that is, if someone demands of thee a service that is not owed, but lawful, thou oughtest to be ready in mind to do more than he requires in forcing thee. But if, in all the cases brought forward, the one who strikes, plunders or forces is confirmed and encouraged in his malice by our patience, it is expedient to resist him by process of law. If, however, there is hope of softening him, namely that his wickedness may be corrected by our goodness, charity and patience, it is to be borne, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:21|overcome evil by good|vince in bono malum]]. Hence Chrysostom says: “Let thy patience overcome his cruelty, and show that the goodness of God in the saints is greater than the malice of the devil in wicked men.” Meanwhile, if a servant of Christ goes willingly with a wicked man, or serves a violent one, he is not forced; it is the other who thinks he is forcing him.

paras.t: Qui autem petit a te, da ei quod postulat, si rationabiliter quærat, et tibi facultas adsit. Da itaque ei secundum exigentiam et possibilitatem tui status ac facultatum tuarum, et si non corporale, tamen spirituale munusculum, ut si inconvenienter vel inconvenientia postulaverit, informes errantem, quia verbum melius quam datum. Nonne ecce verbum super datum bonum ? Ut autem testatur Ambrosius : Ejusdem criminis est habenti sua auferre, et indigenti quod quærit denegare, quum possis tribuere. Quoniam, contestante Chrysostomo, homines non domini, sed dispensatores sunt divitiarum, idcirco omnia quodammodo sunt communia. Huic consonat quod in Actibus dicit Apostolus : Oportet reminisci verbi Domini Jesu, quia beatius est magis dare quam accipere. Denique, secundum principem theologorum, bonum est sui diffusivum ; et caritas non quærit quæ sua sunt. Ideo dicit Apostolus ad Timotheum : Divitibus præcipe facile tribuere. Verumtamen prodigalitas non laudatur. Nec obstat prædictis illud in Ecclesiastico : Benefac humili, et ne dederis impio. Hoc enim intelligendum est de beneficio corporali, quod non est impio dandum, si sit in fomentum et adjutorium sui impietatis. Spirituale autem beneficium nulli negandum est, sicut nec corporale in articulo necessitatis.
paras.en: [[5:42|Give to him that asketh of thee|Qui autem petit a te]] what he asks for, if he asks reasonably and thou hast the means. Give to him, then, according to what the condition and means of thy state require; and if not a bodily gift, yet a small spiritual one; so that if he has asked unfittingly or for unfitting things, thou mayest instruct him in his error, because a word is better than a gift. [[Ecclus 18:17|Lo, is not a word better than a gift?|Nonne ecce verbum super datum bonum]] [Denis adds “good”: “a word above a good gift”.] As Ambrose testifies: “It is the same crime to take from one who has, and to refuse to one in need what he asks, when thou canst give.” Since, as Chrysostom bears witness, men are not the owners but the stewards of riches, therefore all things are in a manner common. With this agrees what the Apostle says in the Acts: We ought [[Acts 20:35|to remember the word of the Lord Jesus|Oportet reminisci verbi Domini Jesu]], that [[Acts 20:35|It is a more blessed thing to give, rather than to receive|beatius est magis dare quam accipere]]. Finally, according to the prince of theologians [that is, Dionysius the Areopagite], good is diffusive of itself; and charity [[1 Cor 13:5|seeketh not her own|non quærit quæ sua sunt]]. Therefore the Apostle says to Timothy: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich|Divitibus præcipe]] [[1 Tim 6:18|to give easily|facile tribuere]]. Prodigality, however, is not praised. Nor does what is in Ecclesiasticus stand in the way of what has been said: [[Ecclus 12:6|Do good to the humble, and give not to the ungodly|Benefac humili, et ne dederis impio]]. For this is to be understood of a bodily benefit, which is not to be given to the wicked man if it would foster and help his wickedness. But a spiritual benefit is to be refused to no one, nor a bodily one in a moment of necessity.

paras.t: Et volenti mutuari a te, id est aliquid sibi concedi, seu mutuum accipere, ne avertaris, negando ei quod petit, si rationabiliter petit, et tibi adsit facultas. Hoc enim spectat ad caritatem, ut necessitatem proximi quasi propriam æstimemus ac sublevemus subveniendo egenti. Imo agendum est quod in Ecclesiastico scribitur : Perde pecuniam propter fratrem et amicum. Teste quoque Psalmista : Jucundus homo qui miseretur et commodat, quia in æternum non commovebitur.
paras.en: [[5:42|and from him that would borrow of thee|et volenti mutuari a te]], that is, who wishes something to be granted him, or to receive a loan, [[5:42|turn not away|ne avertaris]] by refusing him what he asks, if he asks reasonably and thou hast the means. For it belongs to charity that we should regard our neighbour’s need as our own and relieve it by helping the needy. Indeed we must do what is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 29:13|Lose thy money for thy brother and thy friend|Perde pecuniam propter fratrem et amicum]]. As the Psalmist also testifies: [[Ps 111:5|Acceptable is the man that sheweth mercy and lendeth|Jucundus homo qui miseretur et commodat]], [[Ps 111:6|Because he shall not be moved for ever|quia in æternum non commovebitur]].

paras.t: Insuper Christus exponit præceptum legis de dilectione proximi : de qua ait Apostolus, Qui diligit proximum, legem implevit. Audistis quia dictum est in lege Moysis : Diliges proximum tuum, non dilectione carnali, nec solum dilectione naturali, sed et dilectione caritativa atque gratuita, quæ fundatur in communicatione felicitatis æternæ ; et odio habebis inimicum tuum, non odiendo naturam, sed culpam, non personam, sed vitium : quod utique odium ex caritate procedit, et ad perfectionem pertinet. De quo in Psalmo cantatur : Perfecto odio oderam illos; et, Iniquos odio habui. Hoc autem quod de odio inimici subjicitur, quidam Judæorum pessime intellexerunt, dicentes inimicos simpliciter odiendos : ad quod multa veteris Testamenti testimonia adduxerunt. Multa enim sunt quæ superficialiter intellecta, videntur hoc ipsum prætendere : sicut quum Moyses ait, Non quæres ei bona ; et Nehemias, Confundantur, et peccatum eorum non deleatur. Sed talia atque similia intelligenda sunt, quantum ad temporalia bona, vel de inimico secundum vitium inimicitiæ, non secundum esse naturæ; vel dicuntur zelo justitiæ, seu modo prophetiæ, non affectu invidi. Quod autem inimici non sint odiendi secundum verum intellectum legis, hinc liquet, quod in Levitico scribitur : Non oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo, sed publice argue eum, ne habeas super illo peccatum ; et denuo, Non quæres ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. Et Salomon loquitur : Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas, et in ruina illius ne exsultet cor tuum. Job quoque protestatur : Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui me oderat, et exsultavi quod invenisset eum malum.
paras.en: Further, Christ expounds the precept of the law on the love of one’s neighbour, of which the Apostle says: [[Rom 13:8|he that loveth his neighbour hath fulfilled the law|diligit proximum, legem implevit]]. [[5:43|You have heard that it hath been said|Audistis quia dictum est]] in the law of Moses: [[5:43|Thou shalt love thy neighbour|Diliges proximum tuum]], not with a carnal love, nor with a natural love only, but also with the love of charity, freely given, which is founded on the sharing of eternal happiness; [[5:43|and hate thy enemy|et odio habebis inimicum tuum]], not hating his nature but his fault, not the person but the vice; and this hatred certainly proceeds from charity and belongs to perfection. Of it we sing in the Psalm: [[Ps 138:22|I have hated them with a perfect hatred|Perfecto odio oderam illos]]; and, [[Ps 118:113|I have hated the unjust|Iniquos odio habui]]. But what is added about hating one’s enemy some of the Jews understood very wrongly, saying that enemies were simply to be hated; and for this they brought forward many testimonies of the Old Testament. For there are many which, understood superficially, seem to put forward this very thing: as when Moses says, [[Deut 23:6|neither shalt thou seek their prosperity|quæres ei bona]]; and Nehemiah, Let them be confounded, and [[2 Esd 4:5|let not their sin be blotted out|et peccatum eorum non deleatur]]. But such things and the like are to be understood as regards temporal goods; or of the enemy as regards the vice of enmity, not as regards the being of his nature; or they are said out of zeal for justice, or by way of prophecy, not from the feeling of one who bears ill will. That enemies are not to be hated, according to the true understanding of the law, is clear from what is written in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:17|Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy heart: But reprove him openly, lest thou incur sin through him|Non oderis fratrem tuum in corde tuo, sed publice argue eum, ne habeas super illo peccatum]]; and again, [[Lev 19:18|Seek not revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|Non quæres ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. And Solomon says: [[Prov 24:17|When thy enemy shall fall, be not glad, and in his ruin let not thy heart rejoice|Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas, et in ruina illius ne exsultet cor tuum]]. Job also protests: [[Job 31:29|If I have been glad at the downfall of him that hated me, and have rejoiced that evil had found him|Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui me oderat, et exsultavi quod invenisset eum malum]].

paras.t: Judæorum ergo errorem Christus excludens, adjunxit : [Ego autem dico vobis :] Diligite inimicos vestros, quantum ad id quod habent a Deo, puta naturam ad Dei imaginem factam, et beatitudinis susceptivam. Diligere autem, est alicui bonum velle, secundum Philosophum. Debemus ergo adversariis nostris bona spiritualia velle, videlicet gratiam in præsenti, et gloriam in futuro : imo et bona corporalia eis optanda sunt, secundum quod expedit eorum saluti. Benefacite his qui oderunt vos, interiorem affectum extendendo in opus, ut scilicet impendatis eis beneficia spiritualia seu corporalia, secundum congruentiam causæ, loci, ac temporis. Unde et Salomon admonet : Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum ; si sitit, potum da illi. Et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus, hoc est calumniam inferentibus, vos. In generali pro omnibus illis orandum est, et etiam in speciali, si specialis causa orandi occurrit, ut si viderimus inimicum graviter anxiatum, seu damnationis periculo expositum. De necessitate ergo præcepti est, ut omnibus quantumcumque adversariis, appetamus saltem in generali gratiam conversionis, et cetera ad salutem necessaria, nec alicui tali specialiter nos precanti, negemus subsidium ei necessarium, si dare poterimus. In speciali autem alicui adversario caritative affici et auxiliari, speciali necessitate non occurrente, ad supererogationem pertinere videtur.
paras.en: Shutting out, then, the error of the Jews, Christ added: [[5:44|But I say to you|Ego autem dico vobis]]: [[5:44|Love your enemies|diligite inimicos vestros]], as regards what they have from God, for instance a nature made to the image of God and capable of beatitude. Now to love is to will good to someone, according to the Philosopher. We ought, then, to will spiritual goods to our adversaries, namely grace in the present and glory in the future; indeed bodily goods too are to be wished for them, so far as is expedient for their salvation. [[5:44|do good to them that hate you|benefacite his qui oderunt vos]], extending the inward affection into deed, so that you bestow on them spiritual or bodily benefits as cause, place and time make fitting. Hence Solomon too admonishes: [[Prov 25:21|If thy enemy be hungry, give him to eat|Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum]]; [[Prov 25:21|if he thirst|si sitit]], give him drink[[Rom 12:20||]]. [[5:44|and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you|et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos]], that is, who bring false accusations against you. We must pray for all of them in general, and in particular too if a particular cause for praying arises, as if we see an enemy in grave distress, or exposed to the danger of damnation. It is, then, of necessity of precept that for all our adversaries, however hostile, we desire at least in general the grace of conversion and the other things necessary for salvation, and that we do not refuse to any such one who asks us in particular the help he needs, if we can give it. But to be charitably disposed towards, and to help, some adversary in particular, when no particular necessity arises, seems to belong to supererogation.

paras.t: Ut sitis filii adoptivi Patris vestri qui in cœlis est, scilicet Dei Patris, vel totius superbeatissimæ Trinitatis, quæ est unus Creator ac Deus et Pater omnium nostrum ; qui solem suum: corporalem, i cœlo fulgentem ac discurrentem, oriri facit super bonos et malos : omnibus enim hominibus sol ministrat et nascitur, radios suos omnibus influendo ; et pluit super justos et injustos. Invitat ergo nos Christus ad inimicorum dilectionem exemplo Dei, qui naturalia beneficia nemini subtrahit, ut simus filii ejus, id est, ut ei assimilemur, conformando nos ejus bonitati ac pietati. Ratio enim filiationis in quadam assimilatione consistit. Propter quod dicit Apostolus : Estote imitatores Dei sicut filii carissimi. Unde Joannes loquitur : Sicut ille est, et nos sumus in hoc mundo, videlicet adversariis nostris affectum et effectum caritatis impendendo.
paras.en: [[5:45|That you may be the children|ut sitis filii]], by adoption, [[5:45|of your Father who is in heaven|Patris vestri qui in cælis est]], namely of God the Father, or of the whole most blessed Trinity, which is the one Creator and God and Father of us all; [[5:45|who maketh his sun to rise|qui solem suum oriri facit]], the bodily sun that shines and runs its course in the sky, [[5:45|upon the good, and bad|super bonos et malos]]; for the sun serves and rises for all men, pouring its rays upon all; [[5:45|and raineth upon the just and the unjust|et pluit super justos et injustos]]. Christ invites us, then, to the love of enemies by the example of God, who withholds His natural benefits from no one, that we may be His children, that is, that we may become like Him by conforming ourselves to His goodness and kindness. For the nature of sonship consists in a certain likeness. For this reason the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:1|Be ye therefore followers of God, as most dear children|imitatores Dei sicut filii carissimi]] [Denis reads “imitators of God”]. Hence John says: [[1 John 4:17|as he is, we also are in this world|Sicut ille est, et nos sumus in hoc mundo]], namely by bestowing on our adversaries the affection and the effect of charity.

paras.t: Consequenter ponit Salvator aliam rationem amandi inimicos. Si enim diligitis eos qui vos diligunt, id est, si solum amatis amantes vos, non tam propter Deum, quam ideo quia vos diligunt, quam mercedem habebitis a Deo in patria? quasi dicat, Nullam. Nonne et publicani, hoc est publici peccatores, hoc faciunt? Utique, et tamen nullam a Deo mercedem sortiuntur. Et si salutaveritis fratres vestros tantum, id est, salutem et bona optaveritis propinquis vestris, quid amplius facitis quam publicani? Nonne et ethnici, id est gentiles, hoc faciunt? Quia in hac clausula additur, Tantum, datur intelligi, quod in præcedenti quoque clausula subaudiendum erat. Sciendum ergo, quod amicos diligere ex caritate, non est immeritorium ; diligere vero amicos alia quacumque dilectione, non est meritorium. Signum autem quod amici diliguntur, quia amici, et non principaliter propter Deum, est quum sic diliguntur, quod inimici non diliguntur. Denique qui unum hominem odit, nullum veraciter diligit, quum sit in peccato mortali, quod caritatem exstinguit. Idcirco qui amat amicos et non inimicos, non amat amicos per caritatem, sed per naturalem, carnalem, sive politicam amicitiam. Non ergo habet a Deo mercedem.
paras.en: Next the Saviour gives another reason for loving enemies. [[5:46|For if you love them that love you|Si enim diligitis eos qui vos diligunt]], that is, if you love only those who love you, not so much for God’s sake as because they love you, [[5:46|what reward shall you have?|quam mercedem habebitis?]] from God in the fatherland; as if to say, None. [[5:46|do not even the publicans this?|nonne et publicani hoc faciunt?]], that is, public sinners. Certainly they do, and yet they receive no reward from God. [[5:47|And if you salute your brethren only|Et si salutaveritis fratres vestros tantum]], that is, wish health and good things to your kinsfolk, [[5:47|what do you more?|quid amplius facitis?]] than the publicans? [[5:47|do not also the heathens this?|nonne et ethnici hoc faciunt?]], that is, the Gentiles. Since in this clause “only” is added, we are given to understand that it was to be understood in the preceding clause too. It must be known, then, that to love one’s friends out of charity is not without merit; but to love one’s friends with any other love is not meritorious. And it is a sign that friends are loved because they are friends, and not chiefly for God’s sake, when they are so loved that enemies are not loved. Moreover, he who hates one man truly loves none, since he is in mortal sin, which extinguishes charity. Therefore he who loves his friends and not his enemies does not love his friends by charity, but by a natural, carnal or civil friendship. He has, then, no reward from God.

paras.t: Quæri potest hoc loco, quid sit magis meritorium, diligere amicum, vel inimicum. Ad hoc diversimode satis a diversis respondetur. Thomas vero respondet hoc modo : Dilectio refertur ad diligentem, et ad Deum, qui est ratio diligendi proximum. Referendo ergo dilectionem ad diligentem, sic dilectio amici eminet dilectioni inimici : quia amicus quum sit melior atque propinquior, est materia aptior dilectioni quam inimicus. Propter quod actus caritatis transiens super talem materiam est melior, et oppositum ejus est pejus, videlicet odium amici quam inimici. Quantum vero ad id quod est ratio diligendi proximum, quod est Deus, dilectio inimici præeminet : primo, quoniam solus Deus est causa hujus dilectionis ; secundo, quia ex dilectione inimici ostenditur amor Dei fortior esse in diligente, quam ex dilectione amici. Nihilo minus dilectio amici secundum se est melior, ferventior, magisque meritoria : quia ad rationem virtutis ac meriti, plus facit bonum quam difficile. Quamvis ergo dilectio inimici sit difficilior, non tamen est melior vel magis meritoria, nisi præmii accidentalis ratione laboris annexi. Præmium vero essentiale correspondet fervori dilectionis.
paras.en: It may be asked in this place which is more meritorious, to love a friend or an enemy. To this various answers are given by various men. Thomas answers in this way: Love is referred to the one who loves, and to God, who is the reason for loving one’s neighbour. Referring love, then, to the one who loves, the love of a friend surpasses the love of an enemy: because a friend, being better and nearer, is more apt matter for love than an enemy. For this reason the act of charity passing over such matter is better, and its opposite is worse, namely hatred of a friend than of an enemy. But as regards what is the reason for loving one’s neighbour, which is God, the love of an enemy is pre-eminent: first, because God alone is the cause of this love; secondly, because the love of an enemy shows the love of God to be stronger in the one who loves than the love of a friend does. Nevertheless the love of a friend is in itself better, more fervent and more meritorious: because for the nature of virtue and merit the good counts for more than the difficult. Although, then, the love of an enemy is more difficult, it is not better or more meritorious, except in respect of the accidental reward on account of the labour joined to it. But the essential reward answers to the fervour of love.

paras.t: Estote ergo vos perfecti, non solum amicos, sed etiam æmulos diligendo, pietatis viscera semper habendo, et in omni virtute viriliter vos habendo, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis perfectus est perfectione simpliciter dicta, et extra omne genus, ita quod nulla ei deest nobilitas, sed omne quod absolute loquendo melius est esse quam deesse, convenit Deo cum plenitudine infinita. Huic ergo perfectioni assimilari non possumus similitudine æqualitatis, sed imitationis. Scriptum est enim : Cui similem fecistis Deum? aut quam imaginem ponetis ei? et cui assimilastis me: dicit Sanctus. De hac perfectione deiformi qua Deo assimilari præcipimur, ait Moyses : Perfectus eris, et absque macula cum Domino Deo tuo. O vere quanta est bonitas atque dignatio Dei, et quanta est dignitas rationalis creaturæ, eo quod Deus immensus, in cujus comparatione totus mundus est velut pulvis exiguus, vult sibi assimilari similemque vocari creaturam suam rationalem ! Ad hanc quippe perfectionem, etiam in veteri Testamento divinitus invitamur, juxta illud : Nolite contaminare animas vestras : ego enim sum Dominus Deus vester. Sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum.
paras.en: [[5:48|Be you therefore perfect|Estote ergo vos perfecti]], loving not only friends but also rivals, always having the bowels of kindness, and bearing yourselves manfully in every virtue, [[5:48|as also your heavenly Father is perfect|sicut et Pater vester cælestis perfectus est]] with a perfection simply so called and outside every genus, so that no nobility is lacking to Him, but everything which, speaking absolutely, it is better to have than to lack belongs to God in infinite fullness. To this perfection, then, we cannot be likened by a likeness of equality, but of imitation. For it is written: [[Is 40:18|To whom then have you likened God? or what image will you make for him?|Cui similem fecistis Deum? aut quam imaginem ponetis ei?]] [[Is 40:25|And to whom have ye likened me|et cui assimilastis me]] [[Is 40:25|saith the Holy One|dicit Sanctus]]? Of this godlike perfection, by which we are commanded to be likened to God, Moses says: [[Deut 18:13|Thou shalt be perfect, and without spot before the Lord thy God|Perfectus eris, et absque macula cum Domino Deo tuo]]. O truly how great is the goodness and condescension of God, and how great the dignity of the rational creature, that the immeasurable God, in comparison with whom the whole world is like a little dust, wills His rational creature to be made like Him and to be called like Him! To this perfection we are invited by God even in the Old Testament, according to the words: [[Lev 11:43|Do not defile your souls|Nolite contaminare animas vestras]]: [[Lev 11:44|For I am the Lord your God. Be holy because I am holy|ego enim sum Dominus Deus vester. Sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum]][[Lev 19:2||]][[Lev 20:7||]][[Lev 20:26||]][[Lev 21:8||]].

6.title: Elucidatio sequentis partis hujus capituli, usque ad finem ipsius, videlicet: Audistis quia dictum est
6.title_en: Explanation of the following part of this chapter, to its end, namely: “You have heard that it hath been said”
6.note: The last part of Art. XI, which begins at Matthew 5:38 (see chapter 5); Denis carries the exposition on to 6:4 before Art. XII.

paras.t: Postquam sublimia perfectaque documenta Salvator proposuit, congruentissime admonet vitare vulpeculam, utpote vanam gloriam, quæ tunc fortius atque latentius ingredi solet sive pulsare, non solum pusillos, sed et proficientes ac fervidos, quando efficacius divinis obtemperaverunt præceptis sive consiliis. Attendite ne justitiam vestram, videlicet opera virtuosa quæ docui, faciatis coram hominibus, ut videamini ab illis, hoc est ad hunc finem quod virtuosi ab illis reputemini, et laudem humanam captetis : hoc enim esset hominibus velle placere ; Deus autem dissipat ossa eorum qui hominibus placent. Alioqui, id est, nisi attenderitis sicut admoneo, mercedem non habebitis apud Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est, id est in conspectu Dei in patria, quoniam ccelestem beatitudinem sortituri non estis. Non enim aliquid meremini sic agendo, quia in moralibus, actus habet speciem a fine; et secundum Ambrosium, Intentio imprimit speciem actui tuo. Si ergo finis est vanus, opus est vitiosum. Denique secundum Dionysium, bonum est ex integra causa, videlicet omnibus circumstantiis concurrentibus; malum vero contingit omnifariam, id est, quacumque circumstantia omittatur. Inter omnes autem circumstantias actus virtuosi, propter quod exstat præcipua : et ideo si opus agatur propter laudem humanam, maxime vitiatur atque inficitur.
paras.en: After setting forth sublime and perfect teachings, the Saviour most fittingly warns us to avoid the little fox [cf. Cant 2:15, “catch us the little foxes that destroy the vines”], namely vainglory, which is wont to enter or knock most strongly and most secretly, not only on the little ones but also on those who are making progress and are fervent, when they have obeyed the divine precepts or counsels most effectively. [[6:1|Take heed|Attendite]] [[6:1|that you do not your justice|ne justitiam vestram faciatis]], namely the virtuous works that I have taught, [[6:1|before men, to be seen by them|coram hominibus, ut videamini ab illis]], that is, to this end, that you may be reckoned virtuous by them and may catch at human praise: for this would be to wish to please men; but [[Ps 52:6|God hath scattered the bones of them that please men|dissipat ossa eorum qui hominibus placent]]. [[6:1|otherwise|Alioqui]], that is, unless you take heed as I warn you, [[6:1|you shall not have a reward of your Father who is in heaven|mercedem non habebitis apud Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est]], that is, in the sight of God in the fatherland, since you will not obtain heavenly beatitude. For you merit nothing by acting so, because in moral matters the act takes its species from its end; and according to Ambrose, “Thy intention stamps its species on thy act.” If, then, the end is vain, the work is vicious. Moreover, according to Dionysius, good comes from an entire cause, namely when all the circumstances concur; but evil happens in every way, that is, when any circumstance whatever is omitted. And among all the circumstances of a virtuous act, the “for the sake of which” [the end] stands out as the chief; and so if a work is done for human praise, it is most of all vitiated and infected.

paras.t: Tu ergo quum facis eleemosynam, noli tuba canere ante te, id est, noli alta voce, vel signo alio manifestare te ipsum, propter laudem hominum obtinendam, sicut hypocritæ faciunt in synagogis et vicis, hoc est templis et plateis. Sic enim multi Judæorum fecerunt. Ut honorificentur ab hominibus. Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam, videlicet laudem humanam. O vanitas ac miseria infinita, propter volatilem, vilem, fallacem et momentaneam hominum laudem, divino, æterno et cœlesti honore privari !
paras.en: [[6:2|Therefore when thou dost an alms-deed|ergo quum facis eleemosynam]], [[6:2|sound not a trumpet before thee|noli tuba canere ante te]], that is, do not make thyself known with a loud voice or by any other sign, to obtain the praise of men, [[6:2|as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets|sicut hypocritæ faciunt in synagogis et vicis]], that is, in the temples and in the squares. For so many of the Jews did. [[6:2|that they may be honoured by men|Ut honorificentur ab hominibus]]. [[6:2|Amen I say to you, they have received their reward|Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam]], namely human praise. O vanity and infinite misery, to be deprived of divine, eternal and heavenly honour for the fleeting, worthless, deceitful and momentary praise of men!

paras.t: Te autem faciente eleemosynam, nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua, id est, tam occulte hanc facias, quantum ad animi intentionem, ut nec ab illo videatur qui tibi tam vicinus est ut una manus alteri. Per talem etenim modum loquendi, datur intelligi, quod homo debet a nemine velle videri propter gloriam hominum capiendam, quamvis ad aliorum ædificationem et Dei honorem, possit eleemosyna fieri in aperto. Vel spiritualiter, Nesciat sinistra, id est cogitatio perversa seu vana affectio, quid faciat dextera tua, id est cogitatio et affectio bona : hoc est, cogitatio vana omnino abjiciatur, nec bonæ cogitationi de qua eleemosyna nascitur, admisceatur. Ut sit eleemosyna tua in abscondito loco, id est, occulte fiat, saltem secundum desiderium cordis, intentionemque animi, ne cupias inaniter apparere.
paras.en: [[6:3|But when thou dost alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doth|Te autem faciente eleemosynam, nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua]]; that is, do it so secretly, as regards the intention of the mind, that it be not seen even by one who is as near to thee as one hand to the other. For by this manner of speaking we are given to understand that a man ought to wish to be seen by no one for the sake of gaining the glory of men; although for the edification of others and the honour of God alms can be given openly. Or spiritually: let not the left hand know, that is, a perverse thought or vain affection, what thy right hand doth, that is, a good thought and affection; that is, let vain thought be cast away altogether, and not mingled with the good thought from which the alms springs. [[6:4|That thy alms may be in secret|Ut sit eleemosyna tua in abscondito]] place, that is, let it be done secretly, at least according to the desire of the heart and the intention of the mind, lest thou desire to appear to no purpose.

paras.t: Et Pater tuus cœlestis, qui videt oculo intellectuali, in abscondito, id est intus in anima, scrutans corda et renes ; et etiam in occultis tenebrosisque locis, quemadmodum Jeremias ait : Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum ? Homo quippe videt quæ foris apparent, Deus autem intuetur cor. Reddet tibi copiosum præmium eleemosyna, quod in præsenti inchoatur, et in futuro perficitur.
paras.en: [[6:4|and thy Father|et Pater tuus]] in heaven, [[6:4|who seeth|qui videt]] with the eye of understanding [[6:4|in secret|in abscondito]], that is, within, in the soul, [[Ps 7:10|the searcher of hearts and reins|scrutans corda et renes]]; and also in hidden and dark places, as Jeremias says: [[Jer 23:24|Shall a man be hid in secret places, and I not see him|Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum]]? For [[1 Kings 16:7|man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart|Homo quippe videt quæ foris apparent, Deus autem intuetur cor]]. [[6:4|will repay thee|reddet tibi]] an abundant reward for the alms, which is begun in the present and perfected in the future.

6.title: Explanatio capituli sexti: Et quum oratis
6.title_en: Explanation of the sixth chapter: “And when ye pray”

paras.t: Post exhortationem operum misericordiæ et caritatis fraternæ, quibus homo ad proximos suos virtuose extenditur, docet Salvator de actu latriæ per quem anima ad Deum elevatur, videlicet de oratione, quæ secundum Damascenum, est ascensus mentis in Deum, vel petitio decentium, id est rerum quas decet peti a Deo. Et quum oratis, Deum suppliciter invocando, non eritis sicut hypocritæ, id est, assimilari non debetis vanis hominibus, humanam laudem potius quam Dei honorem, vel honorationem a Deo, quærentibus ; qui amant in synagogis, id est in publicis conventiculis seu templis, et in angulis platearum stantes orare. Stant enim, ut sic remotius videantur. Quod autem apud Christianos designat ecclesia, hoc apud Judæos significat synagoga, videlicet locum cultus divini, vel collectionem fidelis populi. Secundum Chrysostomum, dicit non, In plateis, sed, In angulis platearum : ad insinuandum quod hypocritæ interdum quærunt secretum locum orandi, non ut lateant, sed ut videantur quasi in abscondito orare, sicque dupliciter commendentur : primo, quoniam orant; secundo, quoniam latere desiderant. Sciunt enim laudabilius esse in occulto orare. Tales sunt multi, qui simulant se honores refugere, nolle præesse, gloriam vanam odire, ut honorem, prælationem, et gloriam consequantur. Sciunt enim, quoniam honor sequitur fugientem, et quod se humilians exaltetur. Ideo scriptum est : Est qui nequiter se humiliat, et interiora ejus plena sunt dolo. Sic igitur orant, ut videantur ab hominibus, id est, devoti putentur, laudentur et honorentur. Amen, id est veraciter, dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam. Imo, etsi a nullo homine videantur neque laudentur, receperunt tamen mercedem suam in præsenti, quantum ad suum propositum et affectum ; nec a Deo præmium sortiuntur, sed pœnam, tanquam sacrilegi qui re sacra abutuntur in vanitatem.
paras.en: After the exhortation to works of mercy and of brotherly charity, by which a man reaches out virtuously to his neighbours, the Saviour teaches about the act of latria [the worship due to God alone] by which the soul is raised to God, namely about prayer, which, according to Damascene, is the ascent of the mind to God, or the asking of fitting things, that is, of things which it is fitting to ask of God. [[6:5|And when ye pray|Et quum oratis]], calling humbly upon God, [[6:5|you shall not be as the hypocrites|non eritis sicut hypocritæ]], that is, you ought not to be like vain men who seek human praise rather than the honour of God or honour from God; [[6:5|that love to stand and pray in the synagogues|qui amant in synagogis]], that is, in public assemblies or temples, [[6:5|and corners of the streets|et in angulis platearum stantes orare]]. For they stand, so that they may be seen from further off. Now what the church signifies among Christians, the synagogue signifies among the Jews, namely the place of divine worship, or the gathering of the faithful people. According to Chrysostom, He does not say, “in the streets”, but, “in the corners of the streets”, to suggest that hypocrites sometimes seek a secret place to pray, not to be hidden but to be seen praying as if in secret, and so be commended twice over: first because they pray, secondly because they wish to be hidden. For they know that it is more praiseworthy to pray in secret. Such are many who pretend to flee honours, not to wish to be over others, to hate vainglory, in order to obtain honour, prelacy and glory. For they know that honour follows him who flees it, and that he who humbles himself is exalted[[Luke 14:11||]][[Luke 18:14||]]. Therefore it is written: [[Ecclus 19:23|There is one that humbleth himself wickedly, and his interior is full of deceit|Est qui nequiter se humiliat, et interiora ejus plena sunt dolo]]. So, then, they pray [[6:5|that they may be seen by men|ut videantur ab hominibus]], that is, that they may be thought devout, and be praised and honoured. [[6:5|Amen I say to you|amen dico vobis]], that is, truly, [[6:5|they have received their reward|receperunt mercedem suam]]. Indeed, even if they are seen and praised by no man, they have nevertheless received their reward in the present, as far as their purpose and desire go; and they obtain from God no reward but punishment, as sacrilegious men who abuse a sacred thing for vanity.

paras.t: His verbis non prohibet Christus in ecclesia materiali ac publicis locis orare, quum dicat Apostolus : Volo viros orare in omni loco, levantes puras manus ; et Psalmista, Vota mea Domino reddam coram omni populo ejus; itemque, Adorate Dominum in atrio sancto ejus. Et quomodo poterimus semper et sine intermissione orare, si non oraverimus ubicumque fuerimus ? Denique sunt orationes solennes ac publicæ, quas faciunt ministri Ecclesiæ pro populo : quas certum est in ipsa ecclesia publice fieri oportere. Orationes quoque privatæ singulorum maxime in ecclesia fieri debent, propter loci sanctitatem et Sacramenti præsentiam, juxta illud : Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur cunctis gentibus, dicit Dominus. Quod ad litteram de materiali ecclesia dictum esse, Christus allegat. Prohibet ergo Dominus in templo et angulis platearum orare, more hypocritarum, videlicet appetitu laudis humanæ, vel commodi temporalis, et ne solum oremus in publicis locis. Ideo subditur :
paras.en: By these words Christ does not forbid praying in the material church and in public places, since the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 2:8|I will therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands|Volo viros orare in omni loco, levantes puras manus]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 115:5|I will pay my vows to the Lord before all his people|Vota mea Domino reddam coram omni populo ejus]]; and again, [[Ps 95:9|Adore ye the Lord in his holy court|Adorate Dominum in atrio sancto ejus]][[Ps 28:2||]]. And how shall we be able to pray always[[Luke 18:1||]] and without ceasing[[1 Thess 5:17||]], if we do not pray wherever we are? Moreover there are solemn and public prayers which the ministers of the Church make for the people, and it is certain that these must be made publicly in the church itself. The private prayers of individuals too ought above all to be made in the church, because of the holiness of the place and the presence of the Sacrament, according to the words: [[Is 56:7|my house shall be called the house of prayer, for all nations|Domus mea domus orationis vocabitur cunctis gentibus]], saith the Lord. That this was said literally of the material church Christ declares when He cites it[[Mark 11:17||]]. What the Lord forbids, then, is praying in the temple and in the corners of the streets after the manner of hypocrites, namely from the desire of human praise or of temporal advantage; and that we should pray only in public places. Therefore it is added:

paras.t: Tu autem quum oraveris, id est, orare intendis vel incipis, intra in cubiculum tuum, id est locum secretum et quietum. Et clauso ostio loci, ne quis accedat, teque impediat, vel ad inanem gloriam excitet, eo quod inveniaris in tam sancto opere, humanum adspectum, præconiumque vitare. Aliqui enim solent subito et inaniter gloriari, quum inveniuntur præter vel contra propositum suum laudabiliter occupari. Ora Patrem tuum cœlestem, Deum trinum ac simplicem, in absconso loco. Et Pater tuus, qui videt in absconso : non enim latent eum quæ fiunt in locis abstractis. Specialiter quoque videt Deus per approbationem in absconso, id est, misericorditer adspicit et acceptat opera bona quæ fiunt in abditis ad vitandum vitium vanitatis. Locus vero secretus et quietus plurimum confert ad orationis puritatem atque fervorem : quia tunc homo securior est, nec a sensibilibus toties inquietatur, unde imaginatio ejus quietior est, et intellectus stabilior ; voluntas quoque tanto ardentius fertur in Deum, stabiliusque in eo permanet fixa, quanto amplius a multis abstrahitur.
paras.en: [[6:6|But thou when thou shalt pray|Tu autem quum oraveris]], that is, intendest or beginnest to pray, [[6:6|enter into thy chamber|intra in cubiculum tuum]], that is, a secret and quiet place, [[6:6|and having shut the door|Et clauso ostio]] of the place, lest anyone come in and hinder thee, or stir thee to vainglory because thou art found in so holy a work; that is, avoid the sight and the praise of men. For some are wont to glory suddenly and vainly when they are found praiseworthily occupied, beside or against their purpose. [[6:6|pray to thy Father|Ora Patrem tuum]] in heaven, God three and simple, [[6:6|in secret|in absconso]] place. [[6:6|and thy father who seeth in secret|Et Pater tuus, qui videt in absconso]]; for the things done in remote places are not hidden from Him. God also sees in a special way, by approval, in secret; that is, He mercifully looks upon and accepts the good works done in hidden places to avoid the vice of vanity. A secret and quiet place contributes very greatly to the purity and fervour of prayer: for then a man is more secure, and is not so often disturbed by the things of sense; hence his imagination is quieter and his understanding steadier; and his will too is borne the more ardently towards God, and remains the more steadily fixed in Him, the more it is drawn away from many things.

paras.t: Potest etiam per cubiculum spiritualiter accipi cor hominis. Sic ergo debemus intrare cubiculum animæ, id est, ad cor nostrum redire, et spiritum nostrum intra nos colligere (juxta illud : Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus, quoniam loquetur pacem in plebem suam, et in eos qui convertuntur ad cor), et Patrem in absconso, id est in cordis secreto soli Deo patenti, orare, sicut ait Salvator : Spiritus est Deus, et eos qui adorant eum, in spiritu et veritate adorare oportet. Hoc modo oravit Anna, cujus tantum labia movebantur, et vox penitus non audiebatur. Et Pater tuus qui videt in absconso, hoc est in intimo cordis fundo, quem nulla latet cogitatio, reddet tibi quod postulas, imo multiplicem orationis effectum tibi præstabit, videlicet dulcem in orando saporem, optata gratiæ infusionem, sempiternamque gloriam, si tamen infatigabiliter oras.
paras.en: By the chamber can also be understood, spiritually, the heart of man. So we ought to enter the chamber of the soul, that is, return to our heart and gather our spirit within us (according to the words: [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me: for he will speak peace unto his people|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus, quoniam loquetur pacem in plebem suam]], [[Ps 84:9|and unto them that are converted to the heart|et in eos qui convertuntur ad cor]]), and pray to the Father in secret, that is, in the secret of the heart, open to God alone, as the Saviour says: [[John 4:24|God is a spirit: and they that adore him must adore him in spirit and in truth|Spiritus est Deus, et eos qui adorant eum, in spiritu et veritate]]. In this way Anna prayed: [[1 Kings 1:13|only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard at all|tantum labia movebantur, et vox penitus non audiebatur]].
