[[6:6|and thy father who seeth in secret|Et Pater tuus qui videt in absconso]], that is, in the inmost depth of the heart, from whom no thought is hidden[[Job 42:2||]], [[6:6|will repay thee|reddet tibi]] what thou askest; indeed He will bestow on thee a manifold fruit of prayer, namely sweet savour in praying, the longed-for infusion of grace, and everlasting glory, if only thou prayest untiringly.

paras.t: Orantes autem, nolite multum loqui, id est verba coram Deo multiplicare, sicut ethnici, id est gentiles, faciunt : qui ideo orando multum loquuntur : putant enim quod in multiloquio suo, hoc est virtute multorum verborum, exaudiantur a diis suis. Et non mirum quod diu orant, et verba multiplicant : nam orant dæmones, qui etsi audiant, exaudire non valent, nec aliquid facere, nisi permissi a Deo. Orant reges mortuos, Jovem, Mercurium, quorum crimina sunt notiora quam nomina, qui etsi viverent, salutem conferre non possent. Orant idola insensata, quæ habent aures, nec audiunt. Nolite ergo assimilari eis, verba multiplicando ea ratione qua illi, ut arbitremini in multiloquio, et non potius in affectu fervido, exaudiri. Patet ergo quod Christus non absolute prohibet verba in oratione protendere, sed ne hoc faciamus more ethnicorum. Nam ipse hortatur nos ut oremus instanter et semper : quod sine multiplicatione verborum mentalium sive vocalium non fit. Ipse quoque in oratione pernoctavit. Scit enim Pater vester, quid opus, id est necesse, vel utile, sit vobis, antequam petatis eum pro quocumque negotio. Scientia enim Dei æterna, perfecta, invariabilisque consistit. Ideo non oportet multum loqui, quasi in multiloquio exaudiret Deus : quia si sic, tunc per nostros sermones aliquid sibi notificaretur, quod antea ignorasset, vel per verborum multitudinem flecteretur, quorum nullum omniscienti et incommutabili competit Deo.
paras.en: [[6:7|And when you are praying, speak not much|Orantes autem, nolite multum loqui]], that is, multiply words before God, [[6:7|as the heathens|sicut ethnici]], that is, the Gentiles, do, who speak much in praying for this reason: [[6:7|For they think that in their much speaking they may be heard|putant enim quod in multiloquio suo exaudiantur]], that is, by the power of many words, by their gods. And it is no wonder that they pray long and multiply words: for they pray to demons, who, even if they hear, cannot grant, nor do anything unless permitted by God. They pray to dead kings, Jupiter and Mercury, whose crimes are better known than their names, and who, even if they were alive, could not bestow salvation. They pray to senseless idols, which [[Ps 113:14|have ears and hear not|Aures habent, et non audient]][[Ps 134:17||]]. [[6:8|Be not you therefore like to them|Nolite ergo assimilari eis]], by multiplying words for the reason they do, so as to think you are heard for much speaking, and not rather for fervent affection. It is plain, then, that Christ does not absolutely forbid drawing out words in prayer, but that we should not do it after the manner of the heathens. For He Himself exhorts us to pray instantly and always[[Luke 18:1||]], which is not done without multiplying words, mental or vocal. He Himself also spent the night in prayer[[Luke 6:12||]]. [[6:8|for your Father knoweth what is needful for you, before you ask him|Scit enim Pater vester, quid opus sit vobis, antequam petatis eum]], that is, what is necessary or useful to you, before you ask Him for any matter. For the knowledge of God is eternal, perfect and unchangeable. Therefore there is no need to speak much, as if God would hear because of much speaking: for if so, something would then be made known to Him by our words of which He was before ignorant, or He would be swayed by the multitude of words; neither of which befits the all-knowing and unchangeable God.

paras.t: Denique circa hunc locum dicit Chrysostomus : De oratione nobis est sermo, quam solam quasi spirituale tributum anima de visceribus suis offert Deo. Vis autem scire, quam pretiosa sit oratio ? Nulla justitia thymiamati comparatur, nisi sola oratio. Sicut enim thymiamata bene confecta delectant hominem odorantem, sic oratio justi suavis est ante Deum. Vis autem scire dignitatem ejus? Mox ut de ore processerit, suscipiunt eam angeli manibus suis sicut Tobiæ angelus dixit : Ego orationem tuam obtuli Deo. Orans autem, nil novi faciat quod adspiciant alii : alte clamando, manus extendendo, pectus tundendo vel oculos impudenter ad cœlos levando. Sed interiora sua ingrediatur, ut nihil cogitet, nisi de quo orat, et quem orat; ut claudat ostium sensus carnalis, omnesque cogitationes carnales et sollicitudines foras expellat. Si autem de extraneis et carnalibus rebus cogitaveris, non introisti in interiorem intellectum tuum, neque clausisti ostium sensus ; sed tacite cum cogitationibus superfluis loquens, tempus orationis amittis. Possumus et per ostium intelligere, ut non clamose oremus. Ex clamosa enim oratione, multa mala sequuntur. Maxime tria hæc : Primum, quia clamose orans, non credit Deum esse ubique, et absconsa audire, id est, ita se habet alte sibilando, ac si non crederet illa. Secundum, quia mysteria orationum tuarum aliis pandis, et non audiris a Deo, quoniam indisciplinate orasti, sed adhuc ab hominibus derideris. Tertium, quoniam alterum juxta te non permittis orare. Vocibus enim tuis rapis sensum illius ad tuos sermones : et non solum non exaudiris, sed adhuc peccatum colligis, dum orare alios non permittis. Sic igitur ora ut Anna, cujus labia movebantur, vox non audiebatur. Hæc Chrysostomus.
paras.en: Further, on this place Chrysostom says: “Our discourse is of prayer, which alone the soul offers to God from its inmost parts as a spiritual tribute. Dost thou wish to know how precious prayer is? No justice is compared to incense except prayer alone. For as well-made incense delights the man who smells it, so the prayer of the just is sweet before God. Dost thou wish to know its dignity? As soon as it has gone forth from the mouth, the angels take it up in their hands, as the angel said to Tobias: [[Tob 12:12|I offered thy prayer to the Lord|ego obtuli orationem tuam Domino]] [Denis: “to God”]. Let him who prays do nothing new for others to look at: crying aloud, stretching out his hands, beating his breast, or shamelessly lifting his eyes to heaven. But let him enter into his inner self, so that he thinks of nothing but what he prays for and Him to whom he prays; so that he shuts the door of carnal sense and drives out all carnal thoughts and cares. But if thou thinkest of outward and carnal things, thou hast not entered into thy inner understanding, nor shut the door of sense; but speaking silently with superfluous thoughts, thou losest the time of prayer. By the door we can also understand that we should not pray noisily. For many evils follow from noisy prayer, above all these three. First, because he who prays noisily does not believe that God is everywhere and hears hidden things; that is, by whistling aloud he behaves as if he did not believe it. Second, because thou layest open the mysteries of thy prayers to others, and art not heard by God, since thou hast prayed without discipline, and art moreover mocked by men. Third, because thou dost not let the man next to thee pray. For by thy voice thou snatchest his mind to thy words; and not only art thou not heard, but thou gatherest sin besides, while thou dost not let others pray. So, then, pray like Anna, whose lips moved, and her voice was not heard[[1 Kings 1:13||]].” So far Chrysostom.

paras.t: Porro, per hoc dictum, Scit Pater vester quid opus sit vobis antequam petatis eum, videretur aliqualiter confirmari opinio Socratis asserentis nihil determinatum petendum a Deo, quoniam melius scit quam nos ipsi quid nobis expediat, nisi immediate subjungeret Christus orationem determinata bona petentem. Sed quum Deus invariabilis non flectatur, nec solum sciat quid nobis necesse sit, sed etiam quid ipse daturus exsistat, cur eum oramus ? Respondendum, quod ideo, ut ipse donet eo ordine quo se daturum prævidit. Quamvis enim prædestinatio non sit ex meritis, tamen in sua æterna prædestinatione disposuit se daturum gratiam in præsenti, et gloriam in futuro, per preces nostras ac merita. Oramus quoque, ut orando ferventius desideremus, et copiosius mereamur, sicque capaciores reddamur, et plura beneficia obtineamus, susceptamque gratiam diligentius custodiamus, in spe divina roboremur acquirendo quod petimus, et Deo familiariores quodammodo efficiamur, cum omni fiducia ad thronum gratiæ accedentes.
paras.en: Further, by this saying, [[6:8|your Father knoweth what is needful for you, before you ask him|Scit Pater vester quid opus sit vobis antequam petatis eum]], the opinion of Socrates might seem in some way confirmed, who asserted that nothing determinate is to be asked of God, since He knows better than we ourselves what is expedient for us; were it not that Christ immediately adds a prayer asking for determinate goods. But since God is unchangeable and is not swayed, and knows not only what we need but also what He Himself is going to give, why do we pray to Him? It must be answered: that He may give in the order in which He foresaw that He would give. For although predestination is not from merits, yet in His eternal predestination He disposed that He would give grace in the present and glory in the future through our prayers and merits. We pray also that by praying we may desire more fervently and merit more abundantly, and so be made more capable, obtain more benefits, guard more carefully the grace we have received, be strengthened in hope in God by gaining what we ask, and become in a manner more familiar with God, going with all [[Heb 4:16|confidence to the throne of grace|fiducia ad thronum gratiæ]].

paras.t: Consequenter docet Filius Dei formam orationis perfectæ, materiamque petendam : Sic ergo vos orabitis.
paras.en: Next the Son of God teaches the form of perfect prayer, and the matter to be asked for: [[6:9|Thus therefore shall you pray|Sic ergo vos orabitis]].

6.title: Expositio Orationis dominicæ: Pater noster
6.title_en: Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father”

paras.t: De hujus Orationis expositione, laude et efficacia, tanta jam a sanctis atque catholicis doctoribus dicta sunt, ut pene tædio sit ea perlegere. Verumtamen nec digna, nec sufficientia dicta sunt, nec usquam dicentur. Tanta nempe est hujus gloriosæ Orationis profunditas in sensu, fecunditas in mysteriis, efficacia in effectu, artificialitas in processu seu ordine, ut nemo capere queat vel eloqui. Immensum igitur æternumque Dei Verbum propter nos incarnatum, et quodammodo breviatum, verbum abbrevians et consummans fecit super terram.
paras.en: On the exposition, praise and efficacy of this Prayer so much has already been said by the holy and catholic doctors that it is almost tedious to read it through. Yet nothing worthy or sufficient has been said, nor ever will be. For so great is the depth of this glorious Prayer in its meaning, its fruitfulness in mysteries, its efficacy in effect, and its artistry in its progress or order, that no one can grasp it or utter it. The immeasurable and eternal Word of God, then, incarnate for our sake and in a manner shortened, has made upon the earth the word that cuts short and finishes, of which it is written: [[Rom 9:28|a short word shall the Lord make upon the earth|verbum abbrevians et consummans fecit super terram]] [the Latin plays on the Word “shortened”, breviatum, and the “short word”].

paras.t: Sic, inquit, vos orabitis : Pater noster. Quid tam auget fiduciam, quid tam inflammat affectum, quid tam lætificat humilem animam, sicut Deum verum et summum velle a fidelibus patrem vocari, eumque fiducialiter patrem vocare? Ut ergo cum plena fiducia postulemus, ejusque quem invocamus, benevolentiam conciliemus seu capiamus, voluit Christus ut sic inchoemus : Pater. Pater utique creatione, provisione, adoptione, redemptione, ad cujus imaginem conditi sumus, cujus providentia gubernamur, cujus gratia adoptati sumus, cujus pietate sumus redempti. Quamvis autem hoc loco nomine patris possit intelligi Deus Pater, prout pater relative accipitur, imo qualibet divina Persona; tamen secundum Augustinum, per patrem Deus Trinitas designatur. Dicit autem, Pater noster, potius quam, Pater meus ; ut dicendo, Noster, intelligamus nos omnes fratres esse, atque ad fraternam dilectionem ac mutuam orationem teneri, sicque oremus pro invicem ut salvemur ; et etiam ideo, ut sciamus quod Deus sit universale bonum, apud quem non est personarum acceptio, qui bonum commune diligit et requirit. Secundum Chrysostomum, libenter exaudit Deus precem, dum orans non solum pro se, sed et pro aliis orat. Pro se enim orare, natura est et necessitatis ; orare autem pro altero, caritatis et gratiæ. Sed pensemus ac satagamus, ne tantæ dignationi, caritati et pietati Creatoris simus ingrati, non considerando beneficia ejus, nec ejus majestatem honorando, ne dicat nobis : Si pater ego sum, ubi est honor meus ?
paras.en: [[6:9|Thus therefore shall you pray|Sic, inquit, vos orabitis]], He says: [[6:9|Our Father|Pater noster]]. What so increases confidence, what so inflames affection, what so gladdens the humble soul, as that the true and highest God wills to be called Father by the faithful, and that they should call Him Father with confidence? That we may ask, then, with full confidence, and win or gain the goodwill of Him whom we call upon, Christ willed that we should begin thus: Father; Father, indeed, by creation, providence, adoption and redemption: to whose image we were made, by whose providence we are governed, by whose grace we have been adopted, by whose kindness we have been redeemed. And although in this place by the name of Father can be understood God the Father, as Father is taken relatively [that is, as the name of the First Person in relation to the Son], indeed any divine Person, yet according to Augustine the Father here designates God the Trinity. And He says “Our Father” rather than “My Father”, so that in saying “our” we may understand that we are all brothers, and are bound to brotherly love and to prayer for one another, and so may pray for one another that we may be saved; and also so that we may know that God is the universal good, with whom there is no respect of persons, who loves and seeks the common good. According to Chrysostom, God gladly hears the prayer of one who prays not only for himself but also for others. For to pray for oneself is of nature and necessity; but to pray for another is of charity and grace. But let us weigh this and take care, lest we be ungrateful to so great a condescension, charity and kindness of the Creator, not considering His benefits nor honouring His majesty, lest He say to us: [[Mal 1:6|if then I be a father, where is my honour?|Si pater ego sum, ubi est honor meus]]

paras.t: Qui es in cœlis, id est in cœlestibus civibus seu Beatis, in quibus es excellentissimo modo per gloriam, beatificamque præsentiam. Vel, In cœlis materialibus, præsertim in cœlo empyreo, ubi specialiter esse et habitare diceris, quoniam ibi excellentius operaris, et te ipsum ostendis : quamvis secundum veritatem, ad nullum locum vel tempus determineris vel habitudinem habeas, quantum in te est, sed sis ante omnia non solus, post omnia non præventus, in omnibus non inclusus, extra omnia non exclusus, supra omnia non elatus, infra omnia non oppressus, manens æternaliter, in tua substantiali simplicitate invariabiliter incircumscriptibiliterque subsistens. Vel, In cœlis, id est sanctis ac virtuosis hominibus, quorum conversatio est in cœlis, qui terrenis non inhiant. Talibus enim dicit Apostolus : Templum Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos. In omnibus quippe est Deus per essentiam, præsentiam, et potentiam, omnia penetrans, ambiens et conservans, singulisque magis propinquus ac intimus quam aliqua pars suo toti, vel aliquid sibimetipsi : quoniam ipse solus illabitur rerum essentiis, nec aliquid alteri adest, nisi virtute divinæ præsentis, seu præsentis, et ut sic loquar, præsentissimi Dei, qui per Jeremiam testatur : Numquid non cœlum et terram ego impleo ?
paras.en: [[6:9|who art in heaven|qui es in cælis]], that is, in the heavenly citizens or the Blessed, in whom Thou art in the most excellent manner by glory and beatifying presence. Or, in the material heavens, above all in the empyrean heaven, where Thou art said to be and to dwell in a special way, because there Thou workest more excellently and showest Thyself; although in truth Thou art not bounded by any place or time, nor hast any relation to them, as far as Thou art concerned, but art before all things without being alone, after all things without being forestalled, in all things without being shut in, outside all things without being shut out, above all things without being lifted up, beneath all things without being pressed down, abiding eternally, subsisting unchangeably and uncircumscribably in Thy substantial simplicity. Or, in heaven, that is, in holy and virtuous men, [[Phil 3:20|our conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]] [Denis: “whose conversation is in heaven”], who do not gape after earthly things. For to such the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:17|the temple of God is holy, which you are|Templum Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos]]. For God is in all things by essence, presence and power, penetrating, encompassing and preserving all things, and nearer and more inward to each thing than any part to its whole, or anything to itself: since He alone enters into the essences of things, and nothing is present to another except by the power of God, who is present, or rather, if I may so speak, most present; who testifies through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:24|do not I fill heaven and earth|Numquid non cœlum et terram ego impleo]]?

paras.t: Sanctificetur, id est, cum omni puritate et reverentia honoretur, sanctum esse sciatur, in sanctitate et justitia ei ministretur, laudetur et glorificetur, nomen tuum nominatum, videlicet tu ipse qui diversis nominibus designaris, qui testatus es : Quicumque glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum. De quo Isaias inducit : Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate ; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester. Ecce hoc ad bonos pertinet filios, ut primo omnium patris sui honorem et gloriam quærant. Deus enim bonorum nostrorum non eget nec nostro obsequio sive præconio aliquid felicitatis aut gloriæ ei accrescit. Sed hoc prorsus justissimum est, ut omnis illi honor et gloria impendatur. Itaque, Sanctificetur ab omnibus nomen tuum, præstaque gratiam adimplendi hoc ipsum. Heu me miserum, ingratum ac frigidum ! qui toties sine attentione, et per consequens sine reverentia et affectu, verba ista pronuntio. Studeamus igitur agere quod ab omnibus fieri cupimus, videlicet, ut Deum ubique et semper honorare conemur, quoniam maledictus qui habet se ad eum intimorate et irreverenter. Unde in Ecclesiastico habetur : Et nunc in omni corde et ore collaudate et benedicite nomen Domini.
paras.en: [[6:9|hallowed be|sanctificetur]], that is, honoured with all purity and reverence, known to be holy, served in holiness and justice, praised and glorified, [[6:9|thy name|nomen tuum]] named, namely Thou Thyself who art designated by divers names, who hast testified: [[1 Kings 2:30|whosoever shall glorify me, him will I glorify|quicumque glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum]]. Of whom Isaias brings in: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread|Dominum exercituum ipsum sanctificate ; ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester]]. Behold, this belongs to good sons: first of all to seek the honour and glory of their father. For God does not need our goods, nor does any happiness or glory accrue to Him from our service or praise; but it is altogether most just that all honour and glory be paid to Him. So, then: Hallowed be Thy name by all, and grant the grace to fulfil this very thing. Ah, wretched, ungrateful and cold man that I am, who so often pronounce these words without attention, and consequently without reverence and affection! Let us strive, then, to do what we desire to be done by all, namely to try to honour God everywhere and always; for cursed is he who behaves towards Him without fear and without reverence. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 39:41|Now therefore with the whole heart and mouth praise ye him, and bless the name of the Lord|Et nunc in omni corde et ore collaudate et benedicite nomen Domini]].

paras.t: Adveniat regnum tuum, id est, ad tuam beatitudinem perducamur, ut ædificentur muri cœlestis Jerusalem, et ruina angelorum suppleatur, numerus Beatorum in patria compleatur, sicque regnum triumphantis Ecclesiæ consummetur, ac cito adveniat, ut transferamur de via ad patriam. Vel, Adveniat regnum tuum, id est Ecclesia militans, in qua per fidem et gratiam regnas ac habitas, perficiatur ac multiplicetur, totoque orbe diffundatur, ut tu solus regnes in ea, hostesque ejus, maxime dæmones, ejiciantur foras. Fiat voluntas tua, id est, omne præceptum tuum ac beneplacitum custodiatur seu impleatur, sicut in cœlo, hoc est in Beatis et comprehensoribus, et in terra, id est in viatoribus : hoc est, da gratiam, per quam nos in hac valle degentes, tibi tam prompte, reverenter ac pure obediamus, sicut Beati in cœlo viventes, quantum nostra fragilitas hoc permittit, videlicet, ut corpore et anima tibi in omnibus pareamus.
paras.en: [[6:10|Thy kingdom come|Adveniat regnum tuum]], that is, may we be brought to Thy beatitude, that the walls of the heavenly Jerusalem may be built up and the fall of the angels made good, the number of the Blessed in the fatherland be completed, and so the kingdom of the Church triumphant be consummated and come quickly, that we may be carried over from the way to the fatherland. Or, Thy kingdom come, that is, may the Church militant, in which Thou reignest and dwellest by faith and grace, be perfected and multiplied and spread through the whole world, that Thou alone mayest reign in it, and its enemies, above all the demons, be cast out. [[6:10|Thy will be done|fiat voluntas tua]], that is, may every precept and good pleasure of Thine be kept or fulfilled, [[6:10|as it is in heaven|sicut in cælo]], that is, in the Blessed and in those who have attained [comprehensores, the Blessed who already possess God, as opposed to viatores, those still on the way], [[6:10|on earth|et in terra]], that is, in wayfarers: that is, give the grace by which we who dwell in this valley may obey Thee as promptly, reverently and purely as the Blessed living in heaven, as far as our frailty allows; namely, that we may obey Thee in all things in body and soul.

paras.t: Panem nostrum supersubstantialem, id est Christum vere superessentialem, et tibi consubstantialem, qui ait, Ego sum panis vivus qui de cœlo descendi, hoc est panem sacramentalem ; da nobis hodie, ut hoc cibo spirituali ac saluberrimo quotidie sustentemur ac roboremur, suscipiendo eum sacramentaliter et spiritualiter, vel spiritualiter solum. Vel, Supersubstantialem, id est præcipuum, secundum Hieronymum, hoc est panem vitæ et intellectus, panem animæ, panem gratiæ ac obedientiæ (de quo dicitur : Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem Patris mei) ; vel certe, ut dictum est, panem Eucharistiæ, quem Dionysius supersubstantialem appellat. Lucas dicit : Panem nostrum quotidianum, id est, quo indigemus quotidie, scilicet sufficientiam alimenti, da nobis hodie, ut licet jam panem pro multis diebus sufficientem habeamus, nihilo minus cibum corporalem cum gratiarum actione et sobrietate, quasi de manu tua accipiamus. Hoc est quod in Proverbiis petitur : Tantum victui meo tribue necessaria.
paras.en: [[6:11|our supersubstantial bread|Panem nostrum supersubstantialem]], that is, Christ, truly superessential and consubstantial with Thee, who says, [[John 6:51|I am the living bread which came down from heaven|Ego sum panis vivus, qui de cœlo descendi]]; that is, the sacramental bread; [[6:11|Give us this day|da nobis hodie]], that we may be sustained and strengthened daily by this spiritual and most wholesome food, receiving it sacramentally and spiritually, or spiritually only. Or, supersubstantial, that is, chief, according to Jerome; that is, the bread of life and of understanding, the bread of the soul, the bread of grace and of obedience (of which it is said: [[John 4:34|My meat is to do the will|Meus cibus est, ut faciam voluntatem]] of my Father); or certainly, as has been said, the bread of the Eucharist, which Dionysius calls supersubstantial. Luke says: [[Luke 11:3|our daily bread|Panem nostrum quotidianum]], that is, which we need daily, namely sufficient food, [[Luke 11:3|Give us this day|da nobis hodie]]; so that even though we already have bread enough for many days, we may nonetheless receive bodily food with thanksgiving and sobriety, as from Thy hand. This is what is asked in Proverbs: [[Prov 30:8|give me only the necessaries of life|Tantum victui meo tribue necessaria]].

paras.t: Et dimitte nobis debita nostra, id est peccata, et pœnas quas peccando meruimus, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris, qui nos offenderunt, et emendare tenentur. Qui igitur non ignoscit, contra se orat. Aliqui vero dicunt se culpam dimittere, non pœnam, quam secundum viam justitiæ proponunt inferre. Qui tales sunt, videant quomodo Deus eis pœnas debitas relaxabit. Non tamen semper dimittenda est pœna, præsertim a prælato, vel judice, quia non expediret delinquenti. Si autem homo quantum in se est, mallet pœnam clementer dimittere, quam juste ulcisci, nisi fraterna caritas et ordo justitiæ aliud flagitarent, potest secure Deum orare pro pœnæ relaxatione.
paras.en: [[6:12|And forgive us our debts|Et dimitte nobis debita nostra]], that is, our sins, and the punishments we have deserved by sinning, [[6:12|as we also forgive our debtors|sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris]], who have offended us and are bound to make amends. He, then, who does not forgive prays against himself. Some, however, say that they forgive the fault, not the punishment, which they purpose to inflict by way of justice. Let those who are such see how God will remit to them the punishments due. Yet the punishment is not always to be remitted, especially by a prelate or judge, because it would not be expedient for the offender. But if a man, as far as in him lies, would rather remit the punishment mercifully than avenge justly, unless brotherly charity and the order of justice demanded otherwise, he can safely pray God for the remission of punishment.

paras.t: Et ne nos inducas in tentationem. Secundum Jacobum, Deus neminem tentat, loquendo de tentatione hostili et deceptoria, quæ ordinatur ad malum tentati. Tentat tamen electos tentatione probationis et exercitationis, quæ ordinatur ad purgationem et perfectionem tentati. Probat autem seu tentat, non ut sibi aliquid innotescat, sed ut homo purificetur, et aliis ostendatur, atque se ipsum cognoscat. Unde locutus est Moyses : Recordaberis itineris per quod adduxit te Dominus, ut affligeret te, atque tentaret, et nota fierent quæ versabantur in animo tuo. In Exodo quoque legitur : Ut probaret vos Deus venit, et ut terror illius semper in vobis esset. Sic et Christus tentavit Philippum. De qua sancta tentatione in Sapientia legitur : Deus tentavit justos, et invenit illos dignos se. De qua sanctus Job contestatur : Probavit me Dominus quasi aurum quod per ignem transit. Non ergo petimus non induci in hanc tentationem, non enim directe inclinat ad culpam. Ideo dicit Psalmista : Proba me, Domine, et tenta me. Et in Judith habetur : Illi qui tentationes non susceperunt in timore Domini, et impatientia sua exterminati sunt. Tobiæ quoque tentato angelus affirmavit : Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te. Nihilo minus orare debemus Deum, ut præstet nobis gratiam patientiæ atque constantiæ in tentatione hujusmodi.
paras.en: [[6:13|And lead us not into temptation|Et ne nos inducas in tentationem]]. According to James, God [[Jas 1:13|tempteth no man|neminem tentat]], speaking of hostile and deceitful temptation, which is ordered to the harm of the one tempted. Yet He tempts the elect with the temptation of proving and exercise, which is ordered to the purification and perfection of the one tempted. And He proves or tempts, not that anything may become known to Him, but that the man may be purified, and shown to others, and know himself. Hence Moses spoke: [[Deut 8:2|And thou shalt remember all the way through which the Lord thy God hath brought thee|Recordaberis itineris per quod adduxit te Dominus]], [[Deut 8:2|to afflict thee and to prove thee|ut affligeret te, atque tentaret]], [[Deut 8:2|and that the things that were known in thy heart might be made known|et nota fierent quæ versabantur in animo tuo]]. In Exodus too we read: [[Ex 20:20|God is come to prove you, and that the dread of him might be in you|Ut probaret vos Deus venit, et ut terror illius semper in vobis esset]]. So too Christ tempted Philip. Of this holy temptation we read in Wisdom: [[Wis 3:5|God hath tried them, and found them worthy of himself|Deus tentavit justos, et invenit illos dignos se]] [Denis: “the just”]. Of it holy Job testifies: [[Job 23:10|has tried me as gold that passeth through the fire|Probavit me Dominus quasi aurum quod per ignem transit]]. We do not, then, ask not to be led into this temptation, for it does not incline directly to fault. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 25:2|Prove me, O Lord, and try me|Proba me, Domine, et tenta me]]. And in Judith it is said: [[Jdt 8:24|they that did not receive the trials with the fear of the Lord|Illi qui tentationes non susceperunt in timore Domini]], [[Jdt 8:24|their impatience|impatientia sua]], [[Jdt 8:25|Were destroyed|exterminati sunt]]. And to Tobias when he was tempted the angel declared: [[Tob 12:13|because thou wast acceptable to God, it was necessary that temptation should prove thee|Quia acceptus eras Deo, necesse fuit ut tentatio probaret te]]. Nevertheless we ought to pray God to grant us the grace of patience and constancy in temptation of this kind.

paras.t: De alia vero tentatione jam dicta, quæ est ab hostibus animæ, scilicet mundo, carne, et demone, petimus ut non inducamur in eam per consensum, quamvis ipsa inducatur in nos per impugnationem. Imbecilles quoque et imperfecti suam infirmitatem scientes, quandoque utiliter orant ne tententur, propter vitandum ruinæ periculum, vel ne graviter impugnentur. Tentatio autem hujusmodi, dum ei non consentimus, est magni profectus occasio. Qui enim non est tentatus, quid scit? Itaque, Et ne nos inducas in tentationem, ne opprimat nos, nec mergamur in ea, nec desinas nos supra vires tentari, sed da fortitudinem resistendi, et fac cum tentatione proventum. In hanc malam tentationem inducit Deus permissive, subtrahendo auxilium. Juxta quem modum dicitur indurasse Pharaonem, Sehon, et Og: et quomodo dicit Apostolus, Mittet illis spiritum erroris, ut credant mendacio.
paras.en: As to the other temptation already mentioned, which comes from the enemies of the soul, namely the world, the flesh and the devil, we ask that we may not be led into it by consent, although it is led into us by assault. The weak and imperfect too, knowing their infirmity, sometimes usefully pray not to be tempted, to avoid the danger of falling, or not to be grievously assailed. But temptation of this kind, while we do not consent to it, is an occasion of great progress. For [[Ecclus 34:11|He that hath not been tried, what manner of things doth he know?|Qui enim non est tentatus, quid scit?]] So, then: and lead us not into temptation, lest it overwhelm us and we sink in it; and do not let us be tempted beyond our strength, but give us strength to resist, and [[1 Cor 10:13|make also with temptation issue|fac cum tentatione proventum]]. Into this evil temptation God leads permissively, by withdrawing His help. In this way He is said to have hardened Pharao, Sehon and Og; and in this way the Apostle says: God [[2 Thess 2:10|shall send them|Mittet illis]] the spirit [[2 Thess 2:10|of error, to believe lying|erroris, ut credant mendacio]].

paras.t: Porro viri perfecti orare possunt ut tententur utroque modo, qui cum Apostolo dicere possunt : Quis nos separabit a caritate Christi? Et : Certus sum, quia neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, neque creatura alia poterit nos separare a caritate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro. Talibus quippe dicitur : Omne gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis. Unde Jeremias oravit : Corripe me, Domine.
paras.en: Moreover, perfect men can pray to be tempted in both ways, men who can say with the Apostle: [[Rom 8:35|Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ?|Quis nos separabit a caritate Christi?]] And: [[Rom 8:38|For I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels|Certus sum, quia neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli]], [[Rom 8:39|nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord|neque creatura alia poterit nos separare a caritate Dei, quæ est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro]]. For to such it is said: [[Jas 1:2|count it all joy, when you shall fall into divers temptations|Omne gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis]]. Hence Jeremias prayed: [[Jer 10:24|Correct me, O Lord|Corripe me, Domine]].

paras.t: Sed libera nos a malo, hoc est ab omni incentivo et occasione peccati, a malis pœnalibus propter originale peccatum inflictis, ab omni periculo, et salutis obstaculo. Amen, id est, fiat. Hæc dictio, Amen, est Hebræa; quam nec Græcus nec Latinus interpres transtulit, propter reverentiam ejus, eo quod Christus toties usus est ea. Est autem orationis signaculum fructuosum, et animi recollectivum. Dicendo enim, Amen, anima summatim fertur ad omnia præinducta, et renovatur affectio impetrandi : sicque oratio cum fervore finita, pleniorem sortitur effectum.
paras.en: [[6:13|But deliver us from evil|Sed libera nos a malo]], that is, from every incentive and occasion of sin, from the penal evils inflicted because of original sin, from every danger and obstacle to salvation. [[6:13|Amen|Amen]], that is, so be it. This word Amen is Hebrew; neither the Greek nor the Latin translator translated it, out of reverence for it, because Christ used it so often. It is a fruitful seal of prayer, and one that gathers the mind together. For in saying Amen the soul is borne in sum to all that has gone before, and the desire of obtaining is renewed; and so prayer finished with fervour obtains a fuller effect.

paras.t: Postremo, de hujus dominicæ Orationis perfectione, et septem petitionum in ea contentarum congruentissimo ordine, dicit Thomas hoc modo : Oratio dominica omnino perfectissima est, quia non solum continetur in ea quidquid orandum est, sed etiam eo ordine quo petenda sunt : ita quod ipsa est informativa totius nostri affectus. Primo enim cadit in desiderio animæ ipse finis, deinde media ad finem. Finis autem noster est Deus, ad quem dupliciter tendimus : Primo, desiderando gloriam Dei, quantum ad ipsum, videlicet, ut ipse honorificetur in omnibus : quod procedit ex caritate qua diligimus Deum in se ipso. Et ad hoc pertinet prima petitio qua dicitur, Sanctificetur nomen tuum. Secundo, prout desideramus perfrui gloria Dei : quod oritur ex caritate qua nos ipsos in Deo diligimus. Ad quod spectat secunda petitio, Adveniat regnum tuum. Ad hunc autem finem ordinat seu adducit nos aliquid dupliciter : Primo per se : et hoc rursus dupliciter, scilicet : principaliter et directe, ut sunt opera virtuosa quibus meremur, ad quod respicit petitio tertia, Fiat voluntas tua ; secundo, instrumentaliter, utpote cooperando seu adjuvando ad opera bona, quod facit alimentum, et hoc quærit quarta petitio, Panem nostrum quotidianum. Secundo, ordinat nos aliquid ad finem prædictum, per accidens, scilicet removendo prohibens sive impedimentum salutis consequendæ, quæ est noster finis. Sunt autem tria quæ nos a salute impediunt : Primum est peccatum, quod directe a felicitate excludit : ideo quinta petitio est, Et dimitte nobis debita nostra, etc. Secundum est tentatio. a Deo nos retrahens : propter quod sexta petitione oramus, Et ne nos inducas, etc. Tertium est præsens pœnalitas, quæ vitæ sufficientiam impedit : ideo septimo petimus, Sed libera nos, etc.
paras.en: Lastly, on the perfection of this Lord’s Prayer, and the most fitting order of the seven petitions contained in it, Thomas speaks in this way: The Lord’s Prayer is altogether most perfect, because not only is everything to be prayed for contained in it, but also in the order in which they are to be asked; so that it shapes the whole of our affection. For first there falls in the desire of the soul the end itself, then the means to the end. Now our end is God, towards whom we tend in two ways. First, by desiring the glory of God as regards Himself, namely that He be honoured in all things; this proceeds from the charity by which we love God in Himself. And to this belongs the first petition, in which it is said, [[6:9|hallowed be thy name|sanctificetur nomen tuum]]. Secondly, as we desire to enjoy the glory of God; this arises from the charity by which we love ourselves in God. To this looks the second petition, [[6:10|Thy kingdom come|Adveniat regnum tuum]]. Now something orders or brings us to this end in two ways. First, of itself; and this again in two ways: principally and directly, as are the virtuous works by which we merit, to which the third petition looks, [[6:10|Thy will be done|Fiat voluntas tua]]; secondly, instrumentally, as by co-operating or helping towards good works, which food does, and this the fourth petition seeks, [[Luke 11:3|our daily bread|Panem nostrum quotidianum]]. Secondly, something orders us to the aforesaid end accidentally, namely by removing what hinders, or the obstacle to attaining salvation, which is our end. Now there are three things that hinder us from salvation. The first is sin, which directly shuts us out from happiness: therefore the fifth petition is, [[6:12|And forgive us our debts|Et dimitte nobis debita nostra]], etc. The second is temptation, drawing us back from God: for which reason in the sixth petition we pray, [[6:13|And lead us not|Et ne nos inducas]], etc. The third is present penalty, which hinders the sufficiency of life: therefore in the seventh we ask, [[6:13|But deliver us|Sed libera nos]], etc.

paras.t: Harum septem petitionum, tres primæ nunc impleri incipiunt, in patria vero perfecte implentur. Aliæ quatuor, ad præsentis vitæ necessitatem atque miseriam pertinent, secundum Augustinum. Sed quia militia est vita hominis super terram, nec a pœnalitatibus originalis peccati liberamur in sæculo isto, videtur quod etiam duæ ultimæ impleantur in patria, in qua neque tentatio locum habet, neque pœnalitas.
paras.en: Of these seven petitions, the first three begin to be fulfilled now, but are fulfilled perfectly in the fatherland. The other four belong to the necessity and misery of the present life, according to Augustine. But since [[Job 7:1|The life of man upon earth is a warfare|Militia est vita hominis super terram]], and we are not freed from the penalties of original sin in this world, it seems that the last two too are fulfilled in the fatherland, where neither temptation nor penalty has any place.

paras.t: Hanc igitur sacratissimam orationem ex divinæ ac sempiterna sapientiæ fonte immediate manantem, devotissime proferamus, et tanto devotius quanto frequentius, ne frequentia incuriam pariat atque fastidium, sed eam sæpius iterando, crescamus semper in ejus affectu, seu gratia, per quam ardentius solito repetatur. Novi fratrem qui ut hanc orationem attentius diceret, quamlibet ejus petitiunculam ad digitum manus per ordinem legit.
paras.en: Let us, then, utter this most sacred prayer, flowing immediately from the fountain of divine and everlasting wisdom, most devoutly, and the more devoutly the more often, lest frequency breed carelessness and weariness; but by repeating it often let us grow always in its affection, or in the grace by which it may be repeated more ardently than usual. I knew a brother who, to say this prayer more attentively, counted each of its little petitions in order on the fingers of his hand.

paras.t: Quod autem harum septem petitionum quinta, videlicet, Dimitte nobis, sit maxime attendenda propter pactum quod in ea cum Domino facimus, constat per hoe, quod hanc solam Christus quasi exponendo prosequitur : Si enim dimiseritis hominibus peccata eorum. Tanquam dicat : Recte docui vos sic orare, et merito sic oratis, Dimitte nobis debita, etc. Si enim dimiseritis hominibus peccata eorum in vos commissa vel omissa, dimittet et vobis Pater vester cœlestis delicta vestra in eum patrata. Si autem non dimiseritis hominibus, nec Pater vester cœlestis dimittet vobis peccata vestra. Hoc inferius magis tractabitur, et ex prehabitis patet. Tenemur enim omnes, etiam persecutores, diligere. Unde in Ecclesiastico dicitur : Qui vindicari vult, a Deo inveniet vindictam, et peccata illius servans servabit ; relinque proximo tuo nocenti te, et tunc deprecanti tibi peccata solventur. Et in libro Judicum : Sicut feci, ita reddidit mihi Dominus.
paras.en: That of these seven petitions the fifth, namely Forgive us, is to be attended to most of all, because of the pact we make with the Lord in it, is clear from this: that Christ follows up this one alone, as if expounding it: [[6:14|For if you will forgive men|Si enim dimiseritis hominibus]] their offences. As if He said: I rightly taught you to pray so, and you rightly pray so, Forgive us our debts, etc. [[6:14|For if you will forgive men|Si enim dimiseritis hominibus]] their offences committed or omitted against you, [[6:14|your heavenly Father will forgive you also your offences|dimittet et vobis Pater vester cælestis delicta vestra]] wrought against Him. [[6:15|But if you will not forgive men, neither will your Father|Si autem non dimiseritis hominibus, nec Pater vester]] in heaven [[6:15|forgive you your offences|dimittet vobis peccata vestra]]. This will be treated more below, and is plain from what has gone before. For we are all bound to love, even our persecutors. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 28:1|He that seeketh to revenge himself, shall find vengeance from the Lord, and he will surely keep his sins in remembrance|Qui vindicari vult, a Deo inveniet vindictam, et peccata illius servans servabit]]; [[Ecclus 28:2|Forgive thy neighbour if he hath hurt thee: and then shall thy sins be forgiven to thee when thou prayest|relinque proximo tuo nocenti te, et tunc deprecanti tibi peccata solventur]]. And in the book of Judges: [[Judg 1:7|as I have done, so hath God requited me|Sicut feci, ita reddidit mihi]] [Denis: “the Lord”].

paras.t: Quæritur, quomodo homo quicumque offensus offensori peccata dimittere possit, quum scriptum sit: Quis potest peccata dimittere, nisi solus Deus? Dicendum, quod solus Deus dimittit peccatum simpliciter per gratiam, tollendo maculam culpæ, relaxandoque pœnam qua secundum divinam æquitatem peccato debetur. Homo autem dimittit peccatum quodam modo, scilicet quantum ad injuriam seu offensam sibi illatam, vel quoad satisfactionem sibi debitam.
paras.en: It is asked how any man who has been offended can forgive sins to the offender, since it is written: [[Mark 2:7|Who can forgive sins, but God only?|Quis potest peccata dimittere, nisi solus Deus?]] It must be said that God alone forgives sin simply, by grace, taking away the stain of guilt and remitting the punishment that is due to sin according to the divine equity. But man forgives sin in a certain way, namely as regards the injury or offence done to himself, or as regards the satisfaction due to himself.

6.title: Declaratio residuæ partis præsentis capituli: Quum jejunatis
6.title_en: Explanation of the rest of the present chapter: “And when you fast”
6.note: A line at the foot of each column of p. 88 is damaged in the scan: one is marked […] (v. 32), the other is supplied by conjecture (v. 33).

paras.t: Quum jejunatis, nolite fieri sicut hypocritæ tristes. Jejunium est actus abstinentiæ, quæ est pars temperantiæ. Est enim jejunium moderata alimenti carentia, et ordinatur ad multa, præsertim ad quatuor, utpote : ad concupiscentiæ refrenationem, ad contemplationis puritatem, ad culpæ emendationem, ad virtutum et gratiæ adeptionem. Unde cantatur : Qui corporali jejunio vitia reprimis, mentem elevas, virtutem largiris et præmia. Quum ergo jejunium sit actus virtutis, ad Dei dumtaxat honorem fieri debet, non ad ostentationem inanem. Ideo ait Salvator : Quum jejunatis, vos ipsos corporaliter affligendo ex parcimonia victus, nolite fieri, id est, non solum non sitis, nec efficiamini, sed nec cupiatis esse vel fieri, sicut hypocritæ tristes. Hoc quod ait, Hypocritæ tristes, legi potest divisim, et conjunctim : divisim sic, Nolite fieri tristes in corde vel apparatu, sicut hypocritæ tristes sunt vel corde vel apparatu : conjunctim sic, Nolite fieri sicut hypocrita tristes, id est, non efficiamini similes hypocritis tristibus, simulando mœrorem in vultu quasi ex magna devotione. Exterminant enim, id est, extra convenientem dispositionem seu naturalem ac solitum terminum ponunt, facies suas, pallorem, attenuationem, seu maciem assumendo in vultu. Secundum diversas enim animæ affectiones facies facile immutatur. Quemadmodum ergo Esther regina tristem animum celavit vultu jueundo, sic hypocritæ inanem animum celant facie mœsta. Aliqui autem hypocritæ jejunant, ut faciem macilentam pallidamque acquirant, et sic sancti ac jejunantes putentur. Aliqui vero non jejunant, et tamen ficta exterminatione vultus jejunare se simulant. Sunt enim quatuor species hypocrisis : prima, qua homo se fingit habere vel facere quod non habet nec facit ; secunda, quum bona facit propter inanem gloriam; tertia, quum mala bonis obumbrationibus depinguntur ac palliantur : unde infra habetur, Væ vobis, qui similes estis sepulcris dealbatis. Quarta, quum homo simulat se velle latere, et tamen hoc facit ut videatur, nec hypocrita, sed humilis reputetur. Ecce quam infelicissimum, vile, et contemptibile est genus hypocritarum : de quibus merito dicitur, Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei. Deus namque est ipsa veritas ; totum autem negotium hypocritarum falsitati innititur. Exterminant igitur facies, ut pareant, id est videantur, hominibus jejunantes, non ad ædificationem intuentium, sed ad propriam laudem. Amen dico vobis, quia receperunt mercedem suam : quæ modica est, quoniam gaudium hypocritæ ad instar puncti.
paras.en: [[6:16|And when you fast, be not as the hypocrites, sad|Quum jejunatis, nolite fieri sicut hypocritæ tristes]]. Fasting is an act of abstinence, which is a part of temperance. For fasting is a moderate going without food, and it is ordered to many things, above all to four: the reining in of concupiscence, the purity of contemplation, the amendment of fault, and the gaining of virtues and grace. Hence it is sung: “Who by bodily fasting dost curb our vices, lift up our minds, and bestow virtue and its rewards” [from the Lenten preface of the Mass]. Since, then, fasting is an act of virtue, it ought to be done for the honour of God alone, not for vain display. Therefore the Saviour says: [[6:16|And when you fast|Quum jejunatis]], afflicting yourselves bodily by sparing food, [[6:16|be not|nolite fieri]]; that is, not only do not be or become, but do not even desire to be or become, [[6:16|as the hypocrites, sad|sicut hypocritæ tristes]]. The words “hypocrites, sad” can be read separately and together. Separately thus: Be not sad in heart or in bearing, as the hypocrites are sad either in heart or in bearing. Together thus: Be not as the sad hypocrites; that is, do not become like the sad hypocrites, feigning grief in the face as if from great devotion. [[6:16|For they disfigure their faces|Exterminant enim facies suas]], that is, they put them outside their fitting disposition, or their natural and usual bound [exterminare, literally “to put beyond the boundary”], taking on pallor, thinness or leanness in the face. For the face is easily changed according to the different affections of the soul. As, then, Queen Esther hid a sad mind under a cheerful face, so the hypocrites hide an empty mind under a sorrowful face. Some hypocrites fast in order to acquire a lean and pale face, and so be thought holy and men of fasting. Others do not fast, and yet pretend to fast by a feigned disfiguring of the face. For there are four kinds of hypocrisy: the first, when a man pretends to have or do what he neither has nor does; the second, when he does good things for vainglory; the third, when evil things are painted over and cloaked with a shadow of good: hence it is said below, [[Matt 23:27|Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites; because you are like to whited sepulchres|Væ vobis, qui similes estis sepulcris dealbatis]]; the fourth, when a man pretends to wish to be hidden, and yet does this in order to be seen and to be reckoned not a hypocrite but humble. Behold how most unhappy, vile and contemptible is the race of hypocrites, of whom it is rightly said: [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]]. For God is truth itself, while the whole business of hypocrites rests on falsehood. They disfigure their faces, then, [[6:16|that they may appear unto men to fast|ut pareant hominibus jejunantes]], that is, may be seen, not for the edification of those who look on, but for their own praise. [[6:16|Amen I say to you, they have received their reward|Amen dico vobis, quia receperunt mercedem suam]], which is slight, since [[Job 20:5|the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment|gaudium hypocritæ ad instar puncti]].

paras.t: Tu autem, quum jejunas. Consuetudo Scripturæ est, sæpe mutare personam, tempus, vel numerum : sic modo a plurali ad singulare descenditur. Tu autem, o fidelis, quicumque sis ille, quum jejunas, unge caput tuum, et faciem tuam lava, id est, sincerum vultum pretende, et festivus ac hilaris esto, ne videaris hominibus jejunans, id est, ut vanam gloriam fugias ; sed Patri tuo cœlesti, qui est in abscondito, id est, inaccessibilem lucem inhabitat, et incomprehensibilis est, quemadmodum Isaias testatur : Vere tu es Deus absconditus, Deus Isræl. Posuit nempe tenebras latibulum suum. Vel : Qui est, id est habitat, in abscondito, id est in corde humili, latere optanti, non in manifesto, id est in animo vano apparere volenti. Secundum Hieronymum, Christus loquitur secundum morem provinciæ Palestinæ, in qua diebus festis homines capita ungunt : sicque per capitis unctionem et faciei lotionem, insinuatur celebritas quædam, seu gaudium vultus. In omni enim opere virtuoso lætandum est, præsertim quum dicat Apostolus : Gaudete in Domino semper. Potest quoque per caput, mens, per faciem, conscientia designari, ut sit sensus : Unge caput tuum, id est, mentem tuam spirituali jucunditate perfunde : de qua ait Psalmista, Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ. Est enim oleum pravum, de quo scribitur : Oleum peccatoris non impinguet caput meum. Et est oleum bonum, de quo in Canticis : Oleum effusum nomen tuum, id est dulce, clarum, ac delectabile, quemadmodum oleum. Hoc oleum non competit hypocritis, juxta illud : Numquid hypocrita poterit in Omnipotente delectari? faciem, id est conscientiam, tuam lava ab intentione corrupta, omnique macula, prout per Jeremiam consulitur : Lava a malitia cor tuum, ut salva fias. Et Isaias inquit : Lavamini, mundi estote, auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum.
paras.en: [[6:17|But thou, when thou fastest|Tu autem, quum jejunas]]. It is the custom of Scripture often to change person, tense or number; so here it goes down from the plural to the singular. But thou, O faithful soul, whoever thou art, [[6:17|when thou fastest|quum jejunas]], [[6:17|anoint thy head, and wash thy face|unge caput tuum, et faciem tuam lava]], that is, show an open countenance, and be festive and cheerful, [[6:18|That thou appear not to men to fast|ne videaris hominibus jejunans]], that is, so that thou flee vainglory; [[6:18|but to thy Father who is in secret|sed Patri tuo cœlesti, qui est in abscondito]], that is, who dwells in light inaccessible and is incomprehensible, as Isaias testifies: [[Is 45:15|Verily thou art a hidden God, the God of Israel|Vere tu es Deus absconditus, Deus Israel]]. For [[Ps 17:12|he made darkness his cover|Posuit tenebras latibulum suum]]. Or: who is, that is, dwells, in secret, that is, in the humble heart that wishes to be hidden, not in the open, that is, in the vain mind that wishes to be seen. According to Jerome, Christ speaks according to the custom of the province of Palestine, in which men anoint their heads on feast days; and so by the anointing of the head and the washing of the face a certain festivity, or gladness of countenance, is suggested. For in every virtuous work we should rejoice, especially since the Apostle says: [[Phil 4:4|Rejoice in the Lord always|Gaudete in Domino semper]]. By the head too can be designated the mind, and by the face the conscience, so that the sense is: Anoint thy head, that is, pour spiritual gladness over thy mind; of which the Psalmist says: [[Ps 44:8|God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness|Unxit te Deus, Deus tuus, oleo lætitiæ]]. For there is a bad oil, of which it is written: [[Ps 140:5|let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head|Oleum peccatoris non impinguet caput meum]]. And there is a good oil, of which it is said in the Canticles: [[Cant 1:2|Thy name is as oil poured out|Oleum effusum nomen tuum]], that is, sweet, bright and delightful, like oil. This oil does not belong to hypocrites, according to the words: [[Job 27:10|can he delight himself in the Almighty|poterit in Omnipotente delectari]]? — said of the hypocrite. [[6:17|wash thy face|faciem tuam lava]], that is, thy conscience, from corrupt intention and every stain, as is counselled through Jeremias: [[Jer 4:14|Wash thy heart from wickedness|Lava a malitia cor tuum]], [[Jer 4:14|that thou mayst be saved|ut salva fias]]. And Isaias says: [[Is 1:16|Wash yourselves, be clean, take away the evil of your devices|Lavamini, mundi estote, auferte malum cogitationum vestrarum]].

paras.t: Et Pater tuus cœlestis, qui videt in abscondito, id est, intima cordis agnoscit, et in abscondito facta bona acceptat, approbandoque inspicit. Hoc modo Deus non videt inaniter facta in manifesto, juxta quod Sapiens ait : Non respicit Dominus in oblationes injustorum. Reddet tibi salutarem effectum jejunii, et premium copiosum, videlicet indulgentiam, concupiscentiarum mitigationem, contemplationisque gratiam. Denique, quod jejunium mereatur divinæ sapientiæ illustrationem, patet in Daniele, Anania, Azaria, et Misæle, quibus Deus præstitit sapientiam et scientiam propter abstinentiam. Meretur et precum exauditionem, sicut ad Danielem angelus loquitur : Ex die quo posuisti cor tuum ut affligeres te in conspectu Dei tui, exaudita sunt verba tua. Tanta nempe est virtus jejunii, ut de pessimis dæmonibus Christus dicat : Hoc genus dæmoniorum in nullo potest exire, nisi in oratione et jejunio.
paras.en: [[6:18|and thy Father who seeth in secret|Et Pater tuus cœlestis, qui videt in abscondito]], that is, knows the inmost things of the heart, and accepts the good things done in secret, and looks on them with approval. In this way God does not see what is done vainly in the open, according to what the Wise Man says: The Lord hath no respect to the offerings of the unjust [cf. Ecclus 34:23]. [[6:18|will repay thee|Reddet tibi]] the saving effect of the fast and an abundant reward, namely forgiveness, the easing of concupiscences, and the grace of contemplation. Moreover, that fasting merits the enlightenment of divine wisdom is plain in Daniel, Ananias, Azarias and Misael, to whom God gave wisdom and knowledge because of their abstinence. It merits also the hearing of prayers, as the angel says to Daniel: [[Dan 10:12|from the first day that thou didst set thy heart to understand, to afflict thyself in the sight of thy God, thy words have been heard|Ex die quo posuisti cor tuum ut affligeres te in conspectu Dei tui, exaudita sunt verba tua]]. For so great is the power of fasting that Christ says of the worst demons: [[Mark 9:28|This kind can go out by nothing, but by prayer and fasting|Hoc genus dæmoniorum in nullo potest exire, nisi in oratione et jejunio]].

paras.t: Sed quoniam parum prodest abstinere a cibis, nisi abstineatur a vitiis, prout Dominus asserit : Ecce in die jejunii vestri invenitur voluntas vestra ; ecce ad lites et contentiones jejunatis. Numquid hoc est jejunium quod elegi ? Nonne hoc est magis jejunium quod elegi? dissolve colligationes impietatis, solve fasciculos deprimentes. Et rursus, quoniam jejunii tres sunt comites, scilicet eleemosyna, humilitas, et oratio : unde in Tobia legitur, Bona est oratio cum jejunio et eleemosyna. Ideo consequenter Christus docet vitia exstirpare, avaritiamque vitare per eleemosynarum largitionem.
paras.en: But since it profits little to abstain from food unless one abstains from vices, as the Lord declares: [[Is 58:3|Behold in the day of your fast your own will is found|Ecce in die jejunii vestri invenitur voluntas vestra]]; [[Is 58:4|Behold you fast for debates and strife|ecce ad lites et contentiones jejunatis]]. [[Is 58:5|Is this such a fast as I have chosen|Numquid hoc est jejunium quod elegi]]? [[Is 58:6|Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? loose the bands of wickedness, undo the bundles that oppress|Nonne hoc est magis jejunium quod elegi? dissolve colligationes impietatis, solve fasciculos deprimentes]]. And again, since fasting has three companions, namely almsgiving, humility and prayer (hence we read in Tobias, [[Tob 12:8|Prayer is good with fasting and alms|Bona est oratio cum jejunio et eleemosyna]]), Christ accordingly teaches us next to root out vices and to avoid avarice by the giving of alms.

paras.t: Nolite thesaurizare vobis, id est immoderate colligere, thesauros, id est temporales divitias naturales, ut sunt blada, gemmæ, etc., vel artificiales, ut sunt pecunia, vasa et vestes, in terra, id est in sæculo isto, ubi non habetis manentem locum, sed peregrini et advenæ estis : juxta illud in Psalmo, Ne sileas, quoniam advena ego sum apud te et peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei. Unde in libro Paralipomenon David fatetur : Peregrini sumus coram te, Domine ; dies nostri quasi umbra sunt super terram, et nulla est mora. Ubi ærugo, id est rubigo, et tinea demolitur, id est, corrumpit divitias seu thesauros, et ubi fures effodiunt domos vel loca in quibus occultantur thesauri, et furantur eos. Thesaurus enim est vel de metallis, et hunc demolitur rubigo; vel de vestibus, quem destruit tinea ; vel de lapidibus, quem subtrahunt fures. Hinc scriptum est : Agite nunc, divites, plorate ululantes in miseriis quæ advenient vobis : divitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, et vestimenta vestra a tineis comesta sunt: aurum vestrum et argentum vestrum æruginavit, et ærugo eorum in testimonium vobis erit. Hanc thesaurizationem seu avaritiam gravissime damnat Scriptura. Dicit enim Apostolus, quod avaritia sit idolorum servitus, omniumque malorum radix sit cupiditas ; et, Qui volunt (inquit) divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli. Sapiens quoque ait : Avaro nihil est scelestius, et nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam : hic enim animam suam habet venalem. Quum enim temporalia ad spiritualia ordinantur, habent rationem instrumenti ac medii : ideo non sunt amplius appetenda vel exquærenda, quam ad spiritualia bona adipiscenda, augenda, seu conservanda, prosunt et conferunt. Propter quod dicit Apostolus : Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Verumtamen thesaurizatio procedens ex causa honesta, et nemini nocens, atque ad pium finem relata, non est illicita, neque his verbis prohibita.
paras.en: [[6:19|Lay not up to yourselves|Nolite thesaurizare vobis]], that is, do not gather beyond measure, [[6:19|treasures|thesauros]], that is, temporal riches, natural ones such as corn, jewels, etc., or artificial ones such as money, vessels and garments, [[6:19|on earth|in terra]], that is, in this world, where you have no abiding place, but are pilgrims and strangers; according to the words in the Psalm: [[Ps 38:13|Be no silent: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were|Ne sileas, quoniam advena ego sum apud te et peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei]]. Hence in the book of Paralipomenon David confesses: [[1 Par 29:15|For we are sojourners before thee|Peregrini sumus coram te]], O Lord; [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|dies nostri quasi umbra sunt super terram, et nulla est mora]]. [[6:19|where the rust|Ubi ærugo]], that is, corrosion, [[6:19|and moth consume|et tinea demolitur]], that is, corrupt riches or treasures, [[6:19|and where thieves break through|et ubi fures effodiunt]] houses or places where treasures are hidden, [[6:19|and steal|et furantur]] them. For treasure is either of metals, and this the rust consumes; or of garments, which the moth destroys; or of stones, which thieves carry off. Hence it is written: [[Jas 5:1|Go to now, ye rich men: weep and howl in your miseries, which shall come upon you|Agite nunc, divites, plorate ululantes in miseriis quæ advenient vobis]]. [[Jas 5:2|Your riches are corrupted: and your garments are motheaten|divitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, et vestimenta vestra a tineis comesta sunt]]. [[Jas 5:3|Your gold and silver is cankered: and the rust of them shall be for a testimony against you|aurum vestrum et argentum vestrum æruginavit, et ærugo eorum in testimonium vobis erit]]. This treasuring, or avarice, Scripture condemns most gravely. For the Apostle says that covetousness is [[Eph 5:5|a serving of idols|idolorum servitus]], and that [[1 Tim 6:10|the desire of money is the root of all evils|Radix enim omnium malorum est cupiditas]]; and: [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil|qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem, et laqueum diaboli]]. The Wise Man also says: [[Ecclus 10:9|nothing is more wicked than the covetous man|Avaro nihil est scelestius]], [[Ecclus 10:10|There is not a more wicked thing than to love money: for such a one setteth even his own soul to sale|et nihil est iniquius quam amare pecuniam : hic enim animam suam habet venalem]]. For since temporal things are ordered to spiritual ones, they have the nature of an instrument and a means; therefore they are not to be desired or sought further than they help and contribute to gaining, increasing or preserving spiritual goods. For this reason the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 6:8|But having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. Yet laying up treasure that proceeds from an honest cause, harms no one, and is referred to a holy end, is not unlawful, nor is it forbidden by these words.

paras.t: Thesaurizate autem, id est, copiose colligite, et prudenter reponite, vobis, id est ad vestram salutem, thesauros, id est cumulum operum meritoriorum, in cœlo empyreo, id est ad hunc finem, ut ad cœlestem perducamini mansionem, committendo opera vestra Deo, et mercedem ab eo tantum quærendo. Hoc est quod Apostolus monet : Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe, non sublime sapere, nec sperare in incerto divitiarum, divites fieri in operibus bonis, thesaurizare sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, ut apprehendant veram vitam. Avari autem, et divites qui in terra, non in cœlo, thesaurizant, experientur verum esse quod in Job scribitur : Dives quum dormierit, nihil secum auferet ; apprehendet eum quasi aqua inopia. Denique quidam thesaurizant sibi in inferno, sicut affirmat Apostolus : Secundum duritiam tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ et revelationis justi judicii Dei. Tales sunt peccatores in peccatis assidui, de quibus Propheta Nescierunt (inquit) facere rectum, thesaurizantes impietatem. Peccator enim adjiciet ad peccandum. Ubi neque ærugo neque tinea demolitur thesauros, et ubi fures non effodiunt neque furantur. In regno enim cœlorum nihil esse potest nocivum aut corruptivum, juxta illud : Non intrabit in illam civitatem aliquid coinquinatum, nisi qui scripti sunt in libro vitæ.
paras.en: [[6:20|But lay up to yourselves|Thesaurizate autem vobis]], that is, gather plentifully and store away prudently, for yourselves, that is, for your salvation, [[6:20|treasures|thesauros]], that is, a heap of meritorious works, [[6:20|in heaven|in cœlo]], the empyrean, that is, to this end, that you may be brought to the heavenly mansion, committing your works to God and seeking reward from Him alone. This is what the Apostle counsels: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich of this world not to be highminded nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches|Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe, non sublime sapere, nec sperare in incerto divitiarum]], [[1 Tim 6:18|to be rich in good work|divites fieri in operibus bonis]], [[1 Tim 6:19|To lay up in store for themselves a good foundation against the time to come, that they may lay hold on the true life|thesaurizare sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, ut apprehendant veram vitam]]. But the covetous, and the rich who lay up treasure on earth and not in heaven, will find true what is written in Job: [[Job 27:19|The rich man when he shall sleep shall take away nothing with him|Dives quum dormierit, nihil secum auferet]]; [[Job 27:20|Poverty like water shall take hold on him|apprehendet eum quasi aqua inopia]]. Moreover some lay up treasure for themselves in hell, as the Apostle affirms: [[Rom 2:5|according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath, against the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God|Secundum duritiam tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die iræ et revelationis justi judicii Dei]]. Such are sinners constant in their sins, of whom the Prophet says: [[Amos 3:10|they have not known to do the right thing|Nescierunt (inquit) facere rectum]], [[Amos 3:10|storing up iniquity|thesaurizantes impietatem]]. For [[Ecclus 3:29|the sinner will add sin to sin|Peccator enim adjiciet ad peccandum]]. [[6:20|where neither the rust nor moth doth consume, and where thieves do not break through, nor steal|Ubi neque ærugo neque tinea demolitur thesauros, et ubi fures non effodiunt neque furantur]]. For in the kingdom of heaven there can be nothing harmful or corruptible, according to the words: [[Apoc 21:27|There shall not enter into it any thing defiled|Non intrabit in illam civitatem aliquid coinquinatum]], [[Apoc 21:27|but they that are written in the book of life|nisi qui scripti sunt in libro vitæ]].

paras.t: Propterea vero in cœlo thesaurizare debes, o quilibet Christiane : Ubi enim est thesaurus tuus, ibi est et cor tuum. Thesaurus namque est quod præcipue amatur, colligitur, et custoditur. Ubi ergo thesaurus tuus, ibi est et cor tuum, non per essentiam, sed per affectum, intentionem atque memoriam. Per cor enim, desiderium et cogitatio cordis exprimitur. Quod ergo magis amatur, hoc frequentius cogitatur. Ideo thesaurizantes immoderate in terra, conversationem non habent in cœlo, neque cor supernis ac divinis intentum, sed in sensibilibus pressum et miserabiliter occupatum. Sed quoniam Christianus oculum mentis semper ad cœlum, tanquam ad patriam, erigere debet, incumbit ei thesaurizare in cœlo spirituales divitias meritorum, quas in die mortis inveniat, edat, et sine fine possideat.
paras.en: And therefore thou oughtest to lay up treasure in heaven, O Christian, whoever thou art: [[6:21|For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also|Ubi enim est thesaurus tuus, ibi est et cor tuum]]. For treasure is what is chiefly loved, gathered and guarded. Where, then, thy treasure is, there is thy heart also, not by essence, but by affection, intention and memory. For by the heart is expressed the desire and thought of the heart. What is loved more, then, is thought of more often. Therefore those who lay up treasure on earth beyond measure have not their conversation in heaven, nor a heart intent on the things above and divine, but one weighed down and wretchedly taken up with the things of sense. But since a Christian ought always to raise the eye of his mind to heaven as to his fatherland, it falls to him to lay up in heaven the spiritual riches of merits, which on the day of death he may find, feed on, and possess without end.

paras.t: Lucerna corporis tui est oculus tuus. Non de oeulo exteriori, neque de corpore naturali intelligendum est hoc. Subditur enim : Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit, etc. Oculus enim exterior non proprie dicitur simplex vel nequam, sed sanus vel infirmus. Et quamvis aliquo modo simplex dici possit, non tamen propter ejus simplicitatem, id est custodiam, totum corpus naturale lucidum erit, id est bonis actibus ornatum, et a carnalibus vitiis incontaminatum. Potest enim contingere, ut propter D) incustodiam tactus vel gustus maculetur, quemadmodum et in cæcis. Intelligendum est ergo de oculo interiori et corpore morali, ut sit sensus : Lucerna, id est illuminatrix atque directrix, corporis tui, id est totius operationis tuæ, seu universitatis et congeriei operum tuorum licitorum, est oculus tuus, id est ratio illuminata, vel intentio recta, quæ dirigit animam in agendo sicut lucerna illuminat hominem in eundo. Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex, id est ratio non perversa, et intentio bona, totum corpus tuum, id est omne opus tuum, lucidum erit, id est splendore virtutis ornatum et purum.
paras.en: [[6:22|The light of thy body is thy eye|Lucerna corporis tui est oculus tuus]]. This is not to be understood of the outward eye, nor of the natural body. For it is added: [[6:22|If thy eye be single, thy whole body shall be lightsome|Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex, totum corpus tuum lucidum erit]], etc. For the outward eye is not properly called single or evil, but sound or sick. And although in some way it could be called single, yet it is not because of its singleness, that is, its being guarded, that the whole natural body will be lightsome, that is, adorned with good acts and undefiled by carnal vices. For it can happen that through want of guard over touch or taste it is stained, as happens even in the blind. It is to be understood, then, of the inward eye and the moral body, so that the sense is: [[6:22|The light|Lucerna]], that is, that which lights and directs, [[6:22|of thy body|corporis tui]], that is, of thy whole activity, or of the whole sum and mass of thy lawful works, [[6:22|is thy eye|est oculus tuus]], that is, enlightened reason, or right intention, which directs the soul in acting as a lamp lights a man in walking. [[6:22|If thy eye be single|Si fuerit oculus tuus simplex]], that is, reason not perverted, and good intention, [[6:22|thy whole body|totum corpus tuum]], that is, all thy work, [[6:22|shall be lightsome|lucidum erit]], that is, adorned with the splendour of virtue, and pure.

paras.t: Si autem oculus tuus nequam fuerit, id est intentio obliqua, et ratio errabunda, totum corpus tuum, id est congeries operum, tenebrosum erit, id est vitiosum et maculatum : quamvis ipsa ex genere bona sint et præcepta, ut si quis vadat ad Missam ut videat mulierem, vel præstet eleemosynam ut videatur ab homine. Intentio enim imprimit speciem moralitatis operationi, et a fine maxime pendet bonitas et malitia actionis. Intentio vero et finis est duplex, videlicet : correspondens, connaturalis, seu proportionatus operi. De quo fine et intentione nunc agitur. Alius est finis et intentio improportionate se habens ad actum, sed solum ex parte operantis concipitur. Et sic ex se mala non possunt fieri propter finem bonum, seu bona intentione, loquendo de fine et intentione primo modo acceptis ; sed fieri possunt bono fine et bona intentione, seeundo modo. Hoc tamen non sufficit ad operis bonitatem : ut si quis occidat adversarium suum, quatenus illo occiso, pacifice vivat.
paras.en: [[6:23|But if thy eye be evil|Si autem oculus tuus nequam fuerit]], that is, a crooked intention and wandering reason, [[6:23|thy whole body|totum corpus tuum]], that is, the mass of thy works, [[6:23|shall be darksome|tenebrosum erit]], that is, vicious and stained, even though the works themselves are good in their kind and commanded: as if someone goes to Mass to see a woman, or gives alms to be seen by men. For the intention stamps the species of morality on the act, and the goodness and malice of an action depend most of all on the end. Now the end and intention are twofold. One is corresponding, connatural, or proportioned to the work; and it is of this end and intention that we are now speaking. The other end and intention stands in no proportion to the act, but is conceived only on the part of the one acting. And so things evil in themselves cannot be done for a good end, or with a good intention, speaking of end and intention taken in the first way; but they can be done with a good end and a good intention in the second way. Yet this is not enough for the goodness of the work: as if someone kills his adversary so that, once he is killed, he may live in peace.

paras.t: Si ergo lumen quod in te est, tenebræ sunt, id est, si ratio tua, quæ debuit alia illustrare (quia signatum est super eam lumen vultus divini), tenebris ignorantiæ et peccati fuscatur, ipsa quoque intentio pervertatur, ipsæ tenebræ quantæ erunt? id est, affectiones carnales et operationes injuste quam impia erunt? Erunt quippe dupliciter vitiose : primo, quia in se malæ sunt; seeundo, quia ex prava intentione procedunt.
paras.en: [[6:23|If then the light that is in thee, be darkness|Si ergo lumen quod in te est, tenebræ sunt]], that is, if thy reason, which ought to have enlightened other things (for [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]] [Denis: “the light of the divine countenance is signed upon it”]), is darkened by the darkness of ignorance and sin, and the intention itself is perverted, [[6:23|the darkness itself how great shall it be!|ipsæ tenebræ quantæ erunt]], that is, how wicked will carnal affections and unjust deeds be? They will be vicious in two ways: first, because they are evil in themselves; secondly, because they proceed from a perverse intention.

paras.t: Consequenter ponit Salvator rationem non thesaurizandi in terra, seu contemnendi superfluitatem temporalium divitiarum. Nemo potest duobus dominis non subordinatis, sed contrariam voluntatem habentibus, servire, videlicet Deo et mundo, Deo et carni. Propter quod dicit Apostolus : Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem. Dominis vero subalternatis atque concordibus, potest homo si- mul servire ac obedire, videlicet Deo et ejus vicariis. Imo qui uni eorum repugnat, reluctatur et alteri, sicut ait Salvator : Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit. Aut enim unum odio habebit, quantum ad id quo contrariatur alteri, et alterum diliget, eum videlicet cui ex animo servit, juxta quod dicit Apostolus : Servi, diligite dominos vestros, non ad oculum servientes, quasi hominibus placentes, sed ex animo. Aut unum sustinebit, id est eum cui servit : et si non diligat, tamen tolerabit eum, et jugo ejus subjiciet se; et alterum contemnet, videlicet eum cui non servit neque obedit. Non dicit, Aut unum diliget, et alterum contemnet : quia interdum non diligit eum cui deservit, et tamen sustinet eum quasi durum dominum, ut patet in his qui dæmoni serviunt, quem non diligunt. Item non dicit, Et alterum odio habebit, sed, Contemnet, videlicet Deum : quia secundum Augustinum, etiam illi qui non serviunt Deo, non odiunt eum, sed spernunt, dum quasi de ejus bonitate securi sunt. Dicit enim Augustinus : Nullius vere conscientia Deum potest odisse. Sed videtur contrarium quod de Judæis ait Christus : Nunc autem viderunt et oderunt me et Patrem meum gratis. Et Psalmista : Nonne qui oderunt te, Domine, oderam ? Et rursus : Superbia eorum qui te oderunt, ascendit semper. Dicendum, quod considerando Deum secundum se, et ut causam rerum, nemo eum odit; considerando vero eum ut prohibitorem et punitorem delectationum ac delectabilium, multi odiunt ipsum.
paras.en: Next the Saviour gives the reason for not laying up treasure on earth, or for despising the superfluity of temporal riches. [[6:24|No man can serve two masters|Nemo potest duobus dominis non subordinatis, sed contrariam voluntatem habentibus, servire]] who are not subordinate to one another but have contrary wills, namely God and the world, God and the flesh. For this reason the Apostle says: [[Gal 1:10|If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ|Si hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem]]. But masters who are ranked one under another and in accord a man can serve and obey at once, namely God and His vicars. Indeed he who opposes one of them resists the other too, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 10:16|He that heareth you heareth me: and he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos audit, me audit; et qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. [[6:24|For either he will hate the one|Aut enim unum odio habebit]], as regards that in which he is contrary to the other, [[6:24|and love the other|et alterum diliget]], namely him whom he serves from the heart; according to what the Apostle says: Servants, love your masters, [[Eph 6:6|Not serving to the eye, as it were pleasing men|non ad oculum servientes, quasi hominibus placentes]], but from the heart. [[6:24|or he will sustain the one|Aut unum sustinebit]], that is, him whom he serves: and even if he does not love him, he will yet put up with him and submit to his yoke; [[6:24|and despise the other|et alterum contemnet]], namely him whom he neither serves nor obeys. He does not say, Either he will love the one and despise the other: because sometimes a man does not love him whom he serves, and yet puts up with him as a hard master, as is plain in those who serve the devil, whom they do not love. Again He does not say, And he will hate the other, but, he will despise, namely God: because, according to Augustine, even those who do not serve God do not hate Him, but despise Him, while they are as it were secure of His goodness. For Augustine says: “No one’s conscience can truly hate God.” But against this seems to be what Christ says of the Jews: [[John 15:24|now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father|Nunc autem viderunt et oderunt me et Patrem meum]] without cause. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 138:21|Have I not hated them, O Lord, that hated thee|Nonne qui oderunt te, Domine, oderam]]? And again: [[Ps 73:23|the pride of them that hate thee ascendeth continually|Superbia eorum qui te oderunt, ascendit semper]]. It must be said that, considering God in Himself and as the cause of things, no one hates Him; but considering Him as the forbidder and punisher of pleasures and pleasant things, many hate Him.

paras.t: Non potestis Deo servire, id est vere et obedientialiter subditi esse, et mammonæ, id est divitiis, seu dæmoni de avaritia tentanti. Qui enim Deo servit, præfert spiritualia et æterna sensibilibus ac transitoriis; qui vero divitiis servit, præfert caduca ccelestibus. Divitiis namque servire, est inordinato earum affectu ligari, in eis finem ponere, cupiditatisque vitio superari atque subesse. A quo autem quis victus est, hujus et servus est. Unde Salvator ait : Omnis qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati. Talis potius possidetur et regitur a divitiis, quam regat et possideat eas.
