paras.en: [[6:24|You cannot serve God|Non potestis Deo servire]], that is, be truly and obediently subject to Him, [[6:24|and mammon|et mammonæ]], that is, riches, or the demon who tempts to avarice. For he who serves God prefers spiritual and eternal things to the things of sense and passing things; but he who serves riches prefers perishable things to heavenly ones. For to serve riches is to be bound by a disordered affection for them, to place one’s end in them, and to be overcome by and subject to the vice of cupidity. [[2 Pet 2:19|For by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave|A quo autem quis victus est, hujus et servus est]]. Hence the Saviour says: [[John 8:34|whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin|Omnis qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati]]. Such a man is rather possessed and ruled by riches than he rules and possesses them.

paras.t: Ideo dico vobis discipulis meis, qui ad perfectionem tendere festinatis. Talibus enim præcipue loquitur Christus in sequentibus, quamvis ad omnes Christianos aliquo modo pertineant. Ne solliciti sitis, id est, inordinatam et anxiam curam habeatis, anima vestra, id est vitæ animali alimoniis indigenti, vel vobis ipsis (ut ponatur pars pro toto, scilicet anima pro homine), quid manducetis, id est de cibo et sustentaculo vitæ, sub quo intelligitur potus ; neque corpori vestro solliciti sitis hoc modo, quid induamini, id est de vestitu. Superflua autem sollicitudo circa hujusmodi appellatur, quando homo in tantum circa talia adipiscenda occupatur, quod a spiritualibus debitis impeditur, vel talia abundantius quærit, quam necessaria sint. De sollicitudine tali Salomon loquitur : Exspectatio sollicitorum peribit. Porro sollicitudo ordinata et rationalis vocatur, qua homo secundum exigentiam sui status quærit necessaria vitæ præsentis in ordine ad spiritualia. Talisque sollicitudo est pars prudentiæ; hanc non habere, esset Deum tentare, vel ignaviter se habere.
paras.en: [[6:25|Therefore I say to you|Ideo dico vobis]], My disciples, who hasten to strive for perfection. For it is to such chiefly that Christ speaks in what follows, although it concerns all Christians in some way. [[6:25|be not solicitous|Ne solliciti sitis]], that is, have no disordered and anxious care, [[6:25|for your life|animæ vestræ]], that is, for the animal life that needs nourishment, or for yourselves (the part being put for the whole, namely the soul for the man), [[6:25|what you shall eat|quid manducetis]], that is, about food and the sustenance of life, under which drink is understood; [[6:25|nor for your body|neque corpori vestro]] be solicitous in this way, [[6:25|what you shall put on|quid induamini]], that is, about clothing. Now care about such things is called superfluous when a man is so taken up with obtaining them that he is hindered from the spiritual things he owes, or seeks them more abundantly than is necessary. Of such care Solomon speaks: [[Prov 11:7|the expectation of the solicitous shall perish|Exspectatio sollicitorum peribit]]. On the other hand, care is called ordered and reasonable by which a man, according to what his state requires, seeks the necessaries of the present life in order to spiritual things. Such care is a part of prudence; not to have it would be to tempt God, or to behave slothfully.

paras.t: Prædictam vero superfluam sollicitudinem non esse habendam, probat Salvator multiplici ratione et exemplo. Et primo per locum a majori. Nonne anima plus, id est præstantior, est quam esca corporalis ? et corpus nonne plus, id est dignius, est quam vestimentum ? Utique. Qui ergo sine vestra sollicitudine, ex sua liberalissima bonitate largitus est vobis animam et corpus, alimentum quoque et vestitum præstabit sine immoderata sollicitudine vestra. Ipsi enim cura præcipua est de rationali creatura.
paras.en: That the superfluous care described is not to be had, the Saviour proves by many reasons and examples. And first by an argument from the greater. [[6:25|Is not the life more|Nonne anima plus est]], that is, more excellent, [[6:25|than the meat|quam esca]] of the body? [[6:25|and the body more|et corpus plus]], that is, worthier, [[6:25|than the raiment?|quam vestimentum?]] Certainly. He, then, who without your care, out of His most bountiful goodness, has given you soul and body, will also provide food and clothing without immoderate care on your part. For He takes special care of the rational creature.

paras.t: Deinde ponit aliam rationem ad idem. sumptam ex consideratione irrationabilium creaturarum. Respicite, id est, sapienter attendite, volatilia cœli ærii : quæ dicuntur volucres cœli, quoniam volant in ære, qui infimum cœlum vocatur; quoniam non serunt, neque metunt, neque congregant fructus in horrea. Omnia enim hæc sunt opera rationis, quæ illis convenire non possunt. Videmus tamen, quod multæ aves congregant victum in nidos. Quemadmodum ergo volatilia pergunt ad grana, et colligunt ea secundum naturalem instinctum, sic hominibus committitur labor et providentia, non sollicitudo inquieta vel avaritia. E^ Pater vester cofestis pascit ea per causas secundas. Nam opus naturæ et intelligentiæ, est opus primæ causæ. Unde in Psalmo cantamus : Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum. Et Job ait : Qui præparat corvo escam, quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, vagientes eo quod non habeant cibos. Nonne vos magis pluris, id est majoris dignitatis ac pretii, estis illis volatilibus? Et per consequens magis vobis providebit. In tantum siquidem major cura est Deo de rationabilibus quam irrationabilibus creaturis, ut dicat Apostolus : Numquid cura est Deo de bobus?
paras.en: Then He gives another reason to the same effect, taken from the consideration of irrational creatures. [[6:26|Behold|Respicite]], that is, consider wisely, [[6:26|the birds of the air|volatilia cœli]], which are called birds of heaven because they fly in the air, which is called the lowest heaven; [[6:26|for they neither sow, nor do they reap, nor gather into barns|quoniam non serunt, neque metunt, neque congregant fructus in horrea]] the fruits. For all these are works of reason, which cannot belong to them. Yet we see that many birds gather food into their nests. As, then, birds go to the grain and gather it according to natural instinct, so to men labour and providence are committed, not restless care or avarice. [[6:26|and your heavenly Father feedeth them|Et Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea]] through second causes. For the work of nature and of the intelligences is the work of the first cause. Hence we sing in the Psalm: [[Ps 146:9|Who giveth to beasts their food: and to the young ravens that call upon him|Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum]]. And Job says: [[Job 38:41|Who provideth food for the raven, when her young ones cry to God, wandering about, because they have no meat?|Qui præparat corvo escam, quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, vagientes eo quod non habeant cibos]] [[6:26|Are not you of much more value than they?|Nonne vos magis pluris estis illis?]], that is, of greater dignity and worth? And consequently He will provide for you the more. For God’s care for rational creatures is so much greater than for irrational ones that the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 9:9|Doth God take care for oxen?|Numquid de bobus cura est Deo?]]

paras.t: Quis autem vestrum cogitans potest adjicere ad staturam suam cubitum unum ? id est, quum nemo ex vobis possit cogitando seu alio modo, augere staturam seu quantitatem corporis sui magnitudine unius cubiti, sed Deus dat vobis debitam quantitatem, patet quod etiam de alimento sufficientiam tribuet et de vestitu. Ideo subditur : Et de vestimento quid, id est cur, solliciti estis (modo præfato)? Quod autem sollicitari non debeant, pandit exemplo inanimatorum. Considerate lilia agri, id est, quæ in agris nascuntur, quomodo crescunt. Non laborant, neque nent pro adeptione naturalis decoris seu quantitatis : et tamen speciosissime vestiuntur seu adornantur a Deo in colore et superficie. Ideo subditur : Dico vobis, quoniam nec Salomon, qui erat rex ditissimus, valde potens, et in vestibus atque ornatibus sui et ministrorum suorum plurimum gloriosus : propter quod regina Saba videns vestes servorum ejus, non habuit spiritum ; in omni gloria, id est præclara ac splendida induitione, sua coopertus est, id est, tam speciose vestitus est, sicut unum ex his liliis agri. Quæ enim purpura regum. quæ tinctura artificum æquari poterit pulchritudini florum? Ars namque humana imitatur naturam, sed non adæquat eam ; sed nec natura adæquat artem divinam et exemplarem, quamvis eam aliqualiter imitetur. Si autem, id est quia, fœnum agri, id est herbam, quod hodie est, et cras, id est cito post hæc, vel die sequenti, in clibanum mittitur ad comburendum, Deus sic vestit, id est, ornat viriditate seu alia specie, et pulchra superficie ; quanto magis Deus vestiet vos modicæ fidei, id est, qui de divina providentia imperfectam fidem habetis, et ob id tam immoderatam sollicitudinem de necessariis acquirendis habetis ?
paras.en: [[6:27|And which of you by taking thought, can add to his stature one cubit?|Quis autem vestrum cogitans potest adjicere ad staturam suam cubitum unum?]] That is, since none of you can by thinking or in any other way increase the stature or size of his body by the measure of one cubit, but God gives you the due size, it is plain that He will also give sufficiency of food and of clothing. Therefore it is added: [[6:28|And for raiment why are you solicitous?|Et de vestimento quid solliciti estis?]], that is, why (in the manner described)? That they ought not to be solicitous He shows by the example of inanimate things. [[6:28|Consider the lilies of the field|Considerate lilia agri]], that is, which grow in the fields, [[6:28|how they grow: they labour not, neither do they spin|quomodo crescunt. Non laborant, neque nent]] to gain their natural beauty or size; and yet they are most beautifully clothed or adorned by God in colour and surface. Therefore it is added: [[6:29|But I say to you, that not even Solomon|Dico vobis, quoniam nec Salomon]], who was a very rich king, very powerful, and most glorious in the garments and adornments of himself and his ministers (for which reason the queen of Saba, seeing the garments of his servants, had no more spirit in her), [[6:29|in all his glory|in omni gloria sua]], that is, in his splendid and magnificent array, [[6:29|was arrayed as one of these|coopertus est sicut unum ex istis]], that is, was so beautifully clothed. For what purple of kings, what dye of craftsmen, could equal the beauty of flowers? For human art imitates nature, but does not equal it; nor does nature equal the divine and exemplary art, although it imitates it in some measure. [[6:30|And if|Si autem]], that is, since, [[6:30|the grass of the field|fœnum agri]], that is, the herb, [[6:30|which is to day, and to morrow|quod hodie est, et cras]], that is, soon after this, or the next day, [[6:30|is cast into the oven|in clibanum mittitur]] to be burned, [[6:30|God doth so clothe|Deus sic vestit]], that is, adorns with greenness or other beauty and a fair surface; [[6:30|how much more you, O ye of little faith?|quanto magis vos modicæ fidei?]], that is, you who have an imperfect faith in divine providence, and for that reason have so immoderate a care about getting necessaries?

paras.t: Nolite ergo solliciti esse, cum inquietudine mentis impediente pacem internam et libertatem cordis in Deo dicentes : Quia manducabimus, aut quid bibemus, aut quo operiemur ? Hæc enim omnia, scilicet cibum, potum, et vestimenta, gentes inquirunt cum sollicitudine animi, id est gentiles, qui divinam providentiam vel non attendunt vel negant, præsertim quantum ad hæc inferiora, putantes Deum non agnoscere distincte neque curare actus humanos, neque hæc corruptibilia providenter disponere, juxta illud in Psalmo : Et dixerunt : Quomodo scit Deus ? et, Si est scientia in Excelso? Job quoque dicit : An cogitas quod Deus excelsior cœlo sit, nec nostra considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat. In persona talium dicitur per Sapientem : Æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram, et conversationem vitæ ac lucrum compositam, et oportere undecumque acquirere. Cur autem hæc Christianis cum sollicitudine inquærenda non sint, subditur : Scit enim Pater vester cofestis,eternus et adorandus. Cujus ineffabilis pietas incomprehensibilisque dignatio patet in hoc, quod a nobis vermiculis pater vocari dignatur, imo et præcipit, sicut infra inducitur : Patrem nolite vocare super terram. Sed attendendum est nobis, ne propter ingratitudinem et negligentiam nostram mereamur ab eo audire illud Isaiæ : Filios enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me; et illud, Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit. Scit itaque Pater vester, quia his omnibus, scilicet victu et indumento ac domo, indigetis. Nomine enim indumenti seu operimenti, etiam habitaculum vel hospitium insinuatur : de quo non est major sollicitudo habenda, quam de indumento.
paras.en: [[6:31|Be not solicitous therefore|Nolite ergo solliciti esse]] with restlessness of mind that hinders inward peace and freedom of heart in God, [[6:31|saying: What shall we eat|dicentes : Quid manducabimus]], [[6:31|or what shall we drink, or wherewith shall we be clothed?|aut quid bibemus, aut quo operiemur?]] [[6:32|For after all these things do the heathens seek|Hæc enim omnia gentes inquirunt]], namely food, drink and clothing, with anxiety of mind; that is, the Gentiles, who either do not heed divine providence or deny it, especially as regards these lower things, thinking that God neither knows distinctly nor cares for human acts, nor disposes these corruptible things providently; according to the words in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:11|And they said: How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High?|Et dixerunt : Quomodo scit Deus ? et, Si est scientia in Excelso?]] Job too says: [[Job 22:12|Dost not thou think that God is higher than heaven|An cogitas quod Deus excelsior cœlo sit]], [[Job 22:14|and he doth not consider our things, and he walketh about the poles of heaven|nec nostra considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat]]? In the person of such men it is said by the Wise Man: [[Wis 15:12|they have counted our life a pastime and the business of life to be gain, and that we must be getting every way|Æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram, et conversationem vitæ ac lucrum compositam, et oportere undecumque acquirere]]. But why these things are not to be sought by Christians with anxiety is added: [[6:32|For your Father knoweth|Scit enim Pater vester]] in heaven, eternal and adorable; whose unspeakable kindness and incomprehensible condescension are shown in this, that He deigns to be called Father by us little worms, and indeed commands it, as is brought in below: [[Matt 23:9|call none your father upon earth|Patrem nolite vocare super terram]]. But we must take heed lest, through our ingratitude and negligence, we deserve to hear from Him the words of Isaias: [[Is 1:2|I have brought up children, and exalted them: but they have despised me|Filios enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me]]; and the words: [[Ps 48:13|man when he was in honour did not understand|Homo quum in honore esset, non intellexit]]. Your Father knoweth, then, [[6:32|that you have need of all these things|quia his omnibus indigetis]], namely food and clothing and a house. For under the name of clothing or covering a dwelling or lodging is also suggested, about which no greater care is to be had than about clothing.

paras.t: Ex præinductis infert Magister universæ perfectionis saluberrimum documentum. Quærite ergo, id est, contemplando, amando, et bene agendo adipisci studete, primum, id est principaliter et ante omnia inferiora, regnum Dei, id est cœlestem patriam, vitam æternam, triumphantis Ecclesiæ societatem, hæc bona a longe adspiciendo, salutando, et confitendo quoniam peregrini et advenæ estis super terram. De quo regno scriptum est : Justi accipient regnum decoris et diadema speciei de manu Domini. Hoc regnum est finis noster : ideo debet primo cadere in intentione, et quotidie prima ac summa occupatio nostra esse debet pro adipiscendo hoc regno. Quod quia adipisci non possumus, nisi observando mandata, idcirco post desiderium hujus finis statim quærere debemus et justitiam ejus, id est opera bona ac meritoria, quibus ad regnum perducimur. Hæc vero justitia est quam Christus jam docuit, de qua et professus est : Nisi abundaverit justitia vestra plus quam Scribarum et Pharisæorum, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum.
paras.en: From what has been brought forward the Master of all perfection draws a most wholesome lesson. [[6:33|Seek ye therefore|Quærite ergo]], that is, strive to obtain by contemplating, loving and doing well, [[6:33|first|primum]], that is, principally and before all lower things, [[6:33|the kingdom of God|regnum Dei]], that is, the heavenly fatherland, eternal life, the fellowship of the Church triumphant, beholding these goods from afar, saluting them, and confessing that you are pilgrims and strangers on the earth [cf. Heb 11:13]. Of this kingdom it is written: [[Wis 5:17|shall they receive a kingdom of glory, and a crown of beauty at the hand of the Lord|accipient regnum decoris et diadema speciei de manu Domini]] [Denis: “The just shall receive”]. This kingdom is our end: therefore it ought to fall first in our intention, and our first and highest business every day ought to be to obtain this kingdom. And since we cannot obtain it except by keeping the commandments, therefore after the desire of this end we ought at once to seek [[6:33|and his justice|et justitiam ejus]], that is, good and meritorious works, by which we are led to the kingdom. This is the justice which Christ has already taught, and of which He declared: [[Matt 5:20|unless your justice abound more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven|Nisi abundaverit justitia vestra plus quam Scribarum et Pharisæorum, non intrabitis in regnum cœlorum]].

paras.t: His autem æternis ac spiritualibus bonis digne quæsitis, temporalia necessaria nobis non deerunt, si tamen saluti expediant. Unde subjungitur : et hæc omnia, ad victum et operimentum opportuna, adjicientur, id est superaddentur vobis, quasi bona accidentalia, minus principalia, ac instrumentalia, sine quibus spiritualis conversatio nequit subsistere. Primum autem refertur ad secundum. Per hoc igitur quod Salvator docet regnum Dei et justitiam ejus primo esse quærenda, innuit temporalia quoque secundario esse quærenda cum labore quidem, sed non cum sollicitudine, secundum Chrysostomum. Scriptum est enim : Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis, beatus es. Et Adæ dictum est : In sudore vultus tui (non in sollicitudine) vesceris pane tuo. Unde Apostolus : Ad ea, inquit, quæ mihi necessaria erant, ministraverunt manus istæ. Non ergo sic adjiciuntur, quod homo debeat ponere manum suam in gremio suo, et non facere quod in se est. Sed nonne aliqui martyres ex fame exstincti sunt, et multi justi maximas patiuntur penurias, sicut et Paulus perpessum se asserit? Et respondendum, quod sæpenumero subtrahuntur prædicta electis ad eorum probationem, et copiosius meritum. Salvator vero loquitur in communi. Deus tamen ex causis sibi agnitis facit interdum aliter in particulari.
paras.en: When these eternal and spiritual goods have been worthily sought, the temporal things necessary to us will not be lacking, if only they are expedient for salvation. Hence it is added: [[6:33|and all these things|et hæc omnia]], suitable for food and covering, [[6:33|shall be added unto you|adjicientur vobis]], that is, given over and above, as accidental goods, less principal, and instrumental, without which the spiritual life cannot subsist. Now the first is referred to the second. By teaching, then, that the kingdom of God and His justice are to be sought first, the Saviour suggests that temporal things too are to be sought secondarily, with labour indeed, but not with anxiety, according to Chrysostom. For it is written: [[Ps 127:2|For thou shalt eat the labours of thy hands: blessed art thou|Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis, beatus es]]. And it was said to Adam: [[Gen 3:19|In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread|In sudore vultus tui (non in sollicitudine) vesceris pane tuo]] (not in anxiety). Hence the Apostle says: [[Acts 20:34|such things as were needful for me and them that are with me, these hands have furnished|Ad ea, inquit, quæ mihi necessaria erant, ministraverunt manus istæ]]. They are not, then, added in such a way that a man ought to put his hand in his bosom and not do what is in him. But have not some martyrs died of hunger, and do not many just men suffer the greatest want, as Paul too declares that he suffered? It must be answered that these things are often withdrawn from the elect to prove them and for their more abundant merit. The Saviour is speaking in general; yet God, for causes known to Himself, sometimes acts otherwise in particular cases.

paras.t: Nolite ergo solliciti esse inordinate, ut dictum est, in crastinum, id est in tempus futurum, pro temporalibus quæ vobis tempore futuro necessaria erunt; sed agite quod ait Psalmista : Jacta cogitatum tuum in Dominum, et ipse te enutriet. Et princeps apostolici agminis : Omnem, ait, sollicitudinem vestram projicientes in Deum, quoniam ipsi cura est de vobis. Ideo Paulus quoque dicebat : Volo vos sine sollieitudine esse. Quamvis autem possit homo ordinatam habere sollicitudinem de provisione temporalium, illa tamen non erit nisi tempore congruo. Omnia enim tempus habent, et cuilibet negotio aptum tempus debetur. Qui ergo ante tempus sollicitatur de temporali negotio, sollicitus est in crastinum : sicut qui tempore hiemali occupatur pro messe seu frugibus colligendis. Qui vero instante tempore messis moderatam curam habet de fructibus congregandis, non sollicitatur in crastinum, quia non prævenit debitum tempus. Crastinum ergo hoc loco accipitur non solum pro die proximo subsequente, sed pro tempore futuro; sicque frequenter accipitur in Scripturis : ut quum ait Jacob, Cras respondebit mihi justitia mea ; et Moyses, Quum interrogaverit te filius tuus cras, dicens, etc. Sic in libro Josue duce tribus et semis dixerunt aliis filiis Isræl : Cras filii vestri dicent filiis nostris.
paras.en: [[6:34|Be not therefore solicitous|Nolite ergo solliciti esse]] in a disordered way, as has been said, [[6:34|for to morrow|in crastinum]], that is, for the time to come, about the temporal things that will be necessary to you in the time to come; but do what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 54:23|Cast thy care upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee|Jacta cogitatum tuum in Dominum, et ipse te enutriet]]. And the prince of the apostolic band says: [[1 Pet 5:7|Casting all your care upon him, for he hath care of you|Omnem, ait, sollicitudinem vestram projicientes in Deum, quoniam ipsi cura est de vobis]]. Therefore Paul too said: [[1 Cor 7:32|But I would have you to be without solicitude|Volo vos sine sollicitudine esse]]. Now although a man may have an ordered care about providing temporal things, it will yet be only at the fitting time. For [[Eccles 3:1|All things have their season|Omnia enim tempus habent]], and to every business its proper time is due. He, then, who is anxious about a temporal business before its time is solicitous for to morrow: as one who in winter is busy about gathering the harvest or the crops. But he who, when the time of harvest is at hand, has a moderate care about gathering the fruits, is not solicitous for to morrow, because he does not forestall the due time. To morrow, then, in this place is taken not only for the next following day but for the time to come; and so it is often taken in the Scriptures: as when Jacob says, [[Gen 30:33|And my justice shall answer for me tomorrow|Cras respondebit mihi justitia mea]]; and Moses, [[Ex 13:14|And when thy son shall ask thee to morrow, saying|Quum interrogaverit te filius tuus cras, dicens]], etc. So in the book of Josue the two tribes and a half said to the other children of Israel: [[Jos 22:27|your children to morrow may not say to our children|Cras filii vestri dicent filiis nostris]] [Denis gives it without the negative: “To morrow your children will say to our children”].

paras.t: Denique duæ rationes subtiles subduntur, cur non sit habenda sollicitudo, id est pœnalis et anxia cura de crastino, quantum ad temporalia. Quantum vero ad spiritualia debemus semper esse solliciti de erastino, juxta illud : Vigilate, et estote parati, quia nescitis diem neque horam. Prima ratio est : Crastinus enim dies sollicitus erit sibi ipsi, id est, propriam curam habebit, hoc est, quocumque die futuro occurret vobis sufficiens sollicitudinis causa sive occasio, nec oportet sollicitudinem miserabilem prævenire, seu ante tempus arripere. Secunda ratio est : Sufficit diei, id est cuilibet tempori, malitia sua, id est sollicitudo sua, quæ est malum pœnæ, et etiam malum culpæ interdum. Hoc est : sufficit homini omni die malitia pœnæ et culpæ, multiplicesque miseriæ occurrentes quotidie ; ideo non oportet uno die admittere malum futuræ diei, ne uno die duplex malum affligat. Unde Apostolus dicit : Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt. Dicitur autem diei malitia sua sufficere, et dies malus esse, non quod tempus in se pravum consistat, sed quoniam his qui in tempore hujus ssæculi vivunt, multa mala occurrunt. Nam homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis.
paras.en: Then two subtle reasons are added why there should be no solicitude, that is, painful and anxious care, for to morrow as regards temporal things. As regards spiritual things, however, we ought always to be solicitous for to morrow, according to the words: [[Matt 25:13|Watch ye|Vigilate]], and be ready, [[Matt 25:13|because you know not the day nor the hour|quia nescitis diem neque horam]]. The first reason is: [[6:34|for the morrow will be solicitous for itself|Crastinus enim dies sollicitus erit sibi ipsi]], that is, it will have its own care; that is, on whatever day to come there will meet you sufficient cause or occasion of care, and there is no need to forestall wretched care, or to seize it before its time. The second reason is: [[6:34|Sufficient for the day|Sufficit diei]], that is, for any time, [[6:34|is the evil thereof|malitia sua]], that is, its care, which is the evil of punishment, and sometimes the evil of fault too. That is: sufficient for a man every day is the evil of punishment and of fault, and the manifold miseries that meet him daily; therefore he ought not on one day to let in the evil of a future day, lest a double evil afflict him on one day. Hence the Apostle says: [[Eph 5:16|redeeming the time, because the days are evil|Redimentes tempus, quoniam dies mali sunt]]. And the day is said to have its own evil sufficient, and to be evil, not because time in itself is bad, but because many evils meet those who live in the time of this world. For [[Job 14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries|homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, repletur multis miseriis]].

7.title: Explanatio capituli septimi: Nolite judicare, ut non judicemini
7.title_en: Explanation of the seventh chapter: “Judge not, that you may not be judged”

paras.t: In præsentis capituli exordio prohibet Dominus judicare. Nolite, inquiens, judicare, ut non judicemini. Lucas dicit : Et non judicabimini. Et nonne utique omnes nos adstare oportet ante tribunal Christi, ut referat unusquisque prout gessit? Habet autem hic locus difficultatem præcipuam, propter diversas auctoritates Scripturæ, quæ quantum ad verba, videntur contrariæ. Ubertim quippe ad judicandum invitamur, imo judicare præcipimur. Ut enim Apostolus dicit : Spiritualis homo omnia judicat ; et rursus, Si nos ipsos, inquit, dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Et tamen ait : Neque me ipsum judico; itemque, Tu quis es, qui judicas proximum tuum? Et pene innumerabilia sunt loca Scripturæ, quorum quædam prohibent, quædam jubent vel admonent judicare.
paras.en: At the opening of the present chapter the Lord forbids judging. [[7:1|Judge not|Nolite, inquiens, judicare]], He says, [[7:1|that you may not be judged|ut non judicemini]]. Luke says: [[Luke 6:37|and you shall not be judged|Et non judicabimini]]. And yet must we not all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that every one may give account as he has done? This place has a special difficulty because of the various authorities of Scripture which, as far as the words go, seem contrary. For we are abundantly invited to judge, indeed commanded to judge. For as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:15|the spiritual man judgeth all things|Spiritualis homo omnia judicat]]; and again, [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos, inquit, dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. And yet he says: [[1 Cor 4:3|neither do I judge my own self|Neque me ipsum judico]]; and likewise, [[Jas 4:13|who art thou that judgest thy neighbour?|Tu quis es, qui judicas proximum tuum?]] And almost countless are the places of Scripture of which some forbid judging, while others command or counsel it.

paras.t: Advertendum ergo secundum Thomam, quod judicium proprie sumptum, est actus judicis, in quantum hujusmodi. Judex vero dicitur, quasi jus dicens. Idcirco judicium est determinatio juris seu prolatio sententiæ. Judicium ergo est actus justitiæ tanquam habitus ad judicandum idoneæ inclinantis, rationis vero seu prudentiæ, tanquam judicium proferentis. Judicium itaque in tantum est licitum, in quantum ex justitia et ratione procedit. Tria vero requiruntur ad hoc quod judicium de alio per modum sententiantis sit licitum : Primo, ut procedat ex habitu justitiæ et ratione, non ex impetu passionis. Qui enim in magnis peccatis sunt, judicare non debent eos qui in eisdem vel minoribus sunt peccatis, secundum Chrysostomum. Secundo, ut procedat ex auctoritate præsidentis : quia judicare homo non debet, nisi subjectum. Tertio, ut proferatur secundum rectam rationem prudentiæ. Si primum horum defuerit, vocatur judicium injustum et perversum ; si secundum, erit usurpatum ; si desit tertium, erit suspiciosum ac temerarium. Nihilo minus de manifestis, et quæ bono animo fieri nequeunt, judicare permittimur vel jubemur, juxta illud : Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis ; a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos. Prædicta ergo tria inordinata judicia prohibentur.
paras.en: It must be observed, then, according to Thomas, that judgment properly taken is the act of a judge as such. And a judge [judex] is so called as one who speaks the law [jus dicens]. Judgment, therefore, is the determination of the law, or the passing of sentence. Judgment, then, is the act of justice, as the habit that inclines one to judge rightly, and of reason or prudence, as that which pronounces the judgment. Judgment is lawful, therefore, in so far as it proceeds from justice and reason. Three things are required for a judgment about another, by way of passing sentence, to be lawful. First, that it proceed from the habit of justice and from reason, not from the impulse of passion; for those who are in great sins ought not to judge those who are in the same or lesser sins, according to Chrysostom. Secondly, that it proceed from the authority of one who presides; for a man ought not to judge anyone but a subject. Thirdly, that it be pronounced according to the right reason of prudence. If the first of these is lacking, the judgment is called unjust and perverse; if the second, it will be usurped; if the third is lacking, it will be suspicious and rash. Nevertheless we are permitted or commanded to judge of things that are manifest and that cannot be done with a good mind, according to the words: [[7:15|Beware of false prophets|Attendite vobis a falsis prophetis]]; [[7:16|By their fruits you shall know them|a fructibus eorum cognoscetis eos]]. It is these three disordered judgments, then, that are forbidden.

paras.t: Denique, ut alii dicunt, multiplex est judicium. Primum est judicium discretionis : quod est meritorium, si cum circumstantiis debitis fiat. De quo per Jeremiam loquitur Deus : Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris. De quo et in Job asseritur : Numquid qui non amat judicium, potest sanari ? Unde ait Psalmista : Recte judicate, filii hominum. Aliud est judicium commendabile, scilicet judicium proprie discussionis : de quo Apostolus loquitur, Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, etc. ; et Psalmista, Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio. Job quoque ait : Judicium eligamus, et inter nos videamus quid sit melius. Tertium judicium est tolerabile, utpote judicium definitionis de inexcusabilibus malis. Quartum est utile, puta judicium præsidentis, secundum regulas juris. Unde Christus apud Joannem præcepit, dicens : Nolite secundum faciem judicare, sed justum judicium judicate. Quintum est judicium inutile, scilicet suspicionis, tamen sine consensu rationis. Sextum est detestabile. Quod fit quatuor modis : Primo, quum fertur sententia de secretis cordis sine sufficientibus signis ; secundo, quum dubia in pejorem partem trahuntur; tertio, dum judicatur de futuro hominis statu; quarto, quum contra jus assumitur exsecutio. Porro, secundum Augustinum, duo sunt in quibus judicium est vitandum : quum ignoramus quo animo aliquid factum sit, et quum ignoramus qualis futurus sit qui peccavit. Et quoniam unusquisque quolibet momento, potest a Deo tangi, converti, et emendari, propterea nunquam definitive judicare debemus personam alterius, seu statum ejus futurum.
paras.en: Further, as others say, judgment is manifold. The first is the judgment of discernment, which is meritorious if it is made with due circumstances. Of it God speaks through Jeremias: If [[Jer 15:19|thou wilt separate the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth|Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris]]. Of it too it is asserted in Job: [[Job 34:17|Can he be healed that loveth not judgment?|Numquid qui non amat judicium, potest sanari?]] Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 57:2|judge right things, ye sons of men|Recte judicate, filii hominum]]. Another is the commendable judgment, namely the judgment of self-examination properly so called, of which the Apostle speaks: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus]], etc.; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 1:5|Therefore the wicked shall not rise again in judgment|Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio]]. Job also says: [[Job 34:4|Let us choose to us judgment, and let us see among ourselves what is the best|Judicium eligamus, et inter nos videamus quid sit melius]]. The third judgment is the tolerable one, namely the judgment of definition concerning inexcusable evils. The fourth is the useful one, namely the judgment of one presiding, according to the rules of law. Hence Christ commanded in John, saying: [[John 7:24|Judge not according to the appearance: but judge just judgment|Nolite secundum faciem judicare, sed justum judicium judicate]]. The fifth is the useless judgment, namely that of suspicion, yet without the consent of reason. The sixth is the detestable one. This is done in four ways: first, when sentence is passed on the secrets of the heart without sufficient signs; secondly, when doubtful things are drawn to the worse side; thirdly, when judgment is passed on a man’s future state; fourthly, when execution is undertaken against the law. Further, according to Augustine, there are two things in which judgment is to be avoided: when we do not know with what mind something was done, and when we do not know what he who has sinned will be in the future. And since every man can at any moment be touched by God, converted and amended, we ought therefore never to judge definitively the person of another, or his future state.

paras.t: Quæritur, an per suspiciones sit judicandum. Dicendum, quod suspicio est opinio mali de altero, ex levibus causis concepta, et procedit ex tribus : Primo, ex malitia suspicantis, qui sibi de propria malitiæ conscius, facile putat alios tales, qualis est ipse. Secundo, ex malo affectu ad alterum : sicut qui alium odit vel ei irascitur, facile suspicatur malum de eo. Tales suspiciones sunt perversæ, sicut et causa earum. Tertio procedit ex quadam experientia : unde secundum Philosophum secundo Rhetoric, Senes sunt magis suspiciosi, tanquam aliorum defectus magis experti. Et ista suspicio minus culpabilis est, quoniam causa ejus melior est, et ipse propinquior est certitudini. Insuper triplex est gradus suspicionis : Primus, dum quis ex levibus signis, de bonitate alterius dubitat : quod est veniale peccatum, pertinens ad tentationem humanam, sine qua præsens vita non agitur, et ex humana infirmitate procedit. Secundus gradus est, quando ex levibus signis firmiter æstimat alium esse perversum : quod est mortale peccatum contra caritatem fraternam, et contemptum habet adjunctum, si malum quod de alio æstimat, sit de genere peccati mortalis. Tertius gradus est, quando ex levibus signis proceditur ad punitionem alterius : quod est gravius aliis, et contra justitiam. Quamvis autem dubia sint in partem meliorem interpretanda, quantum ad quamdam piam fiduciam, quoniam non debemus proni esse ad male sentiendum de alio ; tamen, quando impendendum est remedium contra animæ morbum, interpretanda sunt in partem deteriorem, propter securitatem, non simpliciter definiendo, sed de pejori timendo.
paras.en: It is asked whether we should judge by suspicions. It must be said that suspicion is an opinion of evil about another conceived from slight causes, and it proceeds from three things. First, from the malice of the one who suspects, who, conscious of his own malice, easily thinks others are such as he is himself. Secondly, from an evil affection towards the other: as one who hates another or is angry with him easily suspects evil of him. Such suspicions are perverse, as is their cause. Thirdly, it proceeds from a certain experience; hence, according to the Philosopher in the second book of the Rhetoric, old men are more suspicious, as having more experience of the failings of others. And this suspicion is less blameworthy, because its cause is better, and it is nearer to certainty. Moreover, there are three degrees of suspicion. The first, when someone from slight signs doubts the goodness of another: this is a venial sin, belonging to human temptation, without which the present life is not lived, and it proceeds from human weakness. The second degree is when from slight signs one firmly judges another to be wicked: this is a mortal sin against brotherly charity, and has contempt joined to it, if the evil one judges of the other is of the kind of mortal sin. The third degree is when from slight signs one proceeds to punish another: this is graver than the others, and against justice. Now although doubtful things are to be interpreted in the better sense, as regards a certain kindly trust, since we ought not to be prone to think evil of another, yet when a remedy is to be applied against a disease of the soul, they are to be interpreted in the worse sense for safety’s sake, not by settling it simply, but by fearing the worse.

paras.t: Quam autem perversum sit prædictis illicitis modis de alio judicare, innotescit ex plurimis locis epistolarum Pauli. Siquidem ad Romanos fatetur dicens : Inexcusabilis es, o homo omnis qui judicas; in quo enim alium judicas, te ipsum condemnas. Et alibi : Tu quis es, qui judicas alienum servum ? Suo domino stat aut cadit.
paras.en: How perverse it is to judge of another in the unlawful ways described is made known from very many places in the epistles of Paul. For to the Romans he declares, saying: [[Rom 2:1|thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest. For wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself|Inexcusabilis es, o homo omnis qui judicas; in quo enim alium judicas, te ipsum condemnas]]. And elsewhere: [[Rom 14:4|Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? To his own lord he standeth or falleth|Tu quis es, qui judicas alienum servum ? Suo domino stat aut cadit]].

paras.t: Itaque, Nolite judicare judicio usurpatorio, temerario, suspicioso, vel de incertis et ceteris modis inordinatis Jam dictis, ut non judicemini judicio reprobationis a Deo, tanquam transgressores præcepti de non judicando. In quo enim judicio judicaveritis, id est secundum qualitatem meriti vel demeriti vestri, quod incurritis judicando bene vel male, judicabimini a Deo, qui reddet unicuique quod meretur. Si ergo temerarie judicatis, ipsa temeritas vestra vobis nocebit, vosque damnabiles faciet; et si recte judicatis, rectitudo vestra vobis proficiet. Juxta hunc sensum dictum est Petro : Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit, id est, iniquitate quam facit gladium accipiendo, damnabitur, si non poenitentiam egerit. Simili modo scriptum est in Genesi : Omnis qui effuderit sanguinem, effundetur sanguis illius. Uniuscujusque enim peccatum in proprium redundat auctorem. Ideo in Proverbiis dicitur : Iniquitates suæ capiunt impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur. Et Ecclesiastes : Qui fodit (inquit) foveam, incidet in eam ; et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber. Et alio in loco : Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur. Et in qua mensura mensi fueritis, id est, secundum quod aliis feceritis, remetietur, id est, a Deo retribuetur vobis, hoc est, secundum proportionem operis vestri ad alios, erit proportio vestræ mercedis. Judicium enim sine misericordia fiet ei qui non fecerit misericordiam. Qualem ergo vis Deum esse tibi, talem te exhibe alteri.
paras.en: So, then: [[7:1|Judge not|Nolite judicare]] with a usurped, rash or suspicious judgment, or about uncertain things, or in the other disordered ways already mentioned, [[7:1|that you may not be judged|ut non judicemini]] with the judgment of reprobation by God, as transgressors of the precept against judging. [[7:2|For with what judgment you judge|In quo enim judicio judicaveritis]], that is, according to the quality of the merit or demerit you incur by judging well or ill, [[7:2|you shall be judged|judicabimini]] by God, who will render to every man what he deserves. If, then, you judge rashly, your very rashness will harm you and make you worthy of damnation; and if you judge rightly, your rightness will profit you. In this sense it was said to Peter: [[Matt 26:52|all that take the sword shall perish with the sword|Omnis qui acceperit gladium, gladio peribit]]; that is, he will be damned for the iniquity he commits in taking the sword, if he does not do penance. In like manner it is written in Genesis: [[Gen 9:6|Whosoever shall shed man’s blood, his blood shall be shed|Omnis qui effuderit sanguinem, effundetur sanguis illius]]. For each man’s sin redounds upon its own author. Therefore it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 5:22|His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins|Iniquitates suæ capiunt impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur]]. And Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 10:8|He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it: and he that breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him|Qui fodit (inquit) foveam, incidet in eam ; et qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber]]. And in another place: [[Ecclus 27:30|A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back upon the author|Facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur]]. [[7:2|and with what measure you mete|Et in qua mensura mensi fueritis]], that is, according as you have done to others, [[7:2|it shall be measured to you again|remetietur vobis]], that is, it shall be repaid you by God; that is, according to the proportion of your work towards others will be the proportion of your reward. For [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy|Judicium enim sine misericordia fiet ei qui non fecerit misericordiam]]. Such, then, as thou wouldst have God be to thee, show thyself to another.

paras.t: Quid autem vides festucam in oculo fratris tui, hoc est, cur observas et pensas parvum peccatum in conversatione vel corde proximi tui, judicando eum, et arguendo de minori excessu, et trabem, id est grande peccatum, in oculo tuo, id est in animo tuo, seu vita, non vides? quasi dicat Salvator : Hoc irrationabiliter agitur. Caritas namque erit ordinata, ut a se ipso incipiat homo, nec præsumat alium increpare, judicare, seu disciplinare, qui se ipsum non purgat, discutit, et emendat. Dicit enim Apostolus : Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces ; qui gloriaris in lege, per prævaricationem legis Deum inhonoras. Itaque, si peccatum arguentis, seu judicis, publicum est, et tamen judicat alium, peccat peccato præsumptionis ac scandali ; si vero peccatum ejus sit abditum, peccat per præsumptionem. Propter quod dicit Ambrosius : Judicet de errore et culpa alterius, qui in se ipso non habet quod judicet, ne quum de alio judicat, in semetipsum ferat sententiam. Scriptum est enim : Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam. Verumtamen Thomas affirmat, quod si peccatum prælati vel judicis sit occultum, et incumbat ei judicare ratione injuncti officii, potest cum timore et humilitate judicare atque arguere. Cui concordat quod alii dicunt, videlicet, quod si arguens corde poeniteat, potest fratrem cum humilitate arguere.
paras.en: [[7:3|And why seest thou the mote that is in thy brother’s eye|Quid autem vides festucam in oculo fratris tui]], that is, why dost thou observe and weigh a small sin in the life or heart of thy neighbour, judging him and reproving him for a lesser excess, [[7:3|and seest not the beam that is in thy own eye?|et trabem in oculo tuo non vides?]], that is, a great sin in thy mind or life? as if the Saviour said: This is done unreasonably. For charity will be ordered, so that a man begins with himself, and does not presume to rebuke, judge or discipline another who does not cleanse, examine and amend himself. For the Apostle says: [[Rom 2:21|that teachest another, teachest not thyself|Qui alium doces, te ipsum non doces]]; [[Rom 2:23|Thou, that makest thy boast of the law, by transgression of the law dishonourest God|qui gloriaris in lege, per prævaricationem legis Deum inhonoras]]. So, if the sin of the one who reproves, or of the judge, is public, and yet he judges another, he sins with the sin of presumption and of scandal; but if his sin is hidden, he sins by presumption. For this reason Ambrose says: “Let him judge of another’s error and fault who has not in himself what he should judge, lest when he judges of another he pass sentence on himself.” For it is written: [[Luke 19:22|Out of thy own mouth I judge thee, thou wicked servant|Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam]]. Yet Thomas affirms that if the sin of the prelate or judge is hidden, and it falls to him to judge by reason of the office laid upon him, he can judge and reprove with fear and humility. With this agrees what others say, namely that if the one who reproves repents in his heart, he can reprove his brother with humility.

paras.t: Aut quomodo, hoc est qua ratione vel fronte, dicis fratri tuo, Sine, id est, permitte et sta, ejiciam festucam de oculo tuo, id est, parvum peccatum tollam a te teque mundabo per informationem, increpationem, vel correctionem, et ecce trabs hoc est magnum peccatum, in oculo tuo est, imo tua præsumptione auges vitia tua priora? Hypocrita, id est, simulator sanctitatis, qui tuam malitiam pallias : nam aliorum parva mala redarguendo, ostendis te immunem a vitiis, quod tamen non est. Ejice per confessionem et pœnitentiam primum, antequam alium increpes, trabem de oculo tuo, id est magna peccata a corde tuo : quemadmodum scriptum est, Quasi a facie colubri, fuge peccatum ; et tunc videbis ejicere, id est, illuminatus eris ad ejiciendum, festucam de oculo fratris tui. Tunc enim non poterit tibi dicere : Medice, cura te ipsum. — Circa hanc litteram dicit Chrysostomus : Omnis sacerdos qui vult docere populum, prius doceat se ipsum : alioqui nec alium reprehendat aut doceat, ut si judicium Dei non evadit, opprobrium hominum non patiatur. Quemadmodum enim medicus ægrotus, argumentum suæ imperitia in proprio gestat corpore; sic prælatus iniquus se ipsum non curans, suæ stultitia judicium secum portat.
paras.en: [[7:4|Or how|Aut quomodo]], that is, by what reason or with what face, [[7:4|sayest thou to thy brother|dicis fratri tuo]]: Let [me], that is, allow me, and stand still, [[7:4|cast the mote out of thy eye|ejiciam festucam de oculo tuo]], that is, I will take away a small sin from thee, and cleanse thee by instruction, rebuke or correction; [[7:4|and behold a beam is in thy own eye?|et ecce trabs hoc est magnum peccatum, in oculo tuo est]], that is, a great sin; indeed by thy presumption thou increasest thy former vices? [[7:5|Thou hypocrite|Hypocrita]], that is, pretender to holiness, who cloakest thy malice: for by reproving the small evils of others thou showest thyself free from vices, which is not so. [[7:5|cast out first|ejice primum]] by confession and penance, before thou rebuke another, [[7:5|the beam out of thy own eye|trabem de oculo tuo]], that is, great sins out of thy heart; as it is written: [[Ecclus 21:2|Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent|Quasi a facie colubri, fuge peccatum]]; [[7:5|and then shalt thou see to cast out|et tunc videbis ejicere]], that is, thou shalt be enlightened to cast out, [[7:5|the mote out of thy brother’s eye|festucam de oculo fratris tui]]. For then he will not be able to say to thee: [[Luke 4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]]. On this text Chrysostom says: “Let every priest who wishes to teach the people first teach himself; otherwise let him neither reprove nor teach another, so that, if he does not escape the judgment of God, he may at least not suffer the reproach of men. For as a sick physician carries the proof of his unskilfulness in his own body, so a wicked prelate who does not heal himself carries the judgment of his folly with him.”

paras.t: Nolite sanctum, hoc est pura et immaculata mysteria fidei, profunda et secretissima christianæ sapientiæ, vel sacramenta Ecclesiæ, dare, id est propalare seu tradere, canibus, id est irrationabilibus et insanis hæreticis, vel ceteris infidelibus, aut indoctis, impoenitentibus et passionatis hominibus, de quibus dicit Apostolus : Videte canes, videte malos operarios, videte concisionem. Neque mittatis margaritas vestras, hoc est pretiosissima dona cœlestium gratiarum vobis concessa, ante porcos, id est homines carnales, de quibus Paulus : Malæ bestiæ, inquit, ventres pigri. Hinc Dionysius primo Mysticæ theologiæ capitulo, ait ad Timotheum : Vide ne quis indoctorum hæc videat, qui in sensibilibus detinentur. Isti omnino indigni et incapaces sunt prædictorum bonorum, quoniam teste Apostolo, Carnalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia enim est illi. Hoc est quod in Isaia habetur : Quem docebit Dominus scientiam ? et quem intelligere faciet auditum ? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere. Hinc et Apostolus : Sapientiam, inquit, loquimur inter perfectos. Ne forte conculcent eas pedibus suis, hoc est, intellectu et affectu predicta bona contemnant, irrideant, et condemnent, et conversi, non a malo ad bonum, sed a malo in pejus, vel corporaliter ad vos conversi, dirumpant, id est, persequantur, impugnent vel occidant vos.
paras.en: [[7:6|Give not that which is holy|Nolite sanctum, hoc est pura et immaculata mysteria fidei, profunda et secretissima christianæ sapientiæ, vel sacramenta Ecclesiæ, dare]], that is, the pure and spotless mysteries of the faith, the deep and most secret things of Christian wisdom, or the sacraments of the Church; give, that is, divulge or hand over, [[7:6|to dogs|canibus]], that is, to irrational and mad heretics, or the other unbelievers, or to unlearned, impenitent men ruled by their passions, of whom the Apostle says: [[Phil 3:2|Beware of dogs, beware of evil workers, beware of the concision|Videte canes, videte malos operarios, videte concisionem]]. [[7:6|neither cast ye your pearls|Neque mittatis margaritas vestras]], that is, the most precious gifts of heavenly graces granted to you, [[7:6|before swine|ante porcos]], that is, carnal men, of whom Paul says: [[Tit 1:12|evil beasts, slothful bellies|Malæ bestiæ, inquit, ventres pigri]]. Hence Dionysius, in the first chapter of the Mystical Theology, says to Timothy: “See that none of the uninitiated hear these things, who are held fast among the things of sense.” These are altogether unworthy and incapable of the goods described, since, as the Apostle testifies: [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him|Carnalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia enim est illi]]. This is what we have in Isaias: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand the hearing? them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam ? et quem intelligere faciet auditum ? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]]. Hence also the Apostle: [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect|Sapientiam, inquit, loquimur inter perfectos]]. [[7:6|lest perhaps they trample them under their feet|Ne forte conculcent eas pedibus suis]], that is, despise, deride and condemn the goods mentioned with understanding and affection, [[7:6|and turning upon you|et conversi]], not from evil to good but from evil to worse, or bodily turning upon you, [[7:6|they tear you|dirumpant vos]], that is, persecute, assail or kill you.

paras.t: Quoniam vero præinducta Christi præcepta ac hortamenta supernaturalia sunt, et difficilia, quæ humana virtute observari non possunt; idcirco Salvator invitat ad fiduciam deprecandi pro adjutorio gratiæ, per quam omnia faciliter adimplentur. Petite a Deo quæ decent, et vere salubria sunt, et dabitur vobis quod petitis, si instanter petieritis, et pro vobis : quemadmodum ait Salvator, Quidquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam. Quærite, id est, diligenter investigate, et agite ea per quæ oratio redditur exaudibilis, quæ sunt facere quod in se est, disponendo se ad gratiæ postulatæ susceptionem, declinando videlicet a proposito peccandi, et dando se ad observanda præcepta. Unde scriptum est : Si omnipotentem deprecatus fueris, si mundus et rectus incesseris, statim evigilabit ad te. Et Evangelium ait : Scimus quoniam peccatores Deus non audit, sed si quis cultor est Dei. Hoc est quod Salomon dicit : Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Et Joannes : Carissimi, si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum, et quidquid petierimus, accipiemus. Ideo subditur : et invenietis. Pulsate, hoc est, misericordiam Dei clamore sanctæ dilectionis, id est alto desiderio, invocate, et aperietur vobis janua vitæ, thesaurus pietatis divinæ : id est, bonitas Dei effundet se super vos, et vestram precem admittet. Vel sic : Petite, desiderando ; quærite, vocaliter exorando ; pulsate, bene vivendo.
paras.en: But since the precepts and exhortations of Christ set out above are supernatural and difficult, and cannot be observed by human strength, the Saviour therefore invites us to confidence in praying for the help of grace, by which all things are easily fulfilled. [[7:7|Ask|Petite]] of God the things that are fitting and truly wholesome, [[7:7|and it shall be given you|et dabitur vobis]] what you ask, if you ask instantly and for yourselves; as the Saviour says: [[John 14:13|whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, that will I do|Quidquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam]]. [[7:7|seek|Quærite]], that is, search diligently, and do the things by which prayer is made fit to be heard, which are to do what is in one, disposing oneself for the reception of the grace asked for, namely by turning from the purpose of sinning and giving oneself to keeping the precepts. Hence it is written: [[Job 8:5|if thou wilt arise early to God, and wilt beseech the Almighty|Si omnipotentem deprecatus fueris]], [[Job 8:6|If thou wilt walk clean and upright, he will presently awake unto thee|si mundus et rectus incesseris, statim evigilabit ad te]]. And the Gospel says: [[John 9:31|we know that God doth not hear sinners: but if a man be a server of God|Scimus quoniam peccatores Deus non audit, sed si quis cultor est Dei]]. This is what Solomon says: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]]. And John: [[1 John 3:21|Dearly beloved, if our heart do not reprehend us, we have confidence towards God|Carissimi, si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum]]; [[1 John 3:22|whatsoever we shall ask, we shall receive|quidquid petierimus, accipiemus]]. Therefore it is added: [[7:7|and you shall find|et invenietis]]. [[7:7|knock|Pulsate]], that is, call upon the mercy of God with the cry of holy love, that is, with deep desire, [[7:7|and it shall be opened to you|et aperietur vobis]], the door of life, the treasure of divine kindness; that is, the goodness of God will pour itself out upon you and admit your prayer. Or thus: Ask, by desiring; seek, by praying aloud; knock, by living well.

paras.t: Omnis enim qui petit a Deo, modo prædicto, accipit quod precatur, vel aliquid melius ; et qui quærit, invenit, et pulsanti aperietur : hoc est, perseveranter et lacrimose aures divinæ misericordiæ flagitanti, tribuetur ingressus ad bona gratiæ in hoc sæculo, et ad bona gloriæ in futuro. Unde Marci undecimo legitur : Omnia quæcumque orantes petitis, credite quia accipietis, et evenient vobis. In Ecclesiastico quoque legitur : Quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum ? Sed videtur contrarium quod ait de se ipso beatus Job : Clamo, et non exaudis me ; sto, et non respicis me; mutatus es mihi in crudelem. Dicendum, quod hoc ideo dicitur, quoniam Deus interdum dispensative differt exaudire preces fidelium ; tuncque afflicto apparet, quod Deus non attendat, neque exaudiat eum : et tali affectu loquitur Job. Tria autem requiruntur, ut oratio sit exaudibilis : Primo, ut petantur quæ ad salutem pertinent. Ideo Paulus pro stimulo carnis auferendo, ter supplicavit, et exauditus non est, quoniam magis erat ei expediens stimulum illum manere in ipso, eo quod virtus perfectorum in infirmitate perficiatur. Secundo, ut perseveranter oretur. Tertio, ut pro se ipso. Deus tamen quandoque cito exaudit etiam pro aliis.
paras.en: [[7:8|For every one that asketh|Omnis enim qui petit]] of God in the manner described [[7:8|receiveth|accipit]] what he prays for, or something better; [[7:8|and he that seeketh, findeth: and to him that knocketh, it shall be opened|et qui quærit, invenit, et pulsanti aperietur]]: that is, to him who perseveringly and tearfully beats upon the ears of the divine mercy, entrance will be granted to the goods of grace in this world and to the goods of glory in the world to come. Hence in the eleventh chapter of Mark we read: [[Mark 11:24|all things, whatsoever you ask when ye pray, believe that you shall receive: and they shall come unto you|Omnia quæcumque orantes petitis, credite quia accipietis, et evenient vobis]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we read: [[Ecclus 2:12|who hath called upon him, and he despised him?|quis invocavit eum, et despexit illum?]] But against this seems what blessed Job says of himself: [[Job 30:20|I cry to thee, and thou hearest me not: I stand up, and thou dost not regard me|Clamo, et non exaudis me ; sto, et non respicis me]]; [[Job 30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me|mutatus es mihi in crudelem]]. It must be said that this is said because God sometimes, by His dispensation, delays to hear the prayers of the faithful; and then it seems to the afflicted man that God does not attend to him or hear him; and it is with this feeling that Job speaks. Now three things are required for prayer to be heard. First, that things be asked which pertain to salvation. Therefore Paul thrice besought that the sting of the flesh might be taken away, and was not heard, because it was more expedient for him that the sting should remain in him, since the strength of the perfect is made perfect in infirmity. Secondly, that one pray perseveringly. Thirdly, that one pray for oneself. Yet God sometimes hears quickly even for others.

paras.t: Quod autem Deus neminem exaudire contemnat, probat Christus per locum a minori, et per exemplum patris terreni. Aut quis est ex vobis, hoc est de numero vestro, homo pater, quem si petierit filius suus famelicus panem, numquid lapidem porriget ei pro pane? Non utique. Pater enim providet filio de alimento, et sustentaculo vitæ. Aut si piscem petierit filius, numquid serpentem porriget ei pater? Palam quod non. Si ergo vos, quum sitis mali, id est, non obstante quod estis peccatores, et ad peccata proclives, nostis per operis exhibitionem, ona data, id est utilia pro sustentatione vitæ, dare filiis vestris carnalibus, quanto magis Pater vester qui in cœlis est, dabit bona spiritualia et honesta, videlicet virtutes et gratiam, petentibus se? Ipse enim naturaliter bonus est, et omnino misericors, a quo plus habemus, quam a patre carnali, videlicet animam immediate. Idcirco incomparabiliter plus amat nos, et diligentius providet nobis, quam pater carnalis.
paras.en: That God disdains to hear no one, Christ proves by an argument from the lesser, and by the example of an earthly father. [[7:9|Or what man is there among you|Aut quis est ex vobis homo]], that is, of your number, a father, [[7:9|of whom if his son shall ask bread|quem si petierit filius suus panem]], being hungry, [[7:9|will he reach him a stone?|numquid lapidem porriget ei?]] instead of bread? Certainly not. For a father provides his son with food and the sustenance of life. [[7:10|Or if he shall ask him a fish|Aut si piscem petierit]], the son, [[7:10|will he reach him a serpent?|numquid serpentem porriget ei?]] the father? Plainly not. [[7:11|If you then being evil|Si ergo vos, quum sitis mali]], that is, notwithstanding that you are sinners and prone to sins, [[7:11|know how to give good gifts to your children|nostis bona data dare filiis vestris]] by showing it in deed, that is, things useful for the sustenance of life, to your children according to the flesh, [[7:11|how much more will your Father who is in heaven, give good things|quanto magis Pater vester qui in cœlis est, dabit bona]], spiritual and honourable, namely virtues and grace, [[7:11|to them that ask him?|petentibus se?]] For He is good by nature and altogether merciful, and from Him we have more than from our father according to the flesh, namely the soul immediately. Therefore He loves us incomparably more, and provides for us more carefully, than a father according to the flesh.

paras.t: Et quoniam dictum est orationis effectum impediri per impiam conversationem, ideo Christus docet hoc impedimentum esse vitandum. Omnia ergo quæcumque vultis voluntate rationabili et discreta, ut faciant vobis homines proximi vestri, et vos facite eis : id est, quemadmodum vultis ut vobis impendatur a proximis vestris consilium, auxilium, misericordia, et omne quod expedit, sic facite illis pro viribus vestris. Hoc est quod Tobias docet : Quod ab alio oderis fieri tibi, vide ne aliquando alii facias. Aliqua autem irrationabiliter et contra legem divinam volunt homines : de talibus non est nunc sermo. Cur vero Christus hoe dixerit, subditur : Hæc est enim lex et Prophetæ : hoc est, doctrina moralis Mosaicæ legis ac Prophetarum ordinatur et tendit ad hoc, ut faciamus proximis quod fieri nobis ab illis peroptamus. Ad quod reducitur illud : non facere illis quod nobis optamus non fieri ordinata voluntate. Istud est enim unum primum principium naturaliter notum in agibilibus, ad quod naturaliter inclinat synderesis : ex quo deducuntur et eliciuntur reliqua præcepta ad proximum ordinantia hominem. Omnia ergo virtualiter in ipso includuntur.
paras.en: And since it has been said that the effect of prayer is hindered by an ungodly life, Christ therefore teaches that this hindrance is to be avoided. [[7:12|All things therefore whatsoever you would|Omnia ergo quæcumque vultis]] with a reasonable and discerning will [[7:12|that men should do to you|ut faciant vobis homines]], your neighbours, [[7:12|do you also to them|et vos facite eis]]; that is, as you wish counsel, help, mercy and everything expedient to be given you by your neighbours, so do to them according to your strength. This is what Tobias teaches: [[Tob 4:16|See thou never do to another what thou wouldst hate to have done to thee by another|Quod ab alio oderis fieri tibi, vide ne aliquando alii facias]]. But men wish some things unreasonably and against the divine law: of such things there is now no question. Why Christ said this is added: [[7:12|For this is the law and the prophets|Hæc est enim lex et Prophetæ]]; that is, the moral teaching of the Mosaic law and of the Prophets is ordered and tends to this, that we do to our neighbours what we earnestly wish to be done to us by them. To this is reduced the other: not to do to them what with an ordered will we wish not to be done to us. For this is one first principle naturally known in matters of action, to which synderesis [the natural habit of the first principles of moral action] naturally inclines; from which the other precepts that order man towards his neighbour are deduced and drawn out. All of them, then, are virtually included in it.

paras.t: Præterea, Christus ostendit rectam viam perducentem ad patriam. Intrate, id est ad veram beatitudinem pergite, per angustam portam, hoc est per opera pœnitentialia, laboriosa, ac ardua, ut sunt jejunia, abstinentiæ, disciplinæ, vigiliæ, et per ceterarum actus virtutum, videlicet per humiliationem, obeditionem, inimicorum dilectionem, continuam cordis custodiam : quæ omnia sunt angusta itinera, quoniam virtus est circa bonum difficile, et consistit in medio, quod difficile est attingere. Nonne angusta via est, nec ad dexteram, nec ad sinistram divertere, regia via incedere, concupiscentias refrenare, passiones animi superare, odientem diligere, adversanti benefacere? Hoc tamen est via perducens ad finem beatum. Ideo dicit Psalmista : Propter verba labiorum tuorum, ego custodivi vias duras. Denique porta angusta Christus intelligi potest, qui asserit : Ego sum ostium ; per me si quis introierit, salvabitur. Per hanc portam intrare, est Christi vestigia imitari, juxta quod dicit : Qui vult. venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me. Sed et lex evangelica appellari potest porta angusta, et tanto angustior, quanto perfectior, tanquam omnium vitiorum prohibitiva, supernaturalia jubens credi et fieri.
paras.en: Further, Christ shows the right way leading to the fatherland. [[7:13|Enter ye in at the narrow gate|Intrate per angustam portam]], that is, go on to true beatitude through the narrow gate, that is, through penitential, laborious and arduous works, such as fasts, abstinences, disciplines, vigils, and through the acts of the other virtues, namely humility, obedience, love of enemies, continual guard of the heart: all of which are narrow paths, since virtue is concerned with the difficult good, and consists in the mean, which is difficult to reach. Is it not a narrow way to turn aside neither to the right nor to the left, to walk the royal road, to rein in concupiscences, to overcome the passions of the mind, to love him who hates us, to do good to him who opposes us? Yet this is the way leading to the blessed end. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 16:4|for the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways|Propter verba labiorum tuorum, ego custodivi vias duras]]. Further, the narrow gate can be understood as Christ, who declares: [[John 10:9|I am the door. By me, if any man enter in, he shall be saved|Ego sum ostium ; per me si quis introierit, salvabitur]]. To enter by this gate is to imitate the footsteps of Christ, according to what He says: [[Luke 9:23|If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me|Qui vult venire post me, abneget semetipsum, et tollat crucem suam quotidie, et sequatur me]]. But the law of the Gospel too can be called the narrow gate, and the narrower the more perfect it is, as forbidding all vices and commanding supernatural things to be believed and done.

paras.t: Quia lata porta, et spatiosa vía est, qua ducit ad perditionem,id est eternam damnationem. Hæc lata porta spatiosaque via est, in desideriis carnis ambulare, per vitiorum abrupta incedere, mundi vanitatibus inhærere, sine timore peccare. Et multi sunt qui intrant per eam, id est, qui taliter conversantur. Multi enim vocati, et pauci electi. Stultorum quoque, secundum Salomonem, infinitus est numerus. Unde in Osee habetur : Non est veritas, non est misericordia, non est scientia Dei in terra; maledictum et homieidium, mendacium, furtum et adulterium inundaverunt, et sanguis sanguinem tetigit. Quam angusta, hoc est multum stricta, et laboriosa est, porta, et arcta via, jam dicta, quæ ducit ad vitam æternam, et pauci sunt qui inveniunt eam! Nam quamvis eis ostendatur, nolunt tamen per eam incedere. Quamvis autem per portam et viam idem possit intelligi, possumus tamen per portam intelligere actus virtutum theologicarum, præsertim caritatis, cui directe correspondet præmium essentiale (de qua legitur : Hæc porta Domini, justi intrabunt in eam); per viam vero, aliarum seu inferiorum virtutum operationes, quæ disponunt ad perfectum actum caritatis, per hoc quod auferunt passionum vitiorumque impetus. Itaque arcta dicitur via hæc, quoniam omnem qui vult Deo placere, oportet in omnibus divine voluntati, matri Ecclesiæ, et recte rationi obtemperare : quod non est parum difficile homini fragili ac mortali, in carne viventi, quemadmodum Ecclesiastes inquit : Quid est homo, ut sequi possit Regem factorem suum? Et tamen dicitur nobis : Si quis totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus ; et, Nemo coronatur, nisi qui legitime certaverit.
paras.en: [[7:13|for wide is the gate, and broad is the way that leadeth to destruction|Quia lata porta, et spatiosa via est, quæ ducit ad perditionem]], that is, eternal damnation. This wide gate and broad way is to walk in the desires of the flesh, to go along the steep places of vice, to cling to the vanities of the world, to sin without fear. [[7:13|and many there are who go in thereat|Et multi sunt qui intrant per eam]], that is, who live in this way. For [[Matt 20:16|many are called but few chosen|Multi enim vocati, et pauci electi]]. And of fools too, according to Solomon, [[Eccles 1:15|the number of fools is infinite|infinitus est numerus]]. Hence it is said in Osee: [[Osee 4:1|for there is no truth, and there is no mercy, and there is no knowledge of God in the land|Non est veritas, non est misericordia, non est scientia Dei in terra]]. [[Osee 4:2|Cursing, and lying, and killing, and theft, and adultery, have overflowed, and blood hath touched blood|maledictum et homicidium, mendacium, furtum et adulterium inundaverunt, et sanguis sanguinem tetigit]]. [[7:14|How narrow|Quam angusta]], that is, very strait and laborious, [[7:14|is the gate, and strait is the way|est porta, et arcta via]] just spoken of, [[7:14|that leadeth to life|quæ ducit ad vitam]] eternal, [[7:14|and few there are that find it!|et pauci sunt qui inveniunt eam!]] For although it is shown to them, they will not walk by it. And although the same thing can be understood by the gate and the way, yet by the gate we can understand the acts of the theological virtues, especially of charity, to which the essential reward directly corresponds (of which we read: [[Ps 117:20|This is the gate of the Lord, the just shall enter into it|Hæc porta Domini, justi intrabunt in eam]]); and by the way, the activities of the other or lower virtues, which dispose for the perfect act of charity by taking away the onset of passions and vices. This way, then, is called strait, because everyone who wishes to please God must in all things obey the divine will, mother Church, and right reason: which is not a little difficult for frail and mortal man living in the flesh, as Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 2:12|What is man, said I, that he can follow the King his maker?|Quid est homo, ut sequi possit Regem factorem suum?]] And yet it is said to us: [[Jas 2:10|whosoever shall keep the whole law, but offend in one point, is become guilty of all|Si quis totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus]]; and, [[2 Tim 2:5|is not crowned, except he strive lawfully|Nemo coronatur, nisi qui legitime certaverit]].

paras.t: Porro, quoniam teste Scriptura, Cum perverso perverteris, et, Qui tetigerit picem, inquinatur; ideo Christus docet societatem fallacium atque pravorum vitare, ne impediamur ab introitu regni. Attendite. hoc est, vos ipsos custodite, a falsis prophetis, id est perversis doctoribus, hypocritis, et fictis sanctis, qui veniunt ad vos in vestimentis ovium, hoc est cum apparenti religione, et ficta maturitate, seu vestibus abjectis ac religiosis. Ut enim decipiant simplices, simulant se justos ac veros. Unde Apostolus ait : Ipse Satanas transfigurat se in angelum lucis; non est ergo magnum, si ministri ejus transformentur velut ministri justitiæ. De talibus prophetis scriptum est : Visionem mendacem, et divinationem fraudulentam, et seductionem cordis sui prophetant vobis. Vestimenta itaque ovium intelligi possunt corporaliter, ipsa eorporis indumenta decentia, et spiritualiter, opera virtuosa, ut sunt jejunia, orationes, quibus anima adornantur : quorum imaginem simulatam assumunt isti prophetæ atque hæretici. Intrinsecus autem, id est in anima, sunt lupi rapaces, id est rapacibus lupis similes : quia sub pelle seu veste ovina abscondunt ac deferunt cor lupinum, desiderantes animas fidelium strangulare, inducendo eos ad suos errores. De talibus dicit Paulus : Scio quod post discessionem meam, intrabunt in vos lupi rapaces, non parcentes gregi.
paras.en: Further, since, as Scripture testifies, [[Ps 17:27|with the perverse thou wilt be perverted|Cum perverso perverteris]], and, [[Ecclus 13:1|He that toucheth pitch, shall be defiled with it|Qui tetigerit picem, inquinatur]], Christ therefore teaches us to avoid the company of the deceitful and wicked, lest we be hindered from entering the kingdom. [[7:15|Beware|Attendite]], that is, guard yourselves, [[7:15|of false prophets|a falsis prophetis]], that is, perverse teachers, hypocrites and pretended saints, [[7:15|who come to you in the clothing of sheep|qui veniunt ad vos in vestimentis ovium]], that is, with an apparent piety and a feigned gravity, or in mean and religious garments. For to deceive the simple they pretend to be just and true. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 11:14|Satan himself transformeth himself into an angel of light|Ipse Satanas transfigurat se in angelum lucis]]; [[2 Cor 11:15|Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers be transformed as the ministers of justice|non est ergo magnum, si ministri ejus transformentur velut ministri justitiæ]]. Of such prophets it is written: [[Jer 14:14|They prophesy unto you a lying vision, and divination, and deceit, and the seduction of their own heart|Visionem mendacem, et divinationem fraudulentam, et seductionem cordis sui prophetant vobis]]. The clothing of sheep, then, can be understood bodily, as the seemly garments of the body themselves, and spiritually, as virtuous works such as fasts and prayers, with which the soul is adorned; of which these prophets and heretics put on a feigned likeness. [[7:15|but inwardly|Intrinsecus autem]], that is, in the soul, [[7:15|they are ravening wolves|sunt lupi rapaces]], that is, like ravening wolves: for under a sheep’s skin or clothing they hide and carry a wolf’s heart, desiring to strangle the souls of the faithful by leading them into their errors. Of such Paul says: [[Acts 20:29|I know that, after my departure, ravening wolves will enter in among you, not sparing the flock|Scio quod post discessionem meam, intrabunt in vos lupi rapaces, non parcentes gregi]].

paras.t: A fructibus, id est ex operibus, eorum cognoscetis eos, quales intrinsecus sint : quia si diligenter considerentur, inveniuntur vane gloriosi, non humiles, sapientes in oculis suis et proprii sensus, non veraciter patientes, sed pleni privato amore, et aliquibus singularibus vitiis deformati. Hoc in omnibus hæreticis claruit. Operatio igitur arguit formam, quoniam qualis quisquis est, talia operatur. Nec diu potest quis ferre personam fictam, secundum Senecam, sed cito in suam naturam incidunt, quibus non subest veritas. Quod autem isti perversi non possunt opera veraciter bona producere, probat Christus per simile. Numquid colligunt homines de spinis uvas, aut de tribulis ficus? Non utique. Sic nec de cordibus prædictorum fallacium (qui propter suam crudelitatem et passionum suarum aculeos, spinis ac tribulis comparantur) possunt boni fructus procedere, qui uvis et ficubus assimilantur, quoniam animam inebriant atque delectant. Huic similitudini consonat illud Jacobi : Numquid fons de eodem foramine emanat dulcem et amaram aquam ? Numquid potest ficus uvas facere, aut vitis ficus ?
paras.en: [[7:16|By their fruits|a fructibus eorum]], that is, by their works, [[7:16|you shall know them|cognoscetis eos]], what they are within: for if they are carefully considered, they are found to be vainglorious, not humble, wise in their own eyes and their own opinion, not truly patient, but full of self-love, and disfigured by certain singular vices. This has been plain in all heretics. The work, then, shows the form, since such as each man is, such are his works. Nor can anyone long wear a feigned mask, according to Seneca; but those in whom there is no truth soon fall back into their own nature. That these perverse men cannot bring forth truly good works Christ proves by a likeness. [[7:16|Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?|Numquid colligunt homines de spinis uvas, aut de tribulis ficus?]] Certainly not. So neither from the hearts of the deceivers spoken of (who, for their cruelty and the stings of their passions, are compared to thorns and thistles) can good fruits come forth, which are likened to grapes and figs, since they inebriate and delight the soul. With this likeness agrees the saying of James: [[Jas 3:11|Doth a fountain send forth, out of the same hole, sweet and bitter water?|Numquid fons de eodem foramine emanat dulcem et amaram aquam?]] [[Jas 3:12|Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear grapes? Or the vine, figs?|Numquid potest ficus uvas facere, aut vitis ficus?]]

paras.t: Sic omnis arbor bona, fructus bonos facit, si tamen ordinetur ad fructificandum, et non potius ad alios usus. Vel per fructum intelligitur omnis utilitas ex arbore proveniens. Mala autem arbor fructus malos facit. Hæc principaliter de hominibus asseruntur, intelligendo per arborem bonam, rectam voluntatem, seu hominem justum ; per arborem malam, voluntatem perversam, seu hominem vitiosum. Bonus itaque homo, in quantum hujusmodi, facit fructus bonos; et malus, malos. Non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere, in quantum bona, sic nec homo virtuosus, ut talis, facere potest opera mala. Potest tamen malus fieri et peccare. Neque arbor mala, ut talis, fructus bonos facere potest. Sic homo iniquus, secundum quod talis, facere opera bona non potest, quamvis possit fieri bonus. Loquitur ergo Salvator de arbore bona et mala formaliter, non materialiter. Unde hujusmodi propositiones veræ sunt in sensu composito, et non in sensu diviso.
