Alia ratio fuit, ut daret prædicatoribus ac prælatis exemplum sæpius recedendi a strepitu populi ad locum secretum, ad vacandum contemplationi ac orationi, ut sic repleantur gratia illustrationis divinæ, et quæ divinitus perceperunt, aliis affectuose eructent.
paras.en: [[8:18|And Jesus seeing great multitudes about him|Videns autem Jesus turbas multas circa se]], because, as Mark says, [[Mark 1:33|all the city was gathered together at the door|tota civitas erat congregata ad januam]], [[8:18|gave orders to pass over the water|jussit ire trans fretum]], His disciples with Him, that is, beyond the sea of Galilee, which flowed by Capharnaum. He went away by boat, then, from Capharnaum to a desert place, as Luke and Mark record, to teach us to flee human praise and glory, especially when we have done something great and are looked on by all with admiration. For when He worked the miracles described, all broke out in His praise. The demons too cried out abundantly, saying, Thou art Christ and the Son of God, as the other Evangelists relate. Another reason was to give preachers and prelates an example of withdrawing often from the noise of the people to a secret place, to be free for contemplation and prayer, so that they may thus be filled with the grace of divine enlightenment, and pour out lovingly to others what they have received from God.

paras.t: Et accedens ad Jesum unus Scriba, id est eruditus in lege, ait illi : Magister, sequar te quocumque ieris, id est, tibi inseparabiliter adhærebo. Qua intentione hoc dixerit, ex subsequenti Christi responsione elicitur. Et dicit ei Jesus : Vulpes foveas habent, id est latibula sua sub terra, et volucres cœli ærii, in quo volant, habent nidos, in quibus quiescunt et pullos enutriunt; Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet, id est propriam domum. Sed nonne Maria, quæ erat unica suis parentibus, ex parte patris habuit domum parentum suorum? et Joseph (qui adhuc vixit, secundum quosdam) propriam habuit domum? Et respondendum, probabile esse quod Virgo beata omnia sua vendidit, egenisque contulit, similiter Joseph : aliter non implessent quod Christus edocuit alios, et Apostoli perfecerunt, qui relictis omnibus secuti sunt Christum. Christus ergo in summa vixit inopia, proprio carens hospitio. Propter quod Jeremias vehementer admirans, ait ad eum : Quare quasi colonus venturus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum ! Quare venturus es quasi vir vagus? Quæritur, cur Christus pauperem vitam elegit. Dicendum : Primo, ut Scripturas Prophetarum impleret. Sic enim primus Christi adventus in paupertate describitur : Exsulta satis, filia Sion ; ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus et salvator, ipse pauper. Et in Psalmo : Pauper sum ego, et in laboribus a juventute mea. Unde patet cæcitas Judæorum exspectantium regem Messiam in primo suo adventu temporaliter regnaturum, et omnia regna sæculi possessurum. Secundo, ut faceret quod docere volebat. Venit enim ut mundi ac divitiarum prædicaret contemptum : non ergo debuit eas habere. Tertio, ut non solum verbis, sed etiam rebus futuri sæculi vitam doceret. Per hoc enim quod omnia temporalia contemnuntur, maxime declaratur esse vita alia post præsentem. Quarto, ne putaretur collatione divitiarum attraxisse sibi discipulos. Quinto, ut merito suæ paupertatis, veras divitias consequamur, quemadmodum dicit Apostolus : Propter nos egenus factus est, quum dives esset, ut illius inopia divites efficeremur.
paras.en: [[8:19|And a certain scribe came|Et accedens ad Jesum unus Scriba]], that is, one learned in the law, [[8:19|and said to him: Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou shalt go|ait illi : Magister, sequar te quocumque ieris]], that is, I will cleave to Thee inseparably. With what intention he said this is drawn from Christ’s answer that follows. [[8:20|And Jesus saith to him: The foxes have holes|Et dicit ei Jesus : Vulpes foveas habent]], that is, their lurking places under the earth, [[8:20|and the birds of the air nests|et volucres cœli ærii, in quo volant, habent nidos]], of the air, in which they fly, have nests in which they rest and rear their young; [[8:20|but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head|Filius autem hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet]], that is, a house of His own. But did not Mary, who was the only child of her parents, have on her father’s side the house of her parents? And did not Joseph (who, according to some, was still alive) have a house of his own? It must be answered that it is probable that the Blessed Virgin sold all she had and gave it to the needy, and likewise Joseph; otherwise they would not have fulfilled what Christ taught others and the Apostles carried out, who left all things and followed Christ. Christ, then, lived in the greatest want, lacking a lodging of His own. For this reason Jeremias, greatly wondering, says to Him: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus futurus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?]] Why wilt Thou be as a wandering man? It is asked why Christ chose a poor life. It must be said: first, to fulfil the Scriptures of the Prophets. For so the first coming of Christ is described in poverty: [[Zach 9:9|Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Sion|Exsulta satis, filia Sion]]; [[Zach 9:9|BEHOLD THY KING will come to thee, the just and saviour: he is poor|ecce rex tuus veniet tibi justus et salvator, ipse pauper]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:16|I am poor, and in labours from my youth|Pauper sum ego, et in laboribus a juventute mea]]. Hence the blindness of the Jews is plain, who expect the King Messias in His first coming to reign temporally and to possess all the kingdoms of the world. Secondly, to do what He wished to teach. For He came to preach contempt of the world and of riches; He ought not, then, to have them. Thirdly, to teach the life of the world to come not only by words but also by deeds. For by the very fact that all temporal things are despised it is most clearly declared that there is another life after the present. Fourthly, lest He be thought to have drawn disciples to Himself by giving them riches. Fifthly, that by the merit of His poverty we may obtain true riches, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 8:9|that being rich he became poor for your sakes: that through his poverty you might be rich|Propter nos egenus factus est, quum dives esset, ut illius inopia divites efficeremur]].

paras.t: Ex prædicta Christi responsione elicitur, quod Scriba perversa intentione dixit, Sequar te, utpote quatenus conversando cum Christo congregaret sibi divitias. Quoniam enim litteratus fuit, cogitavit multis infirmis sanitatem a Christo acquirere, inducendo Christum ad sanationem illorum : sicque volebat pecuniam multam a sanatis colligere. Simili intentione Simon magus dixit Petro et Joanni : Date mihi hanc potestatem, ut cuicumque manus imposuero, recipiat Spiritum Sanctum. Jesus itaque videns mentem illius, repulit eum, dicendo : Vulpes foveas habent, etc., id est, quum ego tantam paupertatem elegerim, quid quæris mecum conversando congregare divitias ?
paras.en: From Christ’s answer it is drawn that the Scribe said, I will follow thee, with a perverse intention, namely so that by living with Christ he might gather riches for himself. For since he was a learned man, he thought to obtain health from Christ for many sick people by leading Christ to heal them; and so he wished to collect much money from those healed. With a like intention Simon Magus said to Peter and John: [[Acts 8:19|Give me also this power, that on whomsoever I shall lay my hands, he may receive the Holy Ghost|Date mihi hanc potestatem, ut cuicumque manus imposuero, recipiat Spiritum Sanctum]]. Jesus, therefore, seeing his mind, repulsed him, saying: [[8:20|The foxes have holes|Vulpes foveas habent]], etc.; that is, since I have chosen such poverty, why seekest thou to gather riches by living with Me?

paras.t: Alius autem de discipulis ejus, scilicet Jesu Christi, ait illi : Domine, permitte me primum, id est, antequam te inseparabiliter sequar, ire et sepelire patrem meum. Quidam dicunt istud non esse intelligendum, quasi pater hujus discipuli jam defunctus fuisset, et ipse ad sepeliendum patrem ire rogasset, quia hoc ei negatum non esset, quum sit opus pietatis; sed quod discipulus iste tenebatur carnali amore parentum, cum quibus usque ad mortem eorum voluit permanere, eisque sepultis Christo adhærere. Verumtamen Ambrosius, Isidorus, et Glossa super Lucam dicunt, quod pater discipuli hujus mortuus fuit, et ipse ad patris sepulturam ire optavit : quod magis consonat litteræ. Nec ratio illa concludit, videlicet, quod sepelitio patris non fuisset negata discipulo, quum sit opus pietatis. Nam apud divum Lucam. ubi factum istud narratur, alius legitur Christo dixisse : Sequar te, Domine, sed primum permitte mihi renuntiare his quæ domi sunt. Quod quamvis bonum sit, tamen Christus ei id negavit, propter periculum moræ. Similiter negavit huic patris sepelitionem, non quia mala, sed quia majoris boni impeditiva. Dicit itaque Ambrosius : Docet Christus minora bona pro utilitate esse prætermittenda. Majus est enim animas mortuas prædicando suscitare, quam corpus mortui in terra abscondere. Unde elicitur, quod quando parentes aliunde habere possunt sustentaculum vitæ, vel sepulturam, filii non impediuntur a religionis ingressu.
paras.en: [[8:21|And another of his disciples|Alius autem de discipulis ejus]], namely of Jesus Christ, [[8:21|said to him: Lord, suffer me first|ait illi : Domine, permitte me primum]], that is, before I follow Thee inseparably, [[8:21|to go and bury my father|ire et sepelire patrem meum]]. Some say that this is not to be understood as though the father of this disciple were already dead and he had asked to go and bury his father, because this would not have been refused him, since it is a work of piety; but that this disciple was held by carnal love of his parents, with whom he wished to remain until their death, and when they were buried to cleave to Christ. But Ambrose, Isidore and the Gloss on Luke say that this disciple’s father was dead and that he wished to go to his father’s burial; which agrees better with the letter. Nor is that reason conclusive, namely that the burial of his father would not have been refused the disciple because it is a work of piety. For in blessed Luke, where this deed is related, another is read to have said to Christ: [[Luke 9:61|I will follow thee, Lord; but let me first take my leave of them that are at my house|Sequar te, Domine, sed primum permitte mihi renuntiare his quæ domi sunt]]. Though this was good, yet Christ refused it him because of the danger of delay. In like manner He refused this one the burial of his father, not because it was evil but because it hindered a greater good. So Ambrose says: “Christ teaches that lesser goods are to be passed over for the sake of usefulness. For it is greater to raise dead souls by preaching than to hide the body of a dead man in the earth.” From this it is drawn that when parents can have the sustenance of life or burial from elsewhere, children are not hindered from entering religion.

paras.t: Jesus autem ait illi : Sequere me mentis affectu, operis imitatione, et corporis gressu. Nec obviat quod secundum Lucam Christus dixit, Vade et annuntia regnum Dei : quia hoc erat Christum sequi operis imitatione, corporaliter vero sequebatur eum sæpe seu congruis horis. Et dimitte mortuos, scilicet morte culpæ (sicut de vidua deliciosa dicit Apostolus, Vivens mortua est; et Joannes in Apocalypsi, Nomen, inquit, habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es), sepelire mortuos suos morte naturæ.
paras.en: [[8:22|But Jesus said to him: Follow me|Jesus autem ait illi : Sequere me]], with the affection of the mind, the imitation of works, and the steps of the body. Nor does it stand in the way that according to Luke Christ said, [[Luke 9:60|go thou and preach the kingdom of God|Vade et annuntia regnum Dei]]: for this was to follow Christ by the imitation of works; and he followed Him bodily often, or at fitting times. [[8:22|and let the dead|Et dimitte mortuos]], namely by the death of guilt (as the Apostle says of the pleasure-loving widow, [[1 Tim 5:6|is dead while she is living|Vivens mortua est]]; and John in the Apocalypse, [[Apoc 3:1|thou hast the name of being alive. And thou art dead|Nomen, inquit, habes quod vivas, sed mortuus es]]), [[8:22|bury their dead|sepelire mortuos suos]], by the death of nature.

paras.t: Et ascendente eo, videlicet Christo, in naviculam. Nunquam legitur Christus intrasse navim cortinatam negotiatorum aut piratorum, sed naviculam aut navim piscatorum : in quo ejus humilitas commendatur. Secuti sunt eum discipuli ejus, quia cum eo ingressi sunt navim, ut legitur in Luca. Secundum Origenem, Christus quum multa et magna fecisset in terra, perrexit ad mare, ut ibidem excellentiora opera demonstraret, quatenus terræ marisque Dominum se ostenderet. Ascendit autem in naviculam, ut pergeret ad locum secretiorem, et populum fugeret, propter causas paulo ante prætactas. Secundum Hieronymum, iste ascensus Christi in naviculam fuit quando exivit Capharnaum. Sed hoc intelligendum non est de exitu facto statim post sanationem socrus Petri. De navigatione namque seu transfretatione post illum exitum immediate prædictum est. Post quam rursus introivit Capharnaum post dies octo, ut habet Marcus. Et postea egressus Capharnaum, quum fecisset sermonem de parabola seminis eodem die, videlicet tempore vespertino, ingrediebatur naviculam istam, ut patet in Marco.
paras.en: [[8:23|And when he entered into the boat|Et ascendente eo, videlicet Christo, in naviculam]], namely Christ. Christ is never read to have entered a curtained ship of merchants or pirates, but a little boat or a fishermen’s ship; in which His humility is commended. [[8:23|his disciples followed him|Secuti sunt eum discipuli ejus]], because they went into the boat with Him, as we read in Luke. According to Origen, Christ, having done many great things on land, went on to the sea, to show still more excellent works there, so as to show Himself Lord of land and sea. And He went up into the boat to go to a more secret place and to flee the people, for the reasons touched on a little before. According to Jerome, this going up of Christ into the boat was when He went out of Capharnaum. But this is not to be understood of the going out made immediately after the healing of Peter’s mother-in-law. For the voyage or crossing immediately after that going out has been spoken of already. After it He entered Capharnaum again after eight days, as Mark has it. And afterwards, going out of Capharnaum, when He had given the sermon on the parable of the seed on the same day, namely in the evening, He went into this boat, as is plain in Mark.

paras.t: Et ecce motus magnus factus est in mari, id est in stagno Genesareth, ultra quod transfretavit : quod dicitur mare, juxta proprietatem idiomatis Hebræorum, qui quamlibet magnam collectionem aquarum, nominant mare, eo quod in Genesi legitur : Congregationes aquarum appellavit Deus maria. Motus hic maris creditur suscitatus magis virtute divina seu miraculose, quam naturaliter, ut Christi potentia atque divinitas panderentur per motionis hujusmodi sedationem. Naturaliter autem motus maris generatur ex vaporibus inferioribus aquarum ascendentibus, et vento flante ac occurrente in ære. Ita ut navicula operiretur fluctibus maris; nam aqua eam abundanter ingrediebatur. Ipse vero Jesus dormiebat in puppi super cervical, ut Marcus habet. Dormiebat autem secundum assumptam humanitatem, ut ejus veritatem ostenderet, et futurum miraculum gloriosius exhiberet; non secundum divinitatem, juxta illud in Psalmo : Ecce non dormitabit neque dormiet, qui custodit Isræl. Denique, secundum partem sensitivam, non secundum portionem intellectivam dormivit, juxta illud : Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat.
paras.en: [[8:24|And behold a great tempest arose in the sea|Et ecce motus magnus factus est in mari]], that is, in the lake of Genesareth, across which He crossed; which is called a sea according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who call any great gathering of waters a sea, because we read in Genesis: [[Gen 1:10|the gathering together of the waters, he called Seas|Congregationes aquarum appellavit Deus maria]]. This movement of the sea is believed to have been stirred up by divine power, or miraculously, rather than naturally, so that Christ’s power and Godhead might be made known by the calming of such a movement. Naturally, the movement of the sea is produced by vapours rising from the lower waters, and by wind blowing and meeting them in the air. [[8:24|so that the boat was covered with waves|Ita ut navicula operiretur fluctibus]] of the sea; for the water came into it abundantly. [[8:24|but he was asleep|Ipse vero Jesus dormiebat]], Jesus, in the stern, on a pillow, as Mark has it. He slept according to the humanity He had taken, to show its reality and to display the coming miracle more gloriously; not according to the Godhead, according to the words of the Psalm: [[Ps 120:4|Behold he shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel|Ecce non dormitabit neque dormiet, qui custodit Israel]]. Moreover, He slept according to the sensitive part, not according to the intellectual portion, according to the words: [[Cant 5:2|I sleep, and my heart watcheth|Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat]].

paras.t: Et accesserunt discipuli, et suscitaverunt eum, dicentes : Domine, salva nos, id est, a tempestate hac libera ; perimus hoc est, mergi incipimus. Et dicit eis Jesus : Quid timidi estis, inordinato timore qui ex defectu fidei oritur, non solum timore naturali qui ex imminentia periculi nascitur, modicæ fidei, id est, vos qui adhuc parvam, sed tamen aliquantulam fidem habetis? Quod enim dixerunt, Domine, salva nos, ex fide manavit, qua crediderunt eum esse Dei Filium, et ad salvandum potentem ; quod vero dixerunt, Perimus ex timore et pusillanimitate processit : quod autem suscitaverunt eum, ex ignorantia et fidei imperfectione descendit. Putabant enim quod Christo dormienti, minus innotescerent omnia, quam vigilanti quasi somnus actum rationis impediret in ipso. Unde increpari et audire meruerunt: Quid timidi estis, modicæ fidei? Nempe si magnæ fidei exstitissent, imperassent et ipsi tempestati, moxque cessasset, prout alibi ait Salvator : Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti, Tollere, et mitte te in mare, et obediet vobis.
paras.en: [[8:25|And they came to him, and awaked him, saying: Lord, save us|Et accesserunt discipuli, et suscitaverunt eum, dicentes : Domine, salva nos]], that is, deliver us from this tempest; [[8:25|we perish|perimus]], that is, we are beginning to sink. [[8:26|And Jesus saith to them: Why are you fearful|Et dicit eis Jesus : Quid timidi estis]] with a disordered fear that arises from a lack of faith, not only with the natural fear that springs from the nearness of danger, [[8:26|O ye of little faith?|modicæ fidei]], that is, you who still have little faith, yet some? For their saying, Lord, save us, flowed from faith, by which they believed Him to be the Son of God and mighty to save; but their saying, We perish, proceeded from fear and faintheartedness; and their waking Him came from ignorance and imperfection of faith. For they thought that all things were less known to Christ asleep than awake, as if sleep hindered the act of reason in Him. Hence they deserved to be rebuked and to hear: Why are you fearful, O ye of little faith? For if they had been of great faith, they too would have commanded the tempest and it would have ceased at once; as the Saviour says elsewhere: [[Matt 17:19|if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain|Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis huic monti]]: Remove, and cast thyself into the sea, and it will obey you.

paras.t: Tunc surgens Jesus a somno, et puppi, seu loco dormitionis, imperavit, id est per modum imperantis potenter injunxit, mari, id est commotioni tempestatique maris, et ventis, ut cessarent ; et facta est tranquillitas magna, id est plena quies a procella præfata, in instanti, quoniam virtus divinitatis Christi quum sit infinita, agit in instanti. In quo opere Christus suæ divinitatis omnipotentiam demonstravit. Nam vento et mari imperare, et imperialiter subjecta habere ad nutum, non convenit nisi vero Deo. Propter quod Marcus, ut istud miraculum gloriosius commendaret, sic ait : Surgens, comminatus est vento, et dixit mari : Tace et obmutesce. In isto fundatur positio theologorum, ponentium in omni natura creata potentiam obedientialem, qua suo Creatori ad nutum obedit in omnibus.
paras.en: [[8:26|Then rising up|Tunc surgens]], Jesus, from sleep and from the stern, or the place of sleeping, [[8:26|he commanded|imperavit]], that is, enjoined powerfully in the manner of one commanding, [[8:26|the winds, and the sea|mari, id est commotioni tempestatique maris, et ventis]], that is, the commotion and tempest of the sea, that they should cease; [[8:26|and there came a great calm|et facta est tranquillitas magna]], that is, full quiet from the storm described, in an instant, since the power of Christ’s Godhead, being infinite, acts in an instant. In this work Christ showed the omnipotence of His Godhead. For to command the wind and the sea, and to have them subject to one’s nod as a ruler, befits none but the true God. For this reason Mark, to commend this miracle more gloriously, says thus: [[Mark 4:39|And rising up, he rebuked the wind, and said to the sea: Peace, be still|Surgens, comminatus est vento, et dixit mari : Tace et obmutesce]]. On this is founded the position of the theologians who place in every created nature an obediential potency [potentia obedientialis, the capacity of a creature to be raised by God beyond its natural powers], by which it obeys its Creator at His nod in all things.

paras.t: Porro homines exsistentes in navi, mirati sunt, viso tanto prodigio, dicentes : Qualis est hic? quasi dicant : Aliquid supra hominem apparet in eo, videlicet, quod sit Deus, vel Deo carissimus, ac summe familiaris. Quia venti et mare obediunt ei : de quo scriptum est, Tu dominaris potestati maris, motum autem fluctuum ejus tu mitigas. Inanimata autem proprie non obediunt nisi Deo, per auctoritatem. Si ceteris obedire dicantur in his quæ sunt supra naturam, intelligendum est, per ministerium, secundum Hieronymum et Bedam. Quod dicitur, Porro homines mimirati sunt, non de discipulis Christi, sed de nautis et aliis qui aderant intelligendum est. Aliis vero satis probabiliter videtur, quod de discipulis quoque hoc ipsum dicatur : quod ex verbis Marci et Lucæ sequi putatur. Miratio enim consurgit ex inspectione effectus et ignorantia causæ : quemadmodum homines videntes lunam eclipsari, et causam eclipsis ignorantes, mirari cœperunt. Quum ergo causa perfecte cognoscitur, cessat miratio : idcirco astrologus eclipsim non admiratur ut rusticus. Discipuli autem nondum cognoverant Christi divinitatem, cujus virtute facta sunt hæc. Ipsi ergo mimirati sunt, quamvis minus quam alii, quoniam magis soliti erant videre miracula Christi.
paras.en: [[8:27|But the men|Porro homines]] who were in the boat [[8:27|wondered|mirati sunt]], at the sight of so great a wonder, [[8:27|saying: What manner of man is this|dicentes : Qualis est hic]]? as if they said: Something above man appears in Him, namely that He is God, or most dear to God and supremely familiar with Him. [[8:27|for the winds and the sea obey him?|Quia venti et mare obediunt ei]]; of whom it is written: [[Ps 88:10|Thou rulest the power of the sea: and appeasest the motion of the waves thereof|Tu dominaris potestati maris, motum autem fluctuum ejus tu mitigas]]. Inanimate things properly obey no one but God, by authority. If they are said to obey others in things above nature, it is to be understood by way of ministry, according to Jerome and Bede. That it is said, But the men wondered, is to be understood not of Christ’s disciples but of the sailors and others who were present. To others, however, it seems quite probable that this is said of the disciples too; which is thought to follow from the words of Mark and Luke. For wonder arises from seeing an effect and not knowing its cause; as men seeing the moon eclipsed, and not knowing the cause of the eclipse, began to wonder. When, then, the cause is perfectly known, wonder ceases; hence the astronomer does not wonder at an eclipse as the countryman does. But the disciples had not yet known the Godhead of Christ, by whose power these things were done. They therefore wondered, though less than the others, because they were more used to seeing Christ’s miracles.

paras.t: Præterea, per naviculam quidam mystice intelligunt crucem, in qua Salvator moriendo dormivit : quam secum ascenderunt discipuli, postmodum tollentes crucem suam quotidie. Quo pendente in cruce, facta est magna in mundo tempestas, quia a sexta hora usque ad nonam tenebræ factæ sunt, terra mota est, Apostoli quoque turbati fuerunt, suscitaveruntque Christum, ejus resurrectionem optando. Quo resurgente, magna cordis tranquillitas data est Christi discipulis. Chrysostomus per navim intelligit Ecclesiam, id est congregationem fidelium, ad quam Christus descendit per incarnationem et conversationem cum ea. Ipsa quoque portavit Christum, prædicando eum per totum mundum, qui est mare magnum de quo ait Salvator in Psalmo : Veni in altitudinem maris. Christo autem hanc navim ingresso, tentationum et adversitatum commotio irruit suÀ per discipulos; sed clamando ad Christum evaserunt. Navis enim Petri concuti potest, non mergi. Sic et nos in omni gravi tribulatione clamemus ad Christum, dicentes : Domine, salva nos, perimus.
paras.en: Further, by the boat some understand mystically the cross, on which the Saviour slept in dying; which the disciples went up into with Him, afterwards taking up their cross daily. While He hung on the cross a great tempest arose in the world, since from the sixth hour to the ninth there was darkness, the earth was moved, and the Apostles too were troubled, and they woke Christ by longing for His resurrection. When He rose again, great tranquillity of heart was given to Christ’s disciples. Chrysostom understands by the ship the Church, that is, the congregation of the faithful, to which Christ came down by the incarnation and by living with it. It too has carried Christ, preaching Him through the whole world, which is the great sea of which the Saviour says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:3|I am come into the depth of the sea|Veni in altitudinem maris]]. When Christ had entered this ship, the commotion of temptations and adversities fell upon the disciples; but by crying to Christ they escaped. For the ship of Peter can be shaken, not sunk. So let us too, in every grave tribulation, cry to Christ, saying: [[8:25|Lord, save us, we perish|Domine, salva nos, perimus]].

paras.t: Et quum venisset Jesus cum discipulis, ttrans fretum, id est ultra stagnum seu mare prædictum, 22 regionem Gerasenorum, quæ erat ex alio littore hujus maris. Et dicitur regio Gerasenorum a principali civitate terræ illius, quæ dicitur Gerasa, vel Geneser. Occurrerunt ei duo homines habentes dæmonia : quia quilibet eorum, vel saltem unus, a multis dæmonibus fuit obsessus. Lucas enim refert, quod legio dæmonum fuit in eo. Marcus vero et Lucas non loquuntur nisi de uno habente dæmonia ; sed non est contradictio inter eos et Matthæum, quoniam numerus minor non excludit majorem, neque econtra. De monumentis exeuntes : quia non habitabant in domibus, sed in fossis factis pro sepultura; sævi nimis, id est valde feroces in se et in alios, quoniam a dæmonibus obsessi erant, quibus data fuit a Deo licentia exercendi crudelitatem magnam per homines istos ab ipsis obsessos. Et tam sævi erant, ita ut nemo posset illæsus atque securus transire per viam illam.
paras.en: [[8:28|And when he was come on the other side of the water|Et cum venisset trans fretum]], Jesus with His disciples, that is, beyond the lake or sea spoken of, [[8:28|into the country of the Gerasens|in regionem Gerasenorum]], which was on the other shore of this sea. And it is called the country of the Gerasens from the chief city of that land, which is called Gerasa or Geneser. [[8:28|there met him two that were possessed with devils|Occurrerunt ei duo homines habentes dæmonia]]: for each of them, or at least one, was possessed by many demons. For Luke relates that a legion of demons was in him. Mark and Luke speak only of one having demons; but there is no contradiction between them and Matthew, since the smaller number does not exclude the greater, nor the reverse. [[8:28|coming out of the sepulchres|De monumentis exeuntes]]: for they did not live in houses but in pits made for burial; [[8:28|exceeding fierce|sævi nimis]], that is, very savage towards themselves and others, since they were possessed by demons, to whom leave had been given by God to exercise great cruelty through these men whom they possessed. And they were so savage [[8:28|so that none could pass by that way|ita ut nemo posset illæsus atque securus transire per viam illam]] unharmed and safely.

paras.t: Et ecce clamaverunt. Viso enim Jesu, dæmones loquebantur per vascula a se impleta, dicentes : Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu, Fili Dei? id est, quæ conventio vel similitudo inter nos insanos atque obsessos, et te sapientem ac sanctum? quasi dicant : Non debuisti venire ad nos. Hæc verba homines isti loquebantur, sed dæmonibus eos ad loquendum moventibus adscribuntur. Quod autem nominant Jesum Filium Dei, non ex certa cognitione, sed conjectura et suspicione procedit, secundum Hieronymum. Hæc quoque confessio ex necessitate potius quam ex voluntate processit, velut si servi fugitivi verbera metuentes, verba blanda suo domino loquantur, ut eis parcatur. Venisti huc ante tempus, id est valde cito et ante tempus a nobis præfixum, vel ante diem judicii, in quo erit plena et finalis reproborum damnatio, torquere nos, quoniam tua præsentia nobis pœnalis est, et timemus ejici a te : quod nobis grave est valde. Dæmones enim quum maxime odiant homines, delectantur eos torquendo, et dolent dum expelluntur. Ideo autem potissimum dixerunt, ut reor, Venisti ante tempus torquere nos, quoniam verebantur in infernum retrudi, in quem noverant se in die judicii retrudendos. Verumtamen ubique ferunt ignem suum secum.
paras.en: [[8:29|And behold they cried out|Et ecce clamaverunt]]. For at the sight of Jesus the demons spoke through the vessels they had filled, [[8:29|saying: What have we to do with thee, Jesus Son of God?|dicentes : Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu, Fili Dei?]]; that is, what agreement or likeness is there between us, mad and possessed, and Thee, wise and holy? as if they said: Thou oughtest not to have come to us. These words those men spoke, but they are ascribed to the demons moving them to speak. That they name Jesus the Son of God proceeds not from certain knowledge but from conjecture and suspicion, according to Jerome. This confession too proceeded from necessity rather than from will, as if runaway slaves, fearing the lash, should speak soft words to their master that they might be spared. [[8:29|art thou come hither to torment us before the time?|Venisti huc ante tempus]], that is, very soon and before the time fixed by us, or before the day of judgment, on which there will be the full and final damnation of the reprobate, [[8:29|to torment us|torquere nos]]; since Thy presence is a punishment to us, and we fear to be cast out by Thee, which is very grievous to us. For the demons, since they hate men most of all, delight in tormenting them, and grieve when they are expelled. And they said this above all, I think, Thou art come before the time to torment us, because they feared to be thrust back into hell, into which they knew they would be thrust on the day of judgment. Yet everywhere they carry their fire with them.

paras.t: Erat autem non longe ab illis dæmoniacis grex porcorum multorum usque ad duo millia, secundum Marcum, pascens, id est, nutrimentum sumens, in monte, de herbis atque graminibus. Dæmones autem rogabant eum, videlicet Jesum, dicentes : Si ejicis nos ab istis duobus obsessis, mitte, id est, ire permitte, nos in gregem porcorum, id est in porcos. Talis fuit ista petitio, velut si reus timens patibulum, quærat gladium, quia inter duo mala minus malum eligitur. Et ait illis Jesus : Ite. Hoc Christus concessit, non ad instantiam dæmonum, sed propter alias causas. Primo, ut ostenderetur hominibus quantus sit rancor dæmonum contra eos, propter hoc quod quærunt nocere jumentis et pecoribus hominum. Secundo, ut miraculum istud ejectionis dæmonum hac occasione amplius divulgaretur ad hominum informationem : quod et factum est, ut statim subjungitur. Tertio, quoniam homines regionis Gerasenorum suis peccatis hoc damnum meruerunt. Erant quippe gentiles, ut fertur. At illi dæmones exeuntes ab obsessis, abierunt in porcos. Imo in unum porcum plures dæmones intraverunt, secundum quod numerus dæmonum numerum porcorum excessit. In uno siquidem obsesso fuerat legio dæmonum. Et ecce impetu, id est cum strepitu veloci ac vehementi, seu motu celerrimo et rabido cursu, abiit totus grex porcorum per præceps, id est præcipitanter, seu per locum præcipitem et tortuosum, in mare Genesareth, dæmonibus porcos impellentibus. Porci namque potius agebantur, quam agebant. Et mortui sunt porci in aquis, id est submersi et suffocati.
paras.en: [[8:30|And there was, not far from them, a herd of many swine|Erat autem non longe ab illis dæmoniacis grex porcorum multorum]], about two thousand, according to Mark, [[8:30|feeding|pascens]], that is, taking food, on the mountain, of herbs and grass. [[8:31|And the devils besought him, saying: If thou cast us out hence, send us into the herd of swine|Dæmones autem rogabant eum, dicentes: Si ejicis nos hinc, mitte nos in gregem porcorum]]: namely Jesus; if Thou cast us out from these two possessed men, send, that is, let us go, into the herd of swine, that is, into the swine. Such was this petition, as if a criminal fearing the gallows should ask for the sword, because between two evils the lesser is chosen. [[8:32|And he said to them: Go|Et ait illis Jesus : Ite]]. This Christ granted not at the instance of the demons but for other reasons. First, to show men how great is the rancour of the demons against them, in that they seek to harm even the beasts and cattle of men. Secondly, that this miracle of the casting out of demons might by this occasion be spread abroad more widely for the instruction of men; which was done, as is added at once. Thirdly, because the men of the country of the Gerasens deserved this loss by their sins. For they were Gentiles, as is said. [[8:32|But they going out went into the swine|At illi exeuntes abierunt in porcos]], the demons, out of the possessed; indeed several demons entered into one swine, inasmuch as the number of demons exceeded the number of swine. For in one possessed man there had been a legion of demons. [[8:32|and behold the whole herd ran violently down a steep place into the sea|Et ecce impetu abiit totus grex porcorum per præceps in mare]], that is, with swift and violent noise, or most rapid motion and mad running, headlong, or down a steep and winding place, into the sea of Genesareth, the demons driving the swine. For the swine were driven rather than drove themselves. [[8:32|and they perished in the waters|Et mortui sunt porci in aquis]], that is, drowned and suffocated.

paras.t: Pastores autem porcorum fugerunt, territi tam insolito horrendoque facto, et ne damnum ipsis imputaretur, et ne ipsi quoque a dæmonibus invaderentur ; et venientes in civitatem Geneser, metropolim hujus provinciæ : quæ fuit ex opposita Galilææ, ut Lucas commemorat ; nuntiaverunt omnia, civibus, scilicet de submersione porcorum, et de his duobus qui dæmonia habuerant, quomodo curati essent a Christo, de cujus licentia dæmones ingressi sunt porcos. Et ecce tota civitas, id est populus civitatis pro magna vel principaliori parte, exiit obviam Jesu, ut eum honorarent, vel signa facta viderent, ut asserit Marcus. Et viso eo, rogabant eum, ut transiret a finibus eorum, id est, ab ipsis et terra eorum recederet : vel quia se indignos reputabant ejus presentia, sicut centurio; vel ne talia damna amplius paterentur, si Christus plures dæmoniacos in terra ipsorum curaret. Verumtamen, si sapientes fuissent, potius Christum rogassent secum manere, quam omnino terram eorum exire.
paras.en: [[8:33|And they that kept them fled|Pastores autem porcorum fugerunt]], terrified by so unusual and horrible a deed, and lest the loss be imputed to them, and lest they too be seized by the demons; [[8:33|and coming into the city|et venientes in civitatem]] of Geneser, the capital of this province, which was opposite Galilee, as Luke records, [[8:33|told every thing|nuntiaverunt omnia]] to the citizens, namely about the drowning of the swine, [[8:33|and concerning them that had been possessed by the devils|et de his duobus qui dæmonia habuerant]], how they had been healed by Christ, by whose leave the demons entered the swine. [[8:34|And behold the whole city went out to meet Jesus|Et ecce tota civitas exiit obviam Jesu]], that is, the people of the city for the greater or chief part, to honour Him, or to see the signs that had been done, as Mark asserts. [[8:34|and when they saw him, they besought him that he would depart from their coast|Et viso eo, rogabant eum, ut transiret a finibus eorum]], that is, would withdraw from them and their land: either because they reckoned themselves unworthy of His presence, like the centurion; or lest they should suffer further such losses if Christ healed more demoniacs in their land. Yet if they had been wise, they would rather have asked Christ to stay with them than to leave their land altogether.

paras.t: Mystice, per hoc quod Christus post maris transfretationem, dormitionem, et suscitationem, ingressus est terram Gerasenorum gentilem, significatur, quod post conversationem suam in hoc sæculo, turbulentissimo mari, post dormitionem in cruce ac monumento, et resurrectionem, intravit terras gentilium, mittendo ad eos Apostolos, et introeundo corda eorum per fidem et gratiam. Per sanationem quoque sævissimorum dæmoniacorum, designatur conversio habituatorum et obstinatorum in vitiis : qui quum in profundum peccatorum venerint, contemnunt; qui sine ullo timore perpetrant mala; super quos clausit puteus os suum. De quibus ait Psalmista : Prodiit quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum ; et Salomon, Lætantur quum malefecerint. Tales sæpius sanantur et convertuntur a Christo, ita ut omnes qui viderint, obstupescant.
paras.en: Mystically, by Christ’s entering the Gentile land of the Gerasens after crossing the sea, sleeping and being woken, it is signified that after His life in this world, a most turbulent sea, after His sleep on the cross and in the tomb, and His resurrection, He entered the lands of the Gentiles, sending the Apostles to them and entering their hearts by faith and grace. By the healing of the most savage demoniacs, too, is designated the conversion of those hardened and obstinate in vices, who, [[Prov 18:3|when he is come into the depths of sins, contemneth|quum in profundum peccatorum venerint, contemnunt]]; who commit evils without any fear; over whom [[Ps 68:16|the pit|puteus]] has shut [[Ps 68:16|her mouth|os suum]]. Of them the Psalmist says: [[Ps 72:7|Their iniquity hath come forth, as it were from fatness|Prodiit quasi ex adipe iniquitas eorum]]; and Solomon, [[Prov 2:14|Who are glad when they have done evil|Lætantur quum malefecerint]]. Such are often healed and converted by Christ, so that all who see it are astonished.
